title: Reading and Leeds festival review – post-GCSE blowout shows how dominant dance music now is | Reading and Leeds festival | The Guardian
description: Charli xcx and Fontaines DC are spellbinding and there’s an awesome array of genres, but the biggest turnouts are for tech house names like Kettama and Josh Baker
Author: Archie Forde
Headline: Charli xcx and Fontaines DC are spellbinding and there’s an awesome array of genres, but the biggest turnouts are for tech house names like Kettama and Josh Baker
Content: Kettama performing at Leeds festival.Photograph: Matthew Baker/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKettama performing at Leeds festival.Photograph: Matthew Baker/Getty ImagesReading and Leeds festivalReviewReading and Leeds festival review – post-GCSE blowout shows how dominant dance music now isBramham Park, LeedsCharli xcx and Fontaines DC are spellbinding and there’s an awesome array of genres, but the biggest turnouts are for tech house names like Kettama and Josh BakerCharli xcx, Reading festival review – Pretentious? Just a bit. But Nietzsche would have loved itArchie FordeMon 31 Aug 2026 11.45 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 15.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReading and Leeds festival will probably always be a post-GCSE rite of passage: a gleefully riotous taste of freedom before having to make actual life decisions. But the sibling events have been struggling for a sense of identity beyond this, particularly post-Covid. In 2025, the festival decided to theme days based on genre, which felt out of touch – but, this year, organisers have decided to tackle gen Z’s borderless approach head on. There are new stages, such as the chandelier-adorned Ballroom, and overall the lineup is wonderfully mazy.On the festival’s second stage, you can catch everything from UK underground rap selector DJ EJ, warbly US rockers Geese, and raw, live-drummed jungle from 4am Kru. “I dedicate this one to all the bad bitches from small places. Let’s make a song about the bad bitches from Leeds,” Slovakian pop star Adéla gleefully giggles during her own set here, before launching into neon-streaked megahit Ain’t in LA. In a ping-ponging journey across styles, other highlights include London singer Dexter in the Newsagent’s blue-skied bedroom pop, Australian artist Mall Grab’s Game Boy grime beats and Bar Italia’s insouciant rock, which is significantly more fun and dance-y than their recent lukewarm album reviews might suggest.View image in fullscreenAdéla performing at Leeds festival.Photograph: Katja Ogrin/RedfernsThursday is headlined by a tired-sounding Kasabian, who don’t move a crowd of kids that, for good reason, would much rather be at LS23, the trippy dance stage in the woods. Chase and Status’ festival-sized drum’n’bass scratches that dance itch as Friday’s main stage headliner, while Charli xcx (reviewed in full here) and Fontaines DC are a spellbinding double bill on Saturday. The latter play new material from their forthcoming album Dopamine Chamber, including beguiling single Marianne, and an unreleased new track called Happy for You – it’s driven by a Sundays-sounding guitar line and a peppy rimshot, but moves with melancholy, the band members’ features obscured against a humming green light onstage. Their set is the best from a guitar band all weekend.Another new stage, the Canopy, replaces the BBC Introducing stage at both festivals and is a showcase of new artists curated by Festival Republic, who are majority owned by Live Nation – it has been dubbed the“nepo baby” stagefor platforming the offspring of Dave Grohl, Liam Gallagher and the Beckhams. For the most part, the programming is disastrously bad, and the stage is underattended until festivalgoers can catch a perfunctory glimpse of someone semi-famous. Then it swarms, making sets look like amomentthat doesn’t actually exist from the outside, and to the detriment of other artists who would benefit from not being juxtaposed with celebrities’ kids. The two best acts are young alt-rock four-piece Tooth and brilliantly talented singer Sade Olutola, and yet they only get 20-minute opening slots on the Saturday and Sunday.View image in fullscreenGeneral Levy performing with Chase and Status.Photograph: Matthew Baker/Getty ImagesIf Reading and Leeds can be defined by anything this past year, it is young people’s ongoing affinity for tech house DJs like Josh Baker, Omar+, Max Dean and Luke Dean; Irish producer Kettama’s set is one of the most packed-out of the weekend. These artists play perfectly engineered going-out music, with chantable vocal samples and mixes that build and change a little too fast, like doomscrolling in audio form.The dance music is mainly on the Warehouse stage, which is not unlike a mockup of Manchester’s Warehouse Project, and is where the most crowd energy is directed across the weekend. Issues with overcrowding mean that Silva Bumpa and a Skepta b2b with East End Dubs are cancelled, with calls online for Reading and Leeds to recognise the popularity of dance and move it to bigger stages. Baker clashes with Dave on Sunday, and despite cameos from Kano, Tems and Central Cee, the Dave crowd is by far the most sparse out of all the headliners.Daisy Chain Fields review – Olivia Rodrigo’s women-led festival is electric amid extreme heatRead moreYou can really see Reading and Leeds’ transformation at Hedex’s set, when the drum’n’bass DJ drops a mix that begins with a sped-up version of Nirvana’s Smells Like Teen Spirit. There’s a slight bit of confusion at a tune that once embodied this festival. Still, the crowd join in singing the verse, before Hedex pulverises the track to the same effect as the distorted drop in the original and everyone’s back to dancing with that same immediacy, that same teenage freedom.Explore more on these topicsReading and Leeds festivalMusic festivalsFestivalsPop and rockDance musicRapKasabianlive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Lionel Messi’s international retirement serves as a reminder: Watch him while you still can | Argentina | The Guardian
description: The Argentine’s career with Argentina was singular, and his exit is a reminder that all good things come to an end
Author: Pablo Iglesias Maurer
Headline: The Argentine’s career with Argentina was singular, and his exit is a reminder that all good things come to an end
Content: Lionel Messi ended his international career with three major titles.Photograph: Peter Cziborra/ReutersView image in fullscreenLionel Messi ended his international career with three major titles.Photograph: Peter Cziborra/ReutersArgentinaLionel Messi’s international retirement serves as a reminder: Watch him while you still canThe Argentine’s career with Argentina was singular, and his exit is a reminder that all good things come to an endPablo Iglesias MaurerMon 31 Aug 2026 14.51 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 19.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIIt was among the defining moments of the 2026 World Cup: Lionel Messi standing arms akimbo, looking up towards Argentina’s fervent supportersafter losing the final. Tears streamed down his face after his team’s embarrassing loss to Spain in what we now know was Messi’s final match wearing that famous Argentina kit.It was not the first time he’d cried at the tournament. There had been tears of joy in Argentina’s opening match, when Messi rolled back the clock to his glory days with a trio ofspectacular goalsagainst Algeria. There had been more when his brace against Austria pushed Argentina through to the knockout round as group winners, and even more when hisequalizer against Egyptthrewla Albicelestea much-needed lifeline. Later, the world found out that Messi had been struggling all the while with thehealth struggles of his father, Jorge, a fact that clearly weighed heavily on him as Argentina made a dramatic return to the final in a bid to defend their 2022 title.Argentina’s Lionel Messi retires from international football: ‘This hurts me a lot’Read moreThere were tears in the weeks that followed the tournament as well, when Jorge passed away. It led Messi – among the most private, reserved megastars in the world, football or otherwise – to provide a rare moment of public vulnerability as he mourned the loss of his father on social media. But buried in that remembrance was something that caught many football fans off guard.“All I did was play football,”Messi wrote, “and now I have serious doubts that I’ll do it for much longer.”Messiannounced his retirement from international footballthis week at age 39, a move that was somewhat expected given his age and the sheer emotional exhaustion that had clearly accompanied his final tournament. He finishes his Argentina career with the most men’s World Cup appearances of all time – 34 spread across six tournaments, the joint-most tournaments played alongside Cristiano Ronaldo and Guillermo Ochoa. He scored or assisted 185 times in his 207 caps, a record 35 of which came at a major tournament. And of course, he was the leading figure in that legendary run that saw Argentina win the 2021 Copa América, the 2022 World Cup, and then defend their Copa América title in 2024. Internationally, there was little left for him to accomplish.View image in fullscreenMessi won the 2022 World Cup with Argentina, his crowning international honor.Photograph: Friedemann Vogel/EPAYet Monday’s announcement still came as a bit of a surprise to many, largely because Messi’s brilliance is still so readily apparent. Few, if any players, have assembled the run of major tournament performances that Messi just put together, regardless of age.He remains the best player in Major League Soccer as well. Just this past weekend, the Argentinianscored four goalsand provided an assist against Montreal, pushing him into the lead for the league’s golden boot.He remains under a guaranteed contract at Miami through 2028, but Messi’s international exit has now cast understandable doubt on whether he will play that deal out. Messi essentially runs the show at Miami, a club that signs and discards players and coaches at his whim. Guaranteed contracts mean little to the club’s megastars. Just last year, Jordi Alba walked away from a three-year contract after just a few months, choosing retirement and making theMLSCup final his last professional game. Messi is an idol at the club and would seemingly face little resistance if he chose to bring his career to a close at the end of this season.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenLionel Messi scored four goals for Inter Miami over the weekend.Photograph: Chandan Khanna/AFP/Getty ImagesAll of which is to say: If you’re in North America, or if you can make it there, go seeLionel Messinow, while you still have a chance.Three years after his arrival, those of us who live and breathe soccer in Canada and the US have grown almost accustomed to Messi’s presence and all of the magic that accompanies it because it has become so routine. Miami’s traveling bazaar of Messi and aging European megastars was a genuine sensation at first but has since retreated into the shadows at times along with the rest of MLS. Hisfour-goal effort against Montrealwould have made international headlines in 2023 but now does little to move the needle. If anything, it’s to be expected. Even in Miami, where Messi was embraced readily, Messi’s presence no longer guarantees the hysteria it once did.Yet Messi’s level, in MLS at least, has not declined. He remains a must-see player and Miami remain a must-watch team. MLS has a sometimes deserved reputation for being a “retirement league,” yet that same reputation provides fans in North America with an opportunity few of them would have otherwise: to witness global greatness in person, and for a relative bargain.For other players – Thierry Henry, David Beckham and the like – those moments of greatness were sometimes sporadic in MLS. Messi, though, seems to provide those moments at each and every turn.His star no longer shines as brightly as it did years ago at Barcelona or even months ago, in anArgentinashirt. Yet even the slightly dimmed, more fleeting light Messi produces in Miami is worth watching. His first, presumably permanent, exit from the global stage is a good reminder that soon enough it will be gone for ever.Explore more on these topicsArgentinaLionel MessiInter MiamiMLSUS sportsWorld Cup 2026World CupfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Do you have a bespoke ‘dirty zone’? | Emma Beddington | The Guardian
description: Apparently a dedicated mud room will make you less stressed. But I have a very different approach, writes Emma Beddington
Author: Emma Beddington
Headline: Apparently a dedicated mud room will make you less stressed. But I have a very different approach, writes Emma Beddington
Content: ‘I’ve already got a dirty zone by each main door.’Photograph: Catherine McQueen/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘I’ve already got a dirty zone by each main door.’Photograph: Catherine McQueen/Getty ImagesOpinionInteriorsDo you have a bespoke ‘dirty zone’?Emma BeddingtonApparently a dedicated mud room will make you less stressed. But I have a very different approachMon 31 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 12.11 EDTShareIwas excited to learn that the latest interiors essential, according tothe Washington Post, is a “dirty zone”. I’m ahead of the curve – I’ve already got a dirty zone by each main door (and also one directly outside the back door, where, rudely, a mystery animal has defecated). The fridge drawers are dirty zones thanks to the windfall apples I thought I would cook, but predictably left to liquefy. There’s a dirty zone next to the washing machine and a mildewy one inside it. There’s the festering compost bin I’m too chicken to tackle post-heatwave, plus the cupboard under the stairs, which we don’t talk about. Good luck finding a clean zone, basically.Does this make mekinda chic? Unfortunately not: the Post is actually preaching the benefits of confining the sordid ephemera of life to carefully delineated and hidden areas: storage benches, monogrammed totes or even a “mud room” (for coats, shoes, skis, lacrosse sticks and dog-washing sinks – I think posh Britons call it a boot room).A 2021 studyin the Netherlands found that participants who did chores in chaotic environments had higher levels of the stress marker salivary alpha-amylase. I always wonder what’s brewing in my mouth as I fall over piles of filthy shoes yet again while running to answer the door.This dirty zone system sounds nice, but deeply, decadently unrealistic. A mud room, rather than various rooms containing some mud, surely isn’t something most people have. If you do, apparently you’ll also want a $115 (£85) petitgrain and neroli reed diffuser, to help mask the smell. One expert consulted by the Post suggested green as a mud room colour scheme, to coordinate harmoniously with your brown delivery boxes “if you’re a heavy Amazon shopper”, which has a real last-days-of-Rome ring to it.If you don’t have a muted green, neroli-scented mud room, don’t despair – mud is good for you.A 2022 studyin Finland found that exposure to muddy environments improved immune system regulation and decreased levels of harmful bacteria in the microbiomes of nursery-age children. My home may be one big, sprawling dirty zone, but I probably have an awe-inspiringly powerful immune system – and that’s a real chic must-have.Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: ‘Everything’s smashed to bits’: Ukrainians turn anger on those storing weapons near their villages  | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: As Russia hits another ammunition warehouse, killing at least 38, locals put blame on poorly placed depots
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: As Russia hits another ammunition warehouse, killing at least 38, locals put blame on poorly placed depots
Content: Damage in Myla village after a Russian attack on an ammunition warehouse. The detonation affected the residential areas nearby.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianView image in fullscreenDamage in Myla village after a Russian attack on an ammunition warehouse. The detonation affected the residential areas nearby.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianUkraine‘Everything’s smashed to bits’: Ukrainians turn anger on those storing weapons near their villagesAs Russia hits another ammunition warehouse, killing at least 38, locals put blame on poorly placed depotsDan Sabbaghin Myla, Kyiv region. Photography byJulia KochetovaMon 31 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is a day and a half since a Russian jet-powered dronesmashed into an ammunition dump in Myla, a village 15 miles outside central Kyiv. Volodymyr, 61, a security guard, leads visitors from his family’s badly damaged home, its roof blown off, back windows shattered, through the garden towards the impact site 300 metres away.The garden, like so many in Ukraine’s villages and suburbs, is a sizeable allotment. But today the greenhouse is shattered, a vegetable patch is blackened and crisp underfoot. Several metres of grapevine have been destroyed. Even so, Volodymyr finds two surviving bunches to hand to the Guardian.View image in fullscreenInside the damaged house in Myla village, Kyiv region.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianIt is a remarkable moment of generosity, though his family now has no electricity and no water after Thursday night’s extended bombing. The death toll rose by one on Sunday, to 38, and four more people are still missing in an episode that has swiftly raised questions about why ammunition was stored so close to people’s homes.In the yard before the garden, Vira, 65, knows who is at fault. “Those who set up the depot here are to blame. There are people here, this is a village. You can’t keep something like that here,” she says. She and her son Serhii hid for hours in a small bunker by the side of the house waiting out what witnesses said were 30 or 50 explosions that went on for about six hours after the initial strike at 8pm.Map showing where Myla is in relation to Bucha and KyivSerhii says they had no idea ammunition was stored in their village. “I thought it was humanitarian aid that was stored there.” Now the family is presented with a cleanup that will be costly and difficult while starting with next to nothing. He is charging his phone from a car battery via a converter. It is all the power they have.A missile shell from a Grad rocket launcher was found on their property once the explosions subsided, Serhii adds, as well as “several mines and cluster munitions”. They have been removed by the cleanup team, although a burnt-out box of bullets, freshly discovered in another part of the semi-collapsed ceiling, has not and sits by the front door awaiting a further collection.View image in fullscreenVolodymyr shows his working place where he was during the attack.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianVolodymyr’s tour continues out back. A grass line, effectively a track, has been marked out through the wood beyond the garden, between blackened patches where fires burned. There is smouldering, even flames in places, more bullets and boxes of bullets, then, on the right, unmistakably, a detonated anti-tank mine.Finally, the woods open out, revealing a warehouse site, large parts of which are bombed out, an open area of destruction. A sulphurous smell endures, and periodically explosions can be heard, though they may be controlled detonations. Clear-up work by the emergency services is in the process of being halted at lunchtime because there is another drone threat above.View image in fullscreenRescue services are still working on the site.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianVolodymyr was on guard duty at a lumber yard close to the ammunition store on the night of the bombing. He survived the initial strike unscathed, and headed back home promptly, but feels a guard’s need to return. “I’ve been coming back and forth for two days to see these ashes,” he says.Thirty of the dead were from a care home close to the ammunition store, the location of which is now subject of a criminal inquiry by Ukraine’s intelligence service. But it is not the first attack of its kind in recent weeks. There have been other Russian bombings of poorly placed ammunition dumps, as Moscow aggressively targets warehouse sites at a time when Ukraine is doing similar.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe fact this has happened recently in Ukraine is not lost on Liudmyla, whose adult daughter was in the house a couple of doors down when the Shahed drone hit. The home is also heavily damaged, windows facing the warehouse blown in, and Liudmyla recalls that a similar incident happened in early July, on the edge of Kyiv.View image in fullscreenLiudmyla near her damaged house.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian“Look at what’s going on here. Everything’s smashed to bits right here. Vyshneve [the scene of the previous incident, nine miles south-east] wasn’t enough for them, and there was more somewhere else too. No, they’ve dumped all this right by people’s vegetable gardens, right on their doorsteps,” she says, warning that munitions are still strewn around, not yet cleared up.Nine people were killed after a munitions store was hit at Vyshneve, and 280 homes damaged. Two people have been detained on suspicion of allowing weapons to be stored in an inappropriate place after the episode, but as the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said on Saturday, similar has happened again.It is a dismal repetition at a time whenKyiv is already coming under increased attackfrom Moscow, the harm to civilians from attacks on food stores and logistics warehouses increasing. When Liudmyla is pressed to say who is at fault for the deaths and destruction at Myla, she offers a double answer.“Putin! Who else? And those who set up the depot here.”Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Rise of Chicken Shop Date highlights how YouTube turned the tables on TV | YouTube | The Guardian
description: Amelia Dimoldenberg says publicists ignored her interview show for years but she can now be picky over A-list guests
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Amelia Dimoldenberg says publicists ignored her interview show for years but she can now be picky over A-list guests
Content: Shania Twain was a guest on Chicken Shop Date in 2023.Photograph: Chicken Shop DateView image in fullscreenShania Twain was a guest on Chicken Shop Date in 2023.Photograph: Chicken Shop DateYouTubeRise of Chicken Shop Date highlights how YouTube turned the tables on TVAmelia Dimoldenberg says publicists ignored her interview show for years but she can now be picky over A-list guestsMichael SavageMedia editorMon 31 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 14.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJust a decade ago,Amelia Dimoldenbergfound it impossible to drum up any mainstream celebrities to come on her mock date YouTube show, in which she chats awkwardly with guests over chicken and chips.Even persuading a local actor connected with her London youth club to come on took years of prodding. Managers of A-listers with movies or albums to push instead battled to claim a spot on the hallowed cushions of the primetime TV chatshow sofa.Yet after those early years of rejection, Dimoldenberg has said that she has reached a watershed moment. Such is the influence of her Chicken Shop Date show, she says it now ranks alongside Graham Norton’s chatshow or BBC Radio 1 for celebrities seeking media cut-through.“When I started the show in 2014, no publicist and no manager would let their talent come on aYouTubeshow – that was just insane,” she told the Edinburgh TV festival. “I would be banging down the doors, it was just so challenging. Now it’s so fascinating because it’s the opposite.“If your publicist is coming to you and you’ve got a movie out, or you’ve got an album rollout campaign, now I do think one of the first things up there on the list of things to do would be to come on Chicken Shop Date.“That has always been the ambition – my ambition – to make it as important as going on Graham Norton or going on Greg James, Radio 1, for example. So I’ve achieved that goal.”Dimoldenberg’s rise is a prime example of how digital platforms have radically reshaped the media world, with viewers across all ages switching to YouTube,especially under-35s.Dimoldenberg has shared the ketchup with Ed Sheeran, Charli xcx and Jennifer Lawrence, although Lawrence got Dimoldenberg’s name wrong. Even Paul McCartney turned up for a date in a vegan chicken shop this year, declining Dimoldenberg’s suggestion that he adopt a pet otter.Dimoldenberg initially focused on interviewing figures from the UK rap and grime scene when she launched Chicken Shop Date in 2014. She secured her first big name, the actor Daniel Kaluuya, because he was a fan of the show.Her interviews have repeatedly gone viral since then, thanks toLouis Theroux rappingor the chemistry between Dimoldenberg and the actor Andrew Garfield. “I didn’t realise fully how much the audience would catch on to how obsessed he is with me,” she said.View image in fullscreenAmelia Dimoldenberg flirting with Andrew Garfield at the British GQ awards in 2022.Photograph: British GQShe is increasingly picky over guests and rejects anyone who wants to be on the show only as part of a “press run” publicising their latest project.It marks a shift in the media hierarchy and underlines YouTube’s muscle. The platform’s rise has become so all-consuming in the TV world that Pedro Pina, YouTube’s head for Europe, the Middle East and Africa, was invited to give the keynote MacTaggart lecture at the Edinburgh TV festival last week, the industry’s most important get-together of the year.Pina used the speech to insist YouTube was “not the villain” about to destroy the TV industry, though he made clear the age of monopoly for TV networks was over.Sure enough, the temptation of having total creative control – as well as scooping up the ads, sponsors and brand deals that can follow – is now enticing more established media names to try their luck on YouTube.The presenterHolly Willoughbylaunched her YouTube channel over the summer, amassing 22,000 subscribers so far. Amol Rajan will finish as a presenter of BBC Radio 4’s Today programme this week and launch a YouTube show, The Amol Rajan Connection. The road from TV personality to YouTuber is already well established in the US.Yet in a media world that continues to converge, Dimoldenberg is moving in the other direction, seeking success in conventional movies and television. She is writing a teen drama for the BBC, similar to the showSkins, which ran for seven series on E4.She is also writing a Hollywood romcom, in which she will star as a journalist who finds romance with a celebrity after interviewing them. Other than the chicken, it is a plot that sounds close to home.“It’s a character that I’ve been playing half my life, so I feel like I know it very well,” she said. “It’s definitely just an exaggeration of who I am.”Explore more on these topicsYouTubeEdinburgh International Television FestivalTalk showsTelevision industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Forbidden planet: was Pluto’s 2006 demotion a big mistake? | Astronomy | The Guardian
description: Since it was stripped of planetary status, Pluto’s defenders have been fighting the decision – and they’re only getting more passionate
Author: Tim Dowling
Headline: Since it was stripped of planetary status, Pluto’s defenders have been fighting the decision – and they’re only getting more passionate
Content: Status anxiety … an artist concept of Pluto with its moons.Photograph: Universal History Archive/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenStatus anxiety … an artist concept of Pluto with its moons.Photograph: Universal History Archive/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesAstronomyForbidden planet: was Pluto’s 2006 demotion a big mistake?Since it was stripped of planetary status, Pluto’s defenders have been fighting the decision – and they’re only getting more passionateTim DowlingMon 31 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 00.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwenty years ago, Pluto got demoted. After a vote by the International Astronomical Union (IAU) in August 2006, Pluto was relegated from major planet to dwarf planet status. Our solar system dropped from nine planets to eight. At the time, many scientists were unhappy with the decision. Two decades on, the debate is, if anything, even more polarised.“The definition of a planet they created, you can’t use it at all,” says Philip Metzger, the director of the Stephen W Hawking Centre for Microgravity Research and Education at the University of Central Florida. “It makes the definition of a planet completely non-useful in science.”Metzger is one of a number of scientists and lay people who consider Pluto’s demotion a big mistake.For some, Pluto’s downgraded status is the source of their affection for the ex-planet. “Pluto represents the underdog that so many people root for, the small kid on the block that is being picked on,” says Kevin Schindler, historian at the Lowell Observatory in Arizona, where Pluto was discovered in 1930.For others, the IAU’s decision, and the way it was taken, is central to the debate. “My being involved with advocating for Pluto started on the day of the vote,” says writer, actor and amateur astronomer Laurel Kornfeld. “I was like: wait a minute, this is wrong.” When we meet on Zoom she is wearing a T-shirt that says: “Pluto Resistance, 20 years: 2006-2026.”View image in fullscreenSpace oddities … dwarf planets (from left) Ceres, Pluto and Eris.Photograph: Stocktrek Images/AlamyThe campaign to reinstate Pluto – with its passionate advocates, ongoing debates, occasional protests and petitions – seems to be largely confined to the US. “It is more of an issue in the United States,” says Metzger. “This was the one we discovered.” So, the planet’s demotion was a source of wounded pride? “I’ll admit there was some of that – among the public, not the scientists.”More recently, the campaign has taken on a populist tinge, with Trump’sNasaadministrator, Jared Isaacman, telling a congressional committee in April that he was in favour of a rethink. “I am very much in the camp of Make Pluto a Planet Again,” he said.The event that sparked the IAU’s 2006 vote was the discovery of a distant celestial body that would come to be called Eris. Eris was out in the Kuiper Belt, beyond Neptune – where Pluto also resides. It was roughly the same size as Pluto (less volume, but more mass). If Pluto was a planet, the argument went, then so was Eris. And if Eris wasn’t a planet, how could Pluto continue to be one?View image in fullscreenPhilip Metzger, director of the Stephen W Hawking Centre for Microgravity Research and Education.Photograph: Florida Space InstituteEris and Pluto were by no means alone in the Kuiper Belt. Other smaller bodies were discovered around the same time, including Haumea, Makemake and Sedna. Were these also planets? There were likely many more similar objects still to be found. How would schoolchildren manage a planetary roster that might number in the hundreds?In search of a solution, the IAU came up with a three-point definition of a planet: it must orbit the Sun; it must have sufficient mass to pull itself into a round shape; and it must have “cleared its neighbourhood” – meaning it must gravitationally dominate the area in which it orbits. Nothing beyond Neptune that we knew about qualified; Pluto was out.It was the last point in particular that upset a lot of Pluto advocates, because a body’s ability to clear its neighbourhood depends a lot on the neighbourhood. “One of the biggest flaws with the IAU definition is that you can have the same object in two different orbits,” says Kornfeld. “In one, it’s considered a planet, and in the other, it’s not considered a planet.” If the Earth were towed out to Pluto’s position, the planetary scientist Alan Stern argued, it wouldn’t be able to clear its zone either, and would no longer meet the IAU definition of a planet.“You could even have small asteroids, that are too small to be round, clearing an orbit if they’re close to a star,” says Metzger. “It just goes to show that orbit clearing isn’t really that meaningful of a category.”To its detractors, the IAU definition seemed crafted with a specific intent. “A reason was invented to exclude Pluto,” says Kornfeld.View image in fullscreen‘A reason was invented to exclude Pluto’ … the IAU vote on the resolution for planet definition in 2006.Photograph: Michal Čížek/AFP/Getty ImagesPluto’s demotion created two opposing scientific teams: the so-called geophysical camp, which believes the physical properties of a celestial body should count toward its planethood; and the dynamicists, who are more concerned with the position a body occupies, its surroundings and its direction of travel. You could characterise the split as planetary scientists v astronomers. Many planetary scientists, including Metzger, simply do not use the IAU definition.When the New Horizons spacecraft made its flyby of Pluto in 2015, the geophysical camp seized what it saw as an advantage. Pluto definitely had the geophysical makings of a planet, they maintained. It had mountains, evidence of recent geological activity, and water ice hills floating on frozen nitrogen. It might even be able to support life. How could that not be a planet?Those agitating for Pluto’s planetary status do not, by and large, recognise any problems stemming from reinstatement. They welcome a definition broad enough to take in hundreds of new planets, as taxing as that might be for children and their wallcharts. “The more the merrier,” says Paul Byrne, associate professor of earth, environmental and planetary sciences at Washington University in St Louis. “There are 1,025 official Pokémon species, and I’ve never heard a kid say that’s too many.”Those against Pluto’s reinstatement say the problem isn’t with a larger number of planets, per se – but with a primarily geophysical definition that would encompass, among other bodies, planetary moons, including our moon.View image in fullscreenUnderdog story … the surface of Pluto pictured from Nasa’s New Horizons spacecraft.Photograph: AFP/Getty Images“I have no problem with having a larger number of planets,” says the astronomer Mike Brown, over email. “My argument is simply that we decided long ago that the moon is not a planet and that also precludes Pluto.” Brown is often described as The Man Who Killed Pluto, because he led the team that discovered Eris back in 2005, setting the whole de-planetisation in motion. It’s a title he leans into: he even wrote a book called How I Killed Pluto and Why It Had It Coming.Brown often says that the moon is bigger than Pluto; it’s round and has a complex geophysical history, and would certainly meet the criteria for a planet if you excluded any requirement concerning orbit. What he’s saying is: if Pluto’s a planet, so is the moon.“I don’t have an issue with calling the moon a planet,” says Byrne. “Because I can be a brother and a husband at the same time, and it doesn’t require that I be one or the other. And so I don’t see why the moon can’t be a satellite and a planet.”For the outsider, this debate can often seem mired in political, even procedural questions, with Plutonians contending that the IAU vote was incorrectly conducted and therefore void. “You could make the argument that they never officially voted on a planet because they didn’t follow the procedure that was required,” says Metzger.Brown denies there was anything political about the decision. “The only people who complain about the voting procedure were the ones who didn’t like the outcome.”So the question remains: why does any of this matter?“It was almost like a coup,” says Kornfeld. “And as a result, kids are learning less. They’re learning eight planets, and that’s it.”View image in fullscreenCosmic controversy … astronomer Gerard P Kuiper claimed that Pluto is actually one of Neptune’s satellites.Photograph: Bettmann ArchiveFor Metzger, the planetary definition excluding Pluto is based on an outmoded notion of the solar system. “They were creating a reactionary view towards an orderly cosmos, rather than the more modern scientific view where it’s chaotic,” he says. “The second problem was that I think they misread the room. The public of today is not the public of the 1800s. They’re perfectly happy understanding a dynamic, chaotic cosmos, and we missed the opportunity to teach that.”Pluto’s nature has always been elusive. In 1915, the astronomer Percival Lowell published calculations based on peculiarities in the orbits of Uranus and Neptune, predicting the existence of a new, ninth planet, which he called Planet X, with a mass somewhere between Earth’s and Neptune’s. In 1930, the long search for Planet X bore fruit: the new body, discovered at the observatory that bore Lowell’s name, was christened Pluto.Gradually, however, it became clear that whatever Pluto was, it wasn’t Planet X. It didn’t seem anywhere near large enough to account for irregularities in Neptune’s orbit. Scientists offered theories to explain why Pluto looked so small, but the truth was, itwassmall – even smaller than the moon. Only in 1992 did we learn that Lowell’s calculations were based on an overestimation of Neptune’s mass. There was no Planet X.Pluto’s reputation as an underdog, the picked-on kid, may stem from the 2006 vote, but one could argue it was punching above its weight for years. How would they have voted on Pluto’s planetary status if they had known the truth in 1930? And will it take another vote to satisfy Pluto’s defenders?“People have locked in,” says Metzger. “We would have a less useful vote today than we did back in the 2006 timeframe. So we don’t want another vote. What we want is for people to recognise that voting was a mistake, and we’re not going to do that any more. We’re going to go back to the scientific method.”Explore more on these topicsAstronomySpaceNasafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: More public control is the way to grow UK economy, Burnham to tell MPs | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Prime minister wants to ‘bring back hope’ by tackling cost of living as MPs call for electoral reform
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Exclusive: Prime minister wants to ‘bring back hope’ by tackling cost of living as MPs call for electoral reform
Content: Andy Burnham took over from Keir Starmer as prime minister in July, shortly after parliament’s summer recess began.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham took over from Keir Starmer as prime minister in July, shortly after parliament’s summer recess began.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAAndy BurnhamMore public control is the way to grow UK economy, Burnham to tell MPsExclusive: Prime minister wants to ‘bring back hope’ by tackling cost of living as MPs call for electoral reformJessica ElgotDeputy political editorMon 31 Aug 2026 14.13 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham will drive home his pledge to bring more essential services back into public control, telling MPs in the Commons on Tuesday that it will be the only way to improve growth across the country.Burnham will address the house for the first time in 16 years from the frontbench, and six weeks since he became prime minister, after spending the summer recess announcing a slew of policies that will now be put before MPs.He will use the statement to put public control of services at the heart of his priorities for the coming months, sources told the Guardian, saying he would make the case that it would unlock investment, jobs and growth.Burnham will say that the cost of everyday services to family budgets is holding back the economy and promise a plan to regain control of the costs.A No 10 source said: “Andy is optimistic about our country’s future. He has a clear plan for how we turn things round. He is determined we make this the moment we bring back hope.”The prime minister will face an early test of his commitment to public control as he mulls legislation to make it easier to bring struggling utilities such as Thames Water under government ownership. The Guardian reported last week Burnham was considering laws to make it easier to put companies into insolvency proceedings and then take control of them afterwards.View image in fullscreenThe prime minister has said taking water companies such as Thames Water into public control is crucial to his vision for the country.Photograph: Maureen McLean/ShutterstockHe will also face crunch decisions on possible changes to the immigration bill to exempt carers, as well as pressure from MPs to back moves towards electoral reform. A quasi-judicial decision on whether to allow more North Sea drilling is also expected soon: ahighly divisive issue within the party.Burnham will tell MPs that he wants to “bring back hope” in politics and pledge to work constructively with opposition parties.On Monday, the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, sacked her shadow chancellor Mel Stride and shadow foreign secretary Priti Patel, promoting Andrew Griffith in Stride’s place in the hope of making further inroads in attacking Burnham’s economic approach. Patel is replaced byTom Tugendhat.View image in fullscreenAndrew Griffith, right, with Kemi Badenoch and former chancellor Jeremy Hunt, second from right, during a visit to Godalming, Surrey earlier this year.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PABurnham will give a scathing analysis of how privatised services have done little for the public, saying that utilities and transport have not been run in the public interest and are neither reliable nor affordable.He will point to action already being taken to bring more bus routes under public control, including through a partnership between No 10 North and the West Midlands Combined Authority. The Liverpool City Region will start taking control of bus services from next weekend.Burnham has promised a10-year projectto take public control of utilities which is expected to be a major focus of his next few months in power. Allies have said the prime minister is “completely committed” to putting utilities such as energy and water companies into public control, and is looking at every option.As well as setting out key priorities for his first months in office, Burnham will face a two-hour grilling from MPs about policies announced over the summer – including a cut to VAT on energy bills, £2 bus fares, the scrapping of digital ID, a major expansion of devolution and a plan for a national care service.Opposition MPs are expected to ask tough questions on how the pledges will be funded as well as how Burnham expects to filla £4.7bn gap in the defence investment planleft by his predecessor, Keir Starmer.On Tuesday, the justice secretary, Alex Norris, will also present the government’s plans to cut the number of prisoners eligible for early release, including the killers of PC Andrew Harper.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThough the decision will see most of those convicted of manslaughter remain in prison to serve longer sentences, it has also raised alarm that the number of prison places may reach crisis point faster.Why are prisons overcrowded? Because no government will stand up to the tabloids | Zoe WilliamsRead moreLater in the week, Burnham will face Badenoch for his first prime minister’s questions and will also need to navigate the growing number ofLabourMPs who are heaping pressure on him to toughen up the representation of the people bill which returns to the Commons this week.Nearly 100 MPs havecalled on Burnham to back a commission on electoral reform, given the prime minister has previously been a vociferous supporter of changing the voting system. MPs have also been angered by the decision to drop any cap on party donations, after pressure from trade unions, despite the prime minister havingpreviously backed a cap of £500,000.TheLiberal Democratssaid on Monday they would put their full backing behind an amendment from the Labour MP Alex Sobel that calls for a commission on electoral reform to be established within 100 days.The party’s leader,Ed Davey, said it was a chance for Burnham to prove he was different to Starmer. “Reform stand to benefit from our terrible voting system and could manipulate it all the way to No 10,” he said.Davey added: “Keir Starmer never would have agreed to a national commission. He failed to grasp that it is our role as progressives to fix the broken system theConservativescreated. The only question now is: what kind of politician is Andy Burnham? Is he willing to do the right thing?”Reform will host its party conference this week in Birmingham, with Farage speaking on Friday.In the latest poll from More in Common, Labour hold a four-point lead over Reform, with the Tories a point behind. The latest Opinium poll found that Burnham’s net approval rating had increased over the last fortnight by three points.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamLabourEd DaveyKemi BadenochTom TugendhatReform UKLiberal DemocratsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Kyiv suffers hours of daytime air raids as Russia deploys new jet-powered drones | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Volodymyr Zelenskyy says about 800 Shahed drones fired into Ukraine in four days in effort to ‘wear down’ country
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Volodymyr Zelenskyy says about 800 Shahed drones fired into Ukraine in four days in effort to ‘wear down’ country
Content: Kremlin forces have targeted supply warehouses around Kyiv, leading to food shortages.Photograph: Sergey Dolzhenko/EPAView image in fullscreenKremlin forces have targeted supply warehouses around Kyiv, leading to food shortages.Photograph: Sergey Dolzhenko/EPAUkraineKyiv suffers hours of daytime air raids as Russia deploys new jet-powered dronesVolodymyr Zelenskyy says about 800 Shahed drones fired into Ukraine in four days in effort to ‘wear down’ countryDan Sabbaghin KyivMon 31 Aug 2026 11.48 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKyiv is enduring hours of daytime air raids and air raid warnings as Russia has fired 800 jet-powered drones intoUkrainein four days, using the faster weapons to sustain prolonged waves of attacksThe new-model Shahed drones have a cruising speed of 200mph to 250mph , about double the 115mph achieved by the piston-engine version and beyond the speed of Ukraine’s cheap interceptors, making them harder to stop.Volodymyr Zelenskyy,Ukraine’s president, said on Sunday that the jet-powered models now accounted for more than half the drones used by Russia to attack and “wear down” the country.“There were almost 1,500 drones of all types in these four days alone – about 800 of them jet-powered,” the president said. Ukraine was currently relying on combat aircraft to shoot them down, he added.A Geran-4, the latest jet-powered model,struck an ammunition dump at Myla, a village 15 miles west of Kyiv on Thursday. Thirty-eight people were killed as the strike unleashed hours of secondary explosions in one of the deadliest single attacks of the war, destroying warehouses and damaging nearby homes.Germany poised to identify suspect in Leipzig drone attack on Ukrainian planeRead moreRussia has also made heavy use of the drones in waves of daytime attacks in the past five days, leading to hours of air alerts, particularly in Kyiv. Eight air raid alerts sounded in Kyiv by lunchtime on Monday.Daytime attacks, although far from unknown, were uncommon previously, prompting some businesses to halt operations until the alert had passed, and leaving residents with the decision of whether to remain indoors, seek shelter, or ignore the warnings entirely.Close drone threats also force emergency services to leave an attack site, potentially worsening the impact of any fire caused by a hit, as happened whena food storage facility was struck in Boryspil, to the east of Kyiv, earlier this month.Kremlin forces have attacked warehouses aroundKyivin the past month, in retaliation to a Ukrainian campaign targeting the Wildberries and Ozon distribution chains inside Russia. The attacks have led to food shortages in the shops, but a Ukrainian official urged people not to panic.View image in fullscreenUkraine’s capital endures heavy drone strikes.Photograph: Gleb Garanich/ReutersSerhii Beskrestnov, an adviser toZelenskyyon defence technology, urged people “do not give in to rumours, misinformation, and panic” and said that companies were rebuilding supply chains in response to the attacks. “We will not die of hunger,” he wrote in a social media posting.Shahed drones, with a distinctive delta wing, were originally designed in Iran, and the technology transferred to Russia. The jet Shahed, the 238, was first unveiled by Iran in autumn 2023, and appeared in Ukraine shortly after.‘Everything’s smashed to bits’: Ukrainians turn anger on those storing weapons near their villagesRead moreIt was not until spring that Russia began to manufacture and deploy its latest jet-powered variant – the Geran-4 – in numbers. Russia now makes more jet-powered drones than the original piston-engined variants, in two models, the delta winged Geran-4 and the Geran-5, which looks like a missile with wings.Beskrestnov said that at least 2,500 of the jet drones had been launched into Ukraine during August, up from 1,500 the month before. Production date stamps found on the bodywork suggest they are being fired within days after being made at a factory in Yelabuga, he added.Ukraine had successfully devised a range of low-cost ground-launched interceptors fast enough to eliminate a piston-engined Shahed, raising interception rates to above 90%. Over the weekend, the president said that level had to be maintained into the autumn.Engineers are now racing to make faster interceptor drones able to knock out jet-powered Shaheds, though details are scant. “Four companies have developed the relevant interceptor drones, and one company has the most successful technology,” Zelenskky said.Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaDrones (military)KyivnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK houses near top state secondary schools cost £40,000 more, research reveals | House prices | The Guardian
description: Premium of nearly 10% paid by housebuyers comparable with cost of a cheaper private school over seven years
Author: Rob Davies
Headline: Premium of nearly 10% paid by housebuyers comparable with cost of a cheaper private school over seven years
Content: Price differences vary across the country but the biggest premium is 54% in Sutton Coldfield.Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPrice differences vary across the country but the biggest premium is 54% in Sutton Coldfield.Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/Getty ImagesHouse pricesUK houses near top state secondary schools cost £40,000 more, research revealsPremium of nearly 10% paid by housebuyers comparable with cost of a cheaper private school over seven yearsRob DaviesMon 31 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA house near a top state secondary school costs an extra £40,000 on average, according to research that reveals education premiums that rank alongside some private school fees.The average property in a postcode district that includes a top 50 state secondary commands a price tag of £415,791, compared with £375,217 across the wider local authority areas in which those schools are located, a UK-wide analysis by the estate agent Yopa found.The £40,574 extra, a premium of about 11%, can be compared with an average annual fee of £23,000 charged by private schools, according to the GoodSchoolsGuide.However, some charge less than £6,000 a year, indicating that over seven years of secondary education parents could end up paying a similar sum to the average extra cost of a house near a top state school.The increased price tag for such properties varies significantly across the country, according to the research, although individual cases can be less informative than the overall average, due to local market factors.Bishop Vesey’s grammar school in the well-to-do West Midlands town of Sutton Coldfield tops the table of schools where buyers are likely to pay much more than in the surrounding area.Homes across the B74 postcode district go for an average of £509,964, a premium of £275,814 compared with the average of £234,150 in Birmingham, which includes more economically deprived areas.In London, the biggest premium is paid by people living close to Henrietta Barnett school, a grammar academy for girls. The average property across its NW11 postcode is valued at 37% more than in the rest of the surrounding borough of Barnet, equivalent to an additional £354,288.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUK house prices flat in July, says Lloyds, as buyers struggle with affordabilityRead moreHowever, there are some outliers to the trend. Across the postcode district home to Reading school and Kendrick school, the average property costs £276,870. That is £84,373 below the wider Reading average of £361,243.Verona Frankish, the chief executive of Yopa, said: “For many homebuyers with children, the quality of local schools is one of the most important considerations when deciding where to live and, with the new school year approaching, education will be front of mind for many families considering their next move.”Separate research reveals that in London, homebuyers with children who go to a nearby private school are opting in to a double whammy of extra costs, with properties near a top fee-paying establishment – which are often located in the most upmarket areas – going for premiums of up to 77%.Queen’s college, London, tops the table. Homes across the W1 postcode command an average price of £1.92m compared with the wider Westminster average of £854,198.Westminster school and Francis Holland school, Sloane Square follow. Both are located within the SW1 postcode, where the average property price stands at £1.49m, a premium of 54.5% compared with Westminster as a whole.Explore more on these topicsHouse pricesPropertySecondary schoolsPrivate schoolsSchoolsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nepal rescuers race to reach hundreds feared trapped in hydropower tunnels | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Workers thought to be stuck in underground areas at 11 sites after last week’s devastating flash floods
Author: Cait Kelly
Headline: Workers thought to be stuck in underground areas at 11 sites after last week’s devastating flash floods
Content: Nepali soldiers search for survivors in a hydropower tunnel in Rasuwa district, Nepal.Photograph: Prime Minister Secretariat, Nepal/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNepali soldiers search for survivors in a hydropower tunnel in Rasuwa district, Nepal.Photograph: Prime Minister Secretariat, Nepal/AFP/Getty ImagesNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepal rescuers race to reach hundreds feared trapped in hydropower tunnelsWorkers thought to be stuck in underground areas at 11 sites after last week’s devastating flash floodsCait Kellyin Kathmandu andWilliam ChristouMon 31 Aug 2026 11.56 EDTFirst published on Mon 31 Aug 2026 02.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRescue teams are working to reach more than 900 missing hydropower workers, hundreds of whom are feared trapped in the tunnels and underground areas of 12hydropower projects in Nepal after thedevastating flash floods, ​the ⁠country’s disaster ​management authority has said.The death toll from the⁠unprecedented delugeof ice, rock, mud ​and debris on Wednesday last week has risen to 939 people, with 16 more dead reported in Tibet.More than 4,400 are missing on the two sides of the border.About 500 of the missing hydropower workers at projects damaged by the flooding in Nepal’s Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts are thought to be trapped in tunnels built to control the flow of water.As rescue efforts drag on, experts fear the chances of finding survivors in tunnels are diminishing as oxygen levels fall.Some workers called for help when flooding started on Wednesday and those who had managed to escape tunnels said many of their colleagues were still trapped, said Mohan Kumar Dangi, the president of the Nepal Independent Power Producers’ Association.Devastated by floods and overwhelmed by bodies, Nepalis weep for what remains of their homesRead moreRescue efforts have been complicated by difficult terrain, persistently high flood waters and difficult weather. With more than 40 bridges destroyed, rescuers are relying on helicopters, while India andChinaare sending prefabricated truss bridges to help restore access.View image in fullscreenA resident examines his damaged home in Devighat, Nuwakot district.Photograph: Rajesh Kumar Singh/APThe swollen Trishuli River has also continued to change course unpredictably, making planning a challenge. Areas that were dry one day are flooded the next, and further floods are a constant concern.Hundreds of bodies, many unidentified, that were swept down the mountains by the torrent, have been buried in shallow graves after DNA testingon the plains ⁠of the Himalayan region.Nepali officials said on Monday that the focus was on reaching the 933 people missing from ‌hydropower plants. “A large amount of debris has been deposited and that is posing us a big challenge to open the tunnels,” the Nepal army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet told Reuters.About 250 people were rescued from the Upper Trishuli hydroelectric project over the weekend, and army engineers began blasting operations at the site to rescue another 42 workers thought be missing.View image in fullscreenA flood victim being airlifted from Rasuwa district yesterday to a hospital in Kathmandu. More than 4,400 people are now listed as missing.Photograph: Prabin Ranabhat/AFP/Getty ImagesThe damage to hydropower infrastructure is estimated to have taken 700 megawatts out of service, about 10% of the country’s power capacity.Pictures and videos shared by rescue teams ⁠showed earth-moving equipment shovelling mud to try to reach the tunnels.Ashish Gurung, who normally works as a guide, was among the rescuers. “There is just mud everywhere,” he said. “Inside the tunnel it was worse. It’s so difficult to move, the mud is so deep.”His team was trying to access the Chilime hydropower plant in Rasuwa, one of the worst-hit areas. At least eight people are believed missing there, and an Indian team is working alongside the Nepali army using pumps and excavators to locate them.View image in fullscreenAshish Gurung, left, with fellow rescue mountaineer Jenjen Lama at the Chilime hydropower plant in Rasuwa.Photograph: SuppliedThe Nepali prime minister, Balendra Shah, said rescue efforts were “challenging due to adverse weather, difficult terrain and ongoing risks.”Gurung said mountaineers were improvising by using planks of wood to check the depth of the mud, before using them as makeshift bridges along with a system of ropes to keep themselves safe.“Walking in it is very difficult, at one point it was up to our chests,” he said. “We got close to the first station, about 130 metres in. Inside that far … it looked like it was just bodies.”The hydropower company had given his team a map and it looked as if there was a chance people in the tunnels could have survived. “They have a safe area inside,” he said. “Some of them could potentially be alive. I am hoping they are alive.”Young girl rescued from rubble three days after Nepal flash flood – videoThe Red Cross estimates that more than 93,000 people have been affected by the disaster,heightening fears that the climate crisis is destabilising the geology of mountain and polar regions.Shah said the flood was an “unprecedented and devastating natural disaster” and that it was difficult to compile a complete assessment of the damage.“Despite the adverse weather, difficult terrain and continuing risks, we are moving forward with determination to save the lives of our citizens,” he said in a Facebook post late on Sunday. Almost 21,000 security personnel were involved in the rescue operations alongside civilian workers and volunteers, he said.Whole communities had been destroyed by the flooding, leaving families homeless in heavy rain.View image in fullscreenRescuers work to access a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydropower plant in Nuwakot district, Nepal.Photograph: Nepal Army/Reuters“There are no roads, they have all been washed away, and many areas are just not accessible,” said a police officer coordinating rescue efforts in Nuwakot district. “It is very difficult for my men. The area is still flooded, and elsewhere it is all marshland.”Nepal’s disaster agency said on Monday it had counted 903 deaths, with 4,793 people, including 592 foreigners, missing. Chinese authorities had reported 16 deaths and 546 people missing as of Sunday. State media said 261 of the missing were foreigners, including more than 100 Nepalis.Among those missing are more than 30 British nationals. On Saturday, a rapid deployment team from the UK arrived in Nepal to support Britons and their families. The UK government has given a £5m support package to assist Nepal in its disaster response.Amid the soaring toll of death and missing was some hope. On Monday, rescuers pulled a six-year-old girl out of mud after hearing crying. “Her body was trapped in mud, but her head was outside,” the Nepali armed police spokesperson Netra Bahadur Karki told Agence France-Presse.China’s state-run CCTV said Beijing had mobilised more than 2,100 rescue workers and allocated at least ​220m yuan (£24m) to support relief efforts and had been airdropping equipment and supplies to frontline rescuers, while its soldiers used life-detection equipment to look for the missing.locatorNepal has said it does not need foreign help in general search and rescue operations, but it has leaned on its neighbours, India and China, for their expertise in tunnel rescues.Rescue operations have been suspended several times since Friday because of bad weather and concerns that a lake formed across the Nepal-China border by the disaster could trigger fresh flooding after it began overflowing into Nepal’s rivers.The weather was good on Monday, however, and rescue ⁠work picked up pace, said Narendra Pariyar, the district administrator of Rasuwa, one of the two hardest-hit districts.In the holy ​town of Devighat on the banks of the Trishuli, residents walked around the shells ofwhat had once been ​homes, trying to salvage their belongings from the debris.View image in fullscreenPeople try to salvage belongings from their devastated homes in Devighat.Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty ImagesThe flood was “caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming”, CCTV reported, saying ​it was a “new and prominent feature of cryosphere ‌disasters” on the Tibetan plateau.Two ​Nepali officials said China had ​not shared much information on glacier risks and water levels after a meeting to strengthen cooperation earlier this year, and they feared that could hamper future disaster preparedness.China’s foreign ministry said Beijing had continuously provided Nepal with meteorological and hydrological data and will continue to “strongly support” Nepal’s disaster relief efforts and safeguard the two countries’ common interests.With Reuters and Agence France-PresseExplore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalFloodingTibetChinaExtreme weatherSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Police appeal after unidentified woman’s body found in Liverpool park | Liverpool | The Guardian
description: Body of victim thought to be in her 70s found in bin bag in walled garden area of Stanley Park on Friday
Author: Hannah Al-Othman
Headline: Body of victim thought to be in her 70s found in bin bag in walled garden area of Stanley Park on Friday
Content: A woman’s body was found in Stanley Park in the Anfield area of Liverpool.Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA woman’s body was found in Stanley Park in the Anfield area of Liverpool.Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesLiverpoolPolice appeal after unidentified woman’s body found in Liverpool parkBody of victim thought to be in her 70s found in bin bag in walled garden area of Stanley Park on FridayHannah Al-OthmanNorth of England correspondentMon 31 Aug 2026 13.58 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 14.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice inLiverpoolhave urged members of the public to come forward with information after the body of an unknown woman believed to be in her 70s was found in a black bin bag in a popular park.Merseyside police were contacted by a passerby who had found the woman’s body in Stanley Park, in the Anfield area of Liverpool, at about 5.25pm on Friday 28 August.The body was found in a black bin bag in the walled garden area of the park. It is believed that it may have lain there undiscovered for a number of weeks.“A postmortem took place on Saturday 29 August, the result of which has been withheld for investigation reasons,” Det Supt Rachel Wilson said at a press conference on Monday. “Our team have since been carrying out extensive enquiries to identify the woman, but we have so far been unable to do so.”Wilson said forensic work continued, adding: “We’re carrying out house-to-house, CCTV and other enquiries as a matter of urgency, but of course the methodical nature of such work can mean it takes time.”Officers believe the woman was in her 70s. She was described as white, about 1.57 metres (5ft 2in) tall, of small build, and with strawberry-blond hair. She was found wearing a pink Nike T-shirt.“Missing people reports in Merseyside and elsewhere have been checked but, so far, these have not resulted in an identification,” Wilson said. “Sometimes people go missing without those close to them realising, through holidays being planned or simple misunderstandings, and so we may not have received a report of any concerns.“While we do not want to worry people unnecessarily, it is vital that we follow every possible lead, both to rule people out and ultimately to identify the woman, notify her next of kin and apprehend the offender.”Describing the murder as a “shocking crime”, Wilson said police were “doing all we can to identify the person or persons responsible and bring them to justice”.Stanley Park separates the Anfield and Goodison Park football stadiums, which are respectively home to Liverpool FC and Everton Women.Assistant chief constable Andy Ryan said he understood “how unnerving” the discovery and the heightened police presence would be for local people, adding: “This is the exact reason that we are so determined to get answers as soon as we possibly can.”He described the park as “a very busy and popular green space, especially in the recent warm summer weeks”.“It is visited by dog walkers and families, as well as people walking and exercising,” he said. “It is quite possible that one or more of these visitors may have seen something suspicious recently and not reported it at the time.”“I want to reiterate Rachel’s appeal,” Ryan added. “If anyone recognises the description of this woman or you have any concerns whatsoever about someone you may know and haven’t seen or heard from recently, please tell us as a matter of urgency.”Potential witnesses are urged to contact Merseyside police via social media or to call 101, quoting reference number 26000706383.Reports can also be made anonymously by calling Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.Explore more on these topicsLiverpoolMerseysideEnglandNorth of EnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump threatens further action as US and Iran exchange fire in new flare-up | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: Washington says it acted after observing Iran was planning to deploy fresh mines in strait of Hormuz
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Washington says it acted after observing Iran was planning to deploy fresh mines in strait of Hormuz
Content: Vessels in the strait of Hormuz. Washington claims that Iranian control over the waterway has been loosened by repeated US attacks on missile launchers and radars.Photograph: Majid Asgaripour/ReutersView image in fullscreenVessels in the strait of Hormuz. Washington claims that Iranian control over the waterway has been loosened by repeated US attacks on missile launchers and radars.Photograph: Majid Asgaripour/ReutersUS-Israel war on IranTrump threatens further action as US and Iran exchange fire in new flare-upWashington says it acted after observing Iran was planning to deploy fresh mines in strait of HormuzPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorMon 31 Aug 2026 13.13 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US and Iran have exchanged fire for the first time in a month, with missiles and drones fired at Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the strait of Hormuz, and Iran targeting US military bases in Jordan and theUnited Arab Emiratesin response.The US president,Donald Trump, on Monday threatened further action. The US is to trying to prise open Tehran’s grip on shipping going through the strait, which before the war accounted for a fifth of the world’s seaborne energy supply. Washington claimed that Iranian control over the waterway had been loosened by repeated US attacks on Iranian missile launchers and radars.US Central Command said it acted late on Sunday, launching the first strikes onIransince July, after it detected the Iranians were planning to deploy fresh mines in the strait. Last week Trump claimed the US navy had cleared the strait of mines for the first time since the conflict started on 28 February, a claim the Iranians rejected as lies.In response to the US attack, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it “targeted technical infrastructure, maintenance facilities and enemy fighter jet positions at the US-operated King Hussein and al-Azraq airbases in Jordan” with ballistic missiles, causing “heavy damage”. The UAE defence ministry said it intercepted a drone over its territorial waters.Trump responded to the Iranian reprisals by telling Fox News: “We’re going to hit them hard. There will be a response.” The US president called Iran “officially a failed nation without an airforce, a navy or a currency”, adding that inflation was at 300% and its leaders were incapable of representing their country.Iran’s economy in crisis as US launches new sanctions campaignRead moreThe White House last week signalled that Trump was shelving military measures in favour ofa campaign to destroy the Iranian economy by enforcing sanctions.Iranian state TV claimed the military exchanges escalated on Sunday after a tanker caught fire when hitting two Iranian naval mines while attempting to pass through the southern side of the strait close to Oman. Officials later said Iran had targeted three ships trying to navigate the southern route that Tehran says is unauthorised.The IRGC warned that other ships violating ⁠its rules would face ​the ​same fate and ​said compliance with ​its regulations ‌for ​passage ​through the strait was mandatory.However, the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, told Pakistan’s prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, in a bilateral meeting on the margins of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan on Monday that continuing the war was not in Iran’s interest, adding he was still ready to implement the memorandum of understanding with the US that Pakistan had mediated in June.The Iranian currency was under renewed pressure on Monday and the inflationary impact of its rapid depreciation is causing growing concern to MPs.View image in fullscreenPeople buy bread from a street vendor beneath an anti-US billboard in Tehran.Photograph: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/ShutterstockIran and Oman last week reached a verbal agreement on a new single temporary route for shipping through the strait in which Oman retains controls on shipping in Omani waters.One western diplomat familiar with the talks said the message had got through to Washington that this bilateral agreement would not be enough for Iran to open the strait and that to do so would at least require the US to end its blockade of Iranian oil exports, something Trump is not currently prepared to do. “There are many in Iran determined to torment Trump right up to the end of his presidency,” the western diplomat said. “We are stuck.” He said some oil was getting through but not very much.The latest fighting broke out late on Sunday with the US claiming it attacked Larak Island in the strait. A US official said: “I can confirm that earlier today US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak Island. Islamic ⁠Revolutionary Guard Corps forces were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the strait of Hormuz.”The IRGC said the US attack had killed three soldiers and wounded two citizens. Iran’s Mehr news agency quoted the IRGC as saying its air defences shot down a US MQ-9 drone over the strait, causing it to crash ‌into Gulf waters.How the Iran war unfolded: every attack and oil price change – visualisedRead moreThe US said all missiles fired towards US forces in Jordan had been intercepted with no significant impact.The White House claim that the US now controls the strait and ships are free to navigate its waters is heavily contested. Tanker Trackers, an independent tracking agency, said on Sunday: “Past seven days daily average of crude oil exports via the strait of Hormuz was 3.8m barrels per day. During the formal ceasefire period (which in effect only lasted for 25 days), it was 9.8m.” The agency said Iranian crude exports had been at zero for some time.A meeting of G20 finance ministers in the US is likely to lead to a clash over American demands that more countries impose sanctions on Iran or face punitive action by Washington. The German finance minister, Lars Klingbeil, who is facing difficult regional elections, is to urge the US to bring the conflict to a diplomatic end, pointing to the war’s inflationary impact.The US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, echoing Trump, claimed on Monday the resumed exchanges of fire showed Iran was “lashing out” because the fresh sanctions were taking ​a heavy toll on its already battered economy.View image in fullscreenScott Bessent speaks to reporters as he arrives for the G20 finance ministers meeting in Asheville, North Carolina.Photograph: Allison Joyce/AFP/Getty Images“They’re taking it very seriously ... they’re in shock at the state of their ‌economy,” Bessent told reporters at the G20 finance ministers ‌meeting in North Carolina. “I would think that they are lashing out kinetically because they are losing economically.”China, a key Iranian customer for its oil, has said it opposes the new US sanctions campaign. In Kyrgyzstan, Pezeshkian will be looking for concrete assurances from the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, that he will not allow the US to spread economic chaos through Iran.Explore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranIranStrait of HormuzUS foreign policyDonald TrumpMiddle East and north AfricaUS militarynewsShareReuse this content

title: Rising microplastics in soil a threat to UK food security, MPs and campaigners say | Plastics | The Guardian
description: Report calls for legally binding targets to cut microplastic pollution as soil ‘is a complex living ecosystem’
Author: Damien Gayle
Headline: Report calls for legally binding targets to cut microplastic pollution as soil ‘is a complex living ecosystem’
Content: Microplastics are often shed by the breakdown of everyday plastic items such as synthetic textiles, packaging, paints, cosmetics or car tyres.Photograph: pcess609/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenMicroplastics are often shed by the breakdown of everyday plastic items such as synthetic textiles, packaging, paints, cosmetics or car tyres.Photograph: pcess609/Getty Images/iStockphotoPlasticsRising microplastics in soil a threat to UK food security, MPs and campaigners sayReport calls for legally binding targets to cut microplastic pollution as soil ‘is a complex living ecosystem’Damien GayleEnvironment correspondentMon 31 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe accumulation of microplastics in soil presents an emerging threat to the UK’s food security, according to scientists, MPs and campaigners who have called for legally binding targets to cut microplastic pollution.UK agricultural soils have been identified as among the most contaminated by microplastics in Europe, often as a result of repeated applications of sludge from water treatment works as fertiliser, according to a report published by the all-party parliamentary group (APPG) on microplastics.With extreme weather caused by climate breakdown already placing new pressures on agriculture, protecting soil from additional and unknown pressures is becoming increasingly important, it argues.Alberto Costa, the MP for South Leicestershire and chair of the APPG, said: “Despite the evidence, the UK’s response remains limited. Existing measures tackle only a tiny proportion of microplastic emissions. We urgently need a preventative approach focused on reducing microplastic releases at source to protect human health and food security.”Prof Cressida Bowyer, the director of the Revolution Plastics Institute at the University of Portsmouth, was the senior author on the report, produced in collaboration with the APPG and the Women’s Institute. The report follows up an earlier collaboration that focused onplastic microfibres from synthetic textiles.Microplastics are pieces of plastic between 1 micrometre and 5 millimetres in size. They are often shed by the breakdown of everyday plastic items such as synthetic textiles, packaging, paints, cosmetics or car tyres.Nanoplastics are particles smaller than 1 micrometre, which makes them small enough to permeate through biological membranes. “Everywhere we look, we find them,” Bowyer said. “Doesn’t matter how deep, how high, how obscure the sampling site, we will find microplastics. And similarly we’re finding microplastics now throughout the human body.”She added: “We’re starting to realise that our exposure to microplastics is happening across the whole of the plastics lifecycle. So not just during the production phase and at the disposal end, where most people think of microplastics contamination occurring.
