But also during our use of plastic, when we’re using plastic packaging or when we’re wrapping ourselves in that lovely soft, cosy blanket on the sofa, or chopping our mushrooms on that plastic chopping board.”Submissions of evidence to the report showed particular concerns around the presence of microplastics in soil, which Bowyer said “impacts the biological, the chemical and the physical functioning of the soil and the soil fertility itself”.According to Bowyer, plastic particles affect the soil structure, changing the water capacity of soil; they affect the microbial community, the bacteria and fungi that are crucial to soil health; and they affect the soil fauna, with earthworms ingesting microplastics undergoing physiological changes.She said it was important to remember that “soil is not an inert material. It’s a complex living ecosystem; it’s very finely balanced. [It is a] complex ecosystem that supports the growth of crops that feed us. The second thing to remember that’s really important is that microplastics, they’re not just polymer particles … they’re basically chemical cocktails.”There are more than 16,000 chemicals used in plastics. About 4,000 are known to be harmful to health, while most of the rest have never undergone safety testing, the report notes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Microplastics can also pick up from the environment further contaminants,” Bowyer said. “So they become like sponges or magnets for other things like bacteria, heavy metals, viral particles, other chemicals.”The report makes five policy recommendations: legally binding targets for cutting microplastic pollution, regulation of the largest sources of microplastic releases, extended producer responsibility to reduce releases across the plastics lifecycle, improved wastewater, sewage sludge and soil protections, and a coordinated national monitoring and evidence system to oversee the issue.The report’s co-author Dr Antaya March, the director of the RevolutionPlasticsInstitute’s Global Plastics Policy Centre, said: “The UK has an opportunity to move from a fragmented response to a coordinated strategy that tackles microplastics across the plastics lifecycle. We should not wait for every scientific uncertainty to be resolved before acting where the evidence already shows that intervention can prevent pollution and reduce future risks.”The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs was contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsPlasticsSoilPollutionEnvironment policynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Superhuman’ AI tool spots heart disease in less than 2 seconds | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Technology trained on millions of routine ECGs could fast-track high-risk patients for treatment
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: Technology trained on millions of routine ECGs could fast-track high-risk patients for treatment
Content: For heart disease, early diagnosis is vital for saving lives.Photograph: alengo/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFor heart disease, early diagnosis is vital for saving lives.Photograph: alengo/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)‘Superhuman’ AI tool spots heart disease in less than 2 secondsTechnology trained on millions of routine ECGs could fast-track high-risk patients for treatmentAndrew GregoryHealth editor in MunichMon 31 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDoctors have developed a “superhuman” AI tool that can spot heart disease in less than two seconds.The groundbreaking technology has been trained on millions of patients and works by extracting more information from a routine electrocardiogram (ECG) than the human eye can typically see.The traditional ECG, which records electrical activity in the heart, including the rate and rhythm, has been a vital medical tool in diagnosing heart attacks and abnormal heart rhythms for a century.But it cannot detect heart disease. That requires an echocardiogram, a type of ultrasound scan, which patients often have to wait months for.Now a team have developed an AI tool that can spot signs of heart failure and heart valve disease – two of the most common forms of heart disease – from ECG results in “the blink of an eye”.Details of the breakthrough, which could boost early diagnosis of heart disease, were presented to thousands of delegates at the European Society of Cardiology annual congress in Munich, the world’s largest heart conference.Doctors’ AI scribes get names of drugs and diagnoses wrong, NHS watchdog warnsRead moreEarly diagnosis is vital for heart failure and heart valve disease, enabling those who need lifesaving medicines to be spotted sooner, before they become dangerously unwell.The development is being seen as potentially significant, because ECGs are one of the most common tests in medicine, with about a billion performed worldwide each year.In a trial involving 67,000 patients in the US, the AI tool was able to identify up to 81% of those who had heart failure, and up to 90% of those with heart valve disease.Dr Sonya Babu-Narayan, a consultant cardiologist and clinical director of the British Heart Foundation (BHF), which funded the trial, said: “It is exciting to see that AI can now deliver a read-out from an ECG in what feels like the blink of an eye.“Technology like the AI ECG in this research, which has the potential to identify high-risk patients early, will not detect everyone with a heart condition. But it could be a solution to help fast-track the patients who are most likely to have a heart abnormality. When it comes to the heart, earlier diagnosis and treatment saves and improves lives.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAI can detect heart disease in women using mammograms, study suggestsRead moreThe tech cannot be used on its own to definitively diagnose or rule out heart failure or heart valve disease, but it gives a very strong indication someone may have them.Someone judged as highly likely to have either could be sent rapidly for an echocardiogram, rather than wait months on the standard waiting lists. That could mean a quicker diagnosis which would enable them to start treatment earlier.Prof Fu Siong Ng, a professor of cardiology at Imperial College London, said: “Patients can often wait several months for a heart ultrasound scan after being referred for one by their doctor.“This makes it exciting that our technology could identify patients most at risk of heart failure and heart valve disease, so they could be prioritised for scans faster and more urgently.”The aim of the tool is to speed up diagnosis of those suspected to have heart failure or heart valve disease. But Ng said it could also prove lifesaving by spotting signs of the conditions in people who may have undergone an ECG for different reasons.“Another potential application of this AI model is to opportunistically diagnose heart failure and heart valve disease in whom these conditions are not suspected,” he said. “The AI model could be run on all ECGs done in a hospital to flag those at highest risk of these diseases, so that they can be diagnosed earlier.”Dr Ahmed El-Medany, a BHF clinical research fellow, who led the Imperial College London analysis, described the tool as a “superhuman AI” and said the next challenge would be to design handheld AI-led ECG readers for healthcare professionals to use.Delegates in Munich also heard how AI-based analysis of facial videos couldrapidly and accurately detect undiagnosed high blood pressure and type 2 diabetes.Researchers at the University of Tokyo and the Institute of Science Tokyo said AI analysis of five-second facial videos could hep improve diagnosis. Millions of people who have high blood pressure or type 2 diabetes do not know they have the conditions.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)HealthNHSnewsShareReuse this content

title: Conservative reshuffle: who’s who in Kemi Badenoch’s top team?  | Conservatives | The Guardian
description: From a darling of the Tory right to a moderate former army officer, we profile the key players
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: From a darling of the Tory right to a moderate former army officer, we profile the key players
Content: Kemi Badenoch measures up Andrew Griffith, her newly appointed shadow chancellor, for a shirt in December last year.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PAView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch measures up Andrew Griffith, her newly appointed shadow chancellor, for a shirt in December last year.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PAConservativesConservative reshuffle: who’s who in Kemi Badenoch’s top team?From a darling of the Tory right to a moderate former army officer, we profile the key playersAndrew Griffith and Tom Tugendhat join Badenoch’s top team in Tory reshuffleHelena HortonandHarry CockburnMon 31 Aug 2026 14.45 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKemi Badenoch has kicked off the return to parliamentwith a reshuffleof her top team in order to take on Andy Burnham and Reform UK. She has made sweeping changes to the shadow cabinet and ruthlessly axed her shadow chancellor. Here is a run-down of the new characters sitting across from Labour on the opposition frontbench.Andrew GriffithGriffith, the MP for Arundel and South Downs, replaces Mel Stride as shadow chancellor, a role he has reportedly long coveted. He is loyal to Badenoch and was one of her first backers for leader in 2024.Previously the chief financial officer and chief operating officer of Sky and the chair of Just Eat, he entered parliament as an ally of Boris Johnson after allowing the former prime minister to use his £9.5m townhouse as his leadership campaign HQ in 2019. He later became Johnson’s business adviser in government before running for election later that year.Griffith was a backer of Liz Truss for leader and as her treasury minister was partially responsible for the disastrous mini-budget which caused economic chaos. He continued to defend the budget and said the market turmoil was linked to global events.He wasspotted last yearat the launch of a climate denial group with Truss and Nigel Farage. Of his attendance, he said: “In any year, I attend hundreds of external events with business organisations and thinktanks, none of which automatically imply my endorsement.” He also recently spoke at a hard-right Cpac event organised by Truss.Claire CoutinhoWidely tipped as one of the party’s rising stars, Coutinho made a fierce opponent to Ed Miliband when he was energy secretary and she shadowed his brief. A cabinet minister in Rishi Sunak’s government, she has been shifted to Badenoch’s economic unit and made shadow business secretary. Before parliament she was an investment banker at Merrill Lynch and KPMG, and has recently been holding the Labour government’s feet to the fire over rising energy bills.View image in fullscreenClaire Coutinho.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesColleagues describe her as forensic, she delights in doing her own research about what she terms “the hidden cost of net zero” and has spoken up in parliament for whistleblowers at the national energy systems operator.She became the first person to represent a political party at PMQs while pregnant earlier this year. Julia Lopez, the MP for Hornchurch and Upminster, will cover for her until the new year while she is on maternity leave. Coutinho is a keen cook in her spare time and once appeared on Nigella Lawson’s cooking gameshow The Taste.Tom TugendhatBadenoch has made a show of purging the more “woke” MPs from the party, banning those who believe in pursuing net zero from standing at the next election for example, so the choice of the moderate Tugendhat as shadow foreign secretary surprised some.View image in fullscreenTom Tugendhat.Photograph: House of Commons/PAHe replaces Priti Patel, who was sacked from the shadow cabinet. Tugendhat has experience in foreign affairs and previously served in the cabinet as security minister from September 2022 to July 2024. A former British army officer, he served in Afghanistan and Iraq.A remainer, he has also said he does not support leaving the European convention on human rights, which puts him at loggerheads with Badenoch.Tugendhat stood as the moderate option in the Tory party leadership contest in 2022, but was beaten by a long way by Truss. He tried and lost again against Badenoch when Sunak stood down in 2024.He wasbanned from drivingfor six months in 2022 for using his mobile phone at the wheel.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKatie LamA darling of the Tory right, Lam was only elected in 2024. She has been given the role of shadow housing and communities minister, and is likely to relish being Angela Rayner’s opposite number. She is a former special adviser to Johnson, and she worked on Sunak’s first leadership bid. Outside politics she worked at the PR company Portland Communications and the AI company Faculty.View image in fullscreenKatie Lam.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesShe has sometimes been tipped as a potential defector to Reform after saying many immigrants should “go home” and supporting the policy of revoking indefinite leave to remain. Her comments on immigration have gone further than official Conservative policy at some points.Lam has written five musicals, including an adaptation of The Railway Children.Other changes and those staying onChris Philp remains shadow home secretary. He supported Badenoch’s successful leadership campaign and has held the role since she became party leader.James Cartlidge stays on as shadow defence secretary, a position he has held since Sunak appointed him to the role in 2024.Andrew Bowie takes up Coutinho’s previous role as energy secretary.The shadow health secretary, Stuart Andrew, quit the frontbench to “focus on constituency work”, and Damian Hinds assumes his brief.Explore more on these topicsConservativesKemi BadenochTom TugendhatnewsShareReuse this content

title: The London office, the empty boxes and the £1bn tax loophole | Financial sector | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: How a court case over an unoccupied office block could end a widely used tax avoidance scheme
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Exclusive: How a court case over an unoccupied office block could end a widely used tax avoidance scheme
Content: 2 America Square, an office block leased by a Virgin Islands-based company, is at the centre of the court case.Photograph: Brian Anthony/AlamyView image in fullscreen2 America Square, an office block leased by a Virgin Islands-based company, is at the centre of the court case.Photograph: Brian Anthony/AlamyFinancial sectorThe London office, the empty boxes and the £1bn tax loopholeExclusive: How a court case over an unoccupied office block could end a widely used tax avoidance schemeNick SommerladMon 31 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 14.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom the outside, the seven-storey building at 2 America Square looks like any other office block in the heart of London’s financial district.Located about half a mile from Tower Bridge, one might expect it to be a hive of commercial activity, teeming with employees holding important meetings. However, much of the property is home not to staff vying for their next bonus, but to stacks of nondescript black boxes arranged in neat lines.The building, leased by a Virgin Islands-based company called 48th Street Holdings Ltd, has found itself at the centre of a court case that has finally signalled the end of a tax avoidance scheme believed to have cost local authorities more than £1bn.For almost two decades, companies in England have been exploiting a legal loophole to avoid paying business rates on unoccupied commercial buildings.The controversial practice dates back to 2008, when the last Labour government changed business rates rules. This meant occupiers of vacant buildings no longer qualified for a 50% discount on the levy.View image in fullscreenBoxes such as these enabled companies to claim three-month rate holidays on unoccupied properties.Photograph: City of London CorporationHowever, they were entitled to claim a three-month rate holiday at the end of each tenancy – and the “box shifting” scheme was born.With commercial property owners facing higher bills, a lucrative “rate mitigation” industry emerged. Historically, this typically involved boxes being moved into the empty space at the end of the three months and back out after just six weeks. The building then became unoccupied again and the clock was reset, allowing the owner to claim another three-month rate-free period.This cycle continued, designed to cut the rates owed by up to 67%, until a new long-term tenant could be found. It has been costing one London council an estimated £35m a year since the pandemic, when the number of claims for empty property relief doubled.However, last month a landmark ruling by three court of appeal judges looks to have sounded the death knell for box shifting. They ruled that the scheme “cannot amount to beneficial occupation”.locator mapThe case was brought by the City of London Corporation against 48th Street Holding Ltd and a second company, Principled Offsite Logistics Ltd (POLL), which provides “rate mitigation” services.48th Street paid £27.6m for a lease on the office block in 2019 before it brought in POLL to save £111,475.30 in rates across a series of three-month periods in 2022 and 2023.POLL describes itself as “the largest and most reliable” provider of “empty business rates mitigation” in the UK and is jointly owned by a Labour councillor from North Hertfordshire.It claimed by 2021 to have already saved its clients “£500m” in rates and that “every council in the UK now totally recognises Principled as being robust in every way”.That bold claim followed a significant high court win in 2018, when POLL defeated a challenge from Trafford council. The judge in that case accepted that “the purpose of the occupation is not to store goods; it is, so to speak, to plant the occupier’s flag” and that “the motive … is rates avoidance for the landlord”, but added “the morality of that is neither here nor there”.When the case against POLL and 48th Street came before the high court last year, Charles Bagot KC, sitting as a deputy high court judge, also ruled against the City of London.“I agree with POLL that if legislation produces clear tramlines and someone organises themselves to fall within them, then it is not for the court to get involved in moral judgments,” he said. “If the government does not like the position, it can amend it.” He concluded that “the RMS [rate mitigation scheme] is effective”.However, last month the court of appeal overturned that decision, with Lady Justice Falk ruling: “In my judgment, ‘occupation’ for, in effect, the sake of it, and which has no use, value or benefit other than rate saving, does not amount to occupation for the purpose of the statutory scheme.”A City of London Corporation spokesperson said: “We welcome the court of appeal’s decision, which represents a significant victory for local authorities across England.“This landmark ruling closes one of the most widely used tax avoidance schemes in the country and helps safeguard revenues that support essential public services.“We are proud that the City of London Corporation has led the way nationally in pursuing this case.“For more than a decade, councils across the country have seen hundreds of millions of pounds of public revenue lost through artificial business rates avoidance schemes and we believe the decision restores fairness, protects money that funds vital local services, and provides greater certainty for councils, ratepayers and property owners alike.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA government spokesperson said: “We recognise concerns about the misuse of Empty Property Relief, which exists to support genuine property owners between tenants.“Business rates avoidance is unacceptable and we are taking the necessary action to address this, and make sure that businesses are paying the tax they owe.”It is unclear what action the government is planning, but there are calls for a general anti-avoidance rule to control the rate mitigation industry.POLL is not the only business offering box shifting. The same scheme was even used by Public Health England at its future headquarters in Harlow in 2018. The resulting £2.5m dispute with Harlow district council ended up in the high court, where PHE won.It remains to be seen how councils and their rate mitigation opponents will respond.One rating expert said that the total cost to councils of box shifting could have topped £1.5bn, and some of that money should now be reclaimed as a deterrent.Under the terms of POLL’s contracts with clients, its success fees are refundable in the event the scheme fails. The latest accounts show it has just over £500,000 in net assets.POLL did not respond to a request for comment and its website went down this week, replaced with a message which read: “This account has been suspended”.The company’s founder, Steven Dawson, died in 2024 and the POLL was acquired in a management buyout by two of its own executives. One of them is a Labour councillor,Sarah Lucas, who, according to her LinkedIn profile, has been POLL’s director of finance since 2018.View image in fullscreenThe boxes are a key element of a ‘rate mitigation’ scheme estimated to have cost local authorities over £1bn.Photograph: City of London CorporationLucas was elected to North Hertfordshire council in 2024, two months after she took 50% ownership of POLL, and she serves as vice-chair of the council’s finance, audit and risk committee.The Guardian understands that POLL’s application for permission to appeal to the supreme court was refused by the court of appeal this week but an option remains for it to apply to the supreme court directly.The rules on empty property relief changed in 2024 and buildings now need to be occupied for 13 weeks instead of six in order for the three-month holiday to apply. According to one recent judgment, this makes box shifting schemes “less attractive but still effective”.There are still a range of variants of rates mitigation on offer. One involves placing Bluetooth boxes in the offices to broadcast adverts. Another uses charitable exhibitions to claim not only empty property relief but also the extra rates relief available for charities.Some schemes install snail or mushroom farms to claim agricultural reliefs, while others involve opening faith rooms to cut rates.Explore more on these topicsFinancial sectorBritish Virgin IslandsTax and spendingBusiness ratesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tea With Judi Dench Featuring Sir Ian McKellen review – TV that will make you cry thunderous tears | Television | The Guardian
description: Two icons share cake and take us on a touching trip down memory lane. Dench is mesmerising, and McKellen is such a devilish guest that he’ll make you weep and giggle too
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: Two icons share cake and take us on a touching trip down memory lane. Dench is mesmerising, and McKellen is such a devilish guest that he’ll make you weep and giggle too
Content: A gentle celebration … Tea With Judi Dench Featuring Sir Ian McKellen.Photograph: Sky UK/Mindhouse/Sky UK LimitedView image in fullscreenA gentle celebration … Tea With Judi Dench Featuring Sir Ian McKellen.Photograph: Sky UK/Mindhouse/Sky UK LimitedTV reviewTelevisionReviewTea With Judi Dench Featuring Sir Ian McKellen review – TV that will make you cry thunderous tearsTwo icons share cake and take us on a touching trip down memory lane. Dench is mesmerising, and McKellen is such a devilish guest that he’ll make you weep and giggle tooLucy ManganMon 31 Aug 2026 17.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIam writing this in the wake of Dolly Parton’s death, so I am very much in the mood for the gentle celebration of ageing icons while we still have them. An hour of 91-year-old Judi Dench having tea with 87-year-oldIan McKellen? Sign me right up and I will not so much as breathe heavily in their direction lest anything go wrong.McKellen – Sir Ian, “Serena” to his friends – navigates the “treacherous” pavement leading to Dame Judi’s fairytale 15th-century home in Surrey, which is as cosy and sparkling as its owner (if anyone is listening, I will take an hour of just Dench, taking us around the house and garden, like the world’s most mesmerising estate agent), and unwraps two lumps of parkin cake to go with their tea. One from Yorkshire, where Dench is from, and one from Lancashire because McKellen was – is – a Burnley (then Wigan, then Bolton) boy.They go through his childhood as they wire into the cake. Seeing Peter Pan at three, falling in love with panto, being aware of the local professional actors as he reached school age and hoping to become one of them one day. Then a scholarship to Cambridge University in 1958, “where I met all these boys and girls who were as crazy about the theatre as I was”, and he started to dream bigger. I suppose you do when the boys and girls include Trevor Nunn, Corin Redgrave, Derek Jacobi, Miriam Margolyes and Clive Swift. “Well,” says McKellen, “I thought – ifDerek Jacobican do it …” The devilish twist of his lips and Dench’s throaty giggle should be put on Unesco’s intangible cultural heritage list instantly.Some of his pals went on to drama school but the Burnley boy felt he had better start earning a living as soon as possible and was soon treading the boards in regional theatre. He and Dench began their friendship at Oxford Playhouse, appearing with Ian McShane in a 1967 production of The Promise. They remember actorly moments – the time she saved him from stage fright in a George Bernard Shaw play (“It’s nice that you don’t remember it,” he says. “Just an actor helping another actor out, which is what we do, isn’t it, at best?”), whether it’s nice to know that friends are in the audience or not, entire performances that become slightly reorientated towards a Peter Brook or an Olivier in the stalls – and they sigh a bit over the youth of today who can’t manage on stage without microphones.View image in fullscreenLike the world’s most mesmerising estate agent … Tea With Judi Dench.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAIntimations of mortality are briefly dealt with, because while McKellen thinks about death “every day” Dench banishes it firmly from her thoughts. She does look back, though, “with a little bit of everything – but mainly thinking about how lucky I’ve been”.There are, of course, lots of clips of them acting – McKellen especially, as he’s the guest – and they are something to behold. You hope that those who only know him as Gandalf or Magneto (“Lovely jobs”) will one day see footage of him as Edward II or Coriolanus or as Max in Bent, or of the two of them as the Macbeths in Nunn’s minimalist 1976 RSC production (filmed by Philip Casson for ThamesTelevisionin 1978). There are only fleeting glimpses here and you long to see more. The set and costumes cost £250, McKellen notes. And a man of the cloth came to multiple performances to sit in the front row holding up a crucifix. McKellen always thought it was to protect them. Dench thinks it was to protect himself. “Ooh,” says McKellen, who you suddenly see is a sweet optimist at heart, deflating.His work as a gay rights activist is limned. The grace and eloquence of his turn on Wogan in 1988, explaining the ramifications of section 28, evoke a vanished past. So too, in sadder ways still, does his memory of the letter his loving and beloved father wrote to him on his 21st birthday, possibly asking between the lines if there was anything Ian wanted to tell him and assuring him that he could. Both of McKellen’s parents died long before he felt able to come out. So he wonders. He wonders and he reads Armistead Maupin’s Letter to Mama and makes us all cry thunderous tears.There are moments in Tea With … that you find yourself wishing that it was A Drink With … (though McKellen himself doesn’t drink any more – Dench looks suitably aghast). Because put any two actors together, let alone this pair, and the anecdotes are always much, much better than the ones that pass muster here. But perhaps it’s enough to hear about lives well lived, and contentment gained, and pay homage to a few of the tears shed along the way.Tea WithJudi DenchFeaturing Sir Ian McKellen aired on Sky Arts and is on NowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewJudi DenchIan McKellenreviewsShareReuse this content

title: 100 ultramarathons in 100 days: former rugby pro hit by brain injury nears end of feat | Marathon running | The Guardian
description: David ‘Jacko’ Jackson has aimed to raise awareness of brain injuries, with fellow runners sharing their stories
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: David ‘Jacko’ Jackson has aimed to raise awareness of brain injuries, with fellow runners sharing their stories
Content: David 'Jacko' Jackson has not shaved during his challenge – his beard is ‘almost a symbol of how far I’ve run’, he says.Photograph: Francesca Jones/The GuardianView image in fullscreenDavid 'Jacko' Jackson has not shaved during his challenge – his beard is ‘almost a symbol of how far I’ve run’, he says.Photograph: Francesca Jones/The GuardianMarathon running100 ultramarathons in 100 days: former rugby pro hit by brain injury nears end of featDavid ‘Jacko’ Jackson has aimed to raise awareness of brain injuries, with fellow runners sharing their storiesSteven MorrisMon 31 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe key for David “Jacko” Jackson is to take each stage nice and gently. “It’s not about running fast,” he said. “It’s more like the hare and tortoise story. Slow and steady – and do it again tomorrow.”So far, so good. Jackson, a former professional rugby player who retired after a traumatic brain injury, is nearing the end ofan extraordinary bid to run 100 ultramarathons(50km, or about 30 miles) in 100 consecutive days.He began from his home in northWalesin May and, if all goes well, will finish back there, at Caernarfon Castle, on Saturday (5 September).Jackson’s run has taken inScotlandand England, and he has been joined by more than 700 people, aged eight to in their 80s, who have run alongside him. He has used seven pairs of shoes.“I should be feeling tired now,” said Jackson, 44, when the Guardian caught up with him in south Wales. “But I’m getting excited about getting to the end and, hopefully, making a bit of a difference.”View image in fullscreen‘Running is a great way to train better breathing patterns and habits,’ said Jackson, seen here in Newport, south Wales.Photograph: Francesca Jones/The GuardianJackson is raising money for the brain injury charitiesHeadwayandHead for Change, but the idea is also about drawing attention to the issue and hearing people’s experiences.“All the way through, the highlights have been the people,” he said. “We’ve been to some really cool conversations.“When you’re running side by side, people tend to share a lot. So many people have things they wanted to talk about. Some were excited because they’ve overcome something, others were in the midst of something really horrible but find running a great way to … keep them sane. People tell you some really, like, deep stuff.”View image in fullscreenJackson suffered a leg injury on day 14 in the Lake District but has been able to keep on going.Photograph: Francesca Jones/The GuardianJackson’s rugby career ended abruptly in 2013 due to a traumatic brain injury and seizure on the pitch during a training session. For months, he experienced symptoms including fatigue, sensitivity to light and cognitive issues.When he recovered, he became a strength and conditioning coach and became interestedin breathing techniquesand then running. “Running is quite rhythmical and your breathing when it’s good is rhythmical. Running is a great way to train better breathing patterns and habits,” he said.Jackson also became fascinated in the“marathon monks”of Japan, who train for years and run huge distances in search of enlightenment.He set off on this challenge intending to do two marathons a day, but suffered a leg injury on day 14 in the Lake District. “I’d done 26 marathons in 13 days and the wheels fell off. I was hobbling, crying my eyes out. I was in pain and felt like a letdown.”His wife, Catherine, who acts as his physio, nutritionist and logistics supremo, encouraged him to keep going. “The mindset was, if I can move, we’ll keep going until I can’t. If we manage to complete that leg, then we’ll try and do the same thing tomorrow. It sounds really cheesy, but it was one step at a time.”The injury eased and Jackson was able to keep going, though he tweaked the challenge from two marathons a day to one ultramarathon.The support vehicle is the couple’s camper van, where they prepare many of Jackson’s meals and drinks. Making sure he has enough fluids on board has been vital as he ran through the summer’s heatwaves.Post-it notes are dotted around the van with inspiration and questioning messages including: “We choose our attitude”, “Is this a reaction or a choice?” and “Greatest ever comeback”.View image in fullscreenDavid and Catherine Jackson have mainly slept in their camper van, though supporters have offered them accommodation along the way.Photograph: Francesca Jones/The GuardianCatherine Jacksonsaid it had been an adventure. She thought people opened up to Jackson because he was prepared to make himself vulnerable by sharing his story. “Other people seem to follow suit. When he’s low, someone comes along with fresh energy or shares a heartfelt story that he gets locked into and it makes him keep moving.”The couple have mainly slept in the camper van, but along the way well-wishers have offered them more roomy accommodation, cooked them meals and helped them with washing. “People have been very kind,” Catherine said.Being away from home for so long has been a challenge. David said: “We’ve unplugged from society. We have no idea what’s going on. Which has been quite nice.”He has not shaved during the run and has an impressive beard that brings to mind a famous movie runner – Forrest Gump.“A few people have shouted ‘Run Forrest, run’ at me. It wasn’t intentional. You don’t look at yourself much in the mirror when you’re doing something like this and in any spare moment you’re eating or doing recovery. But the beard has become almost a symbol of how far I’ve run, so it’s staying for now.”Explore more on these topicsMarathon runningWalesSports injuriesRunningScotlandEnglandRugby unionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: £4,000 for a teddy bear?! How cuddly toys became luxury items | Toys | The Guardian
description: Designs by Louis Vuitton, suits by Savile Row: these are not your run-of-the-mill teddies. But who’s buying them?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Designs by Louis Vuitton, suits by Savile Row: these are not your run-of-the-mill teddies. But who’s buying them?
Content: A snip … Hamley’s well-dressed gentleman bearsView image in fullscreenA snip … Hamley’s well-dressed gentleman bearsPass notesToys£4,000 for a teddy bear?! How cuddly toys became luxury itemsDesigns by Louis Vuitton, suits by Savile Row: these are not your run-of-the-mill teddies. But who’s buying them?Mon 31 Aug 2026 12.02 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName: Teddy bears.Age: 124 years old.Appearance: Vastly out of your price range.Well, that can’t be. I just lookedonline, and you can pick up a teddyfor a couple of quid. Get some sense, would you? I’m not talking about the flimsy bulk-produced abominations you let your kids play with. I’m talking about quality teddies.What’s the difference?First, these teddies don’t have eyes that will pop out and choke you. But in purely financial terms, the difference is about three and a half grand.For atoy?Oh yes. That’s what Louis Vuitton’s Doudou Vivienne XL retails for, anyway.View image in fullscreenBlooming expensive … Louis Vuitton’s Doudou Vivienne XL.Photograph: Louis VuittonThat’sberserk. Does it cook your dinner for you?No, but according tothe Times, it has leather on the soles of its feet, so that’s something.What a bizarre one-off this must be.Oh no, there is also the Louis Vuitton Collectible Damoflage, made from a fabric created by Pharrell Williams. But that one is admittedly slightly different.Is it?Yes, because it costs nearly £1,000 more.Wait, is this some insane luxury trend I don’t know about?No, of course there are plenty of designer teddies that are much more affordable.Phew. For example, there’s a Kaws bear that’s a snip at £844. Or if you’re really slumming it, you can pick up a giant Jellycat rabbit for the low, low price of £750.The world has gone mad.In fact, Hamleys toyshop is about to releasea limited range of bearsthat have each been dressed by a Savile Row tailor. All 10 bears are going to be auctioned (some in support of children’s charities), so no price has been revealed yet.What in the Jacob Rees-Mogg is this?They’ve been made to mark Hamleys’ 266th anniversary.Oh yes, thebig two six six.Butsurely children would be too scared to play with something that costsso much. What are you talking about? These aren’t for children. That’s the most preposterous thing I’ve ever heard. No, these are for adults only.OK,this just got creepy.Don’t be silly. There are plenty of adults who collect teddy bears. Maybe they have a fascination with the form as it was originally developed by German toy designer Richard Steiff. Or perhaps they have a lingering fondness for the comfort of childhood, and this has manifested in a large and fastidiously maintained teddy bear collection. You know, like …Don’t say it…Like the former prince Andrew. Oh wait, I see it now. Yes, super creepy, sorry.Do say:“Please look after this bear.”Don’t say:“Because it is genuinely worth more than your life.”Explore more on these topicsToysPass notesConsumer affairsCollectingLouis VuittonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Readers reply: If all car tyres were filled with CO2, would this cut atmospheric carbon significantly? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions considers a change that might help the environment
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions considers a change that might help the environment
Content: But what happens when it leaks?Photograph: Westend61/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBut what happens when it leaks?Photograph: Westend61/Getty ImagesNotes and queriesLife and styleReaders reply: If all car tyres were filled with CO2, would this cut atmospheric carbon significantly?The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions considers a change that might help the environmentThis week’s question:Would equal pay create a better society?Mon 31 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf all the vehicles on the planet had their tyres pumped up with CO2, would this lock up enough carbon to lower the amount in the air significantly? Would there be other issues, such as the carbon cost of trapping it all into the tyres?Chris Coldwell, LancasterSend new questions tonq@theguardian.com.Readers replyAre we expecting the car tyres to stay pumped up for geological time, say the next 50,000 years? If they leak and go flat before then, they haven’t helped restore the natural carbon balance. It’s quite sobering how long the damage done by one generation of humans will persist in the environment.Randomusername222An inflated car tyre will contain about 14g of air. CO2weighs about 50% more than air, giving 21g of CO2per tyre, or 105g per car. There are just short of 1.5bn cars on the planet. Multiplying this by 105g gives 157,700 tonnes of CO2in all of the world’s car tyres.CO2emissions in 2025 were 38.1bn tonnes, or about 100,000 tonnes per minute.DrLBlackIt would be interesting to compare the 157,700 tonnes stored here to the area needed to get the same carbon store in a rewilding project. I imagine that it would be a relatively small area of woodland on a map?KP8900Four hundred tonnes per hectare per year. So, in very round terms, either thousands of hectares or thousands of years, to achieve capture of hundreds of thousands of tonnes. Which is well, well short of current emissions.mill1806You have to pull the stuff out of the sky first and stop putting more there afterward. Locking it into tyres is a very short-term, fanciful solution. Bubble it through algae, trap it in basalt, turn it into bicarbonate and chuck it in the ocean. Plant one thing each day – preferably a tree. Turn it into kelp forests and sink it. Educate more girls. Make voting compulsory.king_tubbyFirst off, it is not easy or cheap to get carbon dioxide out of the air – certainly not easier or cheaper than just pumping air into the tyres. Plus, it does nothing about the other gases, such as methane, that are far more powerful drivers of climate change on a by-volume basis. If we could, we’d be better off extracting the CO2and turning it into C and O2. Carbon is far easier to store and the O2could be released to help dilute the CO2remaining in the atmosphere.TotallyTukTukActually while we are still using natural gas for heating, it would be useful to react captured CO2with H2to form methane, which then goes in the gas grid, reducing the amount of fossil gas needed. The energy to capture CO2, make hydrogen by electrolysis of water and run the combining reactions can be wholly renewable.canyoudosoErr, but thermodynamics 101 says that the electricity you use to recreate the methane is equal or greater than the heat you gained by burning the natural gas. Electrolysis in particular is very wasteful of energy. Thermodynamics 102 says that a heat pump gives you four units of heat for every one of electricity you put in. So you’d bemany timesbetter off leaving the natural gas in the ground and heating your home with a heat pump instead. So the gas created in that way will be prohibitively expensive. Even an electric fan heater would be many times cheaper than synthetic methane.Randomusername222The cost of collecting, transporting and storing CO2for the specific purpose of filling car tyres would probably be astronomical compared to the current simple and cheap compressed air method. When punctured or removed, tyres release the same air back into the atmosphere. Billions of CO2-filled tyres would simply add to pollution levels upon deflation. There would be little or no point in using an esoteric gas in pressurised cylinders, particularly in the hands of unskilled operators on petrol station forecourts, etc.FrankieandDexyNo. The total volume of every car tyre on the planet is so much smaller than the size of the atmosphere that filling them all with 100% carbon dioxide would make no noticeable difference. Even if it did, the carbon would be held only until the tyre punctured or wore out, much quicker than the 100-year time carbon dioxide persistsin the atmosphere.Mark, CambridgeshireProbably not. When you change a tyre, or get a puncture or at the end of the vehicle’s life, the CO2has to go somewhere. Maybe it could be reclaimed/recycled, but I suspect the cost would be prohibitive.Pointy_Haired_BossOn the face of it that’s a great idea, but the logistics of doing it would be huge so for that reason and the maths involved I can’t say if it would work. Meanwhile, planting trees and all the other stuff we’ve started doing helps a lot, with the possible exception of electric cars, whose advocates so miss the point that we need much better public transport, not more expensive little boxes that degrade the environment.Alan WebbThis would make the problem a lot worse. Several others in the comments already addressed with simple calculations that it would not make a significant dent in carbon storage. Next to that, it would cause many more problems. First: CO2leaks out of rubber much faster then nitrogen (air). This means much more of it would need to be compressed and people would need to check their tyre pressure daily or have underinflated tyres, which is bad for fuel efficiency. Compressing air is relatively straightforward but compressing CO2and keeping it in containers is harder, for several reasons: one is that if it is not completely dry, it will form carbonic acid that will corrode many materials at high concentrations. Another is the safety aspect of having an infrastructure with so much high-concentration CO2everywhere. Carbon dioxide is not very toxic at low levels but at above 2% in air, it can become quite an issue, as our blood literally turns acidic.PolyphonicPolyGiven the environmental pollution hazard created by billions of tyres anyway, inflating them with CO2seems like the old “lipstick on a pig” situation.DrspeedyPlanting more trees instead – a natural store of CO2– would be a better option.jupiterblueThere are two things you can decide to do today that will reduce your carbon impact – and they don’t involve lashing out money to, for example, eg upgrade your home. 1) Don’t buy anything from the livestock industry; 2) Don’t buy air tickets. There really is no sustainable future which includes the mass-production livestock industry, and the mass aviation industry is very unlikely to be able to produce enough non-fossil aviation fuel within the timeframe required. So it is up to us to stop giving money to those two industries.rockyrexIt wouldn’t help the environment if you filled your tyres with nitrous oxide, but it would be funny if they burst.EddieChorepostExplore more on these topicsLife and styleNotes and queriesGreenhouse gas emissionsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A job that changed me: Being a theatre usher cracked open my heart to beauty | Music | The Guardian
description: The performances often gave me goose bumps, but I also got to observe the highs and lows of audience behaviour
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The performances often gave me goose bumps, but I also got to observe the highs and lows of audience behaviour
Content: ‘Looking back, that place felt like a cradle’ … Freya Bennett worked as an usher in one of Australia’s busiest performing arts theatres.Composite: Getty Images /  Lauren DavidView image in fullscreen‘Looking back, that place felt like a cradle’ … Freya Bennett worked as an usher in one of Australia’s busiest performing arts theatres.Composite: Getty Images /  Lauren DavidA job that changed meMusicA job that changed me: Being a theatre usher cracked open my heart to beautyThe performances often gave me goose bumps, but I also got to observe the highs and lows of audience behaviourRead more inthis series hereFreya BennettMon 31 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 20.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIwas 24, had just moved into a share house I couldn’t afford, and my job as a nanny was proving less than ideal. I’d graduated from my music degree a few years prior and was floating along, feeling a little lost.A friend had told me to apply to become a front-of-house staff member at Australia’s busiest performing arts centre, Arts Centre Melbourne. It was a rare opportunity, as people rarely quit. To be surrounded by art again sounded like a dream.I progressed to the final interview round. Anxious about nailing it and unable to study for it – for some unknown reason, a maths quiz was involved – I focused purely on appearance. I blew my budget on a blow wave, planning to charm the interviewers with my perfect hair and Target office-casual best.Whether it was my hair or the secret texts to my friend asking for help answering the maths quiz, I got the job.A job that changed me: I worked for an infamous clothing brand – but it was one of the most positive workplaces of my lifeRead moreMy first shift was inside door 1 of the centre’s State Theatre. It was the easiest place to avoid royally stuffing things up, and I could be kept under close supervision. I watched Madama Butterfly from my little fold-down seat, goose bumps exploding all over my body. I had never had any interest in opera and, apart from being an unwilling audience to my grandfather’s car DJ set – which consisted entirely of opera – I had rarely listened to it. But watching these incredible performers in a historic theatre, I felt like a wide-eyed kid discovering music for the first time.From there I ricocheted around theatres, learning the labyrinth under the complex’s famous spire. I saw Summer of the Seventeenth Doll no fewer than 17 times; I savoured spine-tingling performances by the Melbourne Symphony Orchestra. When my box seat patrons didn’t show up, I cried alone in my section during the Australian Ballet’s production of Arvo Pärt’s Spiegel im Spiegel.Boyband Human Nature got audience members, of all ages, dancing out of their seats – to this day, their show is one of the best performances I’ve seen.View image in fullscreen‘I felt like a wide-eyed kid discovering music for the first time’ … State Theatre at Arts Centre Melbourne.Photograph: Ellen Smith/The GuardianI also saw the highs and lows of patron behaviour. I thought of the audience as my precious babies, albeit ones I could watch from a distance with love and fascination. I saw a little girl’s first ballet concert; a grown man who, when I said he couldn’t take his ice-cream in, angrily threw his unwrapped Magnum in the bin; a woman, breathless after a coughing fit, graciously accepting that she couldn’t return to the show she’d been so looking forward to because of the door policy. People came as they were – joyful, messy, broken, hopeful, and I relished the hours of people-watching.A few years into the job, I was stationed outside the door of an over-the-top musical when I met a fellow usher who would become my best friend. Within minutes of meeting Stef, we were dancing all over the empty foyer, recreating our version of Chess.We bonded over our feminism and anxiety, and she later became one of my bridesmaids. My kids now call her Aunty Steffy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI’ve never felt safer in a workplace, despite the dark corridors and hidden spaces.Many colleagues were also queer artists who took their ushering jobs seriously, while also having fun on the job. Looking back, having lived and experienced life and now nearing 40, that place felt like a cradle. Being an usher cracked open my heart to the beauty of humans experiencing art and I had the privilege of watching along with them.Explore more on these topicsMusicA job that changed meAustralian lifestyleAustralian theatrefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Why are prisons overcrowded? Because no government will stand up to the tabloids | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: Whatever happens to the early release scheme, Andy Burnham needs to consider the possibility that sentences are just too high, writes Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: Whatever happens to the early release scheme, Andy Burnham needs to consider the possibility that sentences are just too high, writes Zoe Williams
Content: Old Victorian prisons are disintegrating … HMP Wandsworth in London.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOld Victorian prisons are disintegrating … HMP Wandsworth in London.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesOpinionPrisons and probationWhy are prisons overcrowded? Because no government will stand up to the tabloidsZoe WilliamsWhatever happens to the early release scheme, Andy Burnham needs to consider the possibility that sentences are just too highMon 31 Aug 2026 11.58 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrisons in England and Wales are full because sentences have increased, and everybody knows this. Lord chief justices know this – four of them said it outright in areport for the Howard League two years ago– ministers know it, and anyone who can count knows it. The prison population in England and Wales was 40,000 in 1991, 88,000 in 2024 and is estimated to hit 105,000 by 2028. Every government promises to increase capacity; no government this century has been able to do that fast enough to cope with the numbers.One prisons inspector, lamenting conditions that were creating unacceptably high levels of violence,said: “The bath was in danger of overflowing, and they either had to turn the taps off or they had to let some water out.” But the taps have not been turned off, the bigger baths (new, often private jails) have been offset by existing baths (old Victorian prisons) disintegrating, and as soon as a government found the energy and maturity to let some water out – in the form of the early release scheme – it immediately hit the wall of tabloid outrage that created this problem in the first place.The fact is thatAndy Burnhamcan press ahead with the early release scheme; he can create problematic caveats; he can overturn indeterminate sentencing, the measure created in 2003 whereby prisoners could spend years over their tariff in prison because the onus was now on them to prove they weren’t dangerous (which is quite difficult to do from prison, and more difficult still from a failing one). Or he can not do any of these things. But he won’t get a grip on the problem until he allows the possibility that sentences are too high for stupid reasons. The act of murder hasn’t changed in 100 years (or 1,000). There is nothing to stop a prime minister bringing sentences back down to where they were in the 90s.“Tough on crime” is a very easy win, politically speaking: it makes you sound like a firm leader, without having an impact on any ordinary person’s life, except in a good way, and you can modify to it to the right (by being tougher still on crime) and to the left (by also being tough on the causes of crime). This puts you at the mercy, however, of people for whom there is no tough enough. There will always be a murder so heinous that the maximum existing imprisonment doesn’t feel like enough; there will always be a comparison ready that ifxviolent act warranted four years behind bars, how canymerit only three and a half? There will always be people who blankly do not see the point of parole, believing it to be somehow an insult to the expectations of victims, because they have never engaged with its purpose. When you can’t decide when or what to eat and how often to shower, the principle that you will be released sooner if you cooperate is an important buffer between you and the abyss, without which prison populations are hard to manage. You really have to be yelling “Life should mean life” at the top of your voice not to understand this but, regrettably, some people always will be.The purpose of prison itself has always been threefold – punishment, public protection and rehabilitation – which is completely understood except by those who choose not to understand it. Those aims can all be met only if they are complementary. If prisons can’t rehabilitate because they are overcrowded and violent, the public will not be protected when prisoners are released. If the deprivation of freedom is not seen as punishment enough, if only cruel conditions count, then the chances of returning prisoners to society as better-adjusted, more stable people are reduced to nil. Those who argue for a more humane approach in prisons are always painted as living in a fantasy land, while the direct opposite is the case: people who want ever-lengthening sentences in the harshest possible conditions are the fantasists, since they leave us all with only two options, both of them absurd – return prisoners to society as dangerous as before, or keep them inside for ever.Burnham knows all this; Keir Starmer knew it; evenLiz Truss, as justice minister in 2017, sabre-rattling that early release wasn’t the answer, knew it. Tony Blair and David Blunkett knew it in 2003, when they introduced statutory starting points for murder – never again would a lenient judge give them a comms headache on a slow news day. Successive governments have tried to make law to satisfy the tabloids, but they are never satiated, only emboldened.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
