title: Saka settles gruelling battle with Aston Villa to extend Arsenal’s winning start | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Bukayo Saka scored the only goal of the game as Arsenal held off a much improved Aston Villa to make it two wins from two in the Premier League
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: Bukayo Saka scored the only goal of the game as Arsenal held off a much improved Aston Villa to make it two wins from two in the Premier League
Content: Bukayo Saka wheels away, accompanied by Ben White and Kai Havertz, after scoring the only goal of the game.Photograph: David Klein/ReutersView image in fullscreenBukayo Saka wheels away, accompanied by Ben White and Kai Havertz, after scoring the only goal of the game.Photograph: David Klein/ReutersPremier LeagueSaka settles gruelling battle with Aston Villa to extend Arsenal’s winning startBen Fisherat Villa ParkMon 31 Aug 2026 17.08 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe smile on Declan Rice’s face with six minutes of normal time remaining said it all. He had just shut down Ian Maatsen as theAston Villafull-back zoomed into the box. Arsenal, for whom Bukayo Saka scored the only goal, were authoritative and seemingly took great satisfaction in keeping Villa at arm’s length.Unai Emery’s work‑in‑progress side struggled to test the champions, David Raya untroubled. The records will show Villa have lost their first two league matches of a season without scoring for the first time since 2002 but, despite successive defeats, this time there was no capitulation.Emery’s new team begin to emerge as Aston Villa rebuild on and off the pitch | Jonathan WilsonRead moreFor Villa, this was a marked improvement on defeat at Brighton in their opener. After 31 minutes in their previous game, they trailed 4-0 and after 40 were down to 10 men.Here they could take plenty of encouragement from a promising if not fruitless performance, the debutants Zion Suzuki and Nicolas Jackson impressing, having taken the No 1 and No 11 shirts vacated by Emiliano Martínez and Ollie Watkins respectively. Suzuki and Jackson were the only changes to Villa’s starting XI but they appeared far more cohesive. Suzuki’s eye for a pass was particularly noticeable, pinging 50-yard passes to George Hemmings, the 19-year-old who kept his place, and John McGinn within a few minutes of each other.Emi Buendía smacked the crossbar after Boubacar Kamara overawed Christos Tzolis – Martin Ødegaard subsequently asked questions of the referee, Jarred Gillett – but Jackson otherwise created Villa’s best opening. The Senegal forward, who worked under Emery at Villarreal, pinched possession from Gabriel Magalhães a few yards into the Villa half and galloped into the other before sending a near-perfect cross in from the right. Hemmings burst into the six-yard box but was unable to convert. Villa are just the second team to fail to register a shot on target in their first twoPremier Leaguematches in a season since 2003-04, along with Swansea City in 2017-18.This fixture last season ended in despair forArsenal, their players splayed across the turf after Buendía’s 95th-minute winner with the last kick of the game. Arteta said that defeat still haunts him and reminded his players as much before this game. “That was still in my tummy and I spoke to my players about it, the image of the players on the floor, totally gutted,” the Arsenal manager said. “We used that [as inspiration].”View image in fullscreenZion Suzuki, Aston Villa’s new goalkeeper, applauds the home fans after the final whistle.Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesIn that game last season Eberechi Eze was at fault for Matty Cash’s opener and was subsequently hooked at half-time. Here it was a case of role‑reversal, Eze shining after coming on for the second half in place of Christos Tzolis, who was booked after a foul on Cash and muted.“I think he learnt a lesson,” Arteta said of Eze, who was involved in Arsenal seizing the lead approaching the hour. Arsenal slowed things down and then punished Villa for switching off. Cristhian Mosquera pushed a pass to Eze, who was afforded space by Cash, Villa’s defender concerned about an unmarked Riccardo Calafiori. Eze promptly spied Calafiori’s underlapping run and the Italian steered the ball across the six-yard box where Saka beat Maatsen to the punch and scrambled the cross into the net.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis is a new-look Villa, on and off the pitch. A handful of staff in hard hats were positioned in the closed North Stand moonlighting as ball boys; the corner of rubble between the remaining skeleton and the Trinity Road Stand remains akin to an excavation site. Ibrahim Mbaye, whose £47m move from Paris Saint‑Germain is to be announced on Tuesday, was in the directors’ box. Taylor Harwood-Bellis is also poised to sign in a £25m deal from Southampton. Six of Villa’s starting XI from their Europa League triumph may have departed but Emery has made no complaints and has relayed his no-excuses mantra to his squad. “We do not look backwards,” he said.Villa’s frustrations were palpable. McGinn, in a hurry to get Villa level, was booked for wiping out Merino. Aaron Wan-Bissaka replaced Cash for his Villa debut and his first job was to stretch his legs to muffle an advancing Eze. Alejandro Garnacho entered in place of Ross Barkley. Arteta introduced Ezri Konsa for his debut, adding further steel.Villa could not find a way through and Arsenal’s winning habit already appears ominous. “It is painful to lose,” Emery said. “But we can feel optimistic with how we competed.”Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueAston VillaArsenalmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Pain-free’ Alcaraz brushes aside qualifier in US Open return after four months out | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: Carlos Alcaraz beat Roman Safiullin 6-4, 6-4, 6-4 in the first round of the US Open in his first match since April
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Carlos Alcaraz beat Roman Safiullin 6-4, 6-4, 6-4 in the first round of the US Open in his first match since April
Content: Spain's Carlos Alcaraz wore tape under a sleeve on his right arm to protect his wrist.Photograph: Kena Betancur/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSpain's Carlos Alcaraz wore tape under a sleeve on his right arm to protect his wrist.Photograph: Kena Betancur/AFP/Getty ImagesUS Open Tennis 2026‘Pain-free’ Alcaraz brushes aside qualifier in US Open return after four months outSpaniard beats Roman Safiullin 6-4, 6-4, 6-4Alcaraz has not played since April with wrist injuryTumaini Carayolat Flushing MeadowsMon 31 Aug 2026 18.35 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAsCarlos Alcarazedged closer to the conclusion of his first singles set in more than four and a half months, like so many times in his career instinct took over. Up 5-4, 30-15 in set one, Alcaraz swept forward to the net behind a precise wide serve and, when his opponent Roman Safiullin responded with a dipping backhand return directly to his feet, Alcaraz delicately pushed a half-volley over the net for a winner.It was a gorgeous shot, a perfect example of the creativity and feel trademarked by Alcaraz that has been missed throughout his extended injury layoff. That touch of genius was followed, predictably, by a wide smile, a quick hold and a comprehensive victory as the Spaniard returned to competition with a stellar 6-4, 6-4, 6-4 win against Safiullin.Aryna Sabalenka begins US Open title defence with victory against Camila OsorioRead moreWith Alcaraz marking his return to competition at a grand slam tournament with no warmup or match preparation, there was a lot of uncertainty about his level and how his wrist might react to ramping up so dramatically to the best-of-five-sets format. The enormous ball striking of Safiullin, meanwhile, also made this a particularly curious first-round match as it was tough to say how exactly Alcaraz’s wrist would hold up while absorbing such pace.All things considered, this was an incredibly positive start. From the beginning, Alcaraz shook off his own lingering doubts and lack of certainty about the wrist by eviscerating his own forehand, the best in the world, throughout the match. He struck it brilliantly from the outset, dominating from the baseline as he fired down 20 forehand winners to just nine forehand unforced errors. The few times he trailed in service games, he hit himself out of trouble.“It’s pain-free right now,” Alcaraz said of his wrist. “I felt great. I don’t know how it looked from outside but, from inside, my feeling was that I was hitting normal. I was playing pretty normal, playing my style, and the arm, the wrist, everything felt great. I’m going to still take care of it, obviously, these days and before the matches and everything, but I’m just really happy it’s pain-free finally.”The one curiosity, though, is Alcaraz’s serve. As was the case in the mixed doubles, where Serena Williams even served first in their second match, Alcaraz kept his speeds low, averaging just 113mph behind his first serve. Alcaraz has worn tape under an arm sleeve in all of his matches and practices, and it is logical that he should treat the wrist cautiously by not trying to serve as hard as possible so soon into his comeback. However, not being able to win many free points will have a bearing on how far he can go here.For now, Alcaraz has no choice but to take things day by day and see how things unfold with so much uncertainty ahead. On his first day back – as his parents, brothers, his team and even the rapper Travis Scott watched on from his box – things could have hardly gone any better. “It was a difficult day for me, to be honest, but at the same time, a really beautiful one,” Alcaraz said.“[I] started the day really nervous. Really, really nervous, thinking: ‘I’m going to make it, I’m going to compete again.’ I had more nerves than usual, but just happy, because for me, my goal here is to compete, to enjoy, and let’s see how my body’s going to react after the matches, after the competition again.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I don’t know how far I’m going to go in the tournament. I didn’t know if I was going to lose this one, if I’m going to make the second round, final. I don’t know how far I’m going to go. But what I just really want to do is enjoy every time that I’m going to walk into the court feeling the energy from the people, feel the competition, walking up, I’m thinking, all right, it’s match day. That’s what I’m going to do this tournament.”Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026Carlos AlcarazUS Open tennisTennisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Aryna Sabalenka begins US Open title defence with victory against Camila Osorio | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: Aryna Sabalenka said she is determined to look ahead after beginning her US Open women’s singles title defence with a 6-2, 6-4 win against Camila Osorio
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Aryna Sabalenka said she is determined to look ahead after beginning her US Open women’s singles title defence with a 6-2, 6-4 win against Camila Osorio
Content: Aryna Sabalenka: ‘If I win the tournament or lose the tournament, today is a new day, and I have to stay in the moment.’Photograph: Sarah Yenesel/EPAView image in fullscreenAryna Sabalenka: ‘If I win the tournament or lose the tournament, today is a new day, and I have to stay in the moment.’Photograph: Sarah Yenesel/EPAUS Open Tennis 2026Aryna Sabalenka begins US Open title defence with victory against Camila OsorioReigning women’s singles champion wins 6-2, 6-4Men’s 10th seed Arthur Fils beaten by Stefanos TsitsipasTumaini Carayolat Flushing MeadowsMon 31 Aug 2026 15.36 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAryna Sabalenka said she is determined to look ahead, rather than dwell on a difficult past few months, after beginning her US Open title defence with a 6-2, 6-4 victory against Camila Osorio.“The good thing for me is not looking back no matter what, if it’s good or bad, because I feel a good result can also stop you from performing well because you’re basically focusing on the past,” Sabalenka said. “I never look back. If I win the tournament or lose the tournament, today is a new day, and I have to stay in the moment.”Venus Williams bows out after 2am following latest start in US Open historyRead moreSabalenka’s No 1 ranking is at risk after failing to reach a final for four months, with Elena Rybakina having a strong chance of taking top spot. Sabalenka produced a professional opening performance, serving well and overpowering Osorio from the baseline. She eased through the first set, and quickly rolled through the concluding three games of the second to close out the match.“I had opportunities, I tried to step in,” Sabalenka said. “She played great. She brought the fight and she battled really well, and I just tried to stay as aggressive as possible.”The Cincinnati Open champion Arthur Fils, meanwhile, endured the biggest upset of the second day at Flushing Meadows: he was defeated 4-6, 7-6 (3), 6-1, 6-4 by the former world No 3 Stefanos Tsitsipas. Fils, the 10th seed, arrived in New York considered one of the title contenders in an open men’s draw, but after leading 6-4, 5-2 the Frenchman balked while attempting to serve for the second set.Once he allowed Tsitsipas back into the match, the Greek served and struck his forehand brilliantly until the end, while Fils failed to regain the intensity and quality with which he began the match.“Once the energy went down at the end of the second, I never felt again a good energy,” Fils said. “I have to talk with my team, but at my level to do such a mistake is almost unprofessional.”It is an enormous result for Tsitsipas, twice a grand slam singles finalist, who fell as low as No 88 in the ATP rankings this year and now sits at No 53.The 28‑year‑old recently chose to split from his father, who had coached him on‑and-off since his childhood. Their relationship had become increasingly tense this year, leading Tsitsipas to declare that he does not intend to work with him again. This result is a significant step forward as he tries to re-establish himself.A positive run of first‑round results for British players early in the tournament continued on Monday as Harriet Dart followed up her strong performances in the qualifying draw by recovering from a set down to defeat the world No 55 Peyton Stearns, 3-6, 6-3, 6-2.She was followed into the second round by Jacob Fearnley, a lucky loser, who trailed by two sets to one before outlasting the world No 65 Martin Landaluce 4-6, 6-2, 4-6, 7-5, 6-3. Fearnley had fallen in the final round of qualifying in three tight sets before a flurry of late withdrawals allowed him to enter the tournament as a lucky loser.As with Toby Samuel, another qualifier, after his first‑round win on Sunday, Fearnley’s victory moves him back into the top 100 of the live rankings, meaning there will likely be five British men inside the ATP top 100 after the tournament: Arthur Fery, Cameron Norrie, Jan Choinski, Samuel and Fearnley.Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026Aryna SabalenkaUS Open tennisTennisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Argentina’s Lionel Messi retires from international football: ‘This hurts me a lot’ | Lionel Messi | The Guardian
description: Lionel Messi has confirmed he is retiring from international football with immediate effect, seven weeks after Argentina were beaten by Spain in the World Cup final
Author: Billy Munday
Headline: Lionel Messi has confirmed he is retiring from international football with immediate effect, seven weeks after Argentina were beaten by Spain in the World Cup final
Content: Lionel Messi after Argentina’s defeat against Spain in the World Cup final.Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLionel Messi after Argentina’s defeat against Spain in the World Cup final.Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesLionel MessiArgentina’s Lionel Messi retires from international football: ‘This hurts me a lot’Argentina great’s last game was in World Cup finalPlayer’s father Jorge died earlier in AugustBilly MundayMon 31 Aug 2026 11.19 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLionel Messi has announced his retirement from international football seven weeks after Argentinawere beaten by Spain in the World Cup finalin the US. The 39-year-oldcaptained Argentina to World Cup glory in 2022and two Copa América titles after winning his first cap in 2005.On Monday, Messi posted a picture on Instagram of notes that he wrote on 21 July, two days after the World Cup final, confirming he was ending his Argentina career and saidthe death of his father, Jorge, in early Augustmade him feel “more convinced than before”. Messi was often visibly emotional during the tournament and revealed in the knockout stages that Jorge was undergoing medical treatment.Messi’s statement, addressed toArgentinafans, read: “After the time that has passed since the final, thinking a lot, I want to let everyone know that I am retiring from the national team. It is a decision that hurts my soul but I know it is time. I can say for sure that I always gave everything, not only in the last few years when we won everything [but] before as well, and I always fought and gave everything for the shirt, to give you joy and make you proud of being Argentinian through football.“There’s not long left and chapters are coming to an end – and this is one that hurts me a lot. I love, have loved and I will always love being part of the national team. I have emptied myself: now I have nothing more to give and, besides, there are great young players coming through who deserve to be [selected].”Messi thanked his family for accompanying him on a “beautiful but difficult journey”. He previously announced his retirement from international football in 2016 after Argentinalost on penalties to Chile in the 2016 Copa América final– at the time his fourth defeat in a major final out of four. The then Barcelona forward was often criticised for not producing his club form at international level and comparisons were constantly made with the World Cup-winning Diego Maradona. However, Messi was persuaded to continue and finally lifted silverware with his countryat the 2021 Copa América in Brazil.“I take with me unforgettable memories and moments,” his statement said. After victory against Brazil at the Maracanã in the 2021 Copa América final, Messi was central to Argentina’s first World Cup triumph since 1986 and scored in every knockout round in Qatar, including twice in the final against France –two years after the death of Maradona.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Argentinadefended their Copa América title in 2024amid speculation that Messi, by then playing for Inter Miami, would call it a day. He turned 39 during the World Cup this summer, briefly becoming the tournament’s all-time record scorer before being overtaken by Kylian Mbappé.His statement finished by returning to address Argentina fans: “I go with the satisfaction and the pride of having, along with my teammates, giving you moments we dreamed about. I love you! I thank God for making me Argentinian.”Messi retires as Argentina’s record appearance maker – he won the first of his 207 caps in a friendly against Hungary in August 2005 and was sent off almost immediately for catching Vilmos Vanczak with an elbow. He is also Argentina’s record scorer with 125 goals. Before playing for the senior team, he won the Under-20 World Cup and also won Olympic gold in 2008.Since the end of his sixth World Cup, Messi has featured seven times for Inter Miami andscored four goals in the 7-1 rout of Montrealin Major League Soccer on Saturday. Messi signed a contract extension last year to 2028, when he will be 41.Ángel Di María, who scored for Argentina in the 2021 Copa América and 2022 World Cup finals, led tributes from Messi’s former teammates, writing: “All I know is that I was born in the right century to be able to see you, enjoy you and, above all, share with you all these years [together] with the national team.” The midfielder Rodrigo de Paul posted: “Thank you for making us so happy. You can’t imagine how many times you made people smile. You are eternal.”As a teenager, Enzo Fernández wrote to Messi to plead with him to reverse his 2016 decision to retire from Argentina duty, trying to work out if he would be old enough to play alongside him one day. “That kid was so lucky … Thank you for letting me share a part of your story,” Fernández said. “We’re going to miss you so much,capitán,” said the striker Lautaro Martínez.Explore more on these topicsLionel MessiArgentinanewsShareReuse this content

title: Manchester City gazump Spurs over Iliman Ndiaye and eye Enzo Fernández deal | Transfer window | The Guardian
description: Manchester City are poised to bolster their attack by buying Everton’s Iliman Ndiaye for up to £65m and have opened talks with Chelsea over a deal to sign Enzo Fernández
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: Manchester City are poised to bolster their attack by buying Everton’s Iliman Ndiaye for up to £65m and have opened talks with Chelsea over a deal to sign Enzo Fernández
Content: Iliman Ndiaye will have a medical at Manchester City with a £65m deal having been agreed with his club, Everton.Photograph: Robbie Hoad/Every Second Media/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenIliman Ndiaye will have a medical at Manchester City with a £65m deal having been agreed with his club, Everton.Photograph: Robbie Hoad/Every Second Media/ShutterstockTransfer windowManchester City gazump Spurs over Iliman Ndiaye and eye Enzo Fernández dealCity agree £65m deal with Everton for Senegal wingerRicharlison to stay at Spurs, who agree Mudryk loanJacob SteinbergandJamie JacksonMon 31 Aug 2026 15.32 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester City are poised to bolster their attack by buying Everton’s Iliman Ndiaye for up to £65m and have opened talks with Chelsea over a deal to sign Enzo Fernández.City’s hijack of Tottenham’s deal for Ndiaye came after their attempts to sign Liverpool’s Cody Gakpo broke down. The Senegal international is poised to undergo a medical after a fee of £60m plus £5m in add-ons was agreed withEverton, who have little time to find a replacement for one of their most important players before the transfer window shuts on Tuesday night.Chelsea’s perfect yet unserious start to the Premier League season | Jonathan WilsonRead moreIt had seemed that Ndiaye would move to Spurs after they agreed a deal in principle with Everton on Sunday. Richarlison was poised to move in the opposite direction but that transfer stalled on Monday. Richarlison released an emotional statement on social media and said that he would not allow his future to be decided for him. The Brazilian is cool on a move to Everton and is expected to stay at Spurs.City registered their interest in Ndiaye last week and moved in after Liverpool pulled out of an £85m deal for Gakpo. Spurs have moved on and agreed to sign Mykhailo Mudryk on loan fromChelsea.The Ukraine winger, who is free to play again after his doping ban was resolved this summer, played for Roberto De Zerbi at Shakhtar Donetsk and favoured a reunion with the Tottenham manager after Leeds and Brentford also contacted Chelsea about him.Spurs have also agreed a deal to sign Chelsea’s defender Tosin Adarabioyo on a permanent deal.Chelsea are poised for a busy end to the window and have finally been contacted by City about Fernández. The Argentina midfielder wants to leave and has his heart set on a move to City. Fernández has a close relationship with City’s manager, Enzo Maresca, who left Chelsea this year.Chelseaset a price of £120m for Fernández this summerand may push for a higher fee with the deadline drawing close. Another consideration for the Stamford Bridge club as they face up to losing one of their biggest players is the need to improve their squad.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChelsea have sounded out Roma’s Manu Koné and Monaco’s Lamine Camara as potential replacements for Fernández. They have been met with resistance in attempts to sign Bournemouth’s Alex Scott while Crystal Palace want to keep Adam Wharton. Chelsea are tracking Morgan Gibbs‑White but know Nottingham Forest are unlikely to sell at this stage.The goalkeeper Robert Sánchez is poised to leave Chelsea as he nears a loan to Como. Sánchez lost the No 1 spot after Emiliano Martínez’s arrival.Explore more on these topicsTransfer windowManchester CityEvertonChelseaTottenham HotspurnewsShareReuse this content

title: Pakistan sack head coach and send seven players home after England Test series defeat | Pakistan cricket team | The Guardian
description: Sarfaraz Ahmed has been sacked after Pakistan’s heavy defeat at Lord’s, with white-ball coach Mike Hesson stepping in
Author: Ali Martin
Headline: Sarfaraz Ahmed has been sacked after Pakistan’s heavy defeat at Lord’s, with white-ball coach Mike Hesson stepping in
Content: Sarfaraz Ahmed watched his side crumble to a 194-run defeat at Lord’s, which meant England took an unassailable 2-0 lead in the series.Photograph: Saud Ahmed/PPAUK/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSarfaraz Ahmed watched his side crumble to a 194-run defeat at Lord’s, which meant England took an unassailable 2-0 lead in the series.Photograph: Saud Ahmed/PPAUK/ShutterstockPakistan cricket teamPakistan sack head coach and send seven players home after England Test series defeatSarfaraz Ahmed sacked after 194-run loss at Lord’sWhite-ball coach Mike Hesson steps inAli MartinMon 31 Aug 2026 12.37 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 13.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePakistan have decided to rip up their plans during an already chaotic tour of England by announcing that seven players and head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed have been sent home before the third Test at Edgbaston next week.Already confirmed to lose the series after going 2-0 down witha 194-run defeat at Lord’son Sunday, Pakistan have now asked Mike Hesson, the New Zealander who runs their white-ball teams, to replace Sarfaraz as head coach. Umar Gul, their bowling coach, has also been swapped out for the Australian Ashley Noffke.England ‘not going to ease off the gas’ with 3-0 Pakistan series sweep in sightRead moreNo less drastic is the jettisoning of nearly half their squad, including five players who have featured in the series. Of the seven players now being flown over for the series finale in Birmingham that starts on 9 September, five are uncapped, with batters Saim Ayub and Abdullah Fazal the only two with Test experience.Among the discarded players is Salman Ali Agha, who captained the team in the first Test while Babar Azam was injured, only to then be dropped at Lord’s. Opener Imam- ul-Haq, the subject of widespread criticism for not batting in either innings of the second Test due to a low-grade calf strain, has also been sent back to Pakistan.Mohammad Rizwan, their longstanding wicketkeeper, is another to be banished following a string of low scores, likewise spinner Ali Usman, who claimed a five-wicket haul in Leeds, and seamer Khurram Shahzad. Aamir Jamal and Muhammad Awais Zafar, both of whom were still to feature on this tour, will also be joining them on the flight home.Quick GuidePakistan team for third TestShow*Babar Azam (c), Abdullah Fazal*, Abdullah Shafique, Arafat Minhas*, Azan Awais, Mohammad Abbas, Mohammad Ali, Muhammad Imran*, Mohammad Imran Jnr*, Muhammad Ghazi Ghori (wk), Razaullah*, Saad Baig (wk)*, Saim Ayub*, Sajid Khan, Saud Shakeel, Shan Masood, Ubaid Shah*new additions to the squadWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.It continues a messy trip by Pakistan that has seen them fail to pass 200 in any of their four innings with the bat. Their fielding has similarly been abject at times, while 36-year-old Mohammad Abbas, who claimed nine wickets at Lord’s, has practically been a one-man attack in seamer-friendly conditions.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThings have been no better thought through off the field either, with the PakistanCricketBoard lodging a complaint with broadcasters Sky Sports during the second Test after an interview with Imran Khan’s sons – one that highlighted the former Pakistan prime minister’s ongoing health issues in prison – was aired. In doing so, the PCB succeeded in bringing far more attention to the matter.Explore more on these topicsPakistan cricket teamEngland v Pakistan 2026CricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: South African airline defends dramatic low-level flyby before rugby union clash | Rugby union | The Guardian
description: A pre-game stunt involving two passenger jets flying dramatically low over a  stadium in South Africa drew huge cheers from the crowd, but also sparked a major debate over safety risks
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A pre-game stunt involving two passenger jets flying dramatically low over a stadium in South Africa drew huge cheers from the crowd, but also sparked a major debate over safety risks
Content: An aircraft performs a low flyby before the match between South Africa and New Zealand in Cape Town.Photograph: Jamie Rossouw/ReutersView image in fullscreenAn aircraft performs a low flyby before the match between South Africa and New Zealand in Cape Town.Photograph: Jamie Rossouw/ReutersRugby unionSouth African airline defends dramatic low-level flyby before rugby union clashCape Town stunt sparks major debate over safety risksAirlink insists flyby conducted according to regulationsAssociated PressMon 31 Aug 2026 09.44 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA pre-game stunt involving two passenger jets flying dramatically low over a stadium in South Africa drew huge cheers from the estimated crowd of 56,000 people, but also sparked a major debate over safety risks. The flyby by two Embraer jets, operated by the local airline Airlink, happened on Saturday before the second rugby union Testbetween South Africa and New Zealandin Cape Town.The flight tracking service Flightradar24 estimated that the lead jet passed just 41-46 feet (12-14 metres) above the roof of Cape Town Stadium, with the crowd and the world’s top-ranked rugby teams below. The second jet, which was very close behind, flew through a cloud of pink dust that shot up from the stadium roof as part of the show.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueAirlink, a sponsor of theSouth Africarugby union team, said the flyby was conducted according to safety regulations. The airline said that it was carefully planned and rehearsed, with the aircraft flying at 150 knots (172 mph), when they went over the stadium. Each jet had three senior captains on board, Airlink said, operating in the roles of a commander, a co-pilot and a safety officer. The jets were not carrying any passengers.“Airlink notes the concerns expressed in various social media and online forums regarding yesterday’s formation flyby over Cape Town’s DHL Stadium,” Airlink said on Sunday. “The flight demanded careful planning and rehearsal, as it required navigating at low altitude, at around 150 knots. The South African Civil Aviation Authority and Air Traffic Navigation Services provided valuable guidance, approval and support to ensure a safe flyby.”View image in fullscreenThe planes fly above the stadium before kick-off.Photograph: Gallo Images/Getty ImagesSouth African rugby union has a tradition of stadium flybys at big games, starting when a Boeing 747 flew over a stadium in Johannesburg before the 1995 World Cup final between the same teams, who are fierce rivals. But the flyby last weekend was especially low and dramatic, generating global interest after it was shown as part of the pre-game broadcast, and sparking a flurry of videos shot by witnesses.View image in fullscreenThe second jet flies through a cloud of pink dust that shot up from the stadium roof as part of the show.Photograph: APSome aviation experts questioned whether the margin for error was too small. “Basically, that lead aircraft … was kind of like dodging over the roof and climbing over the one side and dipping below and then climbing over the other side. That was a little bit uncomfortable,” Chris Martinus, president of Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association South Africa, said. “[If] something adverse happens, you just don’t have options at that kind of altitude.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKeith Tonkin, an Australian aviation consultant and former military and commercial pilot, said yesteron Monday that the Embraer passenger jets – which are small-to-medium jets designed for regional flights – were not designed or intended for that kind of low-level operation and warned against the precedent.“The bigger picture is that a benchmark has been established and others may expect to do something similar, and that’s not going to end well,” Tonkin said. He added that turbulence or a bird strike at such a low altitude could leave the pilots with too little room to manoeuvre without hitting the stadium.Airlink said flight data recorded by both aircraft confirmed their flights were performed within civil aviation safety limits for speed and altitude.Explore more on these topicsRugby unionSouth AfricaSouth Africa rugby teamNew Zealand rugby union teamAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Harry Edward, Britain’s first black Olympic medallist, inducted into England Athletics hall of fame | Athletics | The Guardian
description: Harry Edward, who won two bronze medals at the 1920 Olympics, will be honoured along with Mo Farah, Sonia Lannaman and Shirley Strong
Author: Neil Duncanson
Headline: Harry Edward, who won two bronze medals at the 1920 Olympics, will be honoured along with Mo Farah, Sonia Lannaman and Shirley Strong
Content: Harry Edward competes in the 1922 AAA Championships – he won the 100, 220 and 440yd titles within a single hour.Photograph: Courtesy of University of Westminster ArchiveView image in fullscreenHarry Edward competes in the 1922 AAA Championships – he won the 100, 220 and 440yd titles within a single hour.Photograph: Courtesy of University of Westminster ArchiveAthleticsHarry Edward, Britain’s first black Olympic medallist, inducted into England Athletics hall of fameEdward and Mo Farah among those to be inductedSonia Lannaman and Shirley Strong also honouredNeil DuncansonMon 31 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain’s first black Olympic medal winner Harry Edward is to be inducted into the EnglandAthleticsHall of Fame. Edward will join the likes of Mo Farah, former sprinter Sonia Lannaman and medal-winning hurdler Shirley Strong, who will all be honoured at a ceremony in Birmingham in November. Edward’s citation includes the tribute: “A true citizen of the world and a pioneer of British sport, England Athletics is proud and humbled to induct Britain’s first black Olympic medallist into the Hall of Fame.”The remarkable story of Harry Edward: Britain’s first black OlympianRead moreEdward was until recent years a forgotten hero of the 1920s, a decade that saw him win two bronze edals, in the 100m and 200m, at the 1920 Antwerp Olympics. He was also three times the AAA 100yd and 220yd champion and won the 100, 220 and 440-yard AAA championships in 1922, inside a single hour. King George V came down from the stands to personally congratulate him.Soon afterwards he emigrated to the US and disappeared from view. When he died in 1973 not a single British newspaper published a line to mark his passing.Born and raised in Berlin, he was forging a promising career as a teenage sprinter when the first world war began. His father came from the British colony of Dominica, so Edward was arrested and interned. After the war he went to London, joined the Polytechnic Harriers and ran for Britain in the Olympics. Harold Abrahams, the British sprinter immortalised in Chariots of Fire, regarded him as one of the greatest sprinters he ever saw. He never beat him.After Edward emigrated in 1923, he devoted his life to fighting for civil rights and leading international programmes to help refugees and foster children. He had written an extraordinary autobiography, entitled When I Passed the Statue of Liberty I Became Black, but it failed to find a publisher. It sat unread in a box in a New Orleans archive, among his medals, photographs, scrapbooks and letters, until it was discovered and published in 2024 – making the William Hill Sports Book of the Year shortlist. Next year, English Heritage plan to erect a blue plaque on his old London home near Euston station.View image in fullscreenHarry Edward (right) crosses the finish line winning the 100 yards race at the 1920 AAA Championships at Stamford Bridge.Photograph: Topical Press Agency/Getty ImagesFarah, Britain’s most successful athlete of all time, is among this year’s other Hall of Fame inductees. Birmingham-born Lannaman was Britain’s premier sprinter of the 1970s and a favourite for medals at the Montreal Olympics in 1976 before injury scuppered her chances. She went on to win 100m gold at the 1978 Commonwealth Games and 4x100m relay bronze at the 1980 Olympics. Strong won silver in the 100m hurdles at the 1984 Olympics, having won Commonwealth gold in 1982.The three other three inductees are triple Paralympic gold medal winner Stephen Miller, who also co-founded the SMILE Through Sport organisation to encourage disabled people to participate in sport, the coach Mike Holmes, who guided Katarina Johnson-Thompson’s early career, and the photographer Mark Shearman, a fixture at major athletics events for more than six decades.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTickets are availablefor the England Athletics Hall of Fame dinner and awards presentationat the Hilton Metropole Hotel, Birmingham, on Saturday 21 November. title: Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 11: Manchester City | Manchester City Women | The Guardian
description: Beth Mead and Niamh Charles are notable additions to the champions’ squad that looks just as strong as last season
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Beth Mead and Niamh Charles are notable additions to the champions’ squad that looks just as strong as last season
Content: Manchester City are jubilant after clinching the 2025-25 Women’s Super League crown with a 4-1 victory against West Ham Women in May. Photograph: Naomi Baker/WSL Football/GettyBeth Mead and Niamh Charles are notable additions to the champions’ squad that looks just as strong as last seasonByTom GarryMon 31 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 19.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuardian writers’ predicted position:1st (NB: this is not necessarily Tom Garry’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)Last season’s position:1stProspectsChampions again at last, after a 10-year wait, Manchester City now face an even tougher task: defending their title. They appear to have a good chance of succeeding, especially after keeping their star striker, Khadija “Bunny” Shaw. The WSL’s top scorer andbest player of 2025-26performed a dramatic U-turnby signing a new four-year contractin May rather than leaving on a free transfer, and that may prove crucial in continuing City’s positive momentum.Their squad looks to be of a similar strength to last season. The Brazil forward Kerolinleft for Barcelonabut Beth Mead arriving from Arsenal in essence replaces her. Similarly, the exit of left-back Leila Ouahabi will be compensated for by the acquisition of Niamh Charles from Chelsea. Perhaps the only minor question is whether there is sufficient depth to sustain a challenge in the Women’s Champions League as well as domestically, but the core of regulars looks as formidable as any club in Europe.The team scored plenty last term and had great success down the flanks, with the right-back Kerstin Casparij providing the joint-most assists in the division. Defensively they look solid. The most intriguing challenge could be psychological, as they switch from hunters to hunted, becoming the team that everybody wants to beat. They start at home to one of the promoted sides, Birmingham City, and first meet a fellow title hopeful – Arsenal – at the start of October, when they will aim to lay down a marker in the title race.Graphic showing how City finished in the past five seasonsOff-field pictureOwned by City Football Group and led off the pitch by the managing director, Charlotte O’Neill, and director of football, Therese Sjögren, City enter the season with anew women’s team buildingat the training centre. The £10m building offers everything from underwater treadmills to a barista-style coffee machine in the canteen, with every element tailored towards maximising performance for female athletes. Previously the women’s team sometimes had to share a gym with City’s boys’ academy.The managerAndrée Jeglertz’s first season could scarcely have gone better, as he oversaw a league and cup double. He arrived in Manchester after a relatively uninspiring spell in charge of Denmark women but his CV is full of extensive high-level experience, including a 2004 European title with the Swedish club Umeå. The 54-year-old is a calm presence on the touchline, unwavering in his belief that his team will “find a way to win”, and has avoided controversy in press conferences, which he handles assuredly.Star signingView image in fullscreenBeth Mead joins the champions from rivals Arsenal.Photograph: Kate Green/WSL/WSL Football/Getty ImagesMead was the headline signing on a free transfer after nine years at Arsenal. City are hoping that the England forward – the Golden Boot winner and player of the tournament at the 2022 European Championship – is not past her best, at 31, and can flourish across a three-year contract. She is the all-time leading assist provider in the WSL. Mead also has 81 caps and will want to be part of any Lionesses squad at next summer’s World Cup.Stat attackIf teams want to defend more effectively against the champions, they could start by focusing on free-kicks and corners. City scored at least twice as many set-piece goals as anyone else in 2025-26. As strong as they were elsewhere, this was their superpower.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGraphic showing Manchester City led the Women’s Super League for set piece goalsSet for a breakthroughThe 18-year-old full-back Sacha Lewis signed her first professional contract with City in August, having been with the club since under-14 level. The younger sister of the club’s men’s first-team full-back Rico Lewis, she has been a regular for England Under-19s and has been named in the England Under-20 squad that will go to Poland for September’s Women’s Under-20 World Cup. She was the player of the season for Manchester City’s “Next Gen” team last term and, with City juggling European and domestic football, may get a chance in the first team.What they say“Our biggest challenge this year is to continue winning and, at the same, compete in other competitions and also want to win those. Winning in one year is one thing, but being able to win in the next year, that is even tougher. Of course we can do that [compete on multiple fronts] and we have good enough players to be able to play with one starting XI on Saturday and do a couple of changes on Wednesday and still win. That was our biggest challenge last year – we had too many good players that were not playing enough games, so this year we will have the possibility to explore the whole squad. Each player will be more important than they’ve ever been for the club” – Jeglertz speaking to BBC Radio 5 Live.Where are they playing their home games?The Joie Stadium is the women’s team’s usual home, across the road from the Etihad Stadium, where they will play two home league fixtures. Those will be against Arsenal on 4 October and against Manchester United on 14 February. The 7,000-capacity Joie Stadium, that hosted matches at Euro 2022, has been the women’s team’s home for more than a decade and they were unbeaten at home in the league last season. They haven’t lost a home WSL game at the Joie Stadiumsince a4-3 thriller against Arsenalin February 2025.On Friday 4 September at 1pm, Suzanne Wrack will be answering readers’ questions about the new WSL season for GuardianConversationsExplore more on these topicsWSL season previews 2026-27Manchester City WomenWomen's footballfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tennessee to wear Dolly Parton tribute on helmets during 2026 college football season | College football | The Guardian
description: The Volunteers will be honoring Dolly Parton with a helmet sticker this season, the college football team’s head coach, Josh Heupel, announced on Monday
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Volunteers will be honoring Dolly Parton with a helmet sticker this season, the college football team’s head coach, Josh Heupel, announced on Monday
Content: Dolly Parton performs before Tennessee’s game against Georgia in 2023.Photograph: Wade Payne/APView image in fullscreenDolly Parton performs before Tennessee’s game against Georgia in 2023.Photograph: Wade Payne/APCollege footballTennessee to wear Dolly Parton tribute on helmets during 2026 college football seasonBeloved singer died last week at the age of 80Parton was born 30 miles from college campusAgenciesMon 31 Aug 2026 16.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Tennessee Volunteers will be honoringDolly Partonwith a helmet sticker this season, the college football team’s head coach, Josh Heupel, announced on Monday.Parton, a Tennessee native,died last weekat the age of 80 from cancer.“I’d be remiss if I didn’t also talk about the passing of Dolly Parton,” Heupel said Monday. “All that she’s meant across the world, this country, and certainly, the queen of EastTennessee– a lady that was extremely proud of her roots.”Dolly Parton obituaryRead moreThe singer grew up in Sevierville, roughly 30 miles east of Knoxville, where the University of Tennessee is located.“You look at [Parton’s] impact, you know, just her ability to give back, make an impact to people, certainly here in East Tennessee. She means a lot to people across this country,” Heupel said. “We’ll be wearing a sticker patch on the back of our helmet to recognize her accomplishments and everything that she’s meant.”Parton often spoke about her upbringing as one of 12 children in what she described as a “dirt poor” family. Inspired by her youth, Parton led several initiatives to give back to her home town, including her nonprofit Imagination Library, which provides children with access to free books.The sticker, in the Volunteers’ signature orange, features a butterfly similar to the one in the logo of Dollywood, Parton’s theme park. The logo also has “Dolly” written at its center.Parton had a close relationship with the university. She twice played on Tennessee’s campus during world tours. In 2023, before a football game, she was walked to the stage at Neyland Stadium by former NFL and Tennessee star Peyton Manning. She then led the crowd in a rendition of Rocky Top, a staple at Volunteers games.Tennessee host Furman in their season-opener on Saturday.Explore more on these topicsCollege footballTennesseeCollege sportsUS sportsDolly PartonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fifa extends ban on man who secretly filmed female footballers in Austria | Women's football | The Guardian
description: Fifa has extended worldwide the ban on a former match official and SCR Altach employee found guilty of taking secret videos and photographs of members of the club’s women’s team
Author: Suzanne Wrack
Headline: Fifa has extended worldwide the ban on a former match official and SCR Altach employee found guilty of taking secret videos and photographs of members of the club’s women’s team
Content: The SCR Altach stadium, pictured in 2022.Photograph: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe SCR Altach stadium, pictured in 2022.Photograph: Getty ImagesWomen's footballFifa extends ban on man who secretly filmed female footballers in AustriaFormer SCR Altach employee now banned worldwideMove follows pressure from players’ unionsSuzanne WrackMon 31 Aug 2026 12.06 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 18.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFifa has extended worldwide the ban on a former match official and SCR Altach employee found guilty oftaking secret videos and photographsof members of the club’s women’s team.In February, a regional court in Feldkirch,Austria, handed the man a seven-month suspended prison sentence, a €1,200 (£1,046) fine and ordered him to pay the victims €625 (£545) each in compensation after he was found guilty of filming and taking photographs of players, including minors, in the changing room, gym and showers of Altach’s women’s team between 2018 and 2025.The sentence provoked outrage from former Altach players and more widely in Austria. After a request from the Austrian players’ union (VdF) and the global players’ union Fifpro, theFifadisciplinary committee extended on 4 August the man’s ban from football-related activities to a global one. A Fifa spokesperson said: “In line with article 70 of the Fifa disciplinary code, the Fifa disciplinary committee has extended the sanction imposed on an official by the Austrian FA to have worldwide effect.”Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.The man did not request a statement of the reasons for the decision within a prescribed timeframe, so the decision has become binding and final. Federations are able to ban individuals from football related activities only in their respective countries.Christos Papadimitriou, the women’s football coordinator at the VdF, said: “Anyone who secretly films players in the locker room crosses a clear line. The fact that the ban now applies worldwide sends an important signal: those who seriously violate players’ rights cannot escape the consequences by moving abroad.”The Czech players’ union, CAFH, hascalled for a lifetime banfrom all football-related activities for Petr Vlachovsky, the former coach of FC Slovacko, who was convicted of similar offences in addition to being in possession of child sexual abuse material. Vlachovsky was convicted in May 2025 and handed a suspended one-year prison sentence and five-year domestic coaching ban.In March Fifpro said: “Because the Czech criminal process and the Czech FA’s administrative proceedings are separate and can run in parallel, the union is challenging the FA to implement a lifetime football ban for Vlachovsky and all sexual offenders. Fifpro is exploring possible legal avenues on behalf of players to achieve a global ban.”Explore more on these topicsWomen's footballFifaAustrianewsShareReuse this content

title: Queensland has passed tough new laws on ebikes and e-scooters. What do they mean for riders, and will the world follow?  | Queensland | The Guardian
description: Transport minister says laws target ‘young hooligans’ holding ‘communities to ransom’, but cycling advocates say changes most affect law-abiding riders
Author: Andrew Messenger
Headline: Transport minister says laws target ‘young hooligans’ holding ‘communities to ransom’, but cycling advocates say changes most affect law-abiding riders
Content: A cyclist riding an ebike in Brisbane. Cycling advocates say the legislation largely targets safe, legal ebike users.Photograph: Darren England/AAPView image in fullscreenA cyclist riding an ebike in Brisbane. Cycling advocates say the legislation largely targets safe, legal ebike users.Photograph: Darren England/AAPQueenslandExplainerQueensland has passed tough new laws on ebikes and e-scooters. What do they mean for riders, and will the world follow?Transport minister says laws target ‘young hooligans’ holding ‘communities to ransom’, but cycling advocates say changes most affect law-abiding ridersFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAndrew MessengerMon 31 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 20.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis week,Queenslandbecame the first Australian state – and one of the first jurisdictions on the planet – to set age limits and licensing requirements for e-vehicle riders.Bicycle Queensland, the advocacy body for cycling in the state, says only a handful of other other jurisdictions around the world have passed similar legislation for ebike or e-scooter riders, such asNew JerseyandIsrael.But how does the new legislation work, and what could other cities, states and countries learn from Queensland’s example?What does the law do?The Transport and Other Legislation (Managing E-mobility Use and Protecting our Communities) Amendment Act 2026 imposes four main new restrictions on ebike and e-scooter riders in Queensland.It bans people under the age of 16 from riding an ebike in public at all, except where supervised by their parents.It also requires a person to get at least a learner’s driving licence to ride, with alimited exemption for disabled people. These two restrictions went into force on Monday.It also imposes a new speed limit of 12km/h near pedestrians and bans e-vehicles that don’t meet a European performance and safety standard, though there is still a grace period on that part of the law.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailIt also gives the police new powers to seize vehicles that were already illegal under prior Queensland law, typically because they were too overpowered or large, which are known as “e-motorbikes”. They can now also fine parents of children breaking the law by riding an ebike and there are new or greater fines for drink riding, speeding and other offences.The larger illegal vehicleshave become controversial, particularly due to media coverage ofhigh-profile gatherings of young peopleriding them.How many people die as a result of ebikes in Queensland?Queensland recorded itsworst road toll in 16 years in 2025, with 306 deaths. There have already been 206 fatalities in 2026, a 7.9% increase on the same time last year, according to Department of Transport and Main Roads data.Queensland ebike laws could cripple Uber Eats, DoorDash and shared e-vehicle schemes, industry warnsRead moreAlmost all of them were people either driving or a passenger in a car, riding a motorbike or killed in a crash involving a heavy freight vehicle.There have been three fatalities involving people using a non-compliant e-mobility device in 2026.There is no specific category covering legal ebikes, but an inquiry into the bill heard that just one person had been killed in a crash involving a legal ebike in Queensland in 2025, a 79-year-old woman who was hit by a car on Bribie Island in July.In March two teenagers died afteran ebike crash with a motorbikesouth of Brisbane, though police could not say at the time whether their ebike was legal.What does the government say?Queensland police say the laws are working.Assistant commissioner Rhys Wildman said there had been “a significant cultural shift in our community” as a result of the legislation, indicated by a visible reduction in the number of people riding an e-vehicle on the state’s bike paths, footpaths and roadway.“They’re using other forms of mobility devices to get around, and they’re doing it safely,” he said on Sunday.0:35Dozens of young ebike riders descend on Sydney golf course in viral rideout – videoQueensland’s minister for transport, Brent Mickelberg, said: “for too long, young hoons and young hooligans have held communities to ransom, and we made a commitment to ensure that we tackled this very challenging issue.”The police minister, Dan Purdie, said the new measures were “the toughest laws in the country”, with about 400 illegal e-devices seized since 1 July – about seven a day.What do advocates and cyclists think?Cycling advocates say the legislation largely targets users of safe, legal ebikes. It permits the continued sale of overpowered vehicles and there is also no buyback scheme.The Bicycle Queensland chief executive, Matt Burke, estimates that the state’s bike stores import and sell about 20 illegal e-motorbikes a day though some retailers are moving to compliance, he said.‘Take them away, crush them’: Australia faces an ebike surge that some say poses a health emergencyRead moreHe said the laws are a barrier to some people switching out of a car into a more sustainable transport model. For instance, they ban children from riding to school, likely forcing their parents to drive them.It may also make ebike riders less safe, he said. The bill’s explanatory notes explain that the new speed limit is expected to force some riders off designated protected cycle lanes into general traffic.Burke said some of the state’s safest riders were being affected by the legislation.“The other people being affected are seniors who who are having to go and get their learner’s permit at the age of 80 plus (after surrendering it due to age).”Is it likely to influence other states?E-mobility iscontroversial across Australiaand many states are consideringhow to crack down.New South Wales is currently developing an age limit similar to Queensland’s,among other changes. There have also been moves in Victoria toroll back council-backed shared ebike schemes.The federal government is also planning to close a loophole created in 2021 by the former Coalition government allowing importation of e-motorbikes.But the head of Asia-Pacific at Lime, Will Peters, said no other Australian jurisdiction was likely to consider licensing, which he said was “ridiculous”.“I think it’s popular, but it’s certainly not the way that we’re seeing governments move at all,” he said.“It’s a very lazy argument to solve a complex problem”.Explore more on these topicsQueenslandEbikesBrisbaneCyclingTransportexplainersShareReuse this content

title: Turkish deep-sea search vessel joins efforts to retrieve 20 still missing after Cyprus ferry disaster | Cyprus | The Guardian
description: TCG Isin expected to play vital role in locating Filo Jet’s voyage data recorder 514 metres below surface
Author: Helena Smith
Headline: TCG Isin expected to play vital role in locating Filo Jet’s voyage data recorder 514 metres below surface
Content: Search and rescue operations continue after the Filo Jet, a high-speed passenger ferry, sank on Sunday near Kyrenia.Photograph: Jewel Samad/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSearch and rescue operations continue after the Filo Jet, a high-speed passenger ferry, sank on Sunday near Kyrenia.Photograph: Jewel Samad/AFP/Getty ImagesCyprusTurkish deep-sea search vessel joins efforts to retrieve 20 still missing after Cyprus ferry disasterTCG Isin expected to play vital role in locating Filo Jet’s voyage data recorder 514 metres below surfaceHelena Smithin AthensMon 31 Aug 2026 14.37 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA deep-sea search and rescue vessel is on its way to Cyprus asTurkeyjoins efforts to retrieve the 20 people still missing after a passenger ferry capsized off the island’s northern coast.The TCG Isinwill join the vast operation to find survivors after the high-speed ferry sank on Sunday barely four nautical miles outside the port town of Kyrenia.Authorities confirmed late on Monday – the first of three days of national mourning in Turkish-held northern Cyprus – that the tragedyhad claimed eight lives, increasing the number of passengers still unaccounted for from 17 to 20.A total of 241 of the 267 people aboard the Filo Jet, bound for Taşucu on the Turkish mainland when it began to take on water, had been rescued, they said. Almost all were either Turkish or Turkish Cypriot.Nearly 20 people still missing after ferry capsizes ⁠off northern CyprusRead moreView image in fullscreenSurvivors arrive on shore. Of the 267 people on board the ferry, 241 have been rescued, authorities have said.Photograph: ReutersInternational sympathy for the victims was highlighted as the Anglo-Cypriot founder of easyJet, Stelios Haji-Ioannou, offered €260,000 (£223,000) in support for the families of the deceased and missing, in a move hailed by Turkish Cypriot officials.Visiting Kyrenia’s new port, where relatives gathered for news of loved ones on Monday,Tufan Erhürman, the self-styled state’s president, vowed search efforts would “continue with the same intensity, with no interruption, through the day and night”.The Isin,capable of searching up to 3,000 metres below the sea surface, was due to arrive on Tuesday, he said, as he comforted the families of those still missing.The ship is expected to play a vital role in recovering the ferry’s voyage data recorder, or black box, now viewed as key in deciphering the cause of a maritime disaster not seen since the breakaway territory declared independence in 1983.Turkish Cypriot officials told the Guardian it was likely “all those responsible” would be charged with gross negligence as the seaworthiness of the 26-year-old ferry was also questioned.The owners and shareholders of the privately owned company operating the passenger vessel have also been ordered to appear in court.View image in fullscreenThe Turkish Cypriot leader, Tufan Erhürman, talks with relatives waiting for news outside the port of Kyrenia.Photograph: Yiannis Kourtoglou/ReutersIt remained unclear whether those still missing had been trapped on board.“Nobody is saying it publicly, but the hope of any survivors being found at this point is very slim,” one official confided. “Those who weren’t rescued very likely didn’t find a lifejacket. We believe many were elderly people and mothers with babies and young kids.”In testimony – and video footage – that emerged on Monday, panic-stricken passengers could be seen desperately looking for lifejackets and screaming before the double-hulled ferry flipped over. One mother, Ayten Biçer, described feeling her 12-year-old daughter slip from her hands and disappear as the ferry capsized and sank in a matter of minutes. “She was saying, ‘Don’t let go.’ And I didn’t let go of my daughter. I swear, I didn’t let her go,” she sobbed. Two of Biçer’s other children are among the 20 still missing.View image in fullscreenAyten and Hayri Biçer wait for news of their two missing children outside the port of Kyrenia.Photograph: Yiannis Kourtoglou/ReutersThe captain of the ferry and seven crew members were detained on Monday as judicial authorities launched an inquiry into the tragedy amid claims they had been among the first to abandon ship.Appearing before a local magistrate, the crew attributed the disaster to the bow of the catamaran-style ferry breaking apart in turbulent seas. But eyewitness accounts contradicted that version of events, with passengers telling officials that appeals to turn back to port had fallen on deaf ears as the ferry began to take on water.Ünal Üstel, the northernCyprusprime minister, told reporters the Filo Jet was lying on the seabed at a depth of 514 metres and that he foresaw the Turkish salvage ship “reaching [it] tomorrow afternoon”. Boats, helicopters, aircraft and other search and rescue teams had joined the operation, he said, adding that search efforts were continuing “on a 24-hour basis”.Cyprus has been divided since 1974 when a coup aimed at union with Greece – engineered by the military junta then in power in Athens – prompted Turkey to invade and seize the island’s northern third. Ever since, as many as 45,000 mainland Turkish troops have been stationed in the north.In 1983, the territory unilaterally declared independence, but in the absence of a settlement, decades of international isolation have ensued.Explore more on these topicsCyprusTurkeyWater transportEuropeStelios Haji-Ioannou (Sir)newsShareReuse this content

title: US supreme court allows Trump to keep building $400m White House ballroom | US supreme court | The Guardian
description: Justices’ 5-4 ruling permits Trump administration appeal to block lower court order halting above-ground work
Author: Chris Stein
Headline: Justices’ 5-4 ruling permits Trump administration appeal to block lower court order halting above-ground work
Content: Donald Trump holds artist’s renderings as he talks to reporters about his proposed White House ballroom next to the worksite in May.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump holds artist’s renderings as he talks to reporters about his proposed White House ballroom next to the worksite in May.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesUS supreme courtUS supreme court allows Trump to keep building $400m White House ballroomJustices’ 5-4 ruling permits Trump administration appeal to block lower court order halting above-ground workChris Steinin WashingtonMon 31 Aug 2026 18.13 EDTFirst published on Mon 31 Aug 2026 16.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA dividedUS supreme courthas permittedDonald Trumpto continuebuildinghis controversial $400m White House ballroom despite legal challenges, raising the likelihood it will be completed.In a 5-4 ruling, the justices permitted the Trump administration’s request to ⁠block a lower court order that hadhaltedabove-ground construction of the project while a lawsuit by a historic preservation group seeks to block it.The US president, whodemolished the historic East Wingof the White House last year to make way for planned ballroom, has repeatedly touted it as “a gift” to the US people.Monday’s decision from the supreme court comes after the court’s conservative chief justice, John Roberts, issued atemporary orderthat had enabled work to continue.Renderings show most detailed vision for Trump’s White House ballroomRead moreHowever, Roberts joined the court’s three liberal justices in dissenting from the majority’s decision and wrote that the construction was “likely unlawful”.The court’s decision may allow Trump to bring to fruition a project that is at the center of his ambition to remake the US capital in his image. Since taking office, he hass ordered the National Mall’sreflecting poolcovered in blue liner, proposed a$250m renovationto the Kennedy Center performing arts center that would see his name emblazoned on its side, and is pursuing plans torenovate a golf courseand build amassive arch.While some projects have hit legal roadblocks, such as when a judgeorderedTrump’s name removed from the Kennedy Center, or descended into farce, like when the reflecting pool line began falling off, the supreme court’s decision today is a victory for the president.Trump celebrated Monday’s ruling in aposton Truth Social, boasting that the White House complex would be “one of the Greatest ever constructed in Washington DC”, with construction to be completed by the summer of 2028.In an unsigned opinion, the five conservative justices said the National Trust for Historic Preservation in the United States lacked standing to bring a lawsuit against the project. The trust had centered its argument on the declaration of a board member, the architectural historian Alison Hoagland, who said the ballroom was an “aesthetic, cultural and historical” affront because of its design, and that she would suffer “injuries” when viewing it inWashington DC.“The government is likely to prevail in showing that the Trust lacks standing to challenge the East Wing project,” the majority opinion read.“This court has not found standing in circumstances like these before. To the contrary, we have repeatedly held that mere offense, disagreement, or distaste does not qualify as a concrete and particularized injury.”The justices also agreed that the government would suffer “irreparable harm” if construction is stopped, or only allowed to continue on a military installation set to be built underneath the ballroom while the above-ground portion remains unfinished.The majority ultimately side stepped the question of whether the president’s decision to tear down a chunk of a building that rotates between presidential officeholders was actually legal.“Today, we do not pass upon the legality of the government’s East Wing project,” they wrote.The dissenting justices – Roberts, together with Democratic-appointed justices Elena Kagan, Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson – argued that the project is unlawful because Congress has not approved it.In his opinion, Roberts wrote that the construction is a “likely infringement of the legislature’s power of the purse and authority to regulate federal property in the District of Columbia to continue”, and says the majority’s ruling “is no victory for the separation of powers”.“The ballroom is a building or structure being erected on federal park grounds – President’s Park – in the District of Columbia. Yet Congress has not passed any law resembling ‘express authority’ for the executive’s construction of it,” the chief writes.He also disagreed that the potential injuries to Hoagland are insufficient for the historic trust to sue, saying she was “deeply committed to the preservation of such historic American buildings” through her work with the association.“Hoagland’s injury suffices for standing,” Roberts wrote, likening the impact of the White House’s transformation on her to how “an environmentalist can sustain a concrete, particularized aesthetic injury from the extinction of a particular animal or the transformation of a particular forest or river that he regularly enjoys”.Explore more on these topicsUS supreme courtDonald TrumpTrump administrationWashington DCUS politicsLaw (US)newsShareReuse this content

title: Anthropic sued over alleged theft of ‘tens of thousands’ of songs  | Music industry | The Guardian
description: AI company faces multibillion dollar lawsuit over misuse of copyrighted songs to train Claude models
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: AI company faces multibillion dollar lawsuit over misuse of copyrighted songs to train Claude models
Content: Music publishers have claimed Anthropic’s models ‘scraped’ smash hits including Mariah Carey’s All I Want For Christmas Is You.Photograph: Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for MCView image in fullscreenMusic publishers have claimed Anthropic’s models ‘scraped’ smash hits including Mariah Carey’s All I Want For Christmas Is You.Photograph: Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for MCMusic industryAnthropic sued over alleged theft of ‘tens of thousands’ of songsAI company faces multibillion dollar lawsuit over misuse of copyrighted songs to train Claude modelsDan MilmoGlobal technology editorMon 31 Aug 2026 08.42 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAll AI wants for Christmas is a vast back catalogue of songs without paying for it, according to a multibillion-dollar lawsuit against the startup behind the Claude chatbot.Sony Music Publishing and Warner Chappell, music publishers who manage the copyright of songs on behalf of songwriters and composers, are seeking damages for alleged misuse of “tens of thousands” of copyrighted works byAnthropic.The compositions include Mariah Carey’s All I Want for Christmas is You, Ain’t No Mountain High Enough, originally performed by Marvin Gaye and Tammi Terrell, and Survivor’s Eye of the Tiger.The plaintiffs claim they are victims of “one of the largest and most blatant ongoing thefts of intellectual property in history”.The lawsuit, filed in a California court, targets Anthropic and its chief executive, Dario Amodei, as well as co-founder Benjamin Mann. It alleges the defendants breached copyright law by “torrenting, scraping and downloading” lyrics from copyrighted works to train its family of Claude AI models – as well as reproducing those lyrics in responses to users’ prompts.It claims that Mann and Anthropic downloaded at least 7m copies of books from pirate websites, including the lyrics and sheet music to songs such as Bon Jovi’s Livin’ on a Prayer and Leonard Cohen’s Hallelujah.The figures are from a recent copyright case against Anthropic brought by US authorswhich the company settled for $1.5bn.Thelawsuit, filed on 28 August, was first reported by trade publication Music Business Worldwide. Other songs allegedly having their copyright infringed included Mark Ronson’s Uptown Funk and Katy Perry’s California Gurls.It also claims that Anthropic acquired copies of songs in other ways including scraping lyrics from legal sites like Musixmatch and LyricFind, and datasets on archive sites such as Common Crawl. In another section of the claim, the publishers allege that Anthropic stripped identifying information from songs while processing the texts, which denied copyright owners “valuable attribution” to their work.“Defendants specifically elected to harvest unauthorized copies of Music Publishers’ works so that they would not have to pay Music Publishers a licensing fee to use their works in AI training and development,” said the plaintiffs.The music publishers are seeking damages that could run into billions of dollars, based on a claim of up to $150,000 per infringed piece of work and $25,000 for each removal or alteration of identifying data.The suit implies at least 20,000 works are involved in the suit, referring to the unlawful copying of “tens of thousands of Music Publishers’ copyrighted musical compositions”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEd Newton-Rex, a UK-based composer and campaigner for protecting artists’ copyright, said he was “not surprised” that rights holders were defending themselves against a company with a “history of downloading and training their AI models on huge libraries”.Alongside the authors’ lawsuit, Anthropic has also faced claims from Universal Music Group and Concord Music Group.In a separate case this month, AI music generator Suno lost a copyright infringement case against German licensing agency GEMA, which alleged illegal use of songs including Boney M’s Daddy Cool to train its technology.A spokesperson for Anthropic, which is preparing for a stockmarket listing that could value the company at $2tn, said: “We disagree with the publishers’ claims and we intend to defend ourselves robustly in court.”Explore more on these topicsMusic industryAnthropicAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: Dolly Parton laid to rest in private Nashville funeral | Dolly Parton | The Guardian
description: The queen of country was interred next to her late husband in an intimate ceremony attended by close family
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: The queen of country was interred next to her late husband in an intimate ceremony attended by close family
Content: Dolly Parton at a Los Angeles event in 2019.Photograph: Mario Anzuoni/ReutersView image in fullscreenDolly Parton at a Los Angeles event in 2019.Photograph: Mario Anzuoni/ReutersDolly PartonDolly Parton laid to rest in private Nashville funeralThe queen of country was interred next to her late husband in an intimate ceremony attended by close familyOwen MyersMon 31 Aug 2026 12.17 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 14.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDolly Partonwas laid to rest in a private ceremony in Nashville on Friday, her family has confirmed.The queen of country music, whodied aged 80 on 25 August“after bravely facing a brief battle with cancer”, was interred at Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum alongside her husband of 60 years, Carl Thomas.From Jolene to Islands in the Stream: Dolly Parton’s 10 best recordingsRead moreParton’s great-niece Lainey Parton wrote onInstagramon Saturday: “I wanted to wait until after my granny was laid to rest yesterday before I tried to put any of this into words.“From the time I was little, my granny always had a way of making me feel like I was enough. She never made my dreams feel too big or made me feel like I couldn’t do something. She believed in me before I even knew how to believe in myself.“Because she couldn’t have kids of her own, she always made us feel like we were hers,” Lainey continued. “She loved us that way, and I’ll forever be grateful for that.”View image in fullscreenDolly Parton’s burial site next to her late husband at Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum in Nashville.Photograph: Tammie Arroyo/AFF-USA/ShutterstockOnly immediate family attended the small ceremony,Peoplereported. Parton had her name engraved on the large mausoleum plaque at the cemetery before she died, as well as an engraving of the cabin in Sevier county, Tennessee, where she grew up.On Saturday, Parton’s niece Jada Star took to the stage at Nashville’s Grand Ole Opry as part of a tribute concert to the country legend. Starperformeda song titled The Orchard that she had recorded with Parton for her 2024 album Smoky Mountain DNA: Family, Faith and Fables.Dolly Parton was a rare singer who proved herself to be an electric movie starRead moreIn anInstagram postahead of the performance, Star said, “I am walking around in a fog of sadness, like all of you have.“I do not take this honor lightly. I will stand on that stage tonight, the stage she loved so much, and share my song I wrote for her and for my whole family.”On Monday, the estate of Parton announced DollyFest, a two-weekend event which will take place in Nashville and London next year.
