Before her death, Parton had been planning the festival for January 2026 but had to take a step back due to health issues.“As far as a traditional memorial goes, that is not something Dolly wanted,” said Parton’s manager, Danny Nozell, in a press release. “So, instead, it feels more appropriate for us to take a beat, let all the tributes that immediately make sense occur naturally, and then, see through this festival-style concept that was truly dreamed up by Dolly.”View image in fullscreenDolly Parton’s niece Jada Star performs at a tribute to Parton at the Grand Ole Opry, Nashville, Tennessee, on Saturday.Photograph: Seth Herald/ReutersLast week, Parton’s team confirmed that the projects she was working on before her death would continue to be brought to life, including a line of coffee grounds, a home decor collection and a Broadway musical to launch in New York later this year.“Dolly worked up until the day she died,” Nozell said. “As the leader of the team responsible for overseeing her legacy, we will ensure the many dreams she had yet to fulfill are brought to life.”Active projects that Parton was working on at the time of her death also include Dolly Parton’s SongTeller Hotel and Dolly’s Life of Many Colors Museum, which are both scheduled to open next month in Nashville. Meanwhile, Dolly Dolls and a range of Dolly’s Dog Treats are scheduled to be released in the coming months.The family has asked for donations in Parton’s memory to be dedicated toImagination Library, the organization she founded to encourage literacy and the love of reading in children.Explore more on these topicsDolly PartonCountrynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Breakthrough’ as Turkmenistan starts fixing ‘mindboggling’ methane mega-leaks | Greenhouse gas emissions | The Guardian
description: Secretive state begins repairs on ageing facilities after being revealed as worst country for leaks of potent greenhouse gas
Author: Damian Carrington
Headline: Secretive state begins repairs on ageing facilities after being revealed as worst country for leaks of potent greenhouse gas
Content: Flares burning off methane and other hydrocarbons in Texas. The US was sent 138 UN alerts to methane plumes in the last year but responded to none and fixed no leaks.Photograph: David Goldman/APView image in fullscreenFlares burning off methane and other hydrocarbons in Texas. The US was sent 138 UN alerts to methane plumes in the last year but responded to none and fixed no leaks.Photograph: David Goldman/APGreenhouse gas emissions‘Breakthrough’ as Turkmenistan starts fixing ‘mindboggling’ methane mega-leaksSecretive state begins repairs on ageing facilities after being revealed as worst country for leaks of potent greenhouse gasDamian CarringtonEnvironment editorMon 31 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTurkmenistan has started plugging the mega-leaks of methane that spew from its ageing oil and gas facilities, the latest UN data shows, in a move hailed as a breakthrough.Methane, also called natural or fossil gas, is a potent greenhouse gas. It traps80 times more heatthan carbon dioxide and causes25% of global heatingtoday. Stopping leaks can be quick and cheap and, because methane breaks down in the atmosphere far quicker than CO2, this has a rapid impact, with some experts calling it the climate “emergency brake”.The Guardian revealed in 2023 that Turkmenistan was theworst country for methane mega-leaks. Sources in Turkmenistan said this scrutiny was the “critical step” in leading the secretive and authoritarian government to engage with foreign partners.A “super-emitter” leak, the escape of tonnes of methane per hour from a single valve or pipeline, heats the planet more than the emissions from a million SUVs or an entire coal-fired power station.Turkmenistan had now stopped eight leaks by repairing corroded pipes, faulty wells and failing flares. The work was an “incredible first step”, said the UN, but much remained to be done.View image in fullscreenA satellite image of a methane leak in Turkmenistan’s Lebap province, which was plugged in March after a corroded pipe was fixed.Illustration: UNEP’s International Methane Emissions ObservatoryThe UNMethane Alert and Response System(Mars) sent 192 alerts of methane plumes to Turkmenistan in the last year. The country had three of the six worst leaks detected in the world by Mars in last six months, and nine of the top 50.Turkmenistan responded to about 20% of the alerts with on-the-ground information about the leaks and potential plans to fix them. In contrast, the US was sent the second highest number of alerts – 138 – but responded to none and had fixed no leaks in the last year. Other nations that failed to respond to any alerts were Iran, Russia and China.Map showing location and extent of methane ‘mega-leaks’ around the world from February to August 2026The worst methane leak detected was an extraordinary leak in Mexico’s offshore oil and gas industry of 37 tonnes per hour, equivalent to the emissions of more than 7m SUVs. Mexico responded to all 23 Mars alerts in the last year, but had yet to complete a fix.The plugging of leaks in Turkmenistan was encouraging, said Meghan Demeter, the programme manager of Mars, which is part of the UN Environment Programme. “These mitigation cases are a proof point of what can be done with satellite data, especially in situations like Turkmenistan, where there are a lot of detections. We’re seeing that the pipeline of satellite data to mitigation action works, and it can work quite quickly.”“This is a breakthrough in terms of having real documented mitigation action,” she told the Guardian. “But it is not yet a breakthrough in the overall magnitude of emissions. Eight cases is an incredible first step, but there’s also a lot more sources in Turkmenistan that need to be addressed. We are in pretty constant communication and the response rate is growing month by month. We’re seeing steady progress.”View image in fullscreenA major methane leak detected in the US in June.Illustration: UNEP’s International Methane Emissions ObservatoryIn March 2023, the Guardian revealedTurkmenistan had the most super-emitting methane leaksin the world. It then revealed in May that themethane emissions alonefrom the nation’s two main fossil fuel fields caused more global heating in 2022 than the entire carbon emissions of the UK, which experts described as both “mind-boggling” and “infuriating”.The findings caused a furore in Turkmenistan, prompting the government to engage with the UN, the EU and other nations and institutions to try to end the leaks, according to sources in the capital, Ashgabat. In December 2023, Turkmenistan joined theglobal methanepledge, two years after it had launched.Turkmenistan has huge gas reserves and is a major supplier to China. Previously, leaks were ignored due to the enormous volumes on tap. But in November 2024, thefirst leakwas fixed after a faulty well was repaired. Themost recent repair, in March, was to a corroded pipeline. Turkmenistan’s ministry of foreign affairs and state companies Turkmenoil and Turkmengaz did not respond to a request for comment.Themost recent Mars datashows Kazakhstan, another former Soviet republic with ageing oil and gas infrastructure, has stopped eight leaks. However, the overall number of leaks in Kazakhstan is smaller, with 38 Mars alerts in the last year.In total, Mars alerts have led to 43 leaks being sealed so far. Many have been straightforward fixes, with leaks plugged on the spot, while others required more planning and funding. Onemajor leak now stemmed in Algeriahad been running for almost 40 years, due to a faulty flare. Flares burn unwanted methane and turn it into CO2, a much less potent greenhouse gas.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe previous US administration, under President Joe Biden, did engage with Mars and onesmall leak in New Mexico was fixed in 2024after a pressure safety valve was repaired. But this engagement ended with the second presidency of Donald Trump. Last year, Trumpcalled climate change “the greatest con jobever perpetrated on the world” at the UN general assembly.Mexico, Brazil and Argentina have 100% response rates to Mars alerts, while Libya and Azerbaijan have high response rates.View image in fullscreenA methane leak at Baiji, in Iraq, was stopped in May after a corroded pipe was fixed.Illustration: UNEP’s International Methane Emissions Observatory“Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan are home to some of the world’s most significant methane hotspots and their response to satellite alerts is much-needed good news in the global effort to minimise methane pollution,” said Dan Grossman, the vice-president at the Environmental Defense Fund.“Stemming methane emissions from oil and gas operations is the quickest and most cost-effective method to reduce climate pollution available today,” he said. “Alerts only matter if they lead to action, and governments and industry must do a better job.”The UN secretary general, António Guterres, has called for all countries to respond to 80% of alerts.Demeter said: “We’re scaling up a lot in terms of the support that we can offer – knowledge building and technical support – and we are working alongside many partners. There are also a lot of requests for funding for direct mitigation.”The Mars system uses artificial intelligence to analyse data from more than a dozen satellites and detect potential leaks, which are then checked by two layers of review by analysts. Verified leaks are then notified to the relevant government or company. Responses are recorded if they report on-the-ground information and an intention to plug the leak. If a leak is reported as fixed, Mars monitors the site until the data shows emissions have ended before recording it as a success.The Guardian’s climate forum 2026On Tuesday 20 October, join Damian Carrington and our panel of experts, including Prof Andy Haines, Katie White MP, Asad Rehman, Shruti Suresh Gareth Thomas and Amy Fairman, for a hopeful and solutions-focused evening. Book ticketshereor atguardian.liveExplore more on these topicsGreenhouse gas emissionsTurkmenistanClimate crisisFossil fuelsUnited NationsEnergyGas (Environment)newsShareReuse this content

title: Cross-party talks needed to tackle climate crisis, say Lib Dems | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: Andy Burnham urged to seek consensus over response to extreme heat and forthcoming ‘super El Niño’
Author: Fiona Harvey
Headline: Andy Burnham urged to seek consensus over response to extreme heat and forthcoming ‘super El Niño’
Content: The UK has been hit by five heatwaves this summer, drying up lakes such as Hollow Pond, near Leytonstone, east London.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreenThe UK has been hit by five heatwaves this summer, drying up lakes such as Hollow Pond, near Leytonstone, east London.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAClimate crisisCross-party talks needed to tackle climate crisis, say Lib DemsAndy Burnham urged to seek consensus over response to extreme heat and forthcoming ‘super El Niño’Fiona HarveyEnvironment editorMon 31 Aug 2026 07.48 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 07.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham should call a cross-party meeting to discuss the UK’s response to worsening extreme weather, including theforthcoming ‘super El Niño’, the Liberal Democrats have said.The prime ministerchaired a Cobra emergencymeeting on the drought earlier this month but there has been little from the government on the wider threats posed by five successive heatwaves since May and expected global issues with food shortages and inflation.Pippa Heylings, the Lib Dem spokesperson for energy security and net zero, said: “Andy Burnham has shown he is able to commit to talking about things people care about, which is good. But there’s been a baffling silence from him on extreme heat. What we have heard so far has been underwhelming.Banning disposable barbecuesis good, but we need to see more.”Heylings andEd Davey, the Lib Dem leader, wrote to Burnham a fortnight ago, proposing a meeting of the UK’s party leaders “to discuss the long-term measures needed to protect our country from climate impacts and build resilience to the extreme weather we are already experiencing”. They say they have not had a response.Heylings contrastedBurnham’s reluctance to addressthe climate crisis with his prioritising of social care, on which he has called forcross-party support: “We want the same approach [to the climate].”She said even the leaders of Reform and the Conservatives, both of whom havevowed to scrap net zeroanddownplayed the climate crisis, should be able to join in an effort to protect the UK. “I think there is not a single MP who would not want to show their constituents they were trying to prepare us [for the impacts of extreme weather],” she said.The forthcoming El Niño could bring more serious problems, Heylings said. “The scale of this Super El Niño is unprecedented and will have impacts here in the UK exacerbating our extreme weather particularly with more intense flooding and storms over the autumn and winter. We’re looking at a double whammy.”Any cross-party approach should not be limited to discussing preparedness for extreme weather, she said. “The key question is how do we stop it worsening?”View image in fullscreenFlooding in Monmouth in Wales last November.  It is feared that the forthcoming El Niño could result in severe storms this autumn.Photograph: Matthew Horwood/Getty ImagesClive Lewis, the Labour MP for Norwich South, backed the Lib Dem call for a cross-party meeting. “It’s the kind of politics we need,” he said. “We may disagree on how we do it and how far we go, but political cooperation like this is the start of consensus building, something any radical transition has to build across both political parties and society, especially if they’re to take on those vested interests that want the status quo to continue.”But Jon Pearce, the Labour MP for High Peak in Derbyshire, warned it was unlikely a meeting would happen.“The idea the Conservatives and Reform UK would be willing to face up to the risks we face is for the birds,” he said. “The Conservatives and Reform UK have ripped up the political consensus on tackling climate change as they compete to see who can most downplay the need for action.“They are refusing to see what is right in front of their eyes: wildfires, drought, pressure on water supplies and farmers facing growing challenges on food production. There should be political consensus on a matter of such national importance but sadly there is not.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNepal-Tibet flood: this is the cost of not acting in the face of the climate crisis | Sunil AcharyaRead moreIn the past few years,Reform and the Conservatives have brokensharply with the consensus on the need for climate action, despite polls consistently showing alarge majority of voterssupport the idea.A spokesperson for the Conservatives said: “We wouldn’t speculate on hypothetical talks to which we have not been invited.”The Reform party did not respond to a request for comment.Hannah Spencer, a Green party MP, said: “The climate crisis should be a priority across every sector of the economy and every government department. Greens have led this agenda for decades and welcome the consistently strong support shown by voters for all parties for bold climate action.”A spokesperson for the government said: “The UK continues to be a world leader in tackling the climate crisis, accelerating the transition to clean power, and acting to protect people and places from the impacts of climate change that are already being felt across the country.“We are working to adapt to the changing climate through our work with the National Drought Group, building nine new reservoirs across the country and investing at least £10.5bn by March 2036 to construct new flood and coastal erosion schemes, as extreme weather becomes more frequent.”Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisExtreme heatAndy BurnhamEl Niño southern oscillationEd DaveyLiberal DemocratsnewsShareReuse this content

title: How a South African town cleaned up its polluted river using stones, wood and sand | Global development | The Guardian
description: Scientists say system to treat contaminated wastewater offers a model for ensuring food security in a fast-warming climate
Author: Kaamil Ahmed
Headline: Scientists say system to treat contaminated wastewater offers a model for ensuring food security in a fast-warming climate
Content: The Water Hub’s filter beds remove nearly 99% of toxins before most of the water is released back into the river, with some held back to irrigate gardens.Photograph: Courtesy of Water HubView image in fullscreenThe Water Hub’s filter beds remove nearly 99% of toxins before most of the water is released back into the river, with some held back to irrigate gardens.Photograph: Courtesy of Water HubGlobal developmentHow a South African town cleaned up its polluted river using stones, wood and sandScientists say system to treat contaminated wastewater offers a model for ensuring food security in a fast-warming climateKaamil AhmedMon 31 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 09.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAll it took to turn the murky, heavily polluted waters of South Africa’s Stiebeuel River into a resource clean enough for irrigating a community’s vegetable plots was a collection of stones, heat-treated wood and sand.Without chemicals and using renewable energy, researchers from the University of Cape Town are cleaning 36,000 litres of water, polluted by sewage, chemicals, and traces of drugs and medication, every day to make it usable for growing food in a fast-expanding informal settlement along the course of the river.Scientists behind the project think it could be a model for ensuring food security in the climate crisis.“What we’re doing is taking that water, treating it every day, and some of that water is now being used for growing vegetables, for feeding hungry children and people living in the informal settlement,” says Kevin Winter, one of the researchers behind theWater Hub project in Langrug, near Stellenbosch in South Africa’s Western Cape region.View image in fullscreenThe researchers set up the Water Hub in an abandoned wastewater site, turning old drying beds into a network of filtration cells.Photograph: Courtesy of Water HubWinter says of the treated water: “You’d be very hard pressed to know the difference between it and your municipal treated water, which has been through a treatment plant and been chlorinated.”Established in 2018, the project has only this year succeeded in reducing bacteria and pathogens to a level that allows the water to be used for irrigation, though not for drinking.Winter says the system now removes about 99% of the toxins before most of the water is released back into the river, where it feeds surrounding ecosystems. About 3,000 litres is held back to irrigate food-producing gardens at theWaterHub.View image in fullscreenThe Stiebeuel River is polluted with rubbish, sewage and grey water.Photograph: Water HubWorking in the area since 2006, Winter has seen the population of Langrug grow from 3,000 people to more than 26,000, mostly driven by seasonal work on farms and in the wealthy nearby town of Franschhoek.Langrug’s unplanned growth left residents without access to clean water or sewage facilities. Local water plants were stretched beyond their capacity and so Winter’s team took on the task.They built their nature-based system in an abandoned wastewater site, turning old drying beds into a network of filtration cells. The system is off-grid, using solar power to pump water from the river into the cells, where it slowly filters through over five days.Large stones are used to trap particles and chemicals; then a layer of biochar – wood burned at 800C (1,470F) – filters out traces of drugs, pharmaceutical waste and ammonia; and the final layers of smaller stones and sand absorb the remaining toxins and pollutants.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe treatment plant filters toxins from the water, which is then released back to supply surrounding ecosystems.Photograph: Courtesy of Water HubWinter says the filtration system is not designed to replace conventional plants cleaning industrial-levels of water for towns and cities, but that it does provide clean water for rural communities.The Western Cape faced an almostcatastrophic water crisis in 2018, when reservoirs came close to running dry after a period of extended drought. For months, households in the region were forced to ration water and about31,000 farm workerslost their jobs.“It’s absolutely crucial that we start looking at how we do this. Climate in the next 30 years, particularly in our region here, is going to look very, very different,” says Winter. “Yes, it’ll have all the wildfires, it will have all the flooding, but it will have prolonged periods of drought when food and access to water is scarce.“Making water available for food, and for food security, as a climate-change strategy is absolutely crucial worldwide and we’ve got to learn to be able to do that more and more,” he says.Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentSouth AfricaAfricaWaterFood securityPollutionAccess to waterfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: British Museum hosted Palantir founder Peter Thiel in private viewing of Bayeux tapestry | British Museum | The Guardian
description: Concern among staff that fragile artwork’s scarce ‘light hours’ given to someone with no known interest in museum
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Concern among staff that fragile artwork’s scarce ‘light hours’ given to someone with no known interest in museum
Content: Peter Thiel. The museum has a careful plan for light-hour allocations, agreed with colleagues in France.Photograph: Gage Skidmore/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPeter Thiel. The museum has a careful plan for light-hour allocations, agreed with colleagues in France.Photograph: Gage Skidmore/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockBritish MuseumBritish Museum hosted Palantir founder Peter Thiel in private viewing of Bayeux tapestryConcern among staff that fragile artwork’s scarce ‘light hours’ given to someone with no known interest in museumNadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentMon 31 Aug 2026 04.50 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe British Museum privately hosted the Donald Trump-supporting tech billionaire Peter Thiel in the exhibition space of theBayeux tapestryearlier this month, the Guardian understands.The museum’s director of development, Charlotte Appleyard, hosted the PayPal founder at a VIP viewing of the tapestry, which is yet to open to the public, on 18 August.In response to queries from the Guardian, a source at the museum confirmed that the visit took place. It is understood the museum chair, George Osborne, was aware of the viewing but did not attend with Thiel.It is understood that senior museum leaders were warned about the possible public perception of special treatment for someone with connections to Jeffrey Epstein, and whose public software company, Palantir,plays a controversial role in the British state.View image in fullscreenGeorge Osborne and France’s culture minister, Catherine Pégard (C), look at the Bayeux tapestry during a visit to its unveiling at the British Museum in July.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/AFPThere were concerns among some staff that scarce “lux hours” for the tapestry – a combined measure of light intensity and exposure time used to track and limit cumulative light damage to sensitive artefacts – were given up to someone with no known interest in the museum.The exhibition gallery is still under construction, and only limited viewings of the tapestry have been possible across a range of stakeholders. Among those receiving special access are Osborne and his podcasting partner, Ed Balls, who will record the next episode of their Political Currency show from the gallery,the noteson the most recent episode suggest.TheBritish Museumhas a careful plan for light-hour allocation, agreed in partnership with colleagues in France. It is understood that no light hours have been taken from the allocation for public visitors. Thiel is not a donor to the museum and no money has been received via him or his businesses.Members of the public keen to see the Bayeux tapestry faced online queues of up to nine hours when tickets went on sale for the first time earlier this summer. There were reports of 40,000 people queueing by mid-morning, with that figure ballooning to almost 80,000 by mid-afternoon.On Friday, the museum announced that the next wave of public tickets for the tapestry will go on sale on 21 October at 10am.View image in fullscreenMuseum staff adjusting protective covers on the Bayeux tapestry.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/AFP/Getty ImagesGuests at One Aldwych hotel, where rooms cost more than £1,000 a night, are also able to get ticketswithout joining the online queues.Thiel is the founder of Palantir, a public software company that builds data integration, analytics and artificial intelligence platforms for government agencies and large corporations. Palantir has a swathe of British public contracts, including, most controversially, a£330m deal with the NHS, which it has held since 2023.The company also works for the US, Israeli and UK militaries. Its use of its AI-powered software to support military strikes in Gaza and Iran, US ICE immigration raids and access to NHS data has stoked concern.Last month, a second parliamentary committee urged Labour to scrap Palantir’s NHS contract. The cross-party group of MPs cited “serious mistrust” among the public and the medical profession of its NHS system, contested evidence of its benefits, and cited the availability of other tools that could deliver similar results.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBayeux tapestry crosses Channel in dead of night for historic UK exhibitionRead moreIn May, Sadiq Khan, the London mayor,blocked the Metropolitan police from awardinga £50m contract to Palantir after saying Londoners wanted to see public money being paid to companies that “share the values of our city”. Palantir is challenging the decision in the high court.Thiel recently hit the headlines forhosting a series of lecturesphilosophising about who the antichrist could be and warning that Armageddon was coming. He has also recently become powerful in US conservative politics, with close ties to Donald Trump and JD Vance, and has helped bankroll Republicans’ 2026 midterm campaigns.The Epstein files showed that Thiel remained in contact with the financier for years after his 2008 conviction for soliciting prostitution from a minor, with multiple references to lunches and meetings between the pair from about 2014 onwards.Epstein’s Southern Trust Company also invested about $40m (£29.5m) in a venture fund co-founded by Thiel, while correspondence from 2018 shows Epstein inviting Thiel to visit him in the Caribbean. Thiel has said he never visited Epstein’s island and there is no suggestion that he was involved in Epstein’s sexual abuse or trafficking.Thiel and Palantir have been approached for comment.Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsBritish MuseumPeter ThielBayeux tapestryPalantirMuseumsLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: British family pleads with French authorities to release body of relative who died in Channel | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Jasmeet Wadhwa, who fled Taliban persecution in Afghanistan, lost his life while trying to reach UK in April
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: Jasmeet Wadhwa, who fled Taliban persecution in Afghanistan, lost his life while trying to reach UK in April
Content: Relatives of Jasmeet Wadhwa and Nagmeldin Adam held a demonstration outside a courthouse in Dunkirk, France on Monday.Photograph: HandoutView image in fullscreenRelatives of Jasmeet Wadhwa and Nagmeldin Adam held a demonstration outside a courthouse in Dunkirk, France on Monday.Photograph: HandoutImmigration and asylumBritish family pleads with French authorities to release body of relative who died in ChannelJasmeet Wadhwa, who fled Taliban persecution in Afghanistan, lost his life while trying to reach UK in AprilDiane TaylorMon 31 Aug 2026 09.36 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA British family is pleading with French authorities to release the body of a relative that officials have held for five months after he died in the Channel in April.Jasmeet Wadhwa, 32, died whileattempting to reach the UKon a dinghy on 1 April with his mother, Harbans Kaur Wadhwa, after they fled Taliban persecution in Afghanistan in January.They endured a difficult two-month journey under the control of people smugglers before reaching northernFrancein mid-March. A man from Sudan, Nagmeldin Adam, 33, died on the same boat. Eight others were rescued, including Harbans Kaur Wadhwa.Adam’s journey from Sudan involved detention in Libya for an extended period and many attempts to cross the Mediterranean toEurope. He finally reached France in December 2025.At least 16 people have died trying to cross the Channel from France to the UK so far this year, with thelatest reported deathon Saturday in a similar part of the French coast to where the two men lost their lives in April.View image in fullscreenJasmeet Wadhwa and Nagmeldin Adam died in the Channel in April 2026.Photograph: HandoutRelatives of the two men took part in a demonstration on Monday outside the courthouse in Dunkirk in protest against the French authorities’ refusal to release the bodies. Wadhwa’s relatives travelled from the UK to France to participate. Many who lose their lives trying to cross the Channel are never publicly identified and it is rare to see family members stage a protest of this kind.Neither the French interior ministry nor the part of the French police in charge of the bodies responded to questions from the Guardian about why there had been a delay in releasing the two men’s bodies.View image in fullscreen‘We shouldn’t have to fight to say goodbye’: Jasmeet Wadhwa’s relatives are urging the French authorities to release his body.Photograph: Family HandoutIvnit Singh Wadwa, Wadhwa’s cousin, travelled from his home in west London for the protest. “We shouldn’t have to fight to say goodbye,” said Wadwa. “We are very upset with the French judicial system. Our family is waiting for Jasmeet’s body so we can lay him to rest.”After witnessing the loss of her son on the dinghy, Harbans Kaur Wadhwa made an application to the Home Office to come to the UK legally underthe “one in, one out” scheme. This scheme forcibly returns one person to France who has arrived in the UK on a small boat in exchange for accepting another who has applied legally to come to the UK from northern France. She was hoping to join her family in the UK who have offered to accommodate and support her.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTalkTV under fire for not disclosing reporter’s ties to Reform UK in Channel crossing filmRead moreBut the Home Office rejected the application for not meeting the requirements, saying that the identity document submitted was not satisfactory. Afghans generally have an identity document known as a Tazkira.A Home Office spokesperson said: “We are deeply saddened to hear about a death in French waters.“Every death in the Channel is a tragedy and a stark reminder of the dangers posed by criminal gangs exploiting vulnerable people for profit. We will continue working relentlessly with the French and our partners overseas to prevent these perilous journeys.”In anappealfor the release of Jasmeet’s body, the family wrote on social media: “A son. A brother. A life not forgotten. Help us bring Jasmeet back to his family. This is not about politics. It’s about a grieving mother being able to see her son one final time, it’s about a family being able to mourn.”Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumFranceEuropeAfghanistannewsShareReuse this content

title: Can Reform UK recover from its summer horribilis?  | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Clacton, funding, internal divisions – party prepares for annual conference next week after a season of missteps
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Clacton, funding, internal divisions – party prepares for annual conference next week after a season of missteps
Content: Nigel Farage in Clacton for the byelection he triggered in an attempt to neutralise the pressure he was under over an undeclared £5m payment from a megadonor.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNigel Farage in Clacton for the byelection he triggered in an attempt to neutralise the pressure he was under over an undeclared £5m payment from a megadonor.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesReform UKAnalysisCan Reform UK recover from its summer horribilis?Ben QuinnPolitical corresponentClacton, funding, internal divisions – party prepares for annual conference next week after a season of misstepsMon 31 Aug 2026 08.22 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareSeniorReform UKfigures like to boast that the summer time – and parliament’s longest recess – is when the party makes hay.Supposedly, it is whenNigel Farageand co can muscle in on the news cycle with provocative statements and new policies, painting “establishment” opponents as workshy layabouts.Last year’s summer break came with an added opportunity, which the rightwing populist party eagerly grasped, in the form of protests against hotels housing asylum seekers. As Labour and the Tories tempered their language,Farage eagerly weighed in, warning of the prospect of “civil disobedience on a vast scale”.Yet as August comes to an end, and with Reform preparing for its annual conference in Birmingham later this week, the party might look back on summer 2026 as a damp squib, or worse.While almost weekly Reform press conferences have taken place and new policies have been rolled out – Robert Jenrick has been particularly busy withpromises to slash the benefits billand scrap supposed “red tape” for businesses – there has been no repeat of last summer’s unrest in England, aside fromdisturbances in the Norfolk market town of Thetford.There have also been missteps of Reform’s own making, not least the hint of internal divisions related to the noisy pronouncements of its home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf. Farage was eventually forced to reprimand him for calling Ben Wallace, a former Conservative defence secretary and veteran, a “traitor”.Divisions also surfaced around the suspension ofTim Montgomerie, a high-profile activist who defected from the Conservatives.However, perhaps the biggest error was Farage’s decision to spark abyelection in Clactonin an attempt to neutralise the pressure he was under over questions about an undeclared £5m payment by theReform megadonor Christopher Harborne. Farage himself scaled back press events amid scrutiny after thepayment was first revealed by the Guardian.Though hecruised to victoryover his closest challenger – Count Binface – the need to get the vote out meant Farage was pinned down in a corner of Essex for six weeks, rather than being free to roam the UK at will and entice media coverage in a way his lieutenants fail to.‘Disgraceful’: what one election photo tells us about British politics in 2026Read moreThe prospect of a “people versus the establishment” battle which Farage so clearly craved did not materialise when other main parties ignored the contest, while a parliamentary standards investigation into the payment has once again started after it was only paused during the byelection.Opponents have taken note.“You could say that Reform are quite good at tactics but bad at strategy, and with Clacton he made a strategic mistake because it bound him to one part of the country for six weeks,” said Giles Dilnot, the editor of ConservativeHome and a former political adviser who covered Farage for years for the BBC.“He made that decision in anger and you never make good strategic decisions when you are angry. Then he had to take a break because of the understandable toll the byelection and all that went before it this year would have taken.”Dilnot suggested two other issues that will have caused worries in Reform ranks. First, despite Reform consistently attacking the Tories, signs of a knockout blow do not seem to have materialised. Second, the centralised way in which Farage has always run his political projects may now be taking a toll.“Over the 15 years it’s always the case he is both the biggest asset and biggest weakness of any party he has led. Everything is centralised, he falls out with people and voters can also be very polarised,” said Dilnot.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRecent polls have indicated that the surge in support for Reform has stalled, with the party failing to break out beyond core supporters and signs that Farage himself might even be a drag on its further growth.A poll released last weekby More in Commonput the party at 23% – four percentage points behind Labour and Reform’s worst performance in 18 months. Labour also now leads Reform for the first time since the general election in Ipsos polling – 28% to 25%.Nearly two-thirds of the public (65%) do not believe Farage is ready to be prime minister, according to Ipsos, while nearly three-quarters backed continuing the standards investigation even before the Clacton result.Aside from struggling to shake off questions about the £5m, there was yet another reminder last week of another drag – namely Reform having to look over its shoulder at the siren call to its voters from Rupert Lowe’s hard-rightRestore Britainparty.The latter was a factor in a much-watched byelection last Thursday on Dover district council, where Reform had swept the board during Kent local elections last year, but where Farage’s party wasnarrowly pipped by the Greensafter Restore polled 10%.Nonsense, say Reform sources, pointing to new policies and attention-grabbing moves by councils such as Kent, which announced plans to “protect” communities from immigrants.“We’re coming out of this summer with a plethora of policies, our councils are getting on with it and at conference there will be more headlines, a proper fringe discussing ideas and a business engagement programme which is a major step up from last year,” said one.Reform says it will use the conference at the Birmingham NEC to set out the first 100 days of what a government led by it would do. One of the biggest questions will be whether any dissent emerges.Explore more on these topicsReform UKNigel FarageRestore BritainanalysisShareReuse this content

title: UK social mobility watchdog could be axed as ministers plan shake-up | Social mobility | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Labour MPs believe Gordon Brown-era SMC has become ineffective and its work ‘should be a core function of government’
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Exclusive: Labour MPs believe Gordon Brown-era SMC has become ineffective and its work ‘should be a core function of government’
Content: Bridget Phillipson, the equalities minister, is reportedly one of the Labour figures who is keen to disband the SMC.Photograph: WIktor Szymanowicz/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBridget Phillipson, the equalities minister, is reportedly one of the Labour figures who is keen to disband the SMC.Photograph: WIktor Szymanowicz/NurPhoto/ShutterstockSocial mobilityUK social mobility watchdog could be axed as ministers plan shake-upExclusive: Labour MPs believe Gordon Brown-era SMC has become ineffective and its work ‘should be a core function of government’Ben QuinnandPeter WalkerMon 31 Aug 2026 08.23 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 13.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMinisters are considering a shake-up of the government’s social mobility watchdog that could range from giving it more teeth to abolishing it outright.The move comes amid concerns that the Social Mobility Commission (SMC) – originally conceived under Gordon Brown’s government in 2010 – has become ineffective.Bridget Phillipson, the equalities minister, and others are said to feel strongly that work to improve social mobility – and thus the life chances of poorer children and families – should be a core function of government rather than being outsourced to arm’s lengths bodies such as the SMC.It is understood to be within the scope of a Cabinet Office review of such bodies and was considered for closure last year on the basis that central government could carry out its limited functions more effectively.The commission has no powers to determine government policy, hold public bodies to account or make recommendations to ministers. Instead, its sole statutory responsibility is to produce an annual state of the nation report on social mobility in the UK, which evaluates opportunities and inequalities.However, while the SMC was conceived as the ChildPovertyCommission by the previous Labour government in 2010, those in the Burnham government believe its focus on child poverty was diluted under the coalition government and subsequent Tory administrations. “It has essentially become a thinktank inside government,” said a source.It wasrenamed the Child Poverty and Social Mobility Commission in 2012, before becoming the SMC in 2016, when Iain Duncan Smith scrapped then legally binding child poverty targets.Alan Milburn, the former Labour minister now leading areview into the million young people who are Neet(not in education, employment or training), was appointed chair but resigned in 2017, saying government was “unable to devote the necessary energy and focus to the social mobility agenda”.A year later, a report from the education select committee made a series of recommendations to give the SMC “real teeth”, all of which were rejected by the then children’s minister,Nadhim Zahawi.A Whitehall source said: “Reducing inequality and supporting working-class communities is at the heart of this government’s agenda. Tracking progress will always be important, but ultimately this is work that should be a core function of government.“We’re looking at all the options to make sure we’re really set-up to deliver the change people want to see in their lives as quickly and effectively as possible.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘It’s rare to hear: I’m black and middle class’ – Symeon Brown on black Britain’s enduring ‘taboo’Read moreAny changes would be expected to be announced over the course of this parliamentary term, but new legislation would be needed to disband an organisation set out in statute.The body is chaired byAlun Francis, who is also the chief executive of Blackpool and The Fylde college, alongside two deputy chairs andfour commissioners. They are supported by a secretariat of about 20 civil servants working in the Cabinet Office.The SMC’smost recent state of the nation reportsaid former industrial communities across Britain face “entrenched disadvantages” stretching back decades and highlighted “extreme regional differences”, citing poorer childhood conditions, fewer job opportunities, less innovation and lack of growth.The report saidYorkshire, the north-east, the Midlands, Wales and Scotland were still living with the impacts of deindustrialisation, describing “half a century of economic disadvantage and decline”.Burnham, who has previously rejected what he characterised as Westminster’s fixed view of social mobility, has prioritised local devolution, technical education and housing policy at the heart of his vision of social mobility.Phillipson, the former eduction secretary and nowLabourparty chair whose equalities brief includes sponsorship of the SMC, has also consistently spoken about social mobility, drawing on her own experience as a child of a working-class family in England’s north-east.Explore more on these topicsSocial mobilityBridget PhillipsonAndy BurnhamIain Duncan SmithNadhim ZahawiLabourPovertynewsShareReuse this content

title: Hiker, 91, becomes oldest person to complete grueling Appalachian Trail | US news | The Guardian
description: Dale Sanders said he fell 71 times on the trail, but completed the journey as ‘people are motivated … by my efforts’
Author: Lucy Campbell
Headline: Dale Sanders said he fell 71 times on the trail, but completed the journey as ‘people are motivated … by my efforts’
Content: Appalachian Trail hiker Dale Sanders wades across Big Wilson Stream on the 100-Mile Wilderness north of Monson, Maine, Wednesday, July 29, 2026.Photograph: Robert F Bukaty/APView image in fullscreenAppalachian Trail hiker Dale Sanders wades across Big Wilson Stream on the 100-Mile Wilderness north of Monson, Maine, Wednesday, July 29, 2026.Photograph: Robert F Bukaty/APUS newsHiker, 91, becomes oldest person to complete grueling Appalachian TrailDale Sanders said he fell 71 times on the trail, but completed the journey as ‘people are motivated … by my efforts’Lucy Campbelland agenciesMon 31 Aug 2026 18.17 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 18.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 91-year-old hiker has reclaimed his record as the oldest person to complete the more than 2,000-mile Appalachian Trail.By his count, Dale Sanders, ofTennessee, fell 71 times during the feat, six of which he said were hard falls and one which required a brief hospitalization and another just 200 yards from the end. The 2,193-mile trail runs between Springer Mountain in Georgia and Mount Katahdin in Maine.The Appalachian Trail Conservancy defines a thru-hike as completing all of the trail’s sections in any order within a year, allowing for pauses. Sanders began his hike on 6 September 2025 in West Virginia and, allowing for some brief breaks, he completed his journey on Monday atop Maine’s highest peak, where he paused to pray at the sign marking the summit.“I had to thank God, and I had to thank my support team and everybody that got me here,” Sanders, whose trail name is Grey Beard, told the Associated Press.View image in fullscreenDale Sanders celebrates after completing a difficult section of Mt Katahdin in Baxter state park in Piscataquis county, Maine.Photograph: Robert F Bukaty/APSanders first set the Appalachian Trail record in 2017 when he was 82, only to be overtaken four years later by his 83-year-old friend MJ Eberhart, whose trail name is Nimblewill Nomad.Within months, Sanders announced his comeback plan. But despite six months of training, he told the AP, he still was not in the best condition. “And even today, I feel that I should probably be in better shape than I am,” he said last month. “But I just have to always go back and say: ‘But I am 91, so I’m blazing new ground hiking long distances like this.’”In June, Sanders was descending Killington Mountain in central Vermont when he fell forward in a boulder field, scraping his legs, arms and hands. “Thank God nothing got broken, but I was banged up,” he said. “I didn’t rub the blood off, I just kept hiking.”Weeks later, his left arm went numb and he ended up at a hospital in Maine with what turned out to be a pinched nerve. But although he was soon cleared to resume hiking, he at that point considered giving up.When he returned home to Tennessee in early August to be with his wife, whose mother had just died, she convinced him to press on with his mission.Some of Sanders’ best days were inPennsylvania, where he said he enjoyed well-maintained trails and treats delivered by “trail angels”. “When people are taking care of you and bringing you caramel frappes on the trail, the rocks don’t matter,” he said.Also pushing him to keep going were his thousands of followers on social media. “I wanna get [my record] back, but right now, that’s secondary,” he told the AP. “Right now, what’s the most important thing – and it’s one of the things that surprised me – is that people are motivated and given encouragement by my efforts.”View image in fullscreenSanders takes a brief power nap near Monson, Maine, on 28 July 2026.Photograph: Robert F Bukaty/APSanders was born in Kentucky in 1935, two years before the Appalachian Trail was completed. Bullied as a child for his small size, he gained confidence in solo sports such as acrobatics and swimming. He later served in the navy and retired in 2002 after a long career in parks and recreation.He holds numerous other age-related records, including becomingthe oldest personto paddle the entire length of the Mississippi River in 2022, an 87-day trip he started on his 87th birthday.Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsUS newsTennesseePennsylvaniaAdventure travelnewsShareReuse this content

title: Head of Viktor Orbán’s favourite thinktank quits over unpaid wages | Thinktanks | The Guardian
description: Frank Furedi announces resignation with immediate effect after organisation’s staff ‘not paid in July or August’
Author: Jennifer Rankin
Headline: Frank Furedi announces resignation with immediate effect after organisation’s staff ‘not paid in July or August’
Content: Frank Furedi said the thinktank’s failure to provide funds meant it had effectively ceased operations.Photograph: Tibor Illyes/EPA-EFE/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenFrank Furedi said the thinktank’s failure to provide funds meant it had effectively ceased operations.Photograph: Tibor Illyes/EPA-EFE/ShutterstockThinktanksHead of Viktor Orbán’s favourite thinktank quits over unpaid wagesFrank Furedi announces resignation from MCC Brussels after organisation’s staff ‘not paid in July or August’Jennifer Rankinin BrusselsMon 31 Aug 2026 13.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 13.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe head of Viktor Orbán’s favourite Brussels thinktank has quit, citing unpaid wages since the change of government in Hungary.The sociology professor Frank Furedi said he was resigning as the executive director of MCC Brussels with “immediate effect” on Monday over “persistent failure to provide the contractually agreed funds”.‘Attack on civil society’: why Viktor Orbán’s favourite thinktank is in crisisRead moreA spokesperson for MCC Brussels confirmed Furedi’s resignation and said no one working for the organisation in the EU capital had been paid in July or August.MCC Brussels launched in late 2022 with a self-styled mission to shake up political debate in the EU capital, although critics said it defended Orbán’s illiberal rule in Hungary whileusing a well-funded position to attack civil society groups.It was an ostensibly independent offshoot of the Mathias Corvinus Collegium Foundation in Budapest, a training ground for Orbán’s Fidesz party that was lavishly funded by his rightwing nationalist government.The future of MCC Brussels was thrown into doubt whenPéter Magyar won a landslide election victory in Aprilpledging to crack down on corruption in Hungary, which numerous independent organisations said had proliferated during Orbán’s 16 years in power. Soon after his victory, Magyar promised to end state financing for MCC Budapest and to investigate a large transfer of state assets to the organisation, which he described as a crime.Furedihas previously dismissedMagyar’s claims of a criminal transfer of assets to MCC Budapest as “bullshit”, while MCC Brussels said it condemned corruption by all politicians.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Guardian view on the new Hungary: de-Orbánising at pace | EditorialRead moreIn a letter to the senior leadership of MCC Budapest seen by the Guardian, Furedi wrote: “Without the contractually agreed resources, our colleagues cannot function and are facing serious economic hardship. We have been placed in a situation where our individual reputations and the integrity of our intellectual mission are systematically undermined.”The failure to provide funds, Furedi said, meant MCC Brussels had effectively ceased operations and was unable to pay suppliers or meet conditions under Belgian insolvency law.Furedi said he intended to ensure, “along with like-minded individuals, the work and intellectual legacy of our institution will continue to flourish in another form”, without elaborating on future plans.The letter wasfirst reported by Politico. MCC Budapest did not immediately respond to a request for comment.MCC Budapest has also seen change at the top following the election of the new government. The MCC board was previously led by Viktor Orbán’s chief of staff, Balázs Orbán, who is no relation to the former prime minister. Balázs Orbán, now an MP for the Fidesz party, announced he was standing down as chair in June.The MCC Brussels spokesperson said after Furedi’s resignation and a round of lay-offs in June and July, MCC Brussels was down to 12 staff and three research fellows. Before the cuts it had employed 25 people and was one of the best-funded thinktanks in Brussels.Explore more on these topicsThinktanksViktor OrbánBelgiumHungaryEuropeEuropean UnionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Met Gala exhibition honoring John Galliano is cancelled after backlash | John Galliano | The Guardian
description: Fashion designer was convicted of hate crime by French court in 2011 after series of racist and antisemitic remarks
Author: Anna Betts
Headline: Fashion designer was convicted of hate crime by French court in 2011 after series of racist and antisemitic remarks
Content: John Galliano in December 2017.Photograph: Jeff Spicer/BFC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJohn Galliano in December 2017.Photograph: Jeff Spicer/BFC/Getty ImagesJohn GallianoMet Gala exhibition honoring John Galliano is cancelled after backlashFashion designer was convicted of hate crime by French court in 2011 after series of racist and antisemitic remarksAnna BettsMon 31 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 15.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe controversial fashion designerJohn Gallianoannounced on Monday that an exhibition honoring his work that New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art had scheduled to open for the upcoming spring’s Met Gala is not going to go forward.The museum’s decision to honor Galliano, who wasconvictedof a hate crime by a French court in 2011after aseries of racist and antisemitic remarks, had drawn controversy and backlash.“After much reflection and discussion with all those involved, I have decided, with great sadness, that it is best for the exhibition not to take place at this time,” Galliano wrote in astatementposted on Instagram on Monday morning.The exhibition, titledJohn Galliano: Horizons, wasannounced in early Augustand was set to have been kicked off by the annual Met Gala.In his statement on Monday saying that the exhibition was off, Galliano wrote: “I remain fully accountable for the pain caused by my words in the past, particularly the hurt I caused to the Jewish and Asian communities, and I remain deeply sorry.“I understand that meaningful atonement is not achieved through an exhibition, institutional recognition or a single public gesture. It is a continuing responsibility, demonstrated through listening, learning and one’s conduct over time.”He also wrote: “I do not want the debate surrounding me to place the Met in a difficult position or distract from the remarkable work of the Costume Institute. I also recognize and respect that an exhibition honoring my work would be painful for some.”In a separatestatementon Monday, the Metropolitan Museum of Art director and chief executive officer, Max Hollein, said: “Following thoughtful discussions with John Galliano, we have together decided not to proceed with the exhibition.”The Met trustee Anna Wintouradded: “John’s decision that the exhibition devoted to his work should not take place at this time is very courageous and a measure of the man he is.“I believe this is the right decision, and both he and the museum have my full support.”TheNew York Timeshad reported on Friday that opposition to the museum’s plans with respect to Galliano had grown in recent days among Jewish leaders in New York City and beyond. The newspaper also reported that some donors had contacted Met executives and threatened to withdraw gifts to the museum if the exhibition went ahead as planned.The New York City council speaker, Julie Menin, alsosent a letterto the Met leadership, calling the museum’s decision to honor Galliano “a mistake”. Menin also urged the institution to reconsider.On Monday, Menin wrote on social media: “Museums such as The Met must be held to a high standard of inclusiveness and tolerance, and I am pleased that they have listened to the concerns I have raised and reacted with the right decision.”Menin also described herself as the daughter of a Holocaust survivor and the first Jewish speaker of theNew YorkCity council, saying, “This decision was personal to me, and the Jewish community and I felt a strong obligation to speak out.”TheNew York Timesreported that the Met’s board of trustees had been scheduled to gather on Monday morning to discuss the exhibition.The museum said on Monday that details about “a new spring Costume Institute exhibition and the 2027Met Galawill be announced at a later date”.The remarks which resulted in Galliano’s hate crime conviction in France also led to his being fired as creative director of the famous fashion brand Christian Dior.Explore more on these topicsJohn GallianoMet GalaNew YorknewsShareReuse this content

title: Defense lawyers for singer D4vd withdraw from murder case | Los Angeles | The Guardian
description: Singer accused of murder and sexual abuse of teen Celeste Rivas Hernandez to be represented by LA public defender
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Singer accused of murder and sexual abuse of teen Celeste Rivas Hernandez to be represented by LA public defender
Content: Blair Berk, left, and Marilyn Bednarski, right, with their former client D4vd at a hearing in Los Angeles in April.Photograph: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBlair Berk, left, and Marilyn Bednarski, right, with their former client D4vd at a hearing in Los Angeles in April.Photograph: Getty ImagesLos AngelesDefense lawyers for singer D4vd withdraw from murder caseSinger, accused of murder and sexual abuse of teen Celeste Rivas Hernandez, to be represented by LA public defenderAssociated PressMon 31 Aug 2026 15.18 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 15.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSinger D4vd lost his high-profile private lawyers on Monday at a hearing where he entered a new not guilty plea to charges that he killed, sexually abused and dismembered 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez.It is not clear why Blair Berk and her colleagues Marilyn Bednarski and Regina Peter parted ways with the singer, whose legal name is David Anthony Burke. They were replaced by a lawyer from theLos Angelescounty public defender’s office.The defense attorneys said in a statement only that the judge granted their request to withdraw after finding that Burke qualified for a court-appointed lawyer.“We continue to support David and his defense against these serious charges,” the statement said. The lawyers would not answer specific questions about their departure outside the courtroom.Burke earned at least $10m through his music from 2023 through 2025, according to testimony from his money handlers at a previous hearing. It is not clear how he financially qualifies for a public defender whose job is to defend clients who lack the money for a lawyer.Without providing details, the public defender’s office said in an email that it had completed a thorough financial evaluation and found he was eligible.Deputy public defender Walid Kandeel took over the defense. Judge Charlaine F Olmedo denied his first request as the singer’s lawyer to delay the arraignment. Olmedo demanded a plea on Monday instead, and scheduled a status conference for October. No trial date has been set.Olmedo ruled after a five-day evidentiary hearing in July that there was enough evidence for Burke to stand trial on charges of murder, continuous lewd and lascivious acts with a child under 14 and unlawful mutilation of human remains.A second arraignment and plea, like Burke gave on Monday, is standard practice after such a hearing and finding. He is eligible for the death penalty, but the district attorney, Nathan Hochman, said after Monday’s hearing that his office was still deciding whether to pursue it.Hochman said the new lawyers would make no difference in how his office pursues the case, though the switch may delay the process. He said regardless of the timing, his office was “ready to prove all three charges beyond a reasonable doubt”.Outgoing attorney Berk has for years been among the go-to lawyers for A-list clients, who have included Leonardo DiCaprio, Jennifer Aniston, Reese Witherspoon, Harvey Weinstein and Ozzy Osbourne.Kandeel, the new attorney, said in a statement: “We recognize the loss of life underlying the allegations and extend our sympathies to those who are grieving. At the same time, David Burke is entitled to a defense that takes his circumstances seriously and carefully examines the evidence.”Authorities allege Burke stabbed Celeste to death in April of last year after she threatened to expose sexual abuse that began when she was 13 and crater his rising career just days before his debut album dropped.“i will end ur career and ur life,” she told him in a text message sent the night before her death.Prosecutors said the following night Burke sent an Uber for her and stabbed her when she entered his house. They presented evidence that her phone went permanently silent at that moment.Celeste’s dismembered and decomposing body was found in the trunk of Burke’s Tesla in the Hollywood Hills in September while he was on tour.Prosecutors argued at the July hearing that the “mountains of evidence” they presented were overwhelming. Burke’s lawyers argued that the evidence of murder was insufficient.Explore more on these topicsLos AngelesCaliforniaWest CoastUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: BT on track for estimated £2bn windfall from selling old copper amid AI boom | BT | The Guardian
description: Telecoms company to benefit from soaring prices for recycled metal recovered from full-fibre broadband rollout
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: Telecoms company to benefit from soaring prices for recycled metal recovered from full-fibre broadband rollout
Content: BT’s Openreach subsidiary is recovering more copper cabling than expected from the full-fibre broadband rollout.Photograph: Ian Rutherford/AlamyView image in fullscreenBT’s Openreach subsidiary is recovering more copper cabling than expected from the full-fibre broadband rollout.Photograph: Ian Rutherford/AlamyBTBT on track for estimated £2bn windfall from selling old copper amid AI boomTelecoms company to benefit from soaring prices for recycled metal recovered from full-fibre broadband rolloutMark SweneyMon 31 Aug 2026 10.06 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBT is on track for an estimated £2bn-plus windfall over the next decade from selling off old copper cabling, as it cashes in on soaring prices amid the AI market frenzy and switches the UK’s network to full-fibre broadband.Copper is one of the main beneficiaries of the“electrification of everything”, essential for the rapid growth of AI datacentres, electronics and the fast-growing renewable energy industry.The metal hit its highest-ever closing price of $14,294 a metric tonne on Friday, close to the record intraday high of $14,500 reached earlier this year amid global shortage fears.BT has a recycling deal with EMR, the UK’s largest cable granulation company, and has now received £99m upfront for thousands of tonnes of surplus stripped copper.It is the second such payment received by the telecoms company, which is rolling out full-fibre broadband to 30m homes by the end of the decade through its Openreach subsidiary,after £105m in 2024.The forward sale agreements, which are understood to cover the delivery of about 20,000 tonnes of copper over a four-year period each, do not include any revenue BT makes each year if it chooses to sell recycled copper on the spot market.BT recovered a record nearly 10,000 tonnes in the year to the end of March, almost three times the amount it managed in the year to the end of March 2024, and a total of 22,347 tonnes since the telecoms company began stripping and selling the cabling in 2023.The record haul, which is 63% more than the 5,600 tonnes reported in BT’s 2025 results, comes at a time of soaring prices which could handsomely benefit BT.In the year that BT reported its first copper haul the average price for the metal was about $8,500 a tonne.“We recovered even more copper cabling,” said Mike McTighe, the chair of Openreach, acknowledging the potential financial benefit of the market surge, in BT’s latest annual report. “Removing 9,147 tonnes from our network for recycling at a time when global demand has never been higher.”Howeer, the jump in value has also made the metal a target of thieves across Britain’stelephone network,railwaysand evenwindfarms.View image in fullscreenCopper prices have been a beneficiary of the ‘electrification of everything’.Photograph: KHAM/ReutersOpenreach has said it expects to be able to recover up to 200,000 tonnes, with telecoms cabling producing high-grade recycled copper, as the programme runs through the 2030s in line with moving customers on to full-fibre connections.While the precise details of BT’s contract with EMR, which initially runs until 2028, are not known, the market value of the copper it expects to be able to extract hadpreviously been estimated at £1.5bn.However, the soaring price of copper and a future supply crunch – the rating agency S&P Global expects demand to grow from 25m metric tonnes now to about 50m by 2035 – means at current market prices BT’s entire copper tonnage could be valued at £2bn-plus.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Copper has become one of the most strategic materials in the modern economy,” said Abby Chicken, the head of sustainability at Openreach. “As we connect the nation to more reliable full fibre, we’re able to retire parts of the legacy network that are no longer needed.“Recovering and recycling that copper is the right thing to do. It reduces waste, supports the UK’s energy transition towards renewables and helps keep a critical resource in circulation at a time when growing demand is putting pressure on global supply chains.”Amid the soaring prices, Openreach hasactedto prevent copper theft. Last year, thieves struck in St Neots, Cambridgeshire,twice in a month, resulting in nearly a mile of underground cables being damaged.In 2024, Openreach suffered copper thefts in the New Forest,affecting 128 premises,and County Tyrone, Northern Ireland, leaving hundreds of homes and businesses with connectivity issues.Openreach is using a wide range of anti-theft measures including coating miles of underground cables with a synthetic DNA and UV tracer, called SelectaDNA.This is widely used across the Openreach network and the tracer easily transfers to hands and clothing.Openreach reported a30% fall in copper phone and broadband cable theft in 2024, which it attributed to the deployment of the new technology.However, this technology cannot be applied to cables that are already underground, meaning thieves continue to target copper cables.Explore more on these topicsBTTelecommunications industryTelecomsCommoditiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: US trade regulator and 22 states accuse Amazon of taking $20bn with secret surcharges  | Amazon | The Guardian
description: FTC alleges in lawsuit that online retailer ‘secretly and systematically overcharged’ advertisers for years
Author: Dara Kerr
Headline: FTC alleges in lawsuit that online retailer ‘secretly and systematically overcharged’ advertisers for years
Content: ‘Amazon has millions of advertising customers who were misled into paying significantly higher prices,’ the FTC chair says.Photograph: Charles-McClintock Wilson/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Amazon has millions of advertising customers who were misled into paying significantly higher prices,’ the FTC chair says.Photograph: Charles-McClintock Wilson/NurPhoto/ShutterstockAmazonUS trade regulator and 22 states accuse Amazon of taking $20bn with secret surchargesFTC alleges in lawsuit that online retailer ‘secretly and systematically overcharged’ advertisers for yearsDara KerrandBlake MontgomeryMon 31 Aug 2026 15.41 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 17.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US’s main trade regulator and 22 states suedAmazonon Monday, alleging the online retailer “secretly and systematically overcharged” advertisers on Amazon.com.The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) said these practices led to higher costs for customers on items like groceries and other essential goods that are sold onAmazon.“Amazon has millions of advertising customers who were misled into paying significantly higher prices. These higher costs were largely passed on to American consumers,” said Andrew Ferguson, the FTC chair.The agency accused the company of taking in more than $20bn from “hidden surcharges”, in what it deems an “ad-rigging scheme”. Amazon’s advertising business has grown significantly in recent years, becoming the third-largest online advertising marketplace after Google and Meta. The FTC says Amazon generates more than $68bn in ad revenue on its website.The lawsuit alleges that 1.2 million advertising customers were overcharged since 2019, including more than 500,000 small- and medium-sized businesses.An Amazon spokesperson pointed the Guardian to ablog postthe company published in response to the legal action, which calls the legal action a “misguided lawsuit”.“Amazon strongly disagrees,” the post reads.The government’s case hinges on Amazon’s advertising auction system, called “second-price auctions”, that lets the winning bidder pay only slightly more than the second-highest bid. Regulators allege that with this system, Amazon could secretly raise the second-highest bids with a higher “shill” bid of its own.“We believe Amazon manipulated its ad auctions to inflate what sellers had to pay, adding billions of dollars in costs that ultimately get passed on to customers with higher prices,” said Jeff Jackson, the attorney general for North Carolina, one of the states involved in the suit.The suit alleges Amazon tested how much it could increase the amount it charges without advertisers flinching. Internal documents show one manager allegedly describing the company’s pricing strategy as “hoping that advertisers don’t notice and decrease bids or ad spend”.Amazon denied these allegations and said the company gives “customers the lowest prices every day across the widest selection of products”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“After reviewing approximately 1.5 million pages spanning six years, the FTC leans on a handful of simplified communications to allege a companywide effort to deceive,” Amazon wrote in its blog post. “That is patently false.”Rob Bonta, the attorney general for California, noted in a press conference that the lawsuit arises from a partnership between conservative states, liberal ones, and the federal government. He said this lawsuit is focusing on Amazon’s alleged unlawful activities and its deception around those practices.“Amazon’s price inflation is illegal, plain and simple,” Bonta said. “This is a massive corporation. They can be wildly successful and also follow the law.”The federal agency and states are asking the court to bar Amazon from continuing the allegedly deceptive advertising practices, along with paying civil penalties and refunding advertisers.Explore more on these topicsAmazonLaw (US)E-commerceInternetAdvertisingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Properties in UK national parks command 24% premium, study finds | Housing market | The Guardian
description: Nationwide research also shows average 14% premium for housing in national landscapes of England and Wales
Author: Simon Goodley
Headline: Nationwide research also shows average 14% premium for housing in national landscapes of England and Wales
Content: The town of Lyndhurst in the New Forest, which remains the most expensive national park in which to buy a house, according to the building society.Photograph: Greg Balfour Evans/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe town of Lyndhurst in the New Forest, which remains the most expensive national park in which to buy a house, according to the building society.Photograph: Greg Balfour Evans/AlamyHousing marketProperties in UK national parks command 24% premium, study findsNationwide research also shows average 14% premium for housing in national landscapes of England and WalesSimon GoodleyMon 31 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 00.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHousebuyers are paying a premium of almost a quarter to own a property located within a UK national park, with the New Forest the most expensive national park to live in, according to Britain’s biggest building society.Nationwide found that a property located within a national park cost 24% more on average than a similar property elsewhere, while buyers were also stumping up a 6% premium for homes within three miles of a national park.The lender said that, as well as the attractions of the beautiful countryside, restricted development in national parks meant construction of new housing was limited, which kept house prices relatively high.The average property inthe New Forestwas £563,000, followed by the South Downs park at £485,000, and the Peak District at £450,000.Nationwide also found a 14% premium for properties located in the national landscapes ofEnglandand Wales, formerly known as areas of outstanding natural beauty, such as Surrey Hills and the Chilterns.Surrey Hills is the most expensive national landscape in which to buy property, with average prices of £710,000, the building society said. Designated in 1958 and covering approximately a quarter of the county of Surrey, the area is home to about 40,000 people who mostly live in small villages and rural hamlets, such as Shere, Mickleham and Westhumble.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe premiums paid on properties in these areas appear to be remaining remarkably consistent, withsimilar research by Nationwide from 2024showing that homes in national parks attracted a 25% premium, while national landscape properties were 15% more expensive.Explore more on these topicsHousing marketPropertyNational parksHouse pricesEnglandWalesScotlandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Gen Z ‘Chinamaxxers’ fantasise about life in China. This journalist and this artist can never go back there | Comics and graphic novels | The Guardian
description: A graphic novel by Melissa Chan and Badiucao imagines China and the US at war in 2035. They hope to remind young people that ‘authoritarianism everywhere is bad’
Author: Kat Wong
Headline: A graphic novel by Melissa Chan and Badiucao imagines China and the US at war in 2035. They hope to remind young people that ‘authoritarianism everywhere is bad’
Content: ‘The younger generation feel like there is no meaningful method to change society,’ says Badiucao (right) with journalist Melissa Chan at Sydney’s Carriageworks.Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The younger generation feel like there is no meaningful method to change society,’ says Badiucao (right) with journalist Melissa Chan at Sydney’s Carriageworks.Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianComics and graphic novelsInterviewGen Z ‘Chinamaxxers’ fantasise about life in China. This journalist and this artist can never go back thereKat WongA graphic novel by Melissa Chan and Badiucao imagines China and the US at war in 2035. They hope to remind young people that ‘authoritarianism everywhere is bad’Mon 31 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 20.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDrinking Tsingtao beers, eating congee, walking with hands behind their backs: for many young people in western countries, “Chinamaxxing” has become all the rage.
