Some content creators have even gone beyond the jokes about being in “a very Chinese time in my life” and have followed this passion to the Middle Kingdom: making TikToks in Chongqing’s multilayered metropolis, bathing in Chengdu’s 24-hour spas or backflipping on the Great Wall of China.When your culture becomes a meme: the ‘jarring’ effect of ChinamaxxingRead moreThis irreverent, mostly ironic trend is jarring for some, but Chinese Australian artist Badiucao and Chinese American journalist Melissa Chan don’t want to lecture the so-called Chinamaxxers.“The younger generation feel like there is no meaningful method to change society. They feel defeated when they see what’s happening in Gaza – there’s been protests but the government doesn’t care and is collaborating with atrocities in wars. There’s also the Epstein files in America, which show how the elite is corrupt,” says Badiucao, who, along with Chan, is in Sydney to promote their new book, You Must Take Part in Revolution.“When you want to see change, there is the hard way, which is being innovative and finding a solution. And there is the lazy way, which is finding a cheap alternative and fantasising about a faraway, oriental, communist country that might be your future,” he says.View image in fullscreen‘We don’t want to just lecture,’ says Badiucao.Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianChan and Badiucao have both paid the price for criticising China’s one-party system. Chinese officials refused to renew Chan’s press credentials before expelling the former Al Jazeera journalist from China in 2012; and the previously anonymous political cartoonist Badiucao wasforced to reveal his identity in 2019after it was compromised and authorities threatened his family in China.You Must Take Part in Revolution, the pair’s debut graphic novel, portrays a dystopian future where China is at war with the United States in 2035.View image in fullscreenYou Must Take Part in Revolution by Badiucao and Melissa Chan.Illustration: Simon & SchusterThe graphic novel features a variety of characters from the Chinese-speaking diaspora, including from Hong Kong, Taiwan, the US and Tibet, as they decide what choices they are willing to make under authoritarian oppression.“It was intentional to show the panoply of Asian identities that have been impacted by a great power,” Chan says. “It opens up the possibility to get young people to better understand it’s not just a ‘Chinese time in my life’, that there’s a lot going on here … hopefully it can get a few people thinking about resistance movements both present and in the past.”“We don’t want to just lecture,” Badiucao adds. “We really want readers to put themselves in the eyes of those characters as if they were a real human being with a real life.”Chan now lives in Berlin and has written for the Atlantic, the Washington Post, Time, and others, while Badiucao, who lives in Melbourne, has exhibited works across the world. They started working on the graphic novel five years ago after first meeting in Germany during the late 2010s.View image in fullscreen‘If things are shit, they’re shit in any country,’ says Chan.Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianYou Must Take Part in Revolution starts off in the real-life Hong Kong protests of 2019, when almost two million people took to the streets to denounce a controversial law that would allow the extradition of suspects to mainland China. The law was viewed as a sign of growing mainland influence in Hong Kong.While the graphic novel is geographically grounded in an Asia governed by authoritarian China, it also portrays the US as a proto-fascist state, resisting the idea that criticising one necessarily means painting the other in a positive light.“This book happens to focus on China, but authoritarianism everywhere is bad,” Chan says. “We don’t want anyone to engage in whataboutism and I don’t think there needs to be a balance – if things are shit, they’re shit in any country.”Unlike other graphic novels such as Art Spiegelman’s Maus, Badiucao and Chan’s book takes its influence from Japanese manga. “There are great works like Attack on Titan which are not necessarily about specific history or political content that have so many metaphors reflecting important things like racism, war and equity,” Badiucao says.“It’s part of the reason this form is potentially more than just entertainment or some kid stuff, it really influences an entire generation.”You Must Take Part in Revolution was released in the US in 2025, but it is only just getting its Australian release this week and its UK release in October.Badiucao says readers across the world have contacted them about their own histories after reading it, including Ukrainian refugees who have escaped Russia’s invasion, and Czech communities who lived through the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic.View image in fullscreenThe artist recalls one interaction at a comic festival in New York, where a second-generation Chinese Canadian girl told him that she had hesitations about taking the book home. “I don’t think my mum would love it,” she said.A few minutes later, an older woman came up to Badiucao and explained she was an immigrant whose family had been through hardship during the Cultural Revolution. Flipping through the book, she said her daughter might like it, but she didn’t know if she would be open to learning about Chinese politics.Badiucao later discovered the two were mother and daughter.“I told the daughter her mum might be more open about political stuff, and I told the mum that your daughter might be interested too,” he says. “They ended up having an honest conversation, and they got a copy of the book … among all the interactions with readers, that was pretty special to me.”You Must Take Part in Revolutionby Melissa Chan and Badiucao is out now in Australia (Affirm Press; $39.99), as well as in the US. It is out in the UK on 8 October.This article was amended on 1 September 2026 to provide the UK release date of You Must Take Part in Revolution. A previous version said the book had already been published in the UK.Explore more on these topicsComics and graphic novelsFestivalsFictionArt and design booksAustralian booksChinafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The whistling on the theme tune? That’s Dickie Attenborough!’ Hayley Mills on Whistle Down the Wind | Movies | The Guardian
description: ‘I’d just made two films in America. Shooting on a Lancashire farm was very different. There was mud everywhere – and we’d be eating dripping, jam butties and fried eggs in buns’
Author: Chris Broughton
Headline: ‘I’d just made two films in America. Shooting on a Lancashire farm was very different. There was mud everywhere – and we’d be eating dripping, jam butties and fried eggs in buns’
Content: ‘Just a fella’ … Hayley Mills and Alan Bates in the 1961 film Whistle Down the Wind.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Just a fella’ … Hayley Mills and Alan Bates in the 1961 film Whistle Down the Wind.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyHow we madeMovies‘The whistling on the theme tune? That’s Dickie Attenborough!’ Hayley Mills on Whistle Down the Wind‘I’d just made two films in America. Shooting on a Lancashire farm was very different. There was mud everywhere – and we’d be eating dripping, jam butties and fried eggs in buns’Interviews byChris BroughtonMon 31 Aug 2026 09.21 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 10.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHayley Mills,played Kathy BostockWhistle Down the Wind was originally a novel written by my mother, Mary Hayley Bell, about three children living on a farm in Sussex. The children – loosely based on my sister Juliet, my brother Jonathan and myself – discover a man in their barn. Thinking he’s Jesus, they decide to hide him and protect him from the adults because they don’t want the same thing to happen to him as before.Dickie Attenboroughthought it was a wonderful story, and convinced my parents it should be made into a film by the production company he’d set up with the actor and writerBryan Forbes. After the original director,Guy Green, pulled out, Bryan took over at the 11th hour. He’d never directed before. When Dickie asked if he could do it, he apparently said: “I’ve no idea. We’ll soon find out!”Keith WaterhouseandWillis Hallwere engaged as writers and made the brilliant decision to move the story to a remote part of Lancashire. The perfect location was found in the village of Downham, at the foot of Pendle Hill, famous for the witch hunts. Nearly all of the children in the film were local: the only experienced child actors were Roy Holder, who played Jackie, and me. I was 14 and a head and shoulders taller than most of the other kids. The sleeves on my coat were too short and my arms stuck out like a scarecrow’s.double quotation markBryan really whacked me! It wasn’t until cameras stopped rolling that I criedI’d just made two films in America for Disney. Shooting on a Lancashire farm in winter was very different: there was mud everywhere, and we often had to walk very carefully on duckboards. But I always loved filming in England. We’d be eating dripping, jam butties and fried eggs in a bun. Bryan was great at communicating what he wanted from the children without just getting them to parrot him. In the scene where the boy slaps me in the playground, the hand in the closeup was actually Bryan’s. He really whacked me! Kathy isn’t supposed to show that she’s been affected, so it wasn’t until cameras stopped rolling that I cried.Watch a trailer for Whistle Down the WindArthur Ibbetson’s black and white cinematography wonderfully captured the stark, leafless trees and the mist blowing across the hills. It had a sort of film noir quality, and as a child I loved the night shoots. This was all beautifully complemented byMalcolm Arnold’s poignant, nostalgic music. His arrangement of We Three Kings was a perfect fit for the kids’ tiny figures leaping like hares on the brow of the hill – and that’s Dickie himself whistling on the main theme.I’ve always said Alan Barnes stole the show as my little brother, Charles. He was only seven. The first morning on location, there was a row of director’s chairs with the names of adult cast and crew members on them. He pointed at Alan Bates’s chair and said, “Ey up, they’ve spelled me name wrong.” By the next day, the props department had made a tiny chair just for him. One of his lines became the most quoted one from the film: “It isn’t Jesus. It’s just a fella.” He delivered it perfectly.Diane Poole (nee Holgate), played Nan BostockI was 10 when Bryan and Richard visited my school. I didn’t know who they were. The head teacher just said two men would be coming to the playground to watch us play, but not to bother about it. Afterwards, a few of us were grouped together and told the men were looking for children to be in a film. When I told my mum, she said: “Don’t be so ridiculous and get your dinner eaten.” But the next dayRichard Attenboroughturned up at the front door. She was horrified as it was a Wednesday – and she wasn’t due to scrub the front step until Friday.View image in fullscreen‘Us kids didn’t go to the cinema so I didn’t know who Hayley Mills was’ … Diane Poole, centre, with Alan Barnes and Hayley Mills.Photograph: Courtesy BFI National ArchiveI remember doing a screen test up at the farm where a lot of the film was made. We just had to look round the end of a stone wall and say, “Is he coming?” without looking at the camera. I’d done school plays before and played Snow White, which involved learning quite a lot of dialogue, so this seemed easy.Nan wasn’t the child who didn’t believe, and she wasn’t the one who was totally besotted. She kept the peace between the other two. I was probably a quiet child at home: I guess they saw that in my personality. Bryan kept some of our mistakes in the film, which helps make it feel more real. In one scene, I spell “Bible” wrong and in another I mispronounce “Christmas”.In those days, us kids didn’t go to the cinema so I didn’t know who Hayley Mills was. She was like a real big sister, though, and we would act the goat together. It was only when we went to Pinewood to film scenes set inside the farmhouse that we started seeing what footage had been shot. It was a revelation. We thought: “Oh, this is what it’s all about.” They borrowed the actual back door from the real farmhouse to use on the set. My dad had a haulage firm and got one of his drivers to deliver it.View image in fullscreenPoole and Mills with Bernard Lee as Mr Bostock.Photograph: Courtesy BFI National ArchiveAlan Bates was very pleasant and softly spoken, so in the scene where he suddenly shouts at the “disciples”, we thought: “Oh crikey, what have we done?” At the London premiere, he came up and swung me around and I didn’t recognise him until he spoke, because he’d shaved his beard off. I got sent to Harrods to choose a dress for the London premiere, but I insisted on wearing the one my granny had bought me.The scene I’m most proud of is when Kathy first tells Nan about Jesus being in the barn, while they’re in bed together. That was the last thing I did at Pinewood and by then I’d got used to it all. It was a long scene, but looking at it now I think: “Yeah, you did all right there, kid.”A new 35mm print of Whistle Down the Windscreens at the BFI Southbank, London, on 4 September,with a Q&A with Hayley Mills, Diane Poole and Alan Barnes. A BFI Film Classic book, Whistle Down the Wind, is published on 3 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmHow we madeDrama filmsFamily filmsRichard AttenboroughAlan BatesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Judi Dench and Ian McKellen share stories, secrets and a little mischief | Television | The Guardian
description: The stage and screen legends reminisce over tea. Plus: Fred Sirieix checks into one of Marrakech’s grandest hotels. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Priya Elan
Headline: The stage and screen legends reminisce over tea. Plus: Fred Sirieix checks into one of Marrakech’s grandest hotels. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Pure gold … Ian McKellen in Tea With Judi Dench.Photograph: Mindhouse/PAView image in fullscreenPure gold … Ian McKellen in Tea With Judi Dench.Photograph: Mindhouse/PATV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Judi Dench and Ian McKellen share stories, secrets and a little mischiefThe stage and screen legends reminisce over tea. Plus: Fred Sirieix checks into one of Marrakech’s grandest hotels. Here’s what to watch this eveningPriya Elan,Phil Harrison,Hollie Richardson,Jack SealeandSimon WardellMon 31 Aug 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTea With Judi Dench9pm, Sky ArtsJudi and her potty-mouthed parrot Sweetheart invite Ian McKellen for a natter in the return of this charming show. Ian reminds her of when they first met, performing a play in 1967, and how Judi saved him from stage fright. Then it’s a warm, naughty hour as they share anecdotes about Ann Summers knickers, ponder the future (Judi’s eyesight is now very bad) and watch a clip of cinema flopCats: “I was frightful in the film,” says Judi. Pure gold with two icons.Hollie RichardsonMillionaire Hot Seat7.30pm, ITV1The new season of the accelerated version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? opens with six new hopefuls (sadly there’s no “Coughing Major”). The tighter format means that contestants don’t have time to doubt themselves as they ascend the money ladder. And if they get a multiple-choice question wrong, they will be eliminated.Priya ElanThe Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo8pm, BBC OneView image in fullscreenAnswering the call … Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo at Edinburgh Castle.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianRebus star Richard Rankin narrates the annual bonanza at Edinburgh Castle, which takes on the theme A Call to Gather. Expect Highland dancers, a ceremonial performance from the RAF’s King’s Colour Squadron, international music and, of course, lots of bagpipes.HRFred’s Ultimate Hotels8pm, Channel 4Fred Sirieix embarks on a luxurious new travel series, starting in Marrakech. He checks into – and has a go at being the general manager of – the exclusive Royal Mansour hotel, where the personal service is impeccable and the hammams are opulent. Then he leaves the site to check out some souks and fly in a hot-air balloon.Jack SealeMy Life Is Murder8pm, U&AlibiA lawyer is killed at an elite pub quiz, which calls for investigator Alexa Crow and sidekick Madison to – you’ve guessed it – go undercover and schmooze with the wealthy suspects. They’re a competitive bunch with a lot of history behind them, so the pair have got their work cut out before the night is over.HR24 Hours in A&E9pm, Channel 4There’s some brilliant detective work in Queen’s medical centre, Nottingham. Claire has arrived in the unit after collapsing during a run. Her case seems straightforward but doctor David has noticed something very troubling in the results of a routine blood test. As ever, impressive and affirming.Phil HarrisonFilm choiceView image in fullscreenFlair to spare … Milla Jovovich in The Fifth Element.Photograph: Gaumont/Sportsphoto/AllstarThe Fifth Element (Luc Besson, 1997), 7pm, Sky Sci-FiGiven that one of the first sci-fi films was French (Georges Méliès’ A Trip to the Moon, 1902), it’s a pity there have been so few great ones from the country since. But Luc Besson’s hyperactive movie should be up for consideration. Bruce Willis plays a cabby in 23rd-century New York who finds himself in an end-of-days race against time when he meets the “ultimate warrior”, Leeloo (Milla Jovovich), who was created to defeat an evil entity. Featuring costumes by Jean Paul Gaultier, it’s got flair and wit to spare.Simon WardellLive sportSnooker: British Open,12.30pm, Channel 5The first round from the Centaur in Cheltenham.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightJudi DenchIan McKellenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Onslaught review – super soldier slasher doesn’t go hard enough | Thrillers | The Guardian
description: There’s a committed performance from a spunky Adria Arjona in the Guest director Adam Wingard’s decent B-movie but it’s missing some sharper weaponry
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: There’s a committed performance from a spunky Adria Arjona in the Guest director Adam Wingard’s decent B-movie but it’s missing some sharper weaponry
Content: Adria Arjona in Onslaught.Photograph: Richard Foreman/Richard Foreman, Jr  SMPSPView image in fullscreenAdria Arjona in Onslaught.Photograph: Richard Foreman/Richard Foreman, Jr  SMPSPThrillersReviewOnslaught review – super soldier slasher doesn’t go hard enoughThere’s a committed performance from a spunky Adria Arjona in the Guest director Adam Wingard’s decent B-movie but it’s missing some sharper weaponryBenjamin LeeMon 31 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 12.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s something rather fascinating about an indie director who heads to the A-list before returning to their roots, a wider skillset and different perspective gained for better or worse. Working within a stricter system – the tiniest of choices being agreed upon by the largest of committees – can often be a creatively crushing experience that we’ve heard gruesomely detailed by many who survived it but the expansion of what one is allowed to technically do with a bigger budget can also be instructive and enriching. The dream scenario is bringing back the good and allowing the bad to inspire new work that makes the most of how unshackled one again now is.The Whisper Man review – Robert De Niro sleepwalks through silly Netflix potboilerRead moreThere are plenty of examples of how this hasn’t worked.Neill Blomkampfollowing Elysium and Chappie with chintzy low-budget horrorDemonic(easily his least effective film although sinceopening his own AI “studio”I imagine the worst is yet to come), Marc Forster following Quantum of Solace and World War Z witha blind Blake Lively film that, ironically, no one sawwhile Anna Boden and Ryan Fleck went from the greatness of Half Nelson to the blandness of Captain Marvel to the headache ofFreaky Tales. But then we were also gifted with the hometown intimacy of Alfonso Cuarón’sRomaafter he came back from space for Gravity and Hogwarts for the Prisoner of Azkaban while Karyn Kusama brushed off the nightmare of Æon Flux with the brilliantly creepy dinner party thrillerThe Invitation.Adam Wingard is a writer-director who broke out with the original low-budget thrillers You’re Next and The Guest before moving on to franchise fare like 2016’sBlair Witchsequel, a Netflix adaptation ofDeath Noteand then, with a combined budget of about $300m to play with, two Godzilla vs Kong films. He did an excellent job with the first and a so-so one with the second, perhaps reflecting hisgrowing frustrationwith the limitations of wrangling franchise IP and after bowing out of more studio fare (he reportedly turned down Face/Off 2), he’s gone back to basics.He calls his new film Onslaught “an A-plus B-movie” because he tried to deliver all of the gonzo fun of a B-movie but with the A polish he’s learned in recent years. I’d call it a B-minus success, Wingard certainly showcasing that polish (a movie that looks like an actual movie is something to be cherished in 2026) but not quite giving us enough of the raucous fun we were promised. There’s something strangely restrained and at times a little tame, as if he’s still haunted by the ghosts of Warner Bros execs peering over his shoulder and restraint isn’t really what you want in an action slasher about genetically engineered super soldiers …The film imagines what would happen if an unstoppable Michael Myers or Jason Voorhees type was created and weaponised by the government (the first wink, wink scene has a line of Halloween pumpkins getting obliterated). Evil German doctor Hans Kammler (Wingard regularDan Stevens, doing a lot and then some) calls them “the human equivalent of a heat-seeking missile” and after an experiment goes awry at a research facility, they are unleashed on the local population. Out in the desert, that number is rather small, mainly the unfortunate residents of a trailer park, managed by ex-soldier and single mother Celeste (Adria Arjona), battling PTSD while struggling to take care of a young daughter who’s more put together than she is.With her in-trailer armoury of guns, it’s no surprise that Celeste is going to step up to the plate and it’s a deserved lead vehicle for Arjona, who has slowly become one of the more magnetic rising stars of late. She was easily the most attention-securing part of Zoe Kravitz’s patchy Epstein thriller Blink Twice, a film that acted as a perfect sizzle reel of both her action star and final girl capabilities and here she gets to shoot, quip and chainsaw her way to the centre of the frame (I look forward to seeing what she brings to Michael B Jordan’sThomas Crown Affair remakenext year yet theobligatory superhero rolecarries far less excitement). But as suited as Arjona is to the role, there’s a limit to what she’s able to do with it. The shallowness of her character isn’t a problem (there’s very little we needed to know about, say, Laurie Strode or Sarah Connor) but the situations she’s placed into are not quite thrilling or inventive enough.In trying to tick off both action and slasher, Wingard often falls in the unsatisfying gap in-between. Arming slasher villains with guns is just plainly not that interesting (there’s a reason why Michael, Ghostface and Jason rarely touch them while even the killer in the 1981 second world war veteran horror The Prowler prefers a pitchfork) and even when they’re forced to improvise, there’s not enough gnarliness to the carnage. Wingard often decides to not even show it, as if he’s still trying to secure a studio-friendly PG-13 rating and it proves to be a strange mix of sanitised violence and brief flashes of gonzo perversity (Drew Starkey having plenty of fun as an S&M-loving cleanup agent having to hunt the soldiers down after having just taken MDMA or the perennially underusedRebecca Hall, a Wingard favourite, as a cold-hearted German dominatrix) and I wish Wingard had leaned harder on the latter, giving us the balls-to-the-wall mayhem we assumed we would be getting. For an action film it feels like we’re missing a set piece or two and for a slasher it feels like we’re missing some gore and seat-edge suspense. It’s decently entertaining and I appreciated Wingard transferring his sleek studio style but it just never goes hard enough. After all, we were promised an onslaught.Onslaught is out in US cinemas on 4 September, the UK on 11 December and in Australia at a later dateExplore more on these topicsThrillersAction and adventure filmsRebecca HallDan StevensHorror filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Parasomnia review – sleep-schedule horror conjures up a succubus on the loose in waking nightmare | Movies | The Guardian
description: Debut director James Ross II shows promise in this gore fest, but the fear factor suffers from an overly complex plot
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: Debut director James Ross II shows promise in this gore fest, but the fear factor suffers from an overly complex plot
Content: Wandering a hellish labyrinth … Jasmine Mathews as Riley in Parasomnia.Photograph: Courtesy of Shudder. A Shudder Release.View image in fullscreenWandering a hellish labyrinth … Jasmine Mathews as Riley in Parasomnia.Photograph: Courtesy of Shudder. A Shudder Release.MoviesReviewParasomnia review – sleep-schedule horror conjures up a succubus on the loose in waking nightmareDebut director James Ross II shows promise in this gore fest, but the fear factor suffers from an overly complex plotPhil HoadMon 31 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSleep has been part of the horror genre repertoire since The Cabinet of Dr Caligari, and the anxieties around it are spiking as the “sleep economy” becomes a thing. This ambitiously structured gore fest about a woman suffering from waking nightmares comes with an all-black cast, but race isn’t a central preoccupation here. Instead, as night terrors burst the banks into reality, debut director James Ross II concentrates on maintaining an appropriately scrambled and claustrophobic experience – perhaps to the detriment of the fear factor.On her 15th birthday, Riley (Jasmine Mathews) is paralysed in a waking/sleep state at her foster home, able to observe but powerless to intervene to stop a care worker going berserk. Since this massacre, Riley keeps a strict sleep protocol as an adult, making sure anyone under the same roof drops off before her, which apparently protects them from the malevolent presence invading her nights. Old foster home pal David (Stephen Barrington) accepts an invitation to the house where Riley’s dad murdered her mum, but gets the willies when a pallid demon begins manifesting in the small hours. It turns out that Riley’s boyfriend, Cam (RJ Brown), has been lax in letting her fall asleep before him – and now her resident succubus is on the loose again.The levels of cause and effect, reality and fantasy, in Riley’s dreams are confusing at first: she inhabits the perspective of the eyeball-plucking fiend (a nod toETA Hoffmann’s Sandman?) and wanders a hellish labyrinth in which past victims are trapped. Thankfully, Ross clarifies everything with a burst of guiding lore in an ingenious third-act switchback that revises the previous two acts.Despite this sturdy constriction, the film remains only mildly scary – maybe because of the interruptions and vagaries of the complex setup. The middling performances don’t feel extreme enough, and the generic, chalk-faced, taloned bogeyman is a mere stain on Freddy Krueger’s jersey. But there is an undeniable astuteness and agility in the storytelling here on which Ross can build.Parasomnia is on Shudder and AMC+ from 4 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsSleepreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Future Starts With Us by Gordon Brown review – the ex-PM’s recipe for beating populism | Politics books | The Guardian
description: Global crises are tightly linked to how we treat each other at the local level, argues this optimistic book
Author: Gaby Hinsliff
Headline: Global crises are tightly linked to how we treat each other at the local level, argues this optimistic book
Content: Gordon BrownPhotograph: Margaret Mitchell/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGordon BrownPhotograph: Margaret Mitchell/The GuardianPolitics booksReviewThe Future Starts With Us by Gordon Brown review – the ex-PM’s recipe for beating populismGlobal crises are tightly linked to how we treat each other at the local level, argues this optimistic bookGaby HinsliffMon 31 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn times of crisis, there is one person to whom the left still turns for guidance.More than a decade and a half after leaving government,Gordon Brownhas mellowed into the Labour party’s favourite wise elder; one who has never disappointed the faithful by going off to make a ton of money, remaining quietly committed to public service and deeply engaged with the world’s knottier problems. Having successfully led the global response to the financial crash of 2008, and advocated powerfully during the pandemic for global cooperation against the virus, he was never going to simply sit back and shrug as the world spiralled into conflict and chaos under Donald Trump.But still, I thought, as I opened his latest book on the collapse of the old world order, it’s barely three years since his last tome on fixing the general mess (Permacrisis, written with the economists Mohammed El-Erian and Michael Spence). Does he really have anything new to say, or is this prolific output born mostly out of frustration that the world has seemingly stopped listening?A bit of both, it turns out. The new twist involves some polling commissioned to back Brown’s hunch that deep down voters actually crave a return to the more stable, orderly, benevolent world of the 2000s, despite voting repeatedly for the opposite. But to reach this research, readers must first wade through multiple chapters ramming home once again what’s wrong with the world, which will have many readers nodding in agreement without telling them much they didn’t already know. What could have been a deep, rich essay thus becomes a book: essentially a sermon on the moral failings of neoliberalism, ending in a rousing hymn to hope, echoing both the rhythm of his best party conference speeches and the broad themes of Andy Burnham’s first few weeks in power. (So much so, indeed, that you wonder how much the two men have been talking lately.)What is new for Brown, however, is that this book is preoccupied less with economics than with the argument that collapsing civic ties – the fact that we’re less likely now than a generation ago to be part of a club, trade union, church or community group – have helped undermine “the very idea that we are all in this together, that there are common causes worth fighting for”.What could be just another nostalgic, even reactionary, argument for a bygone age when everyone knew their neighbours is tempered by Brown’s willingness to acknowledge that much of this togetherness was built on the unpaid labour of women stuck at home. But it’s also brought up to date by his argument that this fraying of social bonds – especially in towns fallen on hard times, now leaning towards populist politicians – is actively connected to fragmentation and the retreat from multilateralism on the world stage. It’s time, he argues, to stop treating breakdown at home and breakup abroad as separate phenomena.Beating populism obviously means tackling the economic grievances – the disappearing jobs and hollowed-out high streets – on which it feeds in post-industrial communities across the US and Europe. Yet the general rolling chaos that populists tend to unleash on the world stage makes it actively harder for everyone else to build stable and prosperous economies, creating a vicious circle of decline.Brown’s answer is to build a virtuous circle instead, from the ground up. Strengthening civic ties should make people feel less lonely, more secure and trusting, and thus hopefully more relaxed about their governments acting generously and collaboratively at an international level. That, of course, is key to tackling everything from the climate crisis, to global poverty, to forming the kind of alliances with other middle-ranking powers that might prevent a country like the UK being totally steamrollered in a standoff between the US and China. At least, that’s the theory.The idea that dying high streets at home and rogue superpowers overseas are different threads of the same great unravelling does at least create a clear narrative hook on which a new Labour prime minister can hang lots of otherwise seemingly disparate ideas, and seek political buy-in for them both in the “red wall” and among big-city liberals. There’s material here too for a foreign secretary capable – as Ed Miliband arguably is – of thinking big and acting local, connecting foreign policy much more closely to progress at home. But just how plausible is it?Enter the new polling, of 32,000 people across 20 developed countries, from Argentina to the UK to South Korea. It distinguishes between “zero sum” thinkers – people who believe they can only win if others lose, colouring their attitudes to everything from trade to immigration – and a more generous “civic core”, open to some compromise for the greater good, on whom progressive governments depend. In the UK, at least, the latter group still outweighs the former, with a significant group lying between the two that Brown reckons could be persuaded to heed the better angels of their natures.He then calculates the impact of measures like reducing economic grievances, or increasing people’s face-to-face interaction with others from different religious or racial backgrounds, on propensity to vote for populists. To cut a long story short: deploy all the virtuous circle measures together, and with luck (and time), you might have a potent means of tackling populism from the ground up.Rather less convincing, however, is his formula for restoring the international rules-based order, starting with a new universal charter to which responsible countries could sign up. We already have plenty of grand statements of intent and bodies to enforce them, from the international criminal court to the Paris climate change accords: what’s missing is governments prepared to actually stick to the rules.Unusually for Brown, the best of this book isn’t in the big-picture thinking on globalisation or the rise of China, but in lessons learned at neighbourhood level. After a life spent trying to push through huge decisions, he writes, only recently has he begun thinking that he should have started small.One obvious hurdle is that the neighbourly civic engagement he favours is of the decidedly muscular, worthy kind. The clubs Brown sees as capable of teaching “active citizenship” are those that demand the most time and effort from volunteers – and they have died out. Just signing up for fun times doesn’t count. Like the good son of the manse he is, Brown personally practises what he preaches in Kirkcaldy, where he is heavily engaged with local charities. I’m not sure your average Briton, spending their downtime from work scrolling exhaustedly on the sofa, will feel the same.Then again Brown does say that cynicism like mine is part of the problem; that if liberal politics is to compete with demagogues, it can’t simply confine itself to the art of the possible – it must “show it can make the desirable possible”. Even if, just occasionally, that sounds like wishful thinking.The Future Starts With Us by Gordon Brown is published by Simon & Schuster (£25). title: Switzy by Emma Cline review – this Booker-listed account of a man’s last days is profoundly moving | Fiction | The Guardian
description: Struggling with Alzheimer’s, the central character sets out on his final journey to a euthanasia clinic
Author: Chris Power
Headline: Struggling with Alzheimer’s, the central character sets out on his final journey to a euthanasia clinic
Content: Journey’s end … Emma Cline.Photograph: PRView image in fullscreenJourney’s end … Emma Cline.Photograph: PRBook of the dayFictionReviewSwitzy by Emma Cline review – this Booker-listed account of a man’s last days is profoundly movingStruggling with Alzheimer’s, the central character sets out on his final journey to a euthanasia clinicChris PowerMon 31 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 02.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe word “Alzheimer’s” never appears in Switzy, Emma Cline’s third novel, which arrives pre-endorsed as a Booker prize longlistee. But we can be certain that it is the disease afflicting its central character, David Hastings – certain in a way he finds it increasingly hard to be about anything.When the novel begins, David and his assistant Cody are aboard a private jet flying from his home in the US to the UK. Landing at London City airport (which the book, experiencing its own senior moment, situates in the countryside), they visit David’s daughter and her family before travelling on to Zurich (hence “Switzy”). One more appointment, a catchup with an old boarding school roommate called Tom, awaits just over the French border, after which David will be euthanised at a facility resembling Dignitas.David is wealthy. Not wealthy enough to own the jet he’s flying around in – that’s a loan from his boss – but someone to whom its polished doors, “that slid silently and obligingly out of sight”, are of a piece with the comfortable, largely frictionless world through which he moves. He has had a career in business, chief financial officer of some undefined entity – one large enough for a forensic accounting firm to be required when it became apparent David, in an early sign of the seriousness of his impairment, had mistakenly scattered its money into “an archipelago of overseas accounts”.For all the capital he has accumulated, David has been “a support person, a man whose name would never be known”, who sat at a desk and “made certain numbers swell up and other numbers recede”. Has it been a happy life? Well, the revelation or otherwise of that is one of the strands running through this extraordinarily well-made novel.How ill is David? Not so ill as to disqualify him from choosing euthanasia, but enough that navigating the world, from finding his hotel room to operating a phone, holding up his end of a conversation or understanding how and why he has offended someone, has become deeply problematic. He has reached the stage of his illness where, we learn from references to past events, he has woken up in his car uncertain of how he came to be there, soiled himself, upset employees, even lost the ability to tie his shoelaces. Sometimes he forgets he has eaten until a burp, tasting of lunch, reminds him of the fact. At other times he experiences the feeling “of coming into a room and the room offering no answers as to why he was there”. His world is full of aftermath but often frustratingly empty of cause.double quotation markBehind his chaotic decline hums a perfectly calibrated narrative machine, as smooth in its operation as the doors of his private jetHe compares his situation to that of a “mental ice floe, populated only by David, floating off into the polar darkness”. The text elegantly reflects this, its atomised paragraphs separated by white space – treacherous voids across which the thread of David’s awareness might not stretch from one moment to another. Yet as his comprehension thins, our own deepens. As his self-referential and fragmented stream of consciousness, often rich in similes, rebounds between the inputs of wherever he happens to be – in a car, at a restaurant, walking the streets of one city or another, always with Cody beside him – and his piecemeal memories, we begin to catch the resonances he no longer can.I think it is probably impossible to remain unmoved by David’s journey towards death, but as I accompanied him on it, I registered a nagging doubt that became increasingly insistent. David’s condition is worsening; he knows the day is coming when “he’d find that the contents of his brain had been excised with an ice-cream scooper instead of these dainty little teaspoons, here and there”. But in the case of the storyline involving Tom, David’s faltering memory just so happens to fall into precisely the pattern of revelation employed by a traditional trauma-plot novel.Characters in such books, as the New Yorker critic Parul Sehgal noted in her 2021 essay on the subject, “work to fill in the gaps of partial, haunting recollections”. Throughout Switzy, clues bob to the surface of David’s consciousness about some shameful event that soured things between himself and Tom at boarding school in the 1960s. One involves Tom’s sister “narrowing her eyes at him across the lawn at graduation”. No further context for the look is provided, for us or David, but as soon as it was mentioned I felt confident that the closer the meeting with Tom came, the more would be revealed about their shared past.This certainty that novelistic convention would be obeyed works against the uncertainty Cline otherwise evokes so brilliantly. It’s true that with Alzheimer’s long-term memories can persist as short-term memories cease to imprint. But David, too, appears to be searching for precisely what happened between himself and Tom. The memory is conveniently unavailable, provoking suspense, and then, just as conveniently, it returns to provide satisfaction. The reader’s knowledge that David will remember – an expectation drummed into us from myriad stories that work this way – runs counter to the reality of his predicament, to which neither narrative nor real-world logic applies. Behind his chaotic decline, the “unknowable soup” of his reality in which cause and effect have become terrifyingly uncoupled, hums a perfectly calibrated narrative machine as smooth and obliging in its operation as the doors of his private jet.When the novel moves past the Tom storyline, as it does with about 50 pages to go, it becomes its best self. Untethered from the duties of revelation it can fully immerse us in David’s pocked reality: impressionistic, arresting, upsetting, even funny. Earlier in the book, when reflecting on losing the name for the plastic cap on a shoelace (an aglet), he thinks that that one “was probably okay. Sure, toss it overboard.” By contrast – although it’s tempting fate to say it – the last pages of Switzy, which mingle horror, beauty, absurdity, and a sense of profound finality, will probably stay with me for ever.Switzy by Emma Cline is published by Chatto & Windus (£18.99). title: Gems, ghosts and GTA VI: the biggest video games for autumn 2026 | Games | The Guardian
description: There are juggernauts and indie gems aplenty for when the nights draw in, from an ingenious puzzle game to blockbusters such as Marvel’s Wolverine and Call of Duty
Author: Jordan Erica Webber
Headline: There are juggernauts and indie gems aplenty for when the nights draw in, from an ingenious puzzle game to blockbusters such as Marvel’s Wolverine and Call of Duty
Content: Work to be done … There Are No Ghosts at the Grand and GTA VI.Composite: Guardian Design/Friday Sundae/Rockstar GamesView image in fullscreenWork to be done … There Are No Ghosts at the Grand and GTA VI.Composite: Guardian Design/Friday Sundae/Rockstar GamesAutumn arts preview 2026GamesGems, ghosts and GTA VI: the biggest video games for autumn 2026There are juggernauts and indie gems aplenty for when the nights draw in, from an ingenious puzzle game to blockbusters such as Marvel’s Wolverine and Call of DutySee all of our unmissable autumn arts recommendations hereKeith StuartandJordan Erica WebberMon 31 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTShareOnimusha: Way of the SwordAfter 20 years away, Capcom’s hyper kinetic action adventure returns, pitting skilled samurai Miyamoto Musashi against hordes of warriors and demons in Edo-period Kyoto. Master the complex combat then prepare for flashing blades, disembodied limbs and geysers of spraying blood.4 September; PC, PS5, Switch 2, XboxScreenboundBilled as the first ever 5D platformer, Screenbound has you navigating a 3D landscape while simultaneously playing an on-screen handheld console, which contains a 2D mirror world. Everything you do in one affects the other in mind-bending ways. The most ingenious puzzle game we’ve seen in a long time.10 September; PC, PS5, XboxView image in fullscreenMind-bending originality … Screenbound.Photograph: Crescent Moon GamesMarvel’s WolverineThe team behind the brilliant Marvel’s Spider-Man titles is back with a very different kind of hero. The open-world New York setting is gone in favour of a globe-trotting narrative following Logan on his quest to protect vulnerable mutants. The visuals are gorgeous, while the slick combat brings literal meaning to the term bleeding edge.15 September; PS5Fire Emblem: Fortune’s WeaveThe tactical role-playing adventure series returns to the realm explored in the acclaimedFire Emblem: Three Houses. This time, hopeful contestants arrive at the glorious city of Dagsion to compete in a contest where the winner is granted a single wish. Deep combat, lush settings and fraught relationships are guaranteed.17 September; Switch 2Silent Hill: TownfallSilent Hill comes to the east coast of Scotland in a beautifully gloomy new horror adventure. You play as Simon Ordell, returning to a quiet harbour town with no memory of whatever catastrophe has taken place there. The place seems abandoned, but you are not alone for long …24 September; PC, PS5View image in fullscreenBeautiful gloom … Silent Hill: Townfall.Photograph: Screen BurnControl ResonantRemedy Entertainment sets out to disprove the notion that all video game sequels are more of the same. This follow-up to the successful2019 sci-fi shooterhas a new lead character with supernatural powers, a whole new role-playing adventure feel, and a fresh take on Manhattan, where a reality-bending monster awaits …24 September; PC, PS5, XboxRatatanThe latest gorgeously strange game from Patapon creator Hiroyuki Kotani is a rhythm action platformer set in a colourful world where enemies are defeated with songs and players can work together to produce devastating melodies. Imagine Dead Cells merged with PaRappa the Rapper and you’re getting close.15 October; PC, PS, Switch, XboxCall of Duty: Modern Warfare 4The world-beating mega shooter packs its bags full of guns, grenades and macho dialogue and heads for Korea, in another Modern Warfare instalment. There will be epic battles, sanitised politically adjacent themes and rip-roaring online multiplayer – plus, moustached SAS figurehead Captain Price will be tagging along for the ride. Resistance is futile.23 October; PC, PS5, Switch 2, XboxGrand Theft Auto VIAfter a decade in development and several delays, Rockstar’s entertainment behemoth returns, following loved-up criminals Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos as they take on every scumbag Vice City has to offer. Already looking vibrant, expansive and lascivious, this is Bonnie and Clyde for the digital generation.19 November; PS5, XboxThere are No Ghosts at the GrandChris David has inherited a grand old hotel, but now there’s work to be done renovating the decrepit building during the day and then exorcising unwanted ghosts into the night. Like all old English buildings, this charming game is filled with secrets and puzzles, and of course there will be ancestral revelations aplenty.TBC: PC, Xbox

title: A$AP Rocky review – arena spectacular has plenty of helicopters but little sense of direction | Music | The Guardian
description: The polymath rapper’s stage show, which also features SWAT teams and a warship, is truly bravura stuff – but you can’t help feeling this is an artist at a creative crossroads
Author: Stevie Chick
Headline: The polymath rapper’s stage show, which also features SWAT teams and a warship, is truly bravura stuff – but you can’t help feeling this is an artist at a creative crossroads
Content: Quite the spectacle … A$AP Rocky.Photograph: Thepinkrosephotographyltd/Laura RoseView image in fullscreenQuite the spectacle … A$AP Rocky.Photograph: Thepinkrosephotographyltd/Laura RoseMusicReviewA$AP Rocky review – arena spectacular has plenty of helicopters but little sense of directionO2 Arena, LondonThe polymath rapper’s stage show, which also features SWAT teams and a warship, is truly bravura stuff – but you can’t help feeling this is an artist at a creative crossroadsStevie ChickMon 31 Aug 2026 09.47 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA$AP Rocky dangles precariously from a helicopter, while beneath him black-clad SWAT officers brawl with his white-masked followers. This isn’t some cliffhanger setpiece from the rapper/actor’s latest film – it’s just how shows on his Don’t Be Dumb tour open. It’s a big production: there are further prop helicopters, including a smaller one up in the rafters from which he also raps (a reference to his single Helicopter), while the stage recreates the top deck of a naval warship, for reasons that never become clear.The bizarre set underscores a sense of a man in career transition, unsure who he is any more. In the eight years since his last album, this survivor of homelessness and incarceration became a father, three times, with Rihanna; he’s pivoting towards movies –goodones– and co-chairs the Met Gala. His new record sought to redefine him as an artist, juggling more of his trademark pugilistic rap with ambitious stylistic experiments and unexpected collaborations (Damon Albarn! Danny Elfman!).View image in fullscreenGet to the chopper! … A$AP Rocky.Photograph: Laura RoseBut Rocky seemed paralysed by choice, unable to choose a lane. Was he a reformed Lothario declaring his devotion to Rihanna? Or the wildling of yore, “still smoking my weed” and rekindling beef with Drake? The album reached No 1 without offering a definitive answer. Now he’s got a warship to strut along (while pursued by 30 dancers in that SWAT gear), and a besotted audience starting circle pits to wonky fight song STFU, bouncing en masse to the death-rattle funk of Riot (Rowdy Pipe’n), and twirling their white shirts like helicopter blades at his command.Tonight, Rocky seems most energised performing the haunted dream-pop frug of Punk Rocky, or his swoonsome Thundercat collab, Stay Here 4 Life, or the hypnotic slither of L$D. The wildcard sound of these tracks suggests he’s searching for a creative mode that will fit him as well as his earlier sizzurp-slaked anthems. But as he ably negotiates the special effects and gonzo props of his big, bonkers stage show, it’s also hard to shake the suspicion that, if Hollywood offered Rocky a truly career-changing role, hip-hop wouldn’t see him for dust. He is a man in motion, for sure – but his direction remains undefined.A$AP Rocky plays 3Arena, Dublin, 2 September; thentours the UK until 5 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsMusicRapHip-hopA$AP Rockylive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Les Siècles/Lehmann La Damnation de Faust review – vivid colour, soaring solos and a sharp-suited demon | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: Period instrument grain and an energised Jakob Lehmann did a fair job with Berlioz’s concert setting of the drama, but the hall’s murky acoustic buried some of the sparkle
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: Period instrument grain and an energised Jakob Lehmann did a fair job with Berlioz’s concert setting of the drama, but the hall’s murky acoustic buried some of the sparkle
Content: ‘All black suit, scarlet tie and eyebrows’ … Gerald Finley  as Méphistophélès in Berlioz’s La Damnation de Faust, conducted by Jakob Lehmann.Photograph: Mark AllanView image in fullscreen‘All black suit, scarlet tie and eyebrows’ … Gerald Finley  as Méphistophélès in Berlioz’s La Damnation de Faust, conducted by Jakob Lehmann.Photograph: Mark AllanProms 2026ReviewLes Siècles/Lehmann La Damnation de Faust review – vivid colour, soaring solos and a sharp-suited demonRoyal Albert Hall, LondonPeriod instrument grain and an energised Jakob Lehmann did a fair job with Berlioz’s concert setting of the drama, but the hall’s murky acoustic buried some of the sparkleErica JealMon 31 Aug 2026 09.18 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 10.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBerlioz wrote hissetting of the Faust storyfor concert performance, counting on the fact that what went on in his audience’s mind’s eye would be more fantastical than anything that could be portrayed on stage. The forces he employed aren’t on the same scale as those for his Requiem – written almost a decade earlier, in 1837, andheard here earlier this month– but are still huge. Here they came in the form of the period-instrument orchestra Les Siècles, plus the Choeur de Radio France and, joining in the closing five minutes, the Radio France children’s choir – conducted byJakob Lehmann, making an energised Proms debut.Les Siècles’ period instruments brought their own grainy texture to the palette, from the chattering piccolos representing Méphistophélès’s malignant spirits and the silky violin swoops lulling Faust to sleep, down to the inclusion in the orchestra of an ophicleide, an instrument that’s an evolutionary dead end on the tuba’s family tree. The Hungarian March sounded snappy, as did the brass fanfares, echoed at one point by a small band up in the gallery.View image in fullscreenRadiant  … Véronique Gens as Marguerite in La Damnation de Faust.Photograph: Mark AllanYet alongside the vividly colourful passages were some that made you wish you could pick the performance up and put it down in a different, less tricky venue. In this very particular hall, Berlioz’s teemingly detailed music often needed more space from Lehmann or a crisper, more forensic approach to ensemble. As it was, the palette at times turned murky, the accompanying figures merging into a blur. And while it was in some ways a treat to hear the choral music sung so well – the Choeur de Radio France was 80-strong, and you rarely get to hear a professional choir on that scale – their well-blended sound didn’t always cut ideally through the orchestra.The soloists were a strong team, with John Osborn’s tenor soaring incisively yet smoothly up to the heights in the title role, the soprano Véronique Gens singing especially radiantly in Marguerite’s first aria, and Thomas Dolié dispatching Brander’s drinking song with vigour. But it was Gerald Finley’s entrances as Méphistophélès – all black suit, scarlet tie and eyebrows – that made the dramatic aspect of this legend come alive.Available on BBC Soundsuntil 12 October.
