title: Tilda Swinton’s blast from the past, Kevin Bridges at large and a deepfake ballet: theatre, comedy and dance to see this autumn | Stage | The Guardian
description: Swinton takes a dead man’s identity, Glasgow’s heir to Billy Connolly heads on tour and Gillian Anderson, Keira Knightley and Natalia Osipova all hit the stage
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Swinton takes a dead man’s identity, Glasgow’s heir to Billy Connolly heads on tour and Gillian Anderson, Keira Knightley and Natalia Osipova all hit the stage
Content: Kevin Bridges tours his standup show and Tilda Swinton stars in Manfred Karge’s Man to Man.Composite: Guardian Design/Andy Hollingworth/Sølve SundsbøView image in fullscreenKevin Bridges tours his standup show and Tilda Swinton stars in Manfred Karge’s Man to Man.Composite: Guardian Design/Andy Hollingworth/Sølve SundsbøAutumn arts preview 2026StageTilda Swinton’s blast from the past, Kevin Bridges at large and a deepfake ballet: theatre, comedy and dance to see this autumnSwinton takes a dead man’s identity, Glasgow’s heir to Billy Connolly heads on tour and Gillian Anderson, Keira Knightley and Natalia Osipova all hit the stageSee all of our unmissable autumn arts recommendations hereTheatre picksArifa Akbar. Comedy picksBrian Logan. Dance picksLyndsey WinshipMon 31 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTShareTheatreBloodsport: After Helen of TroyAva Pickett has an impressive track record of imaginative historical dramas, including her award-winning Tudor-era play1536, which had a West End run this year.Alongside co-writing a film about Joan of Arc with Baz Luhrmann, she has reconceived this ancient epic, with Michelle Dockery playing Helen returning to war-ravaged Troy.Theatre Royal Stratford East, London, 3 September-10 OctoberMan to ManAt the Edinburgh festival in 1987, Tilda Swinton played a German widow who takes on the identity of her dead husband in a prose poem by the Berliner Ensemble’s Manfred Karge. Almost 40 years later, she returns to the role of Ella/Max in a revised version, again directed by Stephen Unwin.Royal Court theatre, London, 5 September-24 October.Traverse theatre, Edinburgh, 29 October-7 NovemberThe Standard of LivingView image in fullscreenPriceless … Thomas Flynn, Rory Kinnear and Natalia Osipova star in The Standard of LivingWhat greater “event theatre” than a new James Graham play? This one brings a twist to Keynesian economics. Directed by Nicholas Hytner, it stars Rory Kinnear as John Maynard Keynes and explores his relationship with the Bloomsbury group and his impact on arts funding. Royal Ballet principal Natalia Osipova co-stars, making her West End debut.Theatre Royal Haymarket, London, 21 September-12 DecemberWho’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?The celebrification of the West End continues apace with this version of Edward Albee’s 1962 play, bringing two starry screen talents together, although both Gillian Anderson and Billy Crudup have proved themselves on stage before now. Directed by Marianne Elliott, they will engage in toxic slanging matches, psychological warfare and marital meltdown.@sohoplace, London, 21 September-19 DecemberI’ll Be Seeing YouView image in fullscreenRhinestones guaranteed … Simon Russell Beale in rehearsals for I'll Be Seeing You.Photograph: Olivia Attwooll-KeithThere is much to excite about this world premiere – a meta Martin Sherman play about the flamboyant pianist Liberace, with Simon Russell Beale taking the lead role. Fra Fee co-stars in the production directed by Alan Cumming and Ben Occhipinti. It promises rhinestones aplenty.Pitlochry Festival theatre, 22 September-11 OctoberAs You Like ItAn all-male production of Shakespeare’s pastoral comedy comes amid some striking gender reversals at the RSC – Harriet Walter is also reprising her Brutus in Phyllida Lloyd’s all-femaleJulius Caesar. This show, directed by Daniel Evans, features Tony award-winner Jonathan Groff as Rosalind and the talented Fisayo Akinade as Celia.Royal Shakespeare theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon, 26 September-7 NovemberView image in fullscreenEagerly awaited … Inua Ellams.Photograph: Dave Benett/Getty ImagesOnce Upon a Time in SokotoPoet-playwright Inua Ellams earned enormous praise forBarber Shop Chroniclesand his adaptation of Chekhov’sThree Sisters. His Alfred Fagon award-winning drama sounds promising, with the exploration of an unlikely friendship between an enslaved woman and her former master in the lead-up to the formation of Nigeria.Royal & Derngate, Northampton, 28 September-10 October.Touring until 13 FebruaryKing LearView image in fullscreenDavid Threlfall will perform as King Lear at the Royal Exchange, Manchester.Illustration: David StewartThere is more than one big-name Lear in store this autumn. Ian McKellen takes on the role (again!) in Simon Stephens’s radically re-spun production at the Yard in east London,opening in November, while David Threlfall returns to Manchester’s Royal Exchange after almost three decades in director Matthew Dunster’s reimagined adaptation for the theatre’s 50th anniversary.Royal Exchange theatre, Manchester, 2 October-15 NovemberBalloon GirlLouisa Maud Evans, otherwise known as Mademoiselle Albertina, was a young Welsh firebrand who died while parachuting during a balloon flight at the Cardiff Exhibition of 1896. Writer-director Hannah McPake creates an upbeat adventure that honours her spirit of curiosity and endeavour.Sherman theatre, Cardiff, 9-24 OctoberThe Lives of OthersView image in fullscreenHigh stakes … Stephen Dillane, Keira Knightley and Luke Thompson in The Lives of Others.Photograph: Oliver Rosser, Feast CreativeKeira Knightley and Stephen Dillane star in an adaptation of Florian Henckel von Donnersmarck’s 2006 film, a high-stakes love story set in Stasi-era east Germany. It may follow the trend for transposing hit films to the stage but is helmed by Robert Icke, who at his best makes old stories blazingly new.Adelphi theatre, London, 14 October-9 JanuaryComedySam CampbellThe success of Channel 4’s oddball mockumentaryMake That Movie, and his stint on Amazon hit Last One Laughing, broadcast more widely what insiders have long known: Aussie act Sam Campbell is one of comedy’s most unpredictable talents. Touring set Kid Giblet offers new fans a glimpse of the indelible live experience.Bristol Beacon, 31 August. Touring until 1 DecemberKevin BridgesHaving unfussily built a reputation as one of the UK’s greatest live standups, and off the back of his acclaimed World Cup curtain-raiser on the telly, In Search of the Beautiful Game, Glasgow’s heir to Billy Connolly returns with his keenly awaited new tour, Here If You Need Me.Eventim Apollo, London, 1-3 September. Touring until 20 FebruaryFlo & JoanView image in fullscreenKeyed up … Flo and JoanNot many comedy acts ascend to the next level by absenting themselves from the stage. Musical duo Flo & Joan (AKA Rosie and Nicola Dempsey) managed it with One Man Musical, their for-the-ages bio showabout a certain West End composer. In With Feeling, a new suite of comic songs, the pair return to their own spotlight.Gala theatre, Durham, 19 September. Touring until 12 DecemberAhir ShahAfter winning the Edinburgh comedy award three summers ago, then conquering Netflix, with a counterintuitive and feelgood show about multicultural Britain and his family history, the Londoner now takes to the road with its follow-up, Golden, inspired (in typical boffinish fashion) by Nietzsche and Gerard Manley Hopkins.Soho theatre, London, 5-17 October.Touring until 14 MarchView image in fullscreenUnlike anyone else … Frankie Thompson: Horrible Things.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianFrankie Thompson“If you laugh, it’s comedy; if you don’t, it’s live art”: so the cult clown-comic (and live artist!) Frankie Thompson describes her new set, Horrible Things. If we can credit her previous, unlike-anyone-else offerings at the Edinburgh fringe and beyond, expect another heart-and-funny-bone-teasing hour of uncategorisable performance.Soho theatre, London, 12-24 OctoberDanceLondon City BalletA mix of revivals, forgotten gems and brand-new choreography is the signature of London City Ballet. Its autumn tour programme differs at each venue, but all shows include a revival of Glen Tetley’s Firebird, marking Tetley’s centenary – his version is about a young woman breaking free from the constraints of her family.York Theatre Royal, 18-19 September. Touring until 24 OctoberJess & Morgs: DeepfakeThe creators of Scottish Ballet’s award-winning Coppélia – which set the classic ballet in an era of AI – return with a new work exploring the possibilities and pitfalls of technology. Using cutting edge tech, the set-up is an interview between a politician and a journalist. The question is: can you tell what’s really real?Jerwood DanceHouse, Ipswich, 25 September.Sadler’s Wells East, London, 1-3 OctoberEnglish National Ballet: Romeo & JulietView image in fullscreenAction-packed ballet … Isaac Hernández as Romeo and Erina Takahashi as Juliet.Photograph: Laurent LiotardoAlmost 50 years have passed since Rudolf Nureyev created his ballet of Romeo & Juliet, a version less often seen in the UK than Kenneth MacMillan’s but just as powerful. It’s a ballet packed with fast-paced steps and heightened drama from the two feuding families plus Prokofiev’s sumptuous, stirring score.Liverpool Empire, 15-17 October. Touring until 24 JanuaryMeet the HatterJust one dancer and a stageful of magical projections is enough to create a wonderland in this multimedia family show from Joss Arnott Dance. Arnott’s take on one of Lewis Carroll’s best-loved characters sees the Mad Hatter turn up for a tea party – but there’s no one there, so his imagination takes over.Pavilion Dance South West, Bournemouth, 24 October. Touring until 26 JuneThe Last HamletParis’s Théâtre de la Ville is dedicating a whole season this autumn to dance-theatre maker Ben Duke, AKA Lost Dog – quite the honour. On home soil, you can see his new work The Last Hamlet, musing on the idea of Hamlet’s last-ever performance, deconstructing Shakespeare’s tragic hero with characteristic wit.Sadler’s Wells East, London, 4-7 November

title: A Small and Quiet Light review – fractured portrait of a remarkable wartime spy | Theatre | The Guardian
description: A female secret agent’s extraordinary courage never quite comes to life in a drama that struggles to find tension in her high-stakes story
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: A female secret agent’s extraordinary courage never quite comes to life in a drama that struggles to find tension in her high-stakes story
Content: Restrained … Priyanga Burford (right) in A Small and Quiet Light at Minerva theatre, Chichester.Photograph: Marc BrennerView image in fullscreenRestrained … Priyanga Burford (right) in A Small and Quiet Light at Minerva theatre, Chichester.Photograph: Marc BrennerTheatreReviewA Small and Quiet Light review – fractured portrait of a remarkable wartime spyMinerva theatre, ChichesterA female secret agent’s extraordinary courage never quite comes to life in a drama that struggles to find tension in her high-stakes storyArifa AkbarMon 31 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 00.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNoor-un-Nisa Inayat Khan was a second world war spy codenamed Madeleine. A mixed-heritage British Indian and Special Operations Executive (SOE) agent in Nazi-occupied Paris who showed extraordinary courage, her story is ripe for dramatic retelling. So why does it feel so fractured and unsatisfactory in director Elin Schofield’s production?Perhaps because of the limited documentation of this medalled war hero’s life. That is not helped in the delivery of her story in playwright Stephanie Street’s non-sequential narrative, beginning with her interrogation in 1943, after being caught by the Germans, and shuttling back and forth across the years, from early family life to her death in Dachau concentration camp.Because the story is already filled with holes, it gains more lacunae in this broken-up telling to become less than the sum of its parts. It creates unnecessary confusion and does not relay who Khan was beneath the facts of her life, what drove her or exactly what she did in what turned out to be a highly dangerous lone mission.Priyanga Burford plays Khan across the decades, from a girl playing piano with her mother to a young woman getting ready for a date. We are told Khan wrote fiction but not much more. A character likens storytellers to spies but the play lacks the essential conflict and suspense of either. Burford’s performance is solid but workmanlike.View image in fullscreenShadowy … Caoilfhionn Dunne (right) in A Small and Quiet Light at Minerva theatre, Chichester.Photograph: Marc BrennerScenes are often short and static. Accompanying characters include Vera (Amanda Hadingue), the handler who sends Khan to France, as well as Viennot (Léa des Garets), Khan’s sometime lover, and Vogt (Caoilfhionn Dunne), her mild-mannered interrogator. There are others but sometimes it is not clear who they are, and they all remain shadowy.Khan’s American-born mother (also Hadingue) and her musician father (Paksie Vernon), who we hear knew Debussy and Tolstoy, provide backstory but do not illuminate what drove Khan. We are told that she feels a greater purpose on her mission but this sounds pat. There is a tantalising suggestion that she feels more herself as Madeleine, and that life as a spy is more real to her, but there is no follow-through.Overall, the tone is too polite and restrained, Nicola T Chang’s melodramatic compositions and Tingying Dong’s big sound design doing all they can to insert some charge.This is not the first attempt at dramatising Khan’s life.Kali Theatre’s production at the Southwark Playhouse in 2022was imperfect but did manage to capture the peril in her mission by focusing the action on her work in France. This play skirts around dramatising that. So scenes lack tension, despite the best attempts of the all-female cast to convey jeopardy, which seems like a fatal flaw for a drama about high-stakes espionage.It stalls itself at the end to remind us that we cannot nail down the story of Khan’s life (or death) with any certainty, that it is fraught with unknowns. This drama goes some way towards telling us who she was, and certainly conveys her heroism – but she never comes to life through these jagged pieces of a remarkable life.At Minerva theatre, Chichester until12 September, and thenOrange Tree theatre, London, 21 September-24 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreChichester Festival theatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Goodbye to Babylon Berlin, the 1920s TV drama that has eerily foreshadowed real-life politics | Television | The Guardian
description: The long-running drama reaches Hitler’s rise to power in its final season as its creators reflect on the unsettling parallels between Weimar Germany and the present day
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: The long-running drama reaches Hitler’s rise to power in its final season as its creators reflect on the unsettling parallels between Weimar Germany and the present day
Content: ‘We’re in the volcano itself’ … Volker Bruch (second, right) and Liv Lisa Fries on set of the fifth series of  Babylon Berlin.Photograph: Joachim Gern/Beta FilmView image in fullscreen‘We’re in the volcano itself’ … Volker Bruch (second, right) and Liv Lisa Fries on set of the fifth series of  Babylon Berlin.Photograph: Joachim Gern/Beta FilmTelevisionGoodbye to Babylon Berlin, the 1920s TV drama that has eerily foreshadowed real-life politicsThe long-running drama reaches Hitler’s rise to power in its final season as its creators reflect on the unsettling parallels between Weimar Germany and the present dayDeborah Colein BerlinMon 31 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s the global hit TV series that pulled audiences straight into the chaotic hedonism of 1920sGermany, dramatising the brilliance and brittleness of a newly built democratic system with unprecedented ambition.But in the 13 years that the German makers ofBabylon Berlinhave worked on the show, modern democracies from the US to Hungary to South Korea have come under pressure in ways the creators say they could never have imagined when they started.Now they are preparing to unveil the fifth and final season, culminating in Adolf Hitler’s rise to power, the same week that Germany will face one of the biggest tests of its postwar order in a watershed state election.The timing, they insist, is pure coincidence, but is fitting for an ambitious programme set a century ago during theWeimar republicthat has always felt eerily prescient.As the team gets ready to sign off, the inexorable end of the story is now upon the familiar characters of the noirish police procedural, with its lush period sets and frisson of impending doom.“It’s no longer a dance on the rim of the volcano,” said lead actorLiv Lisa Fries, using a German idiom for the explosion of avant garde culture and sexual liberation in the 1920s before the descent into fascism. “We’re in the volcano itself.”Fries plays the series’ intrepid working-class heroine Charlotte Ritter, who works her way up from secretarial duties and underworld sex work to become the first female detective on the Berlin police force.Her co-star Volker Bruch is Gereon Rath, a shellshocked first world war veteran whose eventful odyssey through the trauma of his era bears a resemblance toChristopher Nolan’s summer blockbuster, The Odyssey.But the more striking parallel isGermanyin 2026.View image in fullscreenPower struggle … episode 12 of series four of Babylon Berlin.Photograph: Frédéric Batier/ARD/Sky StudiosThe far-rightAlternative für Deutschland, anextremist, anti-constitutional partyfounded around the same time that work on the series began, is now leading national opinion polls.On Sunday 6 September, it could win its first absolute majority in a state election, in Saxony-Anhalt, and two weeks later may beat its opponents in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. In Berlin, it is polling close to the far-left party Die Linke.With German democracy facing such a stress test, Bruch said the political “parallels” jumped out. But he resisted overly simplistic comparisons, citing an old adage: “History doesn’t repeat itself that way – it rhymes.”The blurred lines between life and art took on sometimes surreal dimensions during the course of the production.Series three was filmed in part at the neo-baroque Villa Adlon, which in November 2023 served as the real-life venue for asecret meetingof AfD officials and neo-Nazis to discuss a “remigration” plan for mass deportations if the party came to power.Series five sees Hitler’s appointment as Reich chancellor, just as an medical file goes missing that casts new light on his time as a soldier in the first world war.Although it was always clear how the series would end, watching Babylon Berlin has meant hoping to the last that history would take another turn.That poignancy transformed a sophisticated crime show into something more affecting, and perhaps more enduring.Across 50-odd hours, the show, based partly on a series ofnovels by Volker Kutscher, helped expand the scale and ambition of European television drama.“It was almost impossible even then when they started,” said Scott Roxborough, the European bureau chief of entertainment trade magazine the Hollywood Reporter.It was the product of a “pioneer time”, he said, when Germany was willing to throw massive resources at a chance to catch up with splashy shows from the US and Britain like Breaking Bad and The Crown.“I think it would be almost impossible to do it nowadays unless an Apple TV or a Netflix decided to finance everything,” something he said was increasingly unlikely as the global streaming companies take a morecautious, profits-first approach.Babylon Berlin has reached audiences around the world – 140 countries at last count – with its cautionary tale of a vibrant civilisation’s inherent fragility.“The secret to the series’s success in capturing the zeitgeist is definitely not that it mirrors the present. I don’t believe that,” one of its three creators, Tom Tykwer, said.Rather, audiences have been drawn to the “transformative force” of Berlin in the 1920s, when a weak government and a churning society left room for women, gay people and new immigrants to rewrite the rules.“That brings forth an incredible number of wonderful, positive, beautiful blossoms, but because it’s so experimental, they’re also destroyed again almost immediately,” he said.“We’ve tried to explore the universal themes that stem from the fact that political systems are people-centred so are always under threat. It will always be that way.”Tykwer also co-composed much of the original music for the series, including the haunting theme song To Ashes, to Dust. The fifth season features a plot excursion to Paris and an on-screen rendition of the tune by French neo-chanson starZaho de Sagazan.In series five, Tykwer and his team have also revived the 1920 queer anthemDas Lila Liedwith its rousing chorus “Wir sind nun einmal anders als die andern” (We’re just different from the others) for the series.It is rousingly sung in a nightclub frequented by cross-dressing patrons and uniformed, gay SA officers – a startling melange the producers say was not uncommon before thebrutal Nazi crackdown on the LGBTQ+ community.While Tykwer bristles at the notion that the series should deliver any sort of “message” to Germans about their choices at the ballot box this month, fellow creator Henk Handloegten said he was proud to have “struck a nerve” with audiences around the world who find themselves at a political crossroads.“I believe that we’ve taken a clear political stand, even now in the final series, and I find it very necessary,” he said.For Handloegten, the pressure on democracy in many countries where the show is watched, “has really motivated me”.“It’s given me the justification to engage with [this era] for so long and so deeply, because I felt there was a relevance to it in today’s world. And for me, in a strange way, that’s political work – something we’ve been doing here for 13 years now.”Explore more on these topicsTelevisionGermanyEuropeAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)featuresShareReuse this content

title: The Mindhunter is a juicy true-crime show indeed: best podcasts of the week | Podcasts | The Guardian
description: Francisco Garcia’s dark, funny new crime show is a rare feat. Plus, an engrossing listen about whether people have ‘awoken’ super intelligent chatbots …
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: Francisco Garcia’s dark, funny new crime show is a rare feat. Plus, an engrossing listen about whether people have ‘awoken’ super intelligent chatbots …
Content: What lies beneath …  Author and journalist Francisco Garcia narrates The Mindhunter.Photograph: PRView image in fullscreenWhat lies beneath …  Author and journalist Francisco Garcia narrates The Mindhunter.Photograph: PRBest podcasts of the weekPodcastsThe Mindhunter is a juicy true-crime show indeed: best podcasts of the weekFrancisco Garcia’s dark, funny new crime show is a rare feat. Plus, an engrossing listen about whether people have ‘awoken’ super intelligent chatbots …Hannah J DaviesandHollie RichardsonMon 31 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 02.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePick of the weekThe MindhunterDark, drily funny and rather meta, thissix-episode podcastmanages a rare feat in the true-crime genre. Hosted by author and journalist Francisco Garcia and producer Brenna Daldorph, it explores the strange case of British criminal profiler Paul Harrison. His myriad identities in the world of both crime writing and regional football journalism intrigue Garcia – before a death hoax makes the story even juicier.Hannah J DaviesAudible, all episodes out nowThe Survivor Files With Elizabeth SmartElizabeth Smart – abducted at the age of 14 in Salt Lake City – and her guests show astonishing bravery inthis seriesabout overcoming abuse, attacks and kidnap. It begins with two episodes featuring Kara Robinson, whose account of her own abduction at the age of 15 is harrowing but also demonstrates huge inner resilience.HJDWidely available, episodes weeklyBlack Box: The ChatbotsView image in fullscreenAI discoveries … Michael Safi.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianMichael Safi returns with the Guardian’s hit AI investigation podcast,this timeexploring claims that people have “awoken” super intelligence in chatbots. It is an engrossing listen as he speaks with those who believe they have made huge discoveries – and as a result developed intense paranoia.Hollie RichardsonWidely available, episodes weekly from Thursday 3 SeptemberSolitaWomen’s solo travel is having a moment – cue this veryfun showfrom Puerto Rican producer Julie Piñero and iHeart. As Julie joins the locals at a pub in Galway, can she reclaim the Spanish diminutive solita from its connotations of pity? There are also travel tales from the likes of comic Kenice Mobley, on her Parisian sexcapades.HJDWidely available, episodes weeklyWho Run the WorldPart of the Listen to Girls initiative at south London’s Oxleas NHS Foundation Trust, thisexcellent seriesputs 11- to 18-year-olds behind the mic to ask important questions on mental health, violence against women and girls, and more. Their episode with the Met police’s Commander Clair Kelland is particularly powerful on concerns such as spiking and stalking.HJDWidely available, episodes weeklyWhat are you listening to this week? title: Caregiver creep: how helping elderly relatives can snowball into a full-time job | Well actually | The Guardian
description: Assisting an ageing loved one can start with small tasks but may lead to full-time caregiving that requires more support
Author: Laura House
Headline: Assisting an ageing loved one can start with small tasks but may lead to full-time caregiving that requires more support
Content: Illustration: Jordan Bohannon/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Jordan Bohannon/The GuardianWell actuallyCaregiver creep: how helping elderly relatives can snowball into a full-time jobAssisting an ageing loved one can start with small tasks but may lead to full-time caregiving that requires more supportLaura HouseMon 31 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 15.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHelping an ageing parent or loved one often begins with easy-to-field requests: Pick up a prescription. Drive them to a doctor’s appointment. Grab groceries.However, light tasks – just “helping out” here and there – may eventually snowball into the avalanche of full-time caregiving, a phenomenon becoming known as “caregiver creep”. Like “caregiver burnout”, it’s not a formal term, but there is growing awareness about this slow build among healthcare providers and experts.A 2025 research report from theAARP and the National Alliance for Caregivingfound that 63 million Americans act as caregivers; one in every four adults is a caregiver and the majority (94%) are caring for an adult. As the population ages – theoldest baby boomers will turn 80this year – the need for care will increase.TheUS Bureau of Labor Statisticsreports the majority (59%) of those providing this unpaid care are women. Many gen X and millennial women are feelingthe sandwich-generationsqueeze of caring for parents and children on top of their careers.Recognizing when responsibilities increase, how to identify when support needs to level up, and where to find resources both for the person receiving care and the caregiver can help manage caregiver creep.What is caregiver creep?According to theCaregiver Alliance, a caregiver is an unpaid individual who helps another person with everyday activities of daily living or medical tasks. (Separately, paid care providers may assist at home or at a care facility.)Caregiver creep is a slow build of tasks and increased responsibilities that may not be apparent at first. It can be distinguished from a more straightforward, sudden plunge into caregiving after an unexpected change in health or circumstances.Kim Elliott, a 45-year-old director of software sales in Denver, Colorado, has experienced both. Elliott was close to her father-in-law. She, rather than his two sons, was the point person for his care. She ordered groceries for him, bought his clothes and made extra dinners to drop off.“I took my father-in-law to a doctor’s appointment and they referred to me as the caregiver … At that moment, I recognized that I was the one caring for him and that there was a term for all of the years of care,” Elliott says.By contrast to this slow creep, in late 2020 Elliott abruptly became the caregiver to her mother. Elliott’s mother was diagnosed with an aggressive form of leukemia that required an urgent stem cell transplant and round-the-clock care. Amid the pandemic, her mother relocated from California to Colorado to move in with Elliott, who became both her stem cell donor and caregiver.“That was an absolute plunge,” Elliott says. “There were minutes between me realizing that she was in need of intense care and the decision to raise my hand to help.”Graphic with three lines of text that say, in bold, ‘Well Actually’, then ‘Read more on living a good life in a complex world,’ then a pinkish-lavender pill-shaped button with white letters that say ‘More from this section’It is very common for people to not recognize the slide into caregiver status – when being a helpful child becomes something more. An estimated 53 million people provide over $870bn worth of unpaid care for loved ones in the US, according to theJohns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.Public health experts say that the tremendous strain on individuals, the grand scale and lack of resourcesconstitutes a crisis.Jackee de Lagarde’s caregiver creep began in 2010 when her father became ill. De Lagarde, a 49-year-old fashion and branding consultant in New Jersey, relocated from San Francisco to New York with her husband to help him. Caregiver roles are often temporary, but following her father’s death in 2012, his medical costs left her mom in need of financial support. When De Lagarde’s son was born in 2013, her mother moved in with them, resulting in a positive multigenerational arrangement – particularly as her mother helped with childcare.In 2021, De Lagarde’s mom was diagnosed with progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), a rare degenerative neurological disease. De Lagarde and her husband, who had already cared for his mother, stepped into full-time caregiver roles.“That’s part of the creep. You are so in the moment. There’s so much that needs to be done that I wasn’t thinking about myself. I wasn’t thinking, how is this gonna affect me, my identity, my family, my career? – it was just go mode,” says De Lagarde.How do you know when an ageing person needs more care?Health shifts may be slow or sudden, but a person’s needs often increase with age-related changes.“Ageing denial is the biggest disease we have,” says Rosanne M Leipzig, a professor of geriatrics and palliative medicine at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai and author of Honest Aging. “You’ve got to be prepared. If you know what’s normal and what to expect, you can gear up for it and adapt,” she says.There are two categories of tasks that are used to assess cognitive and physical health, says Leipzig: activities of daily living (ADL) and instrumental activities of daily living (IADL). These are the everyday tasks required to live independently. Healthcare providers rate the tasksona scale to assess health and ability, and determine if support is needed. “These are clues that something’s going on … and also clues that people need more help than they currently have,” says Leipzig.ADL include daily tasks such as bathing, personal hygiene, using the toilet, eating, getting dressed and moving around the house. Sometimes, people only need temporary assistance with ADL, such as after a surgery. IADL are more advanced skills, such as managing money, organizing a household, cooking, making a phone call, driving and shopping.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIf you notice that an older person needs help with ADL and IADL – for instance, they are wearing the same outfit or taking longer to answer the phone, or have an empty fridge – these are signs that support is needed, says Martin Hernandez, general manager of family sales at A Place for Mom, an agency that helps assess and find in-home support and senior living options for families.Leipzig notes that the Medicare annual wellness visit can be a helpful assessment tool for ADL and IADL. She recommends someone dial in or be at a parent’s wellness visit to understand their overall health needs.What should you do when older relatives or friends need more support?First, start the conversation. “Dialogues are really important,” says Leipzig. Acknowledge that their needs have shifted, then “brainstorm together”, she says. “Make it a team effort. Collaborate if it’s possible.”The best-case scenario is to get ahead of the creep and start the conversation before their needs grow. Invite other point people too, advises Hernandez. “Over half of the families that we speak to wish they would have started their planning sooner. It doesn’t mean that a decision needs to be made, but you need to be prepared for it,” says Hernandez.Want to continue living at home as you age? Here’s what to considerRead moreAs a caregiver, you cannot do it all, so knowing the options can be mutually beneficial. “No one task seems huge on its own. But over time, that mental load, that stress, that worry, that time commitment can become very real,” says Hernandez. Meet with a social worker or senior living adviser to discuss support and safety forageing in place, whether a move is the right option, and budgeting.For transportation, grocery shopping or socialization, connect with a social worker througha community agencyor local senior center, or at a hospital.Many caregivers find themselvesfinancially responsiblefor covering costs or taking a step back from their careers to provide care. This can result in lost earnings. Advance planning can help minimize that impact. A Place for Mom’s2026 Cost of Long-Term Care and Senior Living Reportfound that the national median costs were $34 per hour for home care, $3,200 per month for independent living, $5,419 per month for assisted living and $6,690 per month for skilled memory care.What is the effect on caregivers?Caring for loved ones can deepen relationships, but caregivers need outside support toavoid burnoutand maintain their own health. Leipzig warns that caregivers are often unaware of how burdened they are. She recommends connecting with a social worker for services and support groups for caregivers or groups specific to care for Alzheimer’s, dementia or cancer.Caregiving can be extremely isolating. Resources are scattered, research is often self-led and community can be hard to find. In 2025, Elliott foundedGray Monster, a newsletter dedicated to those supporting ageing parents that features practical resources, tools and interviews with experts.Elliott wanted to help others feel less alone and normalize conversations about care. “The caregiving experience I walked into cannot be the one that 63 million people are also walking into. I can’t let that happen,” Elliott says.De Lagarde also felt that isolation and launched theWho Cares About Me?podcast for caregivers. “Everybody’s going through it. We all have some of the same experiences, and sometimes you just want to be heard and acknowledged,” de Lagarde says.Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyAgeingCarersHealthSocial carefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The one change that worked: I stopped listening to podcasts – and my mind flooded with ideas | Life and style | The Guardian
description: For decades my life was soundtracked by comedy duos, mostly male, discussing their friendships. When I gave them up, I felt as if I was having a mental reboot
Author: Rachel Aroesti
Headline: For decades my life was soundtracked by comedy duos, mostly male, discussing their friendships. When I gave them up, I felt as if I was having a mental reboot
Content: ‘On a trip with no podcast diversions, my mind flooded with ideas, plans and insights’ … Rachel Aroesti on a train.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘On a trip with no podcast diversions, my mind flooded with ideas, plans and insights’ … Rachel Aroesti on a train.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianThe one change that workedLife and styleThe one change that worked: I stopped listening to podcasts – and my mind flooded with ideasFor decades my life was soundtracked by comedy duos, mostly male, discussing their friendships. When I gave them up, I felt as if I was having a mental rebootRachel AroestiMon 31 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 05.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIhave always loved podcasts. The genre of audio I have come to think of as Two Men Talking (In Excessive Detail About Their Lives) has been one of my favourite forms of entertainment for decades. It started with a semi-religious devotion to a Sunday morning XFM show hosted by Jimmy Carr and the comedy writer Iain Morris, but as the years progressed and podcasting boomed, I was soon spoilt for choice. Eventually there were enough comedy duos candidly discussing their hopes, fears and awkward social interactions to fill every moment of my day.I was initially drawn to these podcasts because they made me laugh, but from the start I also found them hugely comforting: there was a period in my teenage years when I couldn’t fall asleep without mainlining episodes of Adam and Joe’s BBC 6 Music show, waking up each morning relieved I hadn’t been strangled by my iPod earphones in the night.As I got older, certain podcasts served specific consolatory functions: I was delighted when Josh Widdicombe and Rob Beckett began sharing their deeply relatable childcare woes in (Lockdown) Parenting Hell during the loneliest days of the pandemic. Sometimes, I desperately needed the reassuring company of the parasocial relationships I’d fostered. During one of my youngest son’s many late-night trips to A&E, I rocked him to sleep in the waiting room while binging episodes of Wolf & Owl – comedians Romesh Ranganathan and Tom Davis’s podcast – to steady my nerves.View image in fullscreen‘As I got older, certain podcasts served specific consolatory functions’ … Rachel Aroesti.Photograph: Alicia Canter/the GuardianAs my consumption ramped up, however, I became aware that I was using this psychological crutch every day: I listened to podcasts while walking, shopping, cleaning, folding laundry, preparing food, getting dressed, having a bath and travelling pretty much anywhere. Although I had occasionally used them to prevent anxious catastrophising, most of the time it wasn’t that I was scared to be alone with my own thoughts – it was more like I couldn’t be bothered to have them in the first place.I can’t remember the precise moment I realised my podcast habit was drowning out my internal monologue but I’m pretty sure I wasn’t wearing my headphones at the time – it is impossible to have an epiphany while eavesdropping on somebody else’s conversation. The seed was definitely sown during a train trip early last year, which involved me gazing at the East Anglian countryside for hours in silence without a single piece of technology to distract me. Along the way, I felt as if I was undergoing a mental reboot; my mind flooded with ideas, plans, insights and reflections at a speed and intensity I hadn’t experienced for years.I knew it hadn’t always been like this; I’m far from the only person who looks back wistfully on an existence not defined by the free, frictionless distraction our phones now provide – these days, there’s rarely a moment in which we lack access to an incessant stream of other people’s thoughts. But there was a simple solution to this particular time-suck: stop pressing play.So I did. Once my days were no longer soundtracked by podcast chatter (much of it entirely trivial, as hundreds of hours of conversation mined from a single friendship is bound to become), I felt some semblance of this lost world returning to me.I began listening to a lot more music – something that actively encouraged my thoughts to drift – but I also got used to silence again. Gradually, my urge to find an escape from day-to-day reality diminished. Mundane household tasks became an opportunity to mentally digest my day, and I actually noticed things when I left the house.These days I’m able to tolerate boredom much more easily. In fact, if I’m in the right mood, I can even savour it. Whereas a 10-minute wait for a bus would have wound me up before, I now see it as an opportunity to prove to myself that I don’t need external stimuli to blot out mild discomfort.I do still listen to podcasts, mainly when I go running – I know I can’t hack exercise without the very highest levels of psychological escapism. But I’d estimate my consumption has reduced by at least 80%. In doing so, I’ve given my mind permission to wander – both productively and pointlessly – again.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe one change that workedPodcastsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rosie Mackean’s quick and easy recipe for cucumber rice with fudgy eggs | Food | The Guardian
description: An intriguing and refreshing hot-cold combo of eggy rice, butter, cold cucumber sauce and pickles
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: An intriguing and refreshing hot-cold combo of eggy rice, butter, cold cucumber sauce and pickles
Content: Rosie Mackean’s cucumber rice with fudgy eggs.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Georgia Rudd.View image in fullscreenRosie Mackean’s cucumber rice with fudgy eggs.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Georgia Rudd.Quick and easyFoodRosie Mackean’s quick and easy recipe for cucumber rice with fudgy eggsAn intriguing and refreshing hot-cold combo of eggy rice, butter, cold cucumber sauce and picklesRosie MackeanMon 31 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen cooking on a weeknight, it’s easy to forget that sometimes experimenting with temperature is as important as flavour. Hot things combined with very cold things are exceptionally refreshing in the summer, and also make the mundane more exciting and playful. This dish of hot rice, hot butter, cold cucumber sauce, hot egg and cold pickles might sound, well, a bit weird, but I promise it’s delicious, comforting and also cooling.Cucumber rice with fudgy eggsPrep10 minCook30 minServes2200g Japanese short-grain riceSalt and black pepper2 medium eggs40g soft salted butter3 spring onions, trimmed and finely slicedFor the pickled cucumbers200g baby cucumbers, or the same quantity of a large cucumber1 tsp flaky sea salt3 tbspcaster sugar75gwhite-wine vinegar1 tbsp olive oil1 small handfulfresh dill, leaves picked and chopped½ tsp dried mintFor the cucumber sauce1 large cucumber, peeled and deseeded100gcreme fraiche1 very generous pinch flaky salt1 garlic clove, peeled1ice cubeStart with the pickles. Slice the cucumber into rounds, put them in a heatproof bowl, add the salt and toss to coat. In a second heatproof bowl, mix 75ml just-boiled water with the sugar and vinegar, then pour this over the cucumber and set aside while you make everything else.Wash the rice under cold water until it runs clear, then drain. If you have a rice cooker, use that. Otherwise, put the rice in a saucepan with a tight-fitting lid and add 250ml cold water and a pinch of salt. Put the pan on a medium heat, bring it to a boil, then turn down the heat as low as possible and cover the pan with the lid. Leave the rice to cook for eight minutes, then take off the heat, and set aside, still covered, for 10 minutes, so it absorbs all the water.Meanwhile, blitz the peeled and deseeded cucumber in a blender with the creme fraiche, salt and garlic, until smooth. Transfer to the fridge with the ice cube to keep it lovely and cool.Cook the eggs in boiling water for seven minutes, then rinse under cold running water until they’re just cool enough to peel.Dress the pickled cucumber with the olive oil, dill and dried mint. Pile spoonfuls of the rice into the centre of two wide, shallow bowls, then dot with the soft butter – it will melt and pool in the rice (heaven). Pour the cucumber sauce around the rice, top with the pickles, the peeled and halved fudgy eggs, and some shredded spring onion, then serve with plenty of salt and pepper on the eggs.Good Time Cooking: Show-Stopping Menus for Easy Entertaining, by Rosie Mackean, is published by Pavilion Books at £26. To order a copy for £23.40, visitguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsFoodQuick and easyMain courseEggsVegetablesVegetarian food and drinkHerbs and spicesPickling, fermenting and preservingrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Squash salad and chocolate mousse: Dean Parker’s recipes for early autumn | Food | The Guardian
description: Celebrate the flavours of the new season via this rewarding salad and rich dessert to share
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Celebrate the flavours of the new season via this rewarding salad and rich dessert to share
Content: Dean Parker’s roast squash and cavolo nero salad with black olive tapenade.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Georgia Rudd.View image in fullscreenDean Parker’s roast squash and cavolo nero salad with black olive tapenade.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Georgia Rudd.FoodSquash salad and chocolate mousse: Dean Parker’s recipes for early autumnCelebrate the flavours of the coming season via this rewarding salad and rich dessert to shareDean ParkerMon 31 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs the days start to shorten and the temperature drops (finally!), the produce becomes richer, sweeter and more comforting, and the onset of autumn is a time of year that naturally brings people together around the table, which is something I’ve always loved about food. At the restaurant, we try to let the ingredients do the talking, and we work closely with growers and producers to make the most of whatever’s in season. Today’s recipes celebrate some of my favourite seasonal flavours: the salad is simple but deeply satisfying, balancing sweet roast squash with bitter greens and a punchy black olive tapenade. For dessert, meanwhile, chocolate mousse with poached fruit is my idea of autumn in a bowl, not least because quince has a beautiful, floral character that develops as it cooks, and pairs perfectly with dark chocolate and the nutty richness of browned butter. The creme fraiche adds freshness and balance, and brings everything together. Both dishes are rooted in the philosophy that guides my cooking: celebrate the season, respect great ingredients and create food that encourages people to slow down and enjoy each other’s company.Roast squash and cavolo nero salad with black olive tapenadeThis is the sort of dish that works just as well as a light lunch or as part of a larger feast shared with friends. If you like, top the finished salad with some crumbled feta, shaved pecorino or a spoonful of thick yoghurt.Prep15 minCook40 minServes4-6For the salad1 medium butternut squash, halved, deseeded, peeled and cut into wedges2 tbsp olive oil, plus a little extra for the cavolo nero1 pinch dried chilli flakesSea salt and black pepper1 roughly 250g bunchcavolo neroJuice of ½ lemon2 tbsp toasted pumpkin seeds, or walnutsFor the tapenade100g black olives, pitted1 small garlic clove, peeled1 tsp capers, drained1 small handful flat-leafparsley2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil1 tsp red-wine vinegarBlack pepperHeat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7. Put the squash in a large roasting tray with the olive oil and chilli flakes, season generously and toss to coat. Spread out the squash into a single layer, then roast for 30-35 minutes, turning once halfway, until golden and tender.Meanwhile, strip off and discard the thick stalks from the cavolo nero and tear the leaves into large pieces. Blanch these in salted boiling water for two minutes, then drain and refresh briefly under cold running water. Squeeze dry, put in a bowl and toss with the lemon juice and a little olive oil.Now make the tapenade. Finely chop the olives, garlic, capers and parsley, either by hand or by pulsing in a food processor, then put them in a medium bowl.Stir in the olive oil and vinegar to form a rough paste, then season lightly with black pepper to taste.Arrange the cavolo nero on a serving plate and top with the warm roast squash. Spoon over the tapenade, finish with a scattering of toasted pumpkin seeds and serve warm or at room temperature.Chocolate mousse with poached quince and brown butter milk crumbView image in fullscreenDean Parker’s chocolate mousse with poached quince and brown butter milk crumb.All the various elements of this dish can be made ahead, ready for assembly on the day. Quince season proper is a few weeks off still, so if you can’t wait, try making this with firm apples or pears instead, until the real thing appears on grocers’ shelves.Prep10 minCook2 hrChill4 hr+Serves6For the mousse200g 70% cocoa dark chocolate3 eggs, separated40g caster sugar300ml double creamCreme fraiche, to serveFor the poached quince55mlclear honey375ml apple juice, or kombucha20ml applecider vinegar1 bay leaf3 black peppercorns¼ cinnamon stick¼ lemon250g quinceFor the brown butter milk crumb60g butter100g milk powder50g plain flour40g caster sugar1 pinch flaky sea saltTo make the mousse, melt the chocolate over a bain-marie, until smooth, then leave to cool slightly. Whisk the egg whites to soft peaks, then gradually work in the sugar until glossy. Lightly whip the cream to soft peaks.Beat the egg yolks, stir into the melted chocolate, then fold in the whipped cream. Gently fold through the whisked egg whites until everything’s well incorporated, then spoon the mix into a container, and chill for at least four hours.Now for the quince. Pour the honey in a medium-sized pan on medium heat and leave to cook until it starts to caramelise. Add all the remaining quince ingredients except the quince itself, and bring to a simmer.Peel and quarter the quince(s), then cut out and discard the core(s). Add the quince to the honey pan, cover, turn down the heat to very low and leave to simmer gently for an hour and a half. Take the pan off the heat, leave to cool, then lift out the quince and cut into 2cm x 2cm dice.For the milk crumb, heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4. Melt the butter in a small saucepan, then cook until it turns nut-brown and smells toasty. Mix the milk powder, flour, sugar and salt in a small bowl, pour in the melted brown butter and stir until the mix turns into small crumbs. Spread these out on a greased and lined oven tray,then bake for 12-15 minutes, stirring once halfway, until golden. Remove and leave to cool completely.To assemble the dish, put a quenelle or spoonful of chocolate mousse on each plate, then dip a spoon in hot water and use the back of it to create a well in the centre of each portion of mousse. Spoon about 10 cubes of quince around one side of each serving of mousse, then generously scatter some brown butter milk crumb on the opposite side. Spoon a generous dollop of creme fraiche on top of the mousse and serve at once.Dean Parker is head chef and co-owner ofCelentano’sin GlasgowExplore more on these topicsFoodVegetablesAutumn food and drinkStarterMain courseDessertFruitrecipesShareReuse this content

title: The pet I’ll never forget: Jerry, the king of dogs, who taught me how to live | Life and style | The Guardian
description: After a burglary, my parents decided we needed extra security. Jerry was the answer – and this hungry, handsome hound helped us all in countless ways
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: After a burglary, my parents decided we needed extra security. Jerry was the answer – and this hungry, handsome hound helped us all in countless ways
Content: Mel Bradman, pictured with Jerry and her niece, at home in Wembley in 1991.Photograph: Courtesy of Mel BradmanView image in fullscreenMel Bradman, pictured with Jerry and her niece, at home in Wembley in 1991.Photograph: Courtesy of Mel BradmanThe pet I'll never forgetLife and styleThe pet I’ll never forget: Jerry, the king of dogs, who taught me how to liveAfter a burglary, my parents decided we needed extra security. Jerry was the answer – and this hungry, handsome hound helped us all in countless waysMel BradmanMon 31 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJerry came into our lives because a burglar had broken in. My mum had woken in the middle of the night to find an intruder in our kitchen. He scarpered, but the psychological damage was done. Two days later, my dad came home with the cutest little rescue puppy, with traces of beagle and labrador in him. He was two months old, had a black, brown and white coat, and big, bashful eyes. We called him Jerry because we had a cat called Tom. “I’m not sure how he’ll protect us,” I said. “He will,” my dad replied.Jerry was very laid-back and Zen. He became part of the family straight away. He also became the therapy dog we hadn’t realised we needed. With two teenagers in the house (me and my older brother) and a hyperactive younger brother, someone was always in a strop and needing to let off steam by taking him out for a walk. Each time, Jerry obliged. I’d bore him with my latest teen-romance trauma; he was a very good listener. Sometimes, he’d have five walks a day, with both of my parents taking their turn. He certainly got his steps in.View image in fullscreenWhere’s my strudel? … Jerry on the dining table, around 1987.Photograph: Courtesy of Mel BradmanHe also dined in style. Most dogs loiter under the table during meal times. Jerry would climb on top of it and make himself comfortable until dinner was served. Often, I would come home from school and catch him lying there regally, waiting for his next banquet. It wasn’t scraps that interested him; he wanted the full three courses. He particularly liked deli food – salt beef, potato salad, pastrami, coleslaw, even apple strudel. One day, a big bowl of chopped liver disappeared. My mum blamed me, my brothers, then my dad, before realising who the culprit was.View image in fullscreenJerry, pictured at home in Wembley in 1985.Photograph: Courtesy of Mel BradmanHis appetite extended into other areas. Jerry was a Lothario with enduring sex appeal. Despite being neutered, he was still emitting something irresistible. He was the local park pin-up – dogs of all shapes and sizes would hurtle towards him, even follow him home. Jerry would flaunt hisje ne sais quoishamelessly while my mum was left trying to fight off his admirers.We never did have another burglar while Jerry was around, though that may have been more to do with luck than anything else. He liked strangers, and would make a fuss of anyone who came to the door.We had Jerry for 14 years. He began spending more time lying quietly in the garden than on top of the dining table, and couldn’t manage more than one walk a day. When I arrived home one evening, my dad broke the news that he was gone.Twenty-five years later, there’s still a huge, Jerry-shaped hole in my life. But now I think of him as our “eat, play, love” dog. He lived life to the full, and whenever I get stuck in a rut I try to take a leaf out of his playbook.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe pet I'll never forgetDogsPetsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Would equal pay create a better society? | Equal pay | The Guardian
description: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions considers the possibility of one wage for all
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions considers the possibility of one wage for all
Content: Who gets what?Photograph: Andrii Yalanskyi/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenWho gets what?Photograph: Andrii Yalanskyi/Getty Images/iStockphotoNotes and queriesEqual payWould equal pay create a better society?The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions considers the possibility of one wage for allLast week’s replies:If all car tyres were filled with CO2, would this cut atmospheric carbon?Mon 31 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIonce worked in an equal pay collective, and the principle has always seemed a good one to me. The person who worked on reception was just as important as the managing director – their actions could be make or break for the company. I remember also meeting someone, a member of the British Communist party, who had been impressed by a visit to East Germany (at that time a communist state). It stuck in my mind that she said the incentive for people to become, for example, surgeons, was that, though they wouldn’t necessarily receive higher pay, was simply that it was more satisfying work than, say, being a road sweeper. So is equal pay possible, desirable even, and would it create a better society overall?Stuart Macmillan, FifePost your answers (and new questions) below or send them tonq@theguardian.com. title: First-time buyer Isa v lifetime Isa – which one should you choose? | Isas | The Guardian
description: Despite plans to scrap the lifetime Isa, experts still advise you open one now and not wait for the new first-time buyer account to launch
Author: Rupert Jones
Headline: Despite plans to scrap the lifetime Isa, experts still advise you open one now and not wait for the new first-time buyer account to launch
Content: Saving to get on the property ladder takes time, and there’s no advantage hanging around for the new product.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreenSaving to get on the property ladder takes time, and there’s no advantage hanging around for the new product.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAIsasExplainerFirst-time buyer Isa v lifetime Isa – which one should you choose?Despite plans to scrap the lifetime Isa, experts still advise you open one now and not wait for the new first-time buyer account to launchRupert JonesMon 31 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you want to start saving towards your first home, don’t wait until a new Isa just for first-time buyers goes on sale. That is the advice from experts after more details emerged about a savings account the government plans to launch to help people get a foot on the property ladder.The first-time buyer Isa is likely to replace the existing lifetime Isa in two years and is supposed to be simpler than the older account. However, it looks as if the financial benefits won’t be as attractive as those offered by the current product, so there’s no advantage in hanging around.Whyscrap the lifetime Isa?It offers a very good deal in the form of free cash, but it also has some downsides.You must be 18 or over, and under 40, to open one, and you can pay in up to £4,000 a year until you turn 50. The money in the account can be saved in cash or invested. It can then be used to help buy a first home, or withdrawn after age 60.The government adds a 25% bonus to your savings, paid monthly, up to a maximum of £1,000 a year. Someone who “maxes out” the account from age 18 to 50 could pocket £32,000 in free cash, which, in turn, will be increased by interest or investment returns, thus further boosting their savings pot.0+0+double quotation markFor those starting to plan the next stage of their life and save towards a first home, there is little reason to delay if they are in a position to start saving nowRachel Vahey, AJ BellBut the property you buy must cost £450,000 or less – a cap that has stayed the same since 2017, while house prices have risen.Savers who withdraw their money to spend on a property costing more than the price cap face a 25% charge for an “unauthorised withdrawal”. This is designed to recover the government bonus, but it also grabs some of the saver’s original investment.Many experts say this would be easy to fix by simply increasing the price cap and reducing the penalty.Instead, the government has decided to ditch the lifetime Isa for new savers, saying there is evidence it “is not working well for many”, and create a new account. It is thought this will not go on sale until 2028 at the earliest.Until then, it will still be possible to open a lifetime Isa, and to carry on saving in line with the existing rules “indefinitely,” the Treasury says.View image in fullscreenThe outgoing lifetime Isa is still worth bagging, say experts.Photograph: Louisa Svensson/AlamyShould I wait?“For those starting to plan the next stage of their life and save towards a first home, there is little reason to delay if they are in a position to start saving now,” says Rachel Vahey, head of public policy at investment platform AJ Bell.“Taking advantage of a lifetime Isa could allow them to benefit from the existing government bonus – and investment growth on it – while they wait for further details of the new product.”There are other reasons why those in the industry are suggesting you don’t wait. The first-time buyer Isa appears to be more user-friendly than the lifetime Isa: it will have no upper age limit and no withdrawal charges.However, savers could end up worse-off than those who use a lifetime Isa. With the new account, the government bonus will not be paid at the end of each month but as a lump sum at the point when the individual is buying their first home. So you will be missing out on any potential interest, or investment growth that the bonus might have attracted.And the bonus will be based on what you have paid in (minus any withdrawals) rather than what your fund ends up being worth – it will not take into account any of the savings interest, or investment growth that you will have enjoyed.“For a saver putting away £333 a month over 10 years at a return of 6%, receiving the bonus at the end, rather than monthly, costs them more than £3,600 in lost growth. That’s assuming a 25% government bonus,” says Brian Byrnes, the director of personal finance at the wealth management platform Moneybox.However, we don’t yet know whether the new account will also offer a 25% government bonus, or if the annual contribution limit will also be £4,000.We also don’t know if the £450,000 property price cap will be increased on either Isa.View image in fullscreenTransferring from a normal stocks and shares Isa, into a cash first-time buyer Isa, will be banned.Photograph: Leonora Oates/AlamyCan I move to the new Isa?If you already have a lifetime Isa, or open one, you won’t be able to transfer it to the new Isa. This is to prevent account holders earning two lots of bonus government cash.You will be able to take out a first-time buyer Isa as well, although you will only be able to save into one type in any single tax year.Someone holding both accounts will be able to use the money saved in both towards the same home purchase.Transferring from a normal stocks and shares Isa, into a cash first-time buyer Isa, will be banned. Transfers from a normal cash Isa into a cash first-time buyer Isa will be permitted, as would transfers from a stocks and shares Isa to a stocks and shares first-time buyer Isa. However, if you do this, as opposed to taking out a lifetime Isa, you will miss out on the 25% government bonus in the meantime.Explore more on these topicsIsasFirst-time buyersPropertySavingsBanks and building societiesexplainersShareReuse this content

title: Is it true that … mental health is affected by inflammation? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Studies have found that anti-inflammatory drugs can improve your mood. But what does that mean for conditions such as depression and anxiety?
Author: Kate Lloyd
Headline: Studies have found that anti-inflammatory drugs can improve your mood. But what does that mean for conditions such as depression and anxiety?
Content: Illustration: Becky Barnicoat/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Becky Barnicoat/The GuardianIs it true that …Life and styleIs it true that … mental health is affected by inflammation?Studies have found that anti-inflammatory drugs can improve your mood. But what does that mean for conditions such as depression and anxiety?Kate LloydMon 31 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleInflammation is the immune system’s response to injury or infection. If you cut yourself and the area becomes red and swollen, that’s inflammation: immune cells are rushing to fight germs and repair tissue.But inflammation can also occur in the body during illnesses, and a low level of inflammation can arise from obesity or ageing. “A marker of that inflammation tends to be elevated cytokines in people’s blood,” says Prof Daniel M Davis, head of life sciences at Imperial College London and author ofImmune Health: A Myth-Busting Guide. “They’re the molecules immune cells use to communicate with each other.”There are more than 100 types of cytokines in your body, and some affect the brain. “If you have a fever, it’s not just physical, you’re also mentally affected,” says Davis. “Some cytokines influence how you feel.”double quotation markWe haven’t disentangled this enough to know what part of the immune system to target to improve people’s mental healthStudies of patients with rheumatoid arthritis have found that cytokine-blocking anti-inflammatory drugs can also improve mood. Scans suggest this may be because blocking cytokines changesactivity in the brain.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIs it true that … you need to detox your scalp?Read moreAstudy of nearly 5,000 childrenfound that those with higher than average levels of the cytokine IL-6 in their blood at the age of nine, with no sign of depression, were more likely to suffer depression at 18. Anotherstudy, this time of adults,found a correlation between the development of an immune-related disease and a previous diagnosis of psychiatric disorders, including depression and anxiety.Scientists don’t yet know enough to use this knowledge to treat conditions such as depression or anxiety. “Several lines of evidence point to an overlap of immune and mental health, but we haven’t disentangled this enough to know who could benefit, and exactly what part of the immune system we could safely target to improve people’s mental health,” says Davis.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleIs it true that …Mental healthHealthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: My search for the perfect Polish dumplings in Gdańsk | Poland holidays | The Guardian
description: Pierogi are a religion in Poland, but I’d never been a believer. Could a recce in the charming Baltic city convert me?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Pierogi are a religion in Poland, but I’d never been a believer. Could a recce in the charming Baltic city convert me?
Content: Gdańsk old town.Photograph: Poike/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenGdańsk old town.Photograph: Poike/Getty Images/iStockphotoPoland holidaysMy search for the perfect Polish dumplings in GdańskPierogi are a religion in Poland, but I’d never been a believer. Could a recce in the charming Baltic city convert me?Ben AitkenMon 31 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 02.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIused to live in Poland.I worked in a fish-and-chip shop in the western city of Poznań, boning cod and peeling potatoes for £1.50 an hour. With the exception of that job, I enjoyed everything about my time in the country, not least the food. I liked the chicken broth with noodles, the slippery herring, the knuckles of pork the size of basketballs, the cold beetroot soup that beats gazpacho hands down.One thing I was less delighted by were Polish dumplings – pierogi. It wasn’t that they weren’t nice – they were – it was more that they didn’t seem to warrant the extreme levels of affection and esteem Poles often bestow on the doughy parcels. By being ambivalent about them, I was going against a well-established grain.It is claimed by some that pierogi arrived in Poland via Marco Polo (actually a myth), and that the oldest written Polish recipe dates to 1682 (true). In short, these things have pedigree, and you denigrate them at your peril. I almost lost a Polish friend once for not being smitten with Poland’s answer to gyoza and ravioli. Such was her reaction, you’d have thought I’d denigrated the late Polish pope, John Paul II.“I don’t understand this mentality,” said Paulina. “Have you tried the ones filled with cheese and potato?”“Yep.”“Have you had the ones from the fancy place on the old square?”“Yep.”“Have you had the frozen ones from the supermarket?”“Uh-huh.”“Have you had the ones from the milk bar near Freedom Street?”“More than once.”“Hm. Have you tried my grandmother’s?”“Erm, no.”“Well there you are. Mystery solved. That explains your mentality. You have to reserve judgment and stop talking nonsense until you’ve tried the dumplings of ababcia.”I had versions of this conversation several times when telling Poles that I was merely fond of pierogi rather than hopelessly devoted. On each occasion, thebabcia(grandmother figure) in question was either dead or otherwise engaged, meaning that their dumplings couldn’t be tested, and my opinion – thatpierogi are just OK – couldn’t be validated.Until now perhaps. Having enjoyed searching forthe perfectsteak fritesin Paris, I set myself the task of giving pierogi a proper crack of the whip in one of Poland’s finest cities – its jewel on the Baltic coast, Gdańsk. Could the old port city cure me of my pierogiscepticism? Would the dumplings of a localbabciabowl me over? The answer was yes … and no.Gdański BowkeView image in fullscreenAfter a mooch around the picturesque old town(during which I learned that Daniel Fahrenheit, inventor of the temperature scale, spent his first years in Gdańsk before leaving as a teen, having realised how cold it got in winter), I pull up a pew on the riverside terrace of this well-regarded establishment. I have a mixed plate of the classics: potato and cheese, cabbage and mushroom, minced pork. They’ve been boiled then shallow fried, ensuring a slightly crisp finish, and are served with the traditional accompaniments: sour cream and bacon bits jostling in their own lardy juices.The first thing that strikes me is the size of these parcels. Boy, are they plump. Of the selection, potato and cheese triumphs, with the optimal mouthful requiring a touch of each topping: the bacon bringing a salty crunch, the lard adding an umami note, the sour cream resolving the whole. In short, solid grub in a lovely spot.£13, 7.5/10,gdanskibowke.comPanoramaView image in fullscreenComposite: Alexander Spatari/Getty ImagesNo chance of just happening on this restaurant: it’s on the 16th floor of what might be charitably called a nondescript building. The view isn’t postcard-perfect but it’s powerful: the vista is dominated by the city’s famous shipyard, where in 1980 trade union leader Lech Wałęsa and his unmerry men downed tools and gave communism the cold shoulder.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe boiled dumplings have been blackened with charcoal or squid ink, filled with a raspberry reduction and white Belgian chocolate, then decorated with strawberries and cream. This is a main course, by the way, not a dessert. I have fun pressing a fork through the foreboding dough and watching the innards spill. Gory but enjoyable. There’s a nice sourness from the raspberries, the chew on the dough allows the flavours to travel and combine, and I like the crunch you get from the tiny raspberry seeds. I had been tempted by the savoury pierogi option – rabbit with thyme sauce – but I went with madam’s suggestion and I’m glad I did. After all,babciaknow best.£11, 7.5/10,panoramarestauracjagdansk.plManduView image in fullscreenThe dumplings here are made on site and it’s a lovely thing to witness – the craft, the culture, the skill of thebabcia. The menu is extensive: 40 types, with baked, boiled and deep-fried options. Some of the fillings require a double take: chorizo, potato, mascarpone and … truffle paste, anyone?I’m pleased to see variety, though. As with the sandwich, conceivably a dumpling can be filled with anything. (In Cleveland, Ohio, I once encountered bacon cheeseburger pierogi – which I interpreted as evidence that multiculturalism was working just fine.)I have a baked half-dozen, filled with a mingling of beef, cheese, red onion and pickled cucumber. Small pies they are, befitting the etymology of pierogi. The filling is excellent, but the heavier carriage of the yeast-risen dumplings starts to weigh on me, and I find myself digging out the interior and foregoing the case. I would have appreciated a mixed plate option, to avoid things getting samey.£12, 8/10,pierogarnia-mandu.plStary MłynView image in fullscreenComposite: Ben AitkenThis pierogi specialist is housed in an old mill – hence the name, which translates as old mill – on the edge of what has become known as booking.com island, on account of its popularity with tourists. I have the mixed plate – nine iterations of Poland’s beloved comfort food. There’s a half-hour wait after ordering, while the dumplings are “cooked on the fly”, the ceaseless prep apparent at the back of the dining room. The wait gives me a chance to read a kids’ book I find on the merchandise stand (yep, there’s merch) about a dumpling that goes on an adventure and ends up as prime minister.The fillings are decent: beef rib, cod fillet, chicken and cheese – but they are somewhat overpowered by the dough. One shortcoming of Polish dumplings is that a plate of them, even a mixed one, can get a bit repetitive.Here’s an idea: individual dumplings, slightly enlarged, handheld, easily taken away and munched on the move? The largest pierogi ever made, incidentally, was about two metres long and weighed nearly 100kg, though the largest recognised by the Guinness World Records weighed 55.7kg – both, unsurprisingly, in the US.£15, 7/10,pierogarnie.comOberża 86View image in fullscreenGdańsk is officially in a relationship with two other cities – Sopot and Gdynia. Together they are known as the Trójmiasto,or Tricity. I take a short train ride to Gdynia, the ugly sister of the three. After vainly wandering around for an hour in search of pierogi, I’m about to abort the mission when I chance on Oberża 86. I confess my head is turned less by the name or the building and more by the word Michelin on the sign. I pop my head in and ask if they do pierogi. They do, as a starter, just the three pieces, filled with broad beans and served with a shallot sauce, which they suggest pairing with a wine from the north-west of Poland.I’m sold. And soon I’m smitten. The sauce has a zing that comes from the onions being slow-cooked with wine and lemon. The dough has the quality of pasta. The filling is gentle, and balances the tangy sauce. And there is the right amount – a lovable trio, rather than a testing half dozen. The wine helps, I must say. It’s lairy, with apple vibes and a slight fizz, the Johnny Rotten of the white wine world. After crowning Oberża 86 my winner, I waddle to the local beach for a swim, wondering if I’ll be more or less buoyant after all the pierogiI’ve taken on board the past couple of days.£12, 9/10,oberza86.plBen Aitken is the author of A Chip Shop in Poznan: My Unlikely Year in Poland. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Author: Alex Bellos
Headline: The solution to today’s underwater conundrums
Content: Photograph: Disney/Sportsphoto/AllstarView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Disney/Sportsphoto/AllstarAlex Bellos's Monday puzzleMathematicsDid you solve it? The fin-tastic fish puzzleThe solution to today’s underwater conundrumsAlex BellosMon 31 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 12.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEarlier today I set you the following puzzles. Here they are again with the solutions.A fish is swimming in a tank that is two metres high, one metre across and one metre deep. The image below shows one path it swam.View image in fullscreenHere is the same path shown from the front, the right side and the top.View image in fullscreenI gave two examples of a front and side view, and asked you to draw the top view of the shortest path that results in those views.1.View image in fullscreenSolutionView image in fullscreenStart off by looking at the cross section defined by the vertical line of the 1. The diagonal of the 7 has to be on that plane, as does the horizontal part of the 7. The final segment has to be on the area I shaded in above right. The top view is thus:View image in fullscreen2.View image in fullscreenSolutionView image in fullscreenThe bottom half of the path must fall on the shaded cross section above left. Likewise, the top section (excluding the very top and middle of the tank) must fall on the shaded cross section above centre. We want the shortest path, so there is only one way to join the bottom part of the path to the top part, and to link the path on the top cross section, above right. The top view is thus:View image in fullscreenI hope you enjoyed these challenges. I’ll be back in two weeks.Today’s puzzles were created by maths educatorGeorge Watkinsto celebrate the opening of the1729 Maths School, which welcomes its first pupils later this month.The school – in Mill Hill, north London – is the first specialist maths secondary school to open in the UK.
