title: ‘I organised my spices – and feel happy every time I cook!’ 12 readers on their most rewarding tiny accomplishments | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Forget writing that novel: the most satisfying tasks are often the smallest. From batch cooking and bird feeding, to filling a kettle with meticulous precision, our readers reveal their favourites
Author: Guardian readers
Headline: Forget writing that novel: the most satisfying tasks are often the smallest. From batch cooking and bird feeding, to filling a kettle with meticulous precision, our readers reveal their favourites
Content: No more fumbling … a well-organised spice cupboard.Photograph: PicturePartners/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenNo more fumbling … a well-organised spice cupboard.Photograph: PicturePartners/Getty Images/iStockphotoLife and style‘I organised my spices – and feel happy every time I cook!’ 12 readers on their most rewarding tiny accomplishmentsForget writing that novel: the most satisfying tasks are often the smallest. From batch cooking and bird feeding, to filling a kettle with meticulous precision, our readers reveal their favouritesGuardian readersMon 31 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSometimes, it’s the smallest accomplishments that bring the biggest feelings of joy. You don’t need to run a marathon or write a novel to get a sense of achievement; something as simple as reorganising your cutlery drawer or repairing a garden fence can prove surprisingly satisfying. Here, readers share the modest achievements that have brought them great pleasure.I really enjoy cooking and have a large collection of spices. Recently, I bought a few dozen glass bottles and organised my herbs and spices in a drawer, with labels on the lids and sides. Every time I cook, I feel pleasure from being able to instantly put my hand on the requisite spice without fumbling through piles of little boxes, and having to open and smell them to be sure which is which.Anna Smith, musician, Utrecht, the NetherlandsView image in fullscreenSawing wood can be simple, yet so satisfying.Photograph: South_agency/Getty ImagesI love using a sharp saw to cut a piece of wood as accurately as I can, then planing the end grain so it is pretty much dead square. The grain glistens beautifully as the light hits it, and the feeling of having done something simple but essential, using only basic hand-tools, is its own reward.Anonymous, teacher,DerbyI love getting arduous tasks done with ease using little hacks. A good example is using sugar soap to clean greasy surfaces in the kitchen. It is also very effective on the grout between tiles. Just give it a little scrub (you can even use an old electric toothbrush), leave overnight, then wipe off with a damp cloth for lovely white grout!Louise Wong, legal assistant, LondonI don’t buy anything new or secondhand; I use what I already have, adapt things and shop my own wardrobe. It means I save a large percentage of my salary (compared with others) and I spend that money on my passions and priorities: pottery, art classes and coastal path walking.Rachel Smith, urban planner,MedwayView image in fullscreenCatch it if you can!Photograph: Artem Stepanov/Getty ImagesOn several occasions, I have dropped a bar of soap in the shower, only to catch it again, eyes closed, without fumbling. I was once washing upwards from my chest to my shoulder and the soap escaped, but I caught it behind my back. It’s even more satisfying than my uncanny ability to load exactly the right number of sheets of paper into the printer when printing long documents.Ed, writer,BebingtonI recently had a second baby and I found so much joy in batch-cooking and labelling containers of food towards the end of my pregnancy. Seeing the freezer full of meals, all neatly stacked, felt great. Top tier nesting activity.Lucy J Huskisson, art technician, BristolI love hollyhocks, but I have never had any success growing them from seeds. Two years ago, I was passing a house where someone was cutting down their hollyhocks – the flowers had died and in their place were little pods of seeds. I asked her for some and planted them – they take two years to grow. Now, I have a front garden full of them.Sarah Linklett, LondonView image in fullscreenDough the right thing.Photograph: ArtistGNDphotography/Getty ImagesI recently learned how to make bread for the first time and it is giving me great joy. It’s so simple, yet hugely satisfying and rewarding. The smell brings me back to my childhood. I hope those same smells are as comforting to my kids as they were to me when I was younger.Caroline, radio producer, IrelandI find joy in hanging the washing on the line in a neat and organised row. Trousers have to be hung up from the waistband, and tops hung from the bottom hem, alternating items for maximum drying. It’s incredibly satisfying to know I’m doing a chore that means my clothes will be dry and fresh for free.Kirsty, social worker, BradfordDiscovering acrylic painting has brought me so much joy. I started learning completely on my own, watching short videos, trying different techniques, making mistakes and simply seeing what happens. When I paint, I become completely absorbed in what I’m doing, and for me it has become one of the best forms of meditation. It calms me, helps me disconnect from everything else, and gives me a nice sense of accomplishment when I see something taking shape on the canvas. I love that there is no pressure for it to be perfect. I can experiment, learn and just enjoy the process. It has become a very special source of calm, creativity and happiness in my life.Cintia Procaci, consultant, LuxembourgView image in fullscreenSuck it and see … vacuuming can be bliss.Photograph: Carol Yepes/Getty ImagesI love vacuuming. It gives me peace and, unlike work-related endeavours that tend to pay dividends days, months or years down the line, once you’re done vacuuming you can enjoy the rewards immediately. It’s the opposite of cooking, a task that involves labouring for an hour in order to enjoy a meal for a whole 10 minutes (or less). With vacuuming, you invest 10 minutes and get several days’ worth of domestic bliss. It’s the one task I refuse to let the robots take away from me.Ana Fota, reporter and content creator, BrusselsI love to feed the birds. My casita is blessed with trees and I’ve grown to love the twitters of the finches, and the hums and clicks of the hummingbirds. I’ve joyously invested in a bird feeder and a suet cake holder, a nectar repository with perches, a nyjer sock and a birdbath with two tiny resin birds decorating the rim. My happiness after cleaning the birdbath, changing out the nectar and replenishing the bird seed can’t be bought. I feel I’m making a difference for companions who reward me daily with their songs and fluttering wings.Susan, writer, USPeople featured in the article responded to a Community callout. You can contribute to open calloutshere.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleHomesInteriorsHealth & wellbeingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: South African airline defends dramatic low-level flyby before rugby union clash | Rugby union | The Guardian
description: A pre-game stunt involving two passenger jets flying dramatically low over a  stadium in South Africa drew huge cheers from the crowd, but also sparked a major debate over safety risks
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A pre-game stunt involving two passenger jets flying dramatically low over a stadium in South Africa drew huge cheers from the crowd, but also sparked a major debate over safety risks
Content: An aircraft performs a low flyby before the match between South Africa and New Zealand in Cape Town.Photograph: Jamie Rossouw/ReutersView image in fullscreenAn aircraft performs a low flyby before the match between South Africa and New Zealand in Cape Town.Photograph: Jamie Rossouw/ReutersRugby unionSouth African airline defends dramatic low-level flyby before rugby union clashCape Town stunt sparks major debate over safety risksAirlink insists flyby conducted according to regulationsAssociated PressMon 31 Aug 2026 09.44 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA pre-game stunt involving two passenger jets flying dramatically low over a stadium in South Africa drew huge cheers from the estimated crowd of 56,000 people, but also sparked a major debate over safety risks. The flyby by two Embraer jets, operated by the local airline Airlink, happened on Saturday before the second rugby union Testbetween South Africa and New Zealandin Cape Town.The flight tracking service Flightradar24 estimated that the lead jet passed just 41-46 feet (12-14 metres) above the roof of Cape Town Stadium, with the crowd and the world’s top-ranked rugby teams below. The second jet, which was very close behind, flew through a cloud of pink dust that shot up from the stadium roof as part of the show.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueAirlink, a sponsor of theSouth Africarugby union team, said the flyby was conducted according to safety regulations. The airline said that it was carefully planned and rehearsed, with the aircraft flying at 150 knots (172 mph), when they went over the stadium. Each jet had three senior captains on board, Airlink said, operating in the roles of a commander, a co-pilot and a safety officer. The jets were not carrying any passengers.“Airlink notes the concerns expressed in various social media and online forums regarding yesterday’s formation flyby over Cape Town’s DHL Stadium,” Airlink said on Sunday. “The flight demanded careful planning and rehearsal, as it required navigating at low altitude, at around 150 knots. The South African Civil Aviation Authority and Air Traffic Navigation Services provided valuable guidance, approval and support to ensure a safe flyby.”View image in fullscreenThe planes fly above the stadium before kick-off.Photograph: Gallo Images/Getty ImagesSouth African rugby union has a tradition of stadium flybys at big games, starting when a Boeing 747 flew over a stadium in Johannesburg before the 1995 World Cup final between the same teams, who are fierce rivals. But the flyby last weekend was especially low and dramatic, generating global interest after it was shown as part of the pre-game broadcast, and sparking a flurry of videos shot by witnesses.View image in fullscreenThe second jet flies through a cloud of pink dust that shot up from the stadium roof as part of the show.Photograph: APSome aviation experts questioned whether the margin for error was too small. “Basically, that lead aircraft … was kind of like dodging over the roof and climbing over the one side and dipping below and then climbing over the other side. That was a little bit uncomfortable,” Chris Martinus, president of Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association South Africa, said. “[If] something adverse happens, you just don’t have options at that kind of altitude.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKeith Tonkin, an Australian aviation consultant and former military and commercial pilot, said yesteron Monday that the Embraer passenger jets – which are small-to-medium jets designed for regional flights – were not designed or intended for that kind of low-level operation and warned against the precedent.“The bigger picture is that a benchmark has been established and others may expect to do something similar, and that’s not going to end well,” Tonkin said. He added that turbulence or a bird strike at such a low altitude could leave the pilots with too little room to manoeuvre without hitting the stadium.Airlink said flight data recorded by both aircraft confirmed their flights were performed within civil aviation safety limits for speed and altitude.Explore more on these topicsRugby unionSouth AfricaSouth Africa rugby teamNew Zealand rugby union teamAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Countries legally obliged to consider slavery reparations, says UN committee | Reparations and reparative justice | The Guardian
description: Guidance says states must implement ‘comprehensive measures’ to address legacy of racial discrimination
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Guidance says states must implement ‘comprehensive measures’ to address legacy of racial discrimination
Content: Protesters in London calling for reparations. At least 12.5 ‌million Africans were taken and sold between the 15th and 19th centuries.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenProtesters in London calling for reparations. At least 12.5 ‌million Africans were taken and sold between the 15th and 19th centuries.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesReparations and reparative justiceCountries legally obliged to consider slavery reparations, says UN committeeGuidance says states must implement ‘comprehensive measures’ to address legacy of racial discriminationReuters in GenevaMon 31 Aug 2026 07.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA UN committee has said countries are legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and take other ⁠measures to address the enduring ⁠legacy of racial ​discrimination.Guidance published on Monday by the committee on the elimination of racial discrimination (CERD) said the obligations arose from ⁠a legally binding 1965 convention on racial discrimination, not from the legal standards that existed when the slave trade took place.The committee described the approach as a “paradigm ⁠shift” away from debates over historical responsibility that have often been used by governments to resist reparations ​claims.“States parties must implement comprehensive reparatory measures for ‌people of African descent, ‌covering all aspects of remedies,” said the UN document, which may be cited in courtrooms.At least 12.5 ‌million Africans were taken and sold between the 15th and 19th centuries in what CERD called the largest forced displacement in history.Calls for reparations – ranging from official apologies to financial compensation – have gained momentum internationally, though opponents argue states and institutions should not be held responsible for historical crimes.The EU and Britain abstained from a UN resolution ‌on slavery in March.Some states have sought to dodge claims for justice in courtrooms by arguing that there were no international laws outlawing the slave trade ​at the time – the so-called intertemporality principle.But the UN document argues that, regardless of whether slavery and the slave trade were illegal under the laws of the day, countries remain responsible under current international obligations to tackle their continuing effects.“Irrespective of the legal characterisation of the original historical acts, states parties remain bound ⁠by their present obligations under the convention to address structural inequalities,” the UN document ​says.Financial compensation alone is ​not sufficient, it adds, urging “transformative” measures including ​opening archives, revising public memorials and establishing independent truth commissions.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long WaveNesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPela Boker Wilson, a committee expert ​from Liberia who helped draft ‌the document, said ​she expected states ​to move beyond broad expressions of regret and review policies and laws.“We are calling on state parties to take concrete and meaningful action,” she told Reuters. “We want to affirm the dignity of those whose suffering was denied, whose suffering was minimised or forgotten.”Explore more on these topicsReparations and reparative justiceSlaveryUnited NationsAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Morocco not to blame for Ceuta border breach, says Spanish PM | Spain | The Guardian
description: Pedro Sánchez says two countries cooperating and accuses Israel and Russia of spreading fake news about migration
Author: Sam Jones
Headline: Pedro Sánchez says two countries cooperating and accuses Israel and Russia of spreading fake news about migration
Content: As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta at the end of July and the start of August.Photograph: Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAs many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta at the end of July and the start of August.Photograph: Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP/Getty ImagesSpainMorocco not to blame for Ceuta border breach, says Spanish PMPedro Sánchez says two countries cooperating and accuses Israel and Russia of spreading fake news about migrationSam Jonesin MadridMon 31 Aug 2026 06.21 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has said there is no evidence to suggest the Moroccan government was behind last month’smassive border crossing into Ceutabut accused Israel and Russia of spreading disinformation.As many as141 people are thought to have diedtrying to enter the Spanish enclave at the end of July. The influx of about 70,000 men, women and children unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency andreignited tensions within the EU over immigration.Despite speculation that Rabat may have engineered the mass crossing as a means of showing its displeasure atSpain’s rapprochement with Algeria, Sánchez said there was nothing to indicate the involvement of the Moroccan authorities.‘We want to find a better future’: teenage girls on why they risked their lives to reach SpainRead more“There’s no information from any intelligence agency that raises doubts over the involvement of Moroccan authorities,” he told Cadena Ser radio on Monday. “Cooperation withMoroccois frankly positive. I’d like to stress that we need to be aware that this crisis can be resolved only through cooperation – and not through a lack of trust in Morocco, which would only further aggravate the already complex situation we have in Ceuta.”Sánchez said fake news had been pumped out on social media accounts “associated with Russia, Israel and the international far right that always use migration to attack not just Spain but also Europe”.The accusation drew a furious response from Israel. The country’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, called it a “brazen lie”, adding: “Continuing to spread defamatory lies will not distract from Sánchez’s disgraceful failure to manage his country’s affairs.”The ⁠Kremlin rejected allegations ⁠that ​Russia was connected to ⁠the Ceuta migration crisis, the ⁠RBC daily ​reported ‌on ‌Monday.Sánchez repeated his assertion that the influx was due to the activities of “criminal gangs” who had used disinformation to falsely claim that a ruling by Spain’s supreme court meant that no one who entered Ceuta by swimming could be deported back to Morocco.Although the overwhelming majority of the migrantscrossed back into Morocco weeks ago, at least 5,000 people, including 1,200 minors, are still on the streets of Ceuta. Their continuing presence has led to clashes between some Ceuta residents and police, while some of the migrants have had their belongings burned while sleeping rough on beaches. On Saturday, four Moroccan migrants were arrested for throwing stones at Spanish soldiers.Sánchez said there would soon be “sufficient capacity” to accommodate all those still in the enclave.Spain’s conservative People’s party has accused the government of failing to protect the people of Ceuta. “It did nothing to avoid the invasion on 30 July and it’s doing nothing to stop the public order crisis that’s getting worse every day,” the PP’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, said last week.Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, has described events in Ceuta as “an invasion and an act of war promoted by Morocco and allowed by Sánchez, who is incapable of responding because he is subservient to Morocco”.Explore more on these topicsSpainMoroccoMigrationAfricaEuropeMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Nepal rescuers race to reach hundreds feared trapped in hydropower tunnels | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Workers thought to be stuck in underground areas at 11 sites after last week’s devastating flash floods
Author: Cait Kelly
Headline: Workers thought to be stuck in underground areas at 11 sites after last week’s devastating flash floods
Content: Nepali soldiers search for survivors in a hydropower tunnel in Rasuwa district, Nepal.Photograph: Prime Minister Secretariat, Nepal/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNepali soldiers search for survivors in a hydropower tunnel in Rasuwa district, Nepal.Photograph: Prime Minister Secretariat, Nepal/AFP/Getty ImagesNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepal rescuers race to reach hundreds feared trapped in hydropower tunnelsWorkers thought to be stuck in underground areas at 11 sites after last week’s devastating flash floodsCait Kellyin Kathmandu andWilliam ChristouMon 31 Aug 2026 11.56 EDTFirst published on Mon 31 Aug 2026 02.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRescue teams are working to reach more than 900 missing hydropower workers, hundreds of whom are feared trapped in the tunnels and underground areas of 12hydropower projects in Nepal after thedevastating flash floods, ​the ⁠country’s disaster ​management authority has said.The death toll from the⁠unprecedented delugeof ice, rock, mud ​and debris on Wednesday last week has risen to 939 people, with 16 more dead reported in Tibet.More than 4,400 are missing on the two sides of the border.About 500 of the missing hydropower workers at projects damaged by the flooding in Nepal’s Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts are thought to be trapped in tunnels built to control the flow of water.As rescue efforts drag on, experts fear the chances of finding survivors in tunnels are diminishing as oxygen levels fall.Some workers called for help when flooding started on Wednesday and those who had managed to escape tunnels said many of their colleagues were still trapped, said Mohan Kumar Dangi, the president of the Nepal Independent Power Producers’ Association.Devastated by floods and overwhelmed by bodies, Nepalis weep for what remains of their homesRead moreRescue efforts have been complicated by difficult terrain, persistently high flood waters and difficult weather. With more than 40 bridges destroyed, rescuers are relying on helicopters, while India andChinaare sending prefabricated truss bridges to help restore access.View image in fullscreenA resident examines his damaged home in Devighat, Nuwakot district.Photograph: Rajesh Kumar Singh/APThe swollen Trishuli River has also continued to change course unpredictably, making planning a challenge. Areas that were dry one day are flooded the next, and further floods are a constant concern.Hundreds of bodies, many unidentified, that were swept down the mountains by the torrent, have been buried in shallow graves after DNA testingon the plains ⁠of the Himalayan region.Nepali officials said on Monday that the focus was on reaching the 933 people missing from ‌hydropower plants. “A large amount of debris has been deposited and that is posing us a big challenge to open the tunnels,” the Nepal army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet told Reuters.About 250 people were rescued from the Upper Trishuli hydroelectric project over the weekend, and army engineers began blasting operations at the site to rescue another 42 workers thought be missing.View image in fullscreenA flood victim being airlifted from Rasuwa district yesterday to a hospital in Kathmandu. More than 4,400 people are now listed as missing.Photograph: Prabin Ranabhat/AFP/Getty ImagesThe damage to hydropower infrastructure is estimated to have taken 700 megawatts out of service, about 10% of the country’s power capacity.Pictures and videos shared by rescue teams ⁠showed earth-moving equipment shovelling mud to try to reach the tunnels.Ashish Gurung, who normally works as a guide, was among the rescuers. “There is just mud everywhere,” he said. “Inside the tunnel it was worse. It’s so difficult to move, the mud is so deep.”His team was trying to access the Chilime hydropower plant in Rasuwa, one of the worst-hit areas. At least eight people are believed missing there, and an Indian team is working alongside the Nepali army using pumps and excavators to locate them.View image in fullscreenAshish Gurung, left, with fellow rescue mountaineer Jenjen Lama at the Chilime hydropower plant in Rasuwa.Photograph: SuppliedThe Nepali prime minister, Balendra Shah, said rescue efforts were “challenging due to adverse weather, difficult terrain and ongoing risks.”Gurung said mountaineers were improvising by using planks of wood to check the depth of the mud, before using them as makeshift bridges along with a system of ropes to keep themselves safe.“Walking in it is very difficult, at one point it was up to our chests,” he said. “We got close to the first station, about 130 metres in. Inside that far … it looked like it was just bodies.”The hydropower company had given his team a map and it looked as if there was a chance people in the tunnels could have survived. “They have a safe area inside,” he said. “Some of them could potentially be alive. I am hoping they are alive.”Young girl rescued from rubble three days after Nepal flash flood – videoThe Red Cross estimates that more than 93,000 people have been affected by the disaster,heightening fears that the climate crisis is destabilising the geology of mountain and polar regions.Shah said the flood was an “unprecedented and devastating natural disaster” and that it was difficult to compile a complete assessment of the damage.“Despite the adverse weather, difficult terrain and continuing risks, we are moving forward with determination to save the lives of our citizens,” he said in a Facebook post late on Sunday. Almost 21,000 security personnel were involved in the rescue operations alongside civilian workers and volunteers, he said.Whole communities had been destroyed by the flooding, leaving families homeless in heavy rain.View image in fullscreenRescuers work to access a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydropower plant in Nuwakot district, Nepal.Photograph: Nepal Army/Reuters“There are no roads, they have all been washed away, and many areas are just not accessible,” said a police officer coordinating rescue efforts in Nuwakot district. “It is very difficult for my men. The area is still flooded, and elsewhere it is all marshland.”Nepal’s disaster agency said on Monday it had counted 903 deaths, with 4,793 people, including 592 foreigners, missing. Chinese authorities had reported 16 deaths and 546 people missing as of Sunday. State media said 261 of the missing were foreigners, including more than 100 Nepalis.Among those missing are more than 30 British nationals. On Saturday, a rapid deployment team from the UK arrived in Nepal to support Britons and their families. The UK government has given a £5m support package to assist Nepal in its disaster response.Amid the soaring toll of death and missing was some hope. On Monday, rescuers pulled a six-year-old girl out of mud after hearing crying. “Her body was trapped in mud, but her head was outside,” the Nepali armed police spokesperson Netra Bahadur Karki told Agence France-Presse.China’s state-run CCTV said Beijing had mobilised more than 2,100 rescue workers and allocated at least ​220m yuan (£24m) to support relief efforts and had been airdropping equipment and supplies to frontline rescuers, while its soldiers used life-detection equipment to look for the missing.locatorNepal has said it does not need foreign help in general search and rescue operations, but it has leaned on its neighbours, India and China, for their expertise in tunnel rescues.Rescue operations have been suspended several times since Friday because of bad weather and concerns that a lake formed across the Nepal-China border by the disaster could trigger fresh flooding after it began overflowing into Nepal’s rivers.The weather was good on Monday, however, and rescue ⁠work picked up pace, said Narendra Pariyar, the district administrator of Rasuwa, one of the two hardest-hit districts.In the holy ​town of Devighat on the banks of the Trishuli, residents walked around the shells ofwhat had once been ​homes, trying to salvage their belongings from the debris.View image in fullscreenPeople try to salvage belongings from their devastated homes in Devighat.Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty ImagesThe flood was “caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming”, CCTV reported, saying ​it was a “new and prominent feature of cryosphere ‌disasters” on the Tibetan plateau.Two ​Nepali officials said China had ​not shared much information on glacier risks and water levels after a meeting to strengthen cooperation earlier this year, and they feared that could hamper future disaster preparedness.China’s foreign ministry said Beijing had continuously provided Nepal with meteorological and hydrological data and will continue to “strongly support” Nepal’s disaster relief efforts and safeguard the two countries’ common interests.With Reuters and Agence France-PresseExplore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalFloodingTibetChinaExtreme weatherSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: China is concealing scale of flood disaster, say Tibet campaigners | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Rights group claims 300 homes were destroyed in Tibet and number of missing people is ‘far higher’ than Beijing admits
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Rights group claims 300 homes were destroyed in Tibet and number of missing people is ‘far higher’ than Beijing admits
Content: Emergency workers carry out disinfection work while searching for victims in an area hit by a mudslide in Gyirong, Tibet.Photograph: Jigme Dorje/Xinhua/APView image in fullscreenEmergency workers carry out disinfection work while searching for victims in an area hit by a mudslide in Gyirong, Tibet.Photograph: Jigme Dorje/Xinhua/APNepal-Tibet flood disasterChina is concealing scale of flood disaster, say Tibet campaignersRights group claims 300 homes were destroyed in Tibet and number of missing people is ‘far higher’ than Beijing admitsDanny Vincent in Hong KongMon 31 Aug 2026 05.18 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Tibetan advocacy group says hundreds of homes were destroyed on the Tibetan side of the border in last week’s deadly floods, raising questions aboutBeijing’s official accountof the scale of the disaster.Public discussion about the flash floods has been restricted, with security officials inTibetannouncing on Sunday that it had penalised at least 10 people for sharing “false disaster information”. There was no further information on the nature of the penalties.Chinese authorities say 16 people have been confirmed dead and 546 are missing, including 261 foreign citizens. But the International Campaign for Tibet says its sources believe the number of casualties is significantly higher, with at least 300 homes destroyed.Tencho Gyatso, the president of the campaign group, told the Guardian: “What is visible inNepalexposes what is being concealed in Tibet. Four villages – Sale, Serchung, Labi and Rizi – were among the hardest hit, with approximately 300 homes reportedly destroyed and many people still missing.”She said the “little information that we can gather from the ground” suggested the numbers affected were “far higher” than Chinese officials had reported.On 26 August, thecollapse of a glacier triggered deadly floodsalong the Nepal-Tibet border, destroying entire villages. The death toll on the Nepal side has passed 900, with more than 4,000 missing.Tourists from India, the US, Britain, Australia and Canada among othersremain unaccounted for in the mountainous region that is popular with trekkers and pilgrims.Advocacy groups say there has been a stark contrast in the amount of information presented on either side of the border. Chinese coverage has been dominated by official state media reports, with few unofficial accounts about the scale of the disaster and its aftermath.View image in fullscreenNepali soldiers retrieve bodies of people swept away by the flash floods and a mudslide on the Narayani River.Photograph: Navesh Chitrakar/ReutersIndependent verification is extremely difficult in Tibet, where foreign journalists face severe restrictions. Tibetans can face imprisonment for sharing information with journalists and advocacy groups outsideChina.Gyatso said: “Officially released glimpses, however important, cannot tell us what is happening across all affected communities.”Her Tibetan advocacy group said several sources reported that survivors had been moved to Gyirong, which is about 30km (18 miles) from the border crossing that was hit by the flooding. They are said to be under strict management and restricted from communicating freely.According to a report posted on 27 August on the Tibet Daily, a state-run newspaper, two Tibetans were detained for questioning for posting “rumours” that more than 1,000 people had been swept away close to the border.Map showing the area of the disasterGyatso said: “The Chinese government portrays it like it’s only happening in Nepal and there’s nothing across the border. For any type of crisis, the way China handles it is that there is no crisis. The party is in control.”Posts relating to the disaster continued to trend on Chinese social media on Monday, with many comments echoing official narratives and supporting rescue efforts.A Weibo post by Hu Xijin – a prominent Chinese commentator and former chief editor of the state-run Global Times – attracted more than 300 comments and thousands of likes. He accused a small number of voices of seeking to “stir controversy by fabricating baseless claims”.However, one comment under his post questioned why all the updates were coming from the Nepali side of the border.View image in fullscreenRescuers use sniffer dogs to search for mudslide victims in Gyirong in Tibet.Photograph: Jigme Dorje/Xinhua/APOn Sunday, Tibetan public security officials said they had penalised people for sharing misleading information or “disrupting online order” with posts about the disaster.In one case, a user identified only as Zhang disputed the official death toll, posting: “Clearly thousands of people were swept away, yet the authorities reported only three deaths and 265 people missing.”How the deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – a visual guideRead moreAnother user named Zhou said: “In this wave of mudslides, one entire village was wiped out. It was definitely more than a thousand [deaths].”Maya Wang of Human Rights Watch said: “The instinct of the Chinese government is always to kind of control and to ensure the narrative which is to portray itself as a very efficient government.“There have been questions raised over how the development of the valleys in an ecologically fragile and geologically fragile area may have related to this disaster.”Human rights groups say that Beijing maintains tight controls over movement, religion and information in Tibet. Tibetan groups in exile have long been critical of large-scale development in the region, which they consider geologically fragile.A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said ⁠on Monday that the ⁠release of ⁠information about the floods and mudslide near its ⁠border with Nepal was transparent and timely.“Malicious smear campaigns ‌and hype using the disaster situation does not align with popular sentiment,” said Guo Jiakun, ‌in response to allegations that China censored videos of the disaster and understated the number of missing people.When asked about allegations ‌that China ignored warnings from scientists over hydropower construction, he said: “We ⁠firmly oppose such baseless and malicious speculation.”Additional reporting by Yu-chen Li in TaipeiExplore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterChinaNepalTibetNatural disastersAsia PacificSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Weather tracker: Warm Yellow Sea strengthens storms in South Korea | South Korea | The Guardian
description: More than 200mm of rain forecast in parts of South Korea, while parts of southern Europe to be 10C above average
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: More than 200mm of rain forecast in parts of South Korea, while parts of southern Europe to be 10C above average
Content: A flooded road after heavy rain in Jeonju, South Korea.Photograph: Yonhap/EPAView image in fullscreenA flooded road after heavy rain in Jeonju, South Korea.Photograph: Yonhap/EPAWeather trackerSouth KoreaAnalysisWeather tracker: Warm Yellow Sea strengthens storms in South KoreaMorgan Thomas for MetDeskMore than 200mm of rain forecast in parts of South Korea, while parts of southern Europe to be 10C above averageMon 31 Aug 2026 03.57 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareSouth Korea’s prime minister, Han Seong-sook, met officials to prepare for heavy rain expected this week, with rainfall totals across central and northern parts of the country forecast to exceed 200mm in some areas.South Korea was battered by heavy rainfall earlier this month and some areas were particularly hard hit. Over the weekend further thunderstorms pushed into the region and these are expected to cause disruption through Monday. This heavy rain is caused by a series of severe thunderstorms that developed over the Yellow Sea, on the western side of South Korea, and will slowly push eastwards on Monday before easing on Tuesday. These storms have been strengthened by the very warm Yellow Sea, which now has a surface temperature of 29C, 4C above the climatological average.Thailand is also under a warning for heavy to very heavy rain as the country passes the middle of its monsoon season, which runs from May to October. In the Philippines, the province of Tarlac has been placed under a state of calamity due to prolonged heavy rain in August.Nearby in the north Pacific, which has had an active typhoon and tropical storm season so far and will continue to do so this week, several tropical systems have the potential to develop. Last week, Typhoon Bang-lang and Tropical Storm Etau developed very close to each other in the north-west Pacific and both travelled northwards, although neither made landfall. Another two systems near the Philippines and China have a medium to high chance of developing into a tropical cyclone. For this to happen, wind speeds need to reach 39mph (63km/h). Across in the eastern north Pacific, Karina has developed into a category 1 hurricane and is expected to head just to the north of Hawaii but is not forecast to make landfall. Tropical Storm Lowell is expected to strengthen into a hurricane on Tuesday before passing just to the south of Hawaii.As Europe reaches the end of its record-breaking meteorological summer, the hot weather is showing no signs of easing off for the start of September. The heat is expected to intensify again later this week across central and southern parts of Europe, with temperatures rising to 10C above the climatological average. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, temperatures could reach about 40C by the weekend, falling just shy of the country’s all-time temperature record of 43.1C, set in 2007.Explore more on these topicsSouth KoreaWeather trackerExtreme weatherAsia PacificanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Investigation into Powerhouse Parramatta museum under way as stop-gap leader steps in | Sydney | The Guardian
description: ‘Opera House of the west’ still slated to open to the public as scheduled on 7 November, NSW arts minister says
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: ‘Opera House of the west’ still slated to open to the public as scheduled on 7 November, NSW arts minister says
Content: The Powerhouse Parramatta is slated to open to the public as scheduled on 7 November.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPView image in fullscreenThe Powerhouse Parramatta is slated to open to the public as scheduled on 7 November.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPSydneyInvestigation into Powerhouse Parramatta museum under way as stop-gap leader steps in‘Opera House of the west’ still slated to open to the public as scheduled on 7 November, NSW arts minister saysFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAustralian Associated PressMon 31 Aug 2026 19.42 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 20.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn investigation is under way into allegations of misconduct involving senior executives at the soon-to-be-opened Powerhouse Parramatta.The $915m museum in westernSydney, billed as one of the world’s most significant new museum projects, is set to open in November.On Thursday, the Powerhouse chief executive, Lisa Havilah, stood aside, pending the investigation of fresh allegations regarding governance and procurement at the museum, theNew South Walesgovernment announced.Allegations had been put to several Powerhouse executives as part of a misconduct investigation ahead of the institution’s formal opening, the NSW arts minister, John Graham, confirmed at a budget estimates hearing on Monday.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“The idea that two of the senior executives were working through this process, this detailed process, and could also make sure that went smoothly was really starting to become unsustainable,” he said.The museum’s chief operating officer, Mark Wilsdon, is on leave and is providing significant information as part of the investigation, Graham said.Havilah agreed to step aside following a conversation about further allegations that had come to light, the department of creative industries secretary, Melanie Hawyes, told the hearing.But she cautioned any interim leadership arrangement should not be interpreted as a sanction or finding.“These allegations that have come to light need to be tested, and that is what this investigation will do,” said Hawyes.NSW government architect Abbie Galvin has been appointed interim chief executive and former Opera House chief executive Louise Herron has been appointed as a strategic advisor, with both to start their roles on Tuesday.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPowerhouse Parramatta: entertainment centre ‘masquerading’ as a museum has high flood risk, inquiry findsRead moreA separate NSW Treasury review of the museum’s operational budget is separate to any allegations, Hawyes said.Spending at the Powerhouse under Havilah’s leadership has included items such as a documentary on the building of the institution, to cost at least $1.7m, about $5m on marketing, and $333,500 on the interior design of on-site accommodation.In response to a whistleblower complaint, an initial investigation was launched in March 2025 and the state’s anti-corruption commission was notified, while a formal misconduct investigation began last December.The procurement deals in question were under about $6m, the amount the chief executive is authorised to spend without ministerial approval, the hearing was told.Graham defended his handling of the controversial project, insisting that issues going back to at least 2023 had been dealt with appropriately.The Powerhouse board members including chair of trustees David Borger were not subject to the the allegations, and the board’s audit committee has assisted with investigations, Graham confirmed.The minister said he was confident the project, which he described as the Opera House of the west, would open to the public as scheduled on 7 November.Explore more on these topicsSydneyNew South WalesNew South Wales politicsMuseumsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Border area between Nepal and China where 33 Australians are missing still almost entirely cut off | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Majority of missing Australians were near Gyirong Port minutes before impact. Rescuers say the area is now destroyed, covered in metres of silt and debris
Author: Cait Kelly
Headline: Majority of missing Australians were near Gyirong Port minutes before impact. Rescuers say the area is now destroyed, covered in metres of silt and debris
Content: Rescuers wade through deep mud while carrying out search and rescue operations at the mudslide-hit Gyirong Port.Photograph: Lhasa fire and rescue mobile detachment/Xinhua/APView image in fullscreenRescuers wade through deep mud while carrying out search and rescue operations at the mudslide-hit Gyirong Port.Photograph: Lhasa fire and rescue mobile detachment/Xinhua/APNepal-Tibet flood disasterBorder area between Nepal and China where 33 Australians are missing still almost entirely cut offMajority of missing Australians were near Gyirong Port minutes before impact. Rescuers say the area is now destroyed, covered in metres of silt and debrisFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastCait Kellyin KathmanduMon 31 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 18.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt has been almost a week since thecatastrophic floods in Nepaland not even a vehicle can get into the area where the majority of missing Australians were last heard from.Gyirong Port, the border area between Nepal and China, was the first to be hit. Images from Chinese rescue teams who have managed to get in by helicopter or hiking show the area has been completely flattened. The immigration building, the power lines, everything, just wiped away.News that phone connectivity to the area was back on spread quickly on Monday around the families of lost Australians who have come to Kathmandu to wait. In WhatsApp groups and over Facebook, they shared any updates they had.‘The house got carried 100 metres away’: some Nepal flood victims had minutes of notice. Others had secondsRead moreOne family member, who did not want to be named, told the Guardian she had been trying to ring her husband all morning after she heard the phone line was back up. He did not answer.“The embassies aren’t helping,” she said.The total number ofAustralians missing in the disasterrose to 43 on Monday, and at least 33 of them were understood to be near Gyirong Port just before the impact.View image in fullscreenMissing Australians in Nepal (clockwise from top left) – Karan Bhardwaj, Bharat Mangwani, Chitra Venkatraman, Venkatraman Balakrishnan, Renee, Sumi Adhikari, Narayan Panthi, Suhasini Kandimalla, The Muralitharan family, and Reshma PatelThe 15 Australians with the Himalaya Glacier Company, 11 travelling with the Isha Foundation, six from Kailash Journeys and one from Kathmandu Holiday Tours and Travel were all near the border – many of them arrived at the immigration building just 10 minutes before the flood hit.Sujan Wasti, the head of Kailash Journeys’ Nepal operations, said the last he heard from the group was at 7.30 am, when the guide touched base to say they were coming back. They were scheduled to land in Kathmandu on Thursday, with many of them flying home from the capital.“In the area, the rescue has been done,” he said. “Now, it will just be about collecting the bodies and bringing them [home].”Rescue efforts continue as 43 Australians remain missing in Nepal – videoSince last Wednesday, Wasti has sent teams up the Trishuli River to look for any signs of the missing trekkers. They have twice flown over the border by helicopter, and have visited local hospitals to see if anyone has shown up.“We are searching every place we can, but still we have not found anyone,” he said. “There is still no sign of them.“Along the border, it was only dead bodies. If they are alive, it will be a miracle.”China is coordinating the search and rescue effort in the area. As of Monday morning, crews reopening the highway towards the port on the Tibet side had 1.15km left of road to clear and reconstruct.A map showing the location of Gyirong PortSince Friday, no one except rescue crews has been able to access the area – some have hiked for 10 hours to get in, before rappelling down into the valley. Others, when the weather allowed, were helicoptered in.Akhilesh Surjan, a humanitarian, emergency and disaster management expert at Charles Darwin University, said one of “the sensitive questions” has become how far everyone keeps the hope alive.“The rescue experts consider the first 72 hours to be very critical,” he says. “Because after the first 72 hours, that is three days, the chance of finding survivors drops sharply.”Despite this, he said surviving after three days “is not uncommon”. In Japan after the 2011 earthquake, two people were found alive after nine days.“Survival usually depends on whether the person has access to the trapped air pockets, protection from extreme weather, no severe internal bleeding or pressure injuries,” he said.View image in fullscreenExcavators repairing a section of damaged road to restore access to Gyirong Port.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockHe said there were possibilities for survival – that people had been swept downstream and were stranded, or had been lucky enough to shelter in a place that wasn’t completely destroyed.Getting into Gyirong Port is not the only challenge. The thick layer of mud and pools of water have made it difficult to use life-detection devices accurately, teams have reported. Instead, rescuers are calling out as they look for survivors.Rain is forecast for the next two days, which will further complicate and slow efforts. There is also the threat of another flood or landslide. A team analysing hazards around the area on Monday found “high-risk geological disaster points”.View image in fullscreenFirefighters and sniffer dogs search for missing people on a road near Gyirong Port.Photograph: cnsphoto/ReutersSurjan said rescue teams would be analysing the landscape to determine where people may have moved to, but it was a dangerous job. In Nepal, at least 85 rescuers, including police and army officers, are now missing.“Continuing rainfall and river flow and the poor visibility for choppers or helicopters, communication failure of the first few days, and the limited ability to get heavy rescue equipment into the area will make it harder,” Surjan said.Three days after the disaster, the first team of Chinese rescue workers were able to reach the border crossing complex. They were the first on the ground and said everything had been destroyed.“There was no road … it was all virgin forest and sheer cliffs,” rescue worker Zou Mingqi told Chinese state media.At the border complex, “as far as the eye could see, there was nothing but ruins”.View image in fullscreenA rescue helicopter delivers supplies at the mudslide-hit area in Gyirong.Photograph: China News Service/Getty ImagesThe Isha Foundation has sent volunteers to Kathmandu and Tibet to help families and find any updates they can. Their loved ones were standing inside the immigration centre and were about to cross the border when the disaster hit.On Sunday, the foundation sent families a message, asking them to “expect the worst”.“We have been informed that the valley at the Gyirong port is covered with significant debris, probably as much as [13-15 metres] of silt and debris,” it said.“The local experts who know the terrain well have told our on-ground team that it is very unlikely that anyone could have possibly survived the force of the flood. The mix of debris and water rose very high, probably as high as [45 metres] with immense force, completely wiping out the whole building complex.“We wish with all our hearts that we could offer you something more hopeful. Everything our teams have seen, and everything those closest to the site have shared with us, has led us to expect the worst.”Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterFloodingExtreme weatherNatural disastersnewsShareReuse this content

title: Qantas ground crews vote for right to strike amid pay dispute – as it happened | Australian politics | The Guardian
description: This blog is now closed
Author: Achol Arok
Headline: This blog is now closed
Content: 18h ago03.48 EDTWhat we learned today, Monday 31 AugustThat’s where we’ll leave our live coverage for the day.Before we go, let’s recap the top headlines:The total number ofAustralians missing in the deadly Nepal floodsis now 43.The death toll from the ⁠unprecedented delugeof ice, rock, mud ​and debris that crashed through valleys of Nepal on Wednesday last week has now risen to 903 people, with 16 more dead reported on the Tibet side of the border. More than 4,000 are missing in Nepal, with another 500 in Tibet.Oscar Jenkins, an Australian man who was captured and sentenced to 13 years in a Russian jail after fighting for Ukraine military,has given his first interview after his conviction.The Australian government said it is working with Russian officials in a bid to secure his release.One Nation’sBarnaby Joycesaid the party wouldn’t get “carried away” afterclaiming a victory in the Secret Harbourstate byelection in Western Australia.According to snowfall data compiled by Snowy Hydro, 2026 is officiallythe worst end to a season since recordsbegan in 1954.The NSW opposition leader,Kellie Sloane,says she has written to Anthony Albanese about the need to tackle violent pornography after a 16-year-old girl died froma suspected sexual strangulationincident.Federal attorney generalMichelle Rowlandsays the government is not immediately planning to ban imports of smartglasses.Queensland has become the first state to makeebike and e-scooter riders hold at least a learner driver’s licence.The New South Wales government will not appeal a supreme courtjudge’s ruling that rejected the state’s request for a terror orderoverMohommed Farhat,who wrote “Fuk Israel” on cars and set another vehicle alight in late 2024.New South Wales police have appealed for information to find the mother of a newborn baby boy, whosebody was discovered in a rubbish bin in Auburnin Sydney’s south-west on Monday morning.Qantasground handling crews may soon walk off the jobafter overwhelmingly voting in favour of taking industrial action to demand better pay and conditions.Thanks for sticking around, we’ll see you tomorrow morning.Share

title: Turkish deep-sea search vessel joins efforts to retrieve 20 still missing after Cyprus ferry disaster | Cyprus | The Guardian
description: TCG Isin expected to play vital role in locating Filo Jet’s voyage data recorder 514 metres below surface
Author: Helena Smith
Headline: TCG Isin expected to play vital role in locating Filo Jet’s voyage data recorder 514 metres below surface
Content: Search and rescue operations continue after the Filo Jet, a high-speed passenger ferry, sank on Sunday near Kyrenia.Photograph: Jewel Samad/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSearch and rescue operations continue after the Filo Jet, a high-speed passenger ferry, sank on Sunday near Kyrenia.Photograph: Jewel Samad/AFP/Getty ImagesCyprusTurkish deep-sea search vessel joins efforts to retrieve 20 still missing after Cyprus ferry disasterTCG Isin expected to play vital role in locating Filo Jet’s voyage data recorder 514 metres below surfaceHelena Smithin AthensMon 31 Aug 2026 14.37 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA deep-sea search and rescue vessel is on its way to Cyprus asTurkeyjoins efforts to retrieve the 20 people still missing after a passenger ferry capsized off the island’s northern coast.The TCG Isinwill join the vast operation to find survivors after the high-speed ferry sank on Sunday barely four nautical miles outside the port town of Kyrenia.Authorities confirmed late on Monday – the first of three days of national mourning in Turkish-held northern Cyprus – that the tragedyhad claimed eight lives, increasing the number of passengers still unaccounted for from 17 to 20.A total of 241 of the 267 people aboard the Filo Jet, bound for Taşucu on the Turkish mainland when it began to take on water, had been rescued, they said. Almost all were either Turkish or Turkish Cypriot.Nearly 20 people still missing after ferry capsizes ⁠off northern CyprusRead moreView image in fullscreenSurvivors arrive on shore. Of the 267 people on board the ferry, 241 have been rescued, authorities have said.Photograph: ReutersInternational sympathy for the victims was highlighted as the Anglo-Cypriot founder of easyJet, Stelios Haji-Ioannou, offered €260,000 (£223,000) in support for the families of the deceased and missing, in a move hailed by Turkish Cypriot officials.Visiting Kyrenia’s new port, where relatives gathered for news of loved ones on Monday,Tufan Erhürman, the self-styled state’s president, vowed search efforts would “continue with the same intensity, with no interruption, through the day and night”.The Isin,capable of searching up to 3,000 metres below the sea surface, was due to arrive on Tuesday, he said, as he comforted the families of those still missing.The ship is expected to play a vital role in recovering the ferry’s voyage data recorder, or black box, now viewed as key in deciphering the cause of a maritime disaster not seen since the breakaway territory declared independence in 1983.Turkish Cypriot officials told the Guardian it was likely “all those responsible” would be charged with gross negligence as the seaworthiness of the 26-year-old ferry was also questioned.The owners and shareholders of the privately owned company operating the passenger vessel have also been ordered to appear in court.View image in fullscreenThe Turkish Cypriot leader, Tufan Erhürman, talks with relatives waiting for news outside the port of Kyrenia.Photograph: Yiannis Kourtoglou/ReutersIt remained unclear whether those still missing had been trapped on board.“Nobody is saying it publicly, but the hope of any survivors being found at this point is very slim,” one official confided. “Those who weren’t rescued very likely didn’t find a lifejacket. We believe many were elderly people and mothers with babies and young kids.”In testimony – and video footage – that emerged on Monday, panic-stricken passengers could be seen desperately looking for lifejackets and screaming before the double-hulled ferry flipped over. One mother, Ayten Biçer, described feeling her 12-year-old daughter slip from her hands and disappear as the ferry capsized and sank in a matter of minutes. “She was saying, ‘Don’t let go.’ And I didn’t let go of my daughter. I swear, I didn’t let her go,” she sobbed. Two of Biçer’s other children are among the 20 still missing.View image in fullscreenAyten and Hayri Biçer wait for news of their two missing children outside the port of Kyrenia.Photograph: Yiannis Kourtoglou/ReutersThe captain of the ferry and seven crew members were detained on Monday as judicial authorities launched an inquiry into the tragedy amid claims they had been among the first to abandon ship.Appearing before a local magistrate, the crew attributed the disaster to the bow of the catamaran-style ferry breaking apart in turbulent seas. But eyewitness accounts contradicted that version of events, with passengers telling officials that appeals to turn back to port had fallen on deaf ears as the ferry began to take on water.Ünal Üstel, the northernCyprusprime minister, told reporters the Filo Jet was lying on the seabed at a depth of 514 metres and that he foresaw the Turkish salvage ship “reaching [it] tomorrow afternoon”. Boats, helicopters, aircraft and other search and rescue teams had joined the operation, he said, adding that search efforts were continuing “on a 24-hour basis”.Cyprus has been divided since 1974 when a coup aimed at union with Greece – engineered by the military junta then in power in Athens – prompted Turkey to invade and seize the island’s northern third. Ever since, as many as 45,000 mainland Turkish troops have been stationed in the north.In 1983, the territory unilaterally declared independence, but in the absence of a settlement, decades of international isolation have ensued.Explore more on these topicsCyprusTurkeyWater transportEuropeStelios Haji-Ioannou (Sir)newsShareReuse this content

title: Head of Viktor Orbán’s favourite thinktank quits over unpaid wages | Thinktanks | The Guardian
description: Frank Furedi announces resignation with immediate effect after organisation’s staff ‘not paid in July or August’
Author: Jennifer Rankin
Headline: Frank Furedi announces resignation with immediate effect after organisation’s staff ‘not paid in July or August’
Content: Frank Furedi said the thinktank’s failure to provide funds meant it had effectively ceased operations.Photograph: Tibor Illyes/EPA-EFE/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenFrank Furedi said the thinktank’s failure to provide funds meant it had effectively ceased operations.Photograph: Tibor Illyes/EPA-EFE/ShutterstockThinktanksHead of Viktor Orbán’s favourite thinktank quits over unpaid wagesFrank Furedi announces resignation from MCC Brussels after organisation’s staff ‘not paid in July or August’Jennifer Rankinin BrusselsMon 31 Aug 2026 13.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 13.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe head of Viktor Orbán’s favourite Brussels thinktank has quit, citing unpaid wages since the change of government in Hungary.The sociology professor Frank Furedi said he was resigning as the executive director of MCC Brussels with “immediate effect” on Monday over “persistent failure to provide the contractually agreed funds”.‘Attack on civil society’: why Viktor Orbán’s favourite thinktank is in crisisRead moreA spokesperson for MCC Brussels confirmed Furedi’s resignation and said no one working for the organisation in the EU capital had been paid in July or August.MCC Brussels launched in late 2022 with a self-styled mission to shake up political debate in the EU capital, although critics said it defended Orbán’s illiberal rule in Hungary whileusing a well-funded position to attack civil society groups.It was an ostensibly independent offshoot of the Mathias Corvinus Collegium Foundation in Budapest, a training ground for Orbán’s Fidesz party that was lavishly funded by his rightwing nationalist government.The future of MCC Brussels was thrown into doubt whenPéter Magyar won a landslide election victory in Aprilpledging to crack down on corruption in Hungary, which numerous independent organisations said had proliferated during Orbán’s 16 years in power. Soon after his victory, Magyar promised to end state financing for MCC Budapest and to investigate a large transfer of state assets to the organisation, which he described as a crime.Furedihas previously dismissedMagyar’s claims of a criminal transfer of assets to MCC Budapest as “bullshit”, while MCC Brussels said it condemned corruption by all politicians.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Guardian view on the new Hungary: de-Orbánising at pace | EditorialRead moreIn a letter to the senior leadership of MCC Budapest seen by the Guardian, Furedi wrote: “Without the contractually agreed resources, our colleagues cannot function and are facing serious economic hardship. We have been placed in a situation where our individual reputations and the integrity of our intellectual mission are systematically undermined.”The failure to provide funds, Furedi said, meant MCC Brussels had effectively ceased operations and was unable to pay suppliers or meet conditions under Belgian insolvency law.Furedi said he intended to ensure, “along with like-minded individuals, the work and intellectual legacy of our institution will continue to flourish in another form”, without elaborating on future plans.The letter wasfirst reported by Politico. MCC Budapest did not immediately respond to a request for comment.MCC Budapest has also seen change at the top following the election of the new government. The MCC board was previously led by Viktor Orbán’s chief of staff, Balázs Orbán, who is no relation to the former prime minister. Balázs Orbán, now an MP for the Fidesz party, announced he was standing down as chair in June.The MCC Brussels spokesperson said after Furedi’s resignation and a round of lay-offs in June and July, MCC Brussels was down to 12 staff and three research fellows. Before the cuts it had employed 25 people and was one of the best-funded thinktanks in Brussels.Explore more on these topicsThinktanksViktor OrbánBelgiumHungaryEuropeEuropean UnionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Germany poised to identify suspect in Leipzig drone attack on Ukrainian plane | Germany | The Guardian
description: Berlin expected to outline response to incident this month widely speculated to have been coordinated by Russia
Author: Kate Connolly
Headline: Berlin expected to outline response to incident this month widely speculated to have been coordinated by Russia
Content: Police officers at Leipzig airport search for a drone that may be connected to a suspected attack on 7 August.Photograph: Sebastian Willnow/DPA/APView image in fullscreenPolice officers at Leipzig airport search for a drone that may be connected to a suspected attack on 7 August.Photograph: Sebastian Willnow/DPA/APGermanyGermany poised to identify suspect in Leipzig drone attack on Ukrainian planeBerlin expected to outline response to incident this month widely speculated to have been coordinated by RussiaKate Connollyin BerlinMon 31 Aug 2026 10.14 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 10.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe German government is imminently expected to announce who it believes was behind a suspecteddrone attack on a Ukrainian cargo planeearlier this month and to outline its response to the incident in coordination with its European and Nato partners.The chancellor, Friedrich Merz, told the public broadcaster ARD in an interview on Sunday evening: “We are in the process of concluding the investigations; we have reached a broad agreement within the federal government on how we will respond, and we will make this clear in the coming days. It won’t take much longer.”The government has so far declined to say officially who it thinks was behind the attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle airport on 4 August. There has beenwidespread speculationthat it was coordinated by Moscow.A drone containing explosives was discovered near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft used to transport military supplies. The drone was apparently intended to land on the wings of the aircraft, which was filled with kerosene, but the explosive device did not detonate, according to a report last week referencing the investigation.About 20 minutes after the discovery of the first drone, a second drone possibly collided with a DHL cargo plane, which had to abort its landing manoeuvre and was diverted.Days later, a third drone was found in a field in a municipality that directly borders the western edge of Leipzig airport. Forensic technicians from the federal criminal police office found residues of a substance that initial assessments indicated could have been the highly explosive substance hexogen.This explosive also failed to detonate but according to media reports, the investigators’ report stated: “The perpetrators may have had a far larger attack in mind than previously known to the public.”Moscow has denied involvement.The Leipzig drone bomb marks a dangerous escalation for EuropeRead moreMerz indicated that the information the government was due to release was being closely communicated with Berlin’s partners, and any response would also be carried out in cooperation with them.“It will be a response fromGermany, but our partners in the European Union and Nato will not be taken by surprise,” he said.It has been speculated in Berlin that meetings this week of EU defence and foreign affairs ministers in Wicklow, Ireland, could be used to make the announcement.Last week Merz stopped short of naming a suspect but said: “They will pay for this.” He underscored the necessity for a decisive response due to the lengths he said those behind the Leipzig plot and other acts of sabotage had been prepared to go.“Attackers are increasingly ruthlessly accepting even serious property damage, and even injuries and deaths,” he said.The daily Die Welt and the news website Politico have reported, citing sources, that the government will blameRussiafor the attack and that its retaliatory measures are likely to include a new, extensive package of sanctions coordinated with Brussels to hinder it financially, as well as more forceful measures against Russia’s shadow fleet, the Russian ships illegally transporting oil.The closure of Russian House, an institution representing Russia’s cultural interests that has a large presence in the centre of Berlin, is also said to be on the cards. In return, Russia would be expected to close Germany’s cultural body in Russia, the Goethe Institute.The political dimensions of the government’s response are potentially considerable owing to the timing. A heated election campaign in eastern German states culminates in a vote this Sunday in which the anti-immigrant, populist AfD is expected to do well. The debate over relations with Russia and whether and how Germany should continue to supportUkraineare playing an important role in the campaign.The AfD’s foreign policy spokesperson, Markus Frohnmaier, said he believed “without a doubt” Germany faced hybrid threats but said he would not speculate over who was behind them, calling on the government to “first establish transparency and provide information about the current state of knowledge”.Explore more on these topicsGermanyUkraineRussiaEuropeDrones (military)newsShareReuse this content

title: British family pleads with French authorities to release body of relative who died in Channel | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Jasmeet Wadhwa, who fled Taliban persecution in Afghanistan, lost his life while trying to reach UK in April
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: Jasmeet Wadhwa, who fled Taliban persecution in Afghanistan, lost his life while trying to reach UK in April
Content: Relatives of Jasmeet Wadhwa and Nagmeldin Adam held a demonstration outside a courthouse in Dunkirk, France on Monday.Photograph: HandoutView image in fullscreenRelatives of Jasmeet Wadhwa and Nagmeldin Adam held a demonstration outside a courthouse in Dunkirk, France on Monday.Photograph: HandoutImmigration and asylumBritish family pleads with French authorities to release body of relative who died in ChannelJasmeet Wadhwa, who fled Taliban persecution in Afghanistan, lost his life while trying to reach UK in AprilDiane TaylorMon 31 Aug 2026 09.36 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA British family is pleading with French authorities to release the body of a relative that officials have held for five months after he died in the Channel in April.Jasmeet Wadhwa, 32, died whileattempting to reach the UKon a dinghy on 1 April with his mother, Harbans Kaur Wadhwa, after they fled Taliban persecution in Afghanistan in January.They endured a difficult two-month journey under the control of people smugglers before reaching northernFrancein mid-March. A man from Sudan, Nagmeldin Adam, 33, died on the same boat. Eight others were rescued, including Harbans Kaur Wadhwa.Adam’s journey from Sudan involved detention in Libya for an extended period and many attempts to cross the Mediterranean toEurope. He finally reached France in December 2025.At least 16 people have died trying to cross the Channel from France to the UK so far this year, with thelatest reported deathon Saturday in a similar part of the French coast to where the two men lost their lives in April.View image in fullscreenJasmeet Wadhwa and Nagmeldin Adam died in the Channel in April 2026.Photograph: HandoutRelatives of the two men took part in a demonstration on Monday outside the courthouse in Dunkirk in protest against the French authorities’ refusal to release the bodies. Wadhwa’s relatives travelled from the UK to France to participate. Many who lose their lives trying to cross the Channel are never publicly identified and it is rare to see family members stage a protest of this kind.Neither the French interior ministry nor the part of the French police in charge of the bodies responded to questions from the Guardian about why there had been a delay in releasing the two men’s bodies.View image in fullscreen‘We shouldn’t have to fight to say goodbye’: Jasmeet Wadhwa’s relatives are urging the French authorities to release his body.Photograph: Family HandoutIvnit Singh Wadwa, Wadhwa’s cousin, travelled from his home in west London for the protest. “We shouldn’t have to fight to say goodbye,” said Wadwa. “We are very upset with the French judicial system. Our family is waiting for Jasmeet’s body so we can lay him to rest.”After witnessing the loss of her son on the dinghy, Harbans Kaur Wadhwa made an application to the Home Office to come to the UK legally underthe “one in, one out” scheme. This scheme forcibly returns one person to France who has arrived in the UK on a small boat in exchange for accepting another who has applied legally to come to the UK from northern France. She was hoping to join her family in the UK who have offered to accommodate and support her.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTalkTV under fire for not disclosing reporter’s ties to Reform UK in Channel crossing filmRead moreBut the Home Office rejected the application for not meeting the requirements, saying that the identity document submitted was not satisfactory. Afghans generally have an identity document known as a Tazkira.A Home Office spokesperson said: “We are deeply saddened to hear about a death in French waters.“Every death in the Channel is a tragedy and a stark reminder of the dangers posed by criminal gangs exploiting vulnerable people for profit. We will continue working relentlessly with the French and our partners overseas to prevent these perilous journeys.”In anappealfor the release of Jasmeet’s body, the family wrote on social media: “A son. A brother. A life not forgotten. Help us bring Jasmeet back to his family. This is not about politics. It’s about a grieving mother being able to see her son one final time, it’s about a family being able to mourn.”Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumFranceEuropeAfghanistannewsShareReuse this content

title: French high schools rush to put Macron’s phone ban into force | France | The Guardian
description: Unions say ban will take time to enact, while president also wants under-15s social media ban as key legacy
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Unions say ban will take time to enact, while president also wants under-15s social media ban as key legacy
Content: A teacher collects students’ mobile phones at a vocational high school in Montsoult, in the northern suburbs of Paris.Photograph: Bertrand Guay/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA teacher collects students’ mobile phones at a vocational high school in Montsoult, in the northern suburbs of Paris.Photograph: Bertrand Guay/AFP/Getty ImagesFranceFrench high schools rush to put Macron’s phone ban into forceUnions say ban will take time to enact, while president also wants under-15s social media ban as key legacyAngelique Chrisafisin ParisMon 31 Aug 2026 06.41 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrench high schools are rushing to put in place a ban on mobile phones this week asEmmanuel Macronpushes for children to spend less time in front of screens.Education unions warned that banning mobile phone use inlycées– where children are aged 15 to 18 – would be hard to implement quickly.Macron approved the high school phone ban this month after another measure he had hoped would be a key legacy, his proposedsocial media banfor under-15s, wasknocked backas unconstitutional.The text of the social media ban is being rewritten in the hope it can be pushed it through before Macron leaves office in May.France has already banned children from using mobile phones inprimary schools and in middle schools, orcollèges,which are attended between the ages of 11 and 15.The government’s focus is now on banning mobile phone use among older teenagers at school from September, as it argues that too much screen time is harming children’s development.In order to enforce the hurriedly signed-off ban, high schools must amend their rules – a lengthy process – and many schools have said they will struggle to implement the measure swiftly.“It’s impossible to put this in place from scratch from 1 September,” said Jérôme Fournier, the national secretary of the SE-Unsa trade union. “Schools will need to change their internal regulations and that requires a full consultation process and a vote, and for high school students to be consulted. So we need time for everyone to meet and work on this.”Fournier said a key challenge was that high school students were often obliged to rely on school smartphone apps to find out even the most basic information for the school day, such as timetables, room changes and homework. “Some even have to use apps on their phones as a badge to enter the canteen to eat lunch or to borrow books from the school library,” he said.Fournier said high schools often hosted students for higher education courses or apprenticeships, some of whom were aged 20 and needed to use their phones for their work.He said the key issue for each high school was to decide where exactly to enforce the ban, whether across the whole school, including corridors, or with exceptions such as in the playground. He said teenagers could be tempted to leave the school grounds in order to use their phones on the street outside, which could have implications for security and road safety.Fournier said students should be consulted on the process rather than being treated as children. “These older teenagers are pre-adults – some in their final school year are going to vote in the upcoming presidential election,” he said.Macron’s office has said he has no plans to give up on his push to bar under-15s from social media platforms such as TikTok and Snapchat, and the government is working redraft the law.France’s constitutional council recently struck down the first version of the law after concerns that its definition of social media was not specific enough.
