This meant a host of sites not generally considered social media but that allowed commentary or communication could be banned, amounting to a “disproportionate restriction” on freedom of expression.The constitutional council alsoraised concerns about the privacy implications of putting in place an age-verification system for all users.Valère Ndior, a law professor at the University of Western Brittany, said it was no surprise to legal experts that the law in its current form had been knocked back, and it would be a challenge to rewrite it. “For the moment, as a legal practitioner, I can’t see how it’s possible to strike a balance between European law and French constitutional law,” he said.Explore more on these topicsFranceSocial media bansEmmanuel MacronEuropeYoung peopleSchoolsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump says US will ‘hit Iran hard’ as hostilities resume – as it happened | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: Iran responded to an assault on its Larak Island by targeting US bases in Jordan
Author: Adam Fulton
Headline: Iran responded to an assault on its Larak Island by targeting US bases in Jordan
Content: 13.00 EDTClosing summaryThe US president, Donald Trump, has told Fox News’s chief foreign correspondent, Trey Yingst, that the US will respond to Iran targeting US military bases inJordanovernight.“We’re going to hit them hard,” Trump told Fox News. “There will be a response,” he added, after Jordan’s army confirmed it had intercepted eight missiles early this morning.Trump was sending a message ⁠toIran⁠with ​his social media post about ⁠Kharg Island, vice-president JD Vance ⁠said on Monday.“The ​president ‌likes to ‌switch it up ‌on social media a little bit. He would be the first to ‌say he doesn’t make announcements about military ​actions on social media, but I think that he’s ⁠sending a message ​to ​the Iranians,” ​Vance said when asked ​about ‌Trump’s ​post.Trump’s one-line social media post on Sunday was accompanied by an AI-generated video clip showing fake attacks by the US military.A US ‌official said on Monday the military had not targeted Kharg Island in overnight ​strikes. An Iranian official dismissed Trump’s post as “laughable”.US ⁠treasury secretary ⁠Scott ⁠Bessent told CNBC ​in an ⁠interview on Monday ⁠that ​the ‌goal ‌of US sanctions ‌onIranis “to create the ‌conditions that they ​will want to come ⁠to the ​table” for ​negotiations.As Bessent opened meetings of the Group of 20 finance ministers in Asheville on Monday, he said he wants to focus on ways to grow the global economy and rein in mounting debt.Bessent also briefly touched on the newIransanctions earlier this morning, before his opening remarks in Asheville.Speaking to reporters, Bessent predicted that, under the latest round of sanctions, Iran’s economy could collapse within “weeks or months”. But he also suggested that a deal, not collapse, was the administration’s primary goal.In a brief post to his Truth Social platform, Trump claimedIranis a “failed nation” with no navy, air force or currency.“IT IS DEAD!” he wrote, saying the only things Tehran have in its favour are a sympathetic US media, a “willingness to kill their protesters” and a “good line of bullshit”. Trump said the Iranian leadership is in “total disarray” and is “incapable” of properly representing the country.The UAE condemned an Iranian drone attack intercepted over its territorial waters, calling it a “dangerous escalation”.In a statement on X, the UAE’s foreign ministry “strongly condemned the hostile Iranian attack on the country involving a drone that was intercepted by air defence systems over UAE territorial waters”.US Central Command (Centcom) has denied claims made byIranstate ⁠TV and the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps that a ship had struck mines in the strait of Hormuz.In a statement posted to social media, Centcom said “Iran’s claim that a supertanker passing through strait of Hormuz struck two mines and was brought to a complete stop is false.”The EU issued a statement saying it will work with the US and other allied countries to maintain economic pressure against Iran.“The ‌EU welcomes efforts at ensuring thatIranceases its destabilising activities and engages in peace negotiations with good ‌faith, also through additional economic pressure, including through ​the US-led Operation Economic Outcast,” it said in reference to the pressure strategy the White House describes as “an unprecedented campaign to sever every remaining economic lifeline sustaining” the Islamic republic.Medics ⁠said two ⁠people ​were killed and several others injured when an Israeli airstrike hit ⁠a crowd of people near the municipal public park in Gaza ⁠City on Monday, an area densely populated with ​families displaced by Israel’s assault. Gaza’s health ministry says at least 1,320 people have been killed by Israeli attacks since a ‘ceasefire’ was signed between Israel and Hamas last October.Israel signed a multibillion-dollar weapons deal with Greece on Monday, the largest between the two countries, AP reports.Israel’s defence ministry said the $3.5bn (€3bn / £2.6bn) export deal, dubbed Achilles Shield, is one of the country’s largest and includes a multilayered air defence system for Greece using Israeli technology.Lebanon’s state-run National News Agency is reporting that Israeli artillery shelling targeted the southern Lebanese town of Houla on Monday.It also reported overnight Israeli attacks in the areas of Mansouri and Buyout Al-Sayyad, also in southern Lebanon.Share

title: Trump threatens further action as US and Iran exchange fire in new flare-up | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: Washington says it acted after observing Iran was planning to deploy fresh mines in strait of Hormuz
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Washington says it acted after observing Iran was planning to deploy fresh mines in strait of Hormuz
Content: Vessels in the strait of Hormuz. Washington claims that Iranian control over the waterway has been loosened by repeated US attacks on missile launchers and radars.Photograph: Majid Asgaripour/ReutersView image in fullscreenVessels in the strait of Hormuz. Washington claims that Iranian control over the waterway has been loosened by repeated US attacks on missile launchers and radars.Photograph: Majid Asgaripour/ReutersUS-Israel war on IranTrump threatens further action as US and Iran exchange fire in new flare-upWashington says it acted after observing Iran was planning to deploy fresh mines in strait of HormuzPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorMon 31 Aug 2026 13.13 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US and Iran have exchanged fire for the first time in a month, with missiles and drones fired at Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the strait of Hormuz, and Iran targeting US military bases in Jordan and theUnited Arab Emiratesin response.The US president,Donald Trump, on Monday threatened further action. The US is to trying to prise open Tehran’s grip on shipping going through the strait, which before the war accounted for a fifth of the world’s seaborne energy supply. Washington claimed that Iranian control over the waterway had been loosened by repeated US attacks on Iranian missile launchers and radars.US Central Command said it acted late on Sunday, launching the first strikes onIransince July, after it detected the Iranians were planning to deploy fresh mines in the strait. Last week Trump claimed the US navy had cleared the strait of mines for the first time since the conflict started on 28 February, a claim the Iranians rejected as lies.In response to the US attack, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it “targeted technical infrastructure, maintenance facilities and enemy fighter jet positions at the US-operated King Hussein and al-Azraq airbases in Jordan” with ballistic missiles, causing “heavy damage”. The UAE defence ministry said it intercepted a drone over its territorial waters.Trump responded to the Iranian reprisals by telling Fox News: “We’re going to hit them hard. There will be a response.” The US president called Iran “officially a failed nation without an airforce, a navy or a currency”, adding that inflation was at 300% and its leaders were incapable of representing their country.Iran’s economy in crisis as US launches new sanctions campaignRead moreThe White House last week signalled that Trump was shelving military measures in favour ofa campaign to destroy the Iranian economy by enforcing sanctions.Iranian state TV claimed the military exchanges escalated on Sunday after a tanker caught fire when hitting two Iranian naval mines while attempting to pass through the southern side of the strait close to Oman. Officials later said Iran had targeted three ships trying to navigate the southern route that Tehran says is unauthorised.The IRGC warned that other ships violating ⁠its rules would face ​the ​same fate and ​said compliance with ​its regulations ‌for ​passage ​through the strait was mandatory.However, the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, told Pakistan’s prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, in a bilateral meeting on the margins of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan on Monday that continuing the war was not in Iran’s interest, adding he was still ready to implement the memorandum of understanding with the US that Pakistan had mediated in June.The Iranian currency was under renewed pressure on Monday and the inflationary impact of its rapid depreciation is causing growing concern to MPs.View image in fullscreenPeople buy bread from a street vendor beneath an anti-US billboard in Tehran.Photograph: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/ShutterstockIran and Oman last week reached a verbal agreement on a new single temporary route for shipping through the strait in which Oman retains controls on shipping in Omani waters.One western diplomat familiar with the talks said the message had got through to Washington that this bilateral agreement would not be enough for Iran to open the strait and that to do so would at least require the US to end its blockade of Iranian oil exports, something Trump is not currently prepared to do. “There are many in Iran determined to torment Trump right up to the end of his presidency,” the western diplomat said. “We are stuck.” He said some oil was getting through but not very much.The latest fighting broke out late on Sunday with the US claiming it attacked Larak Island in the strait. A US official said: “I can confirm that earlier today US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak Island. Islamic ⁠Revolutionary Guard Corps forces were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the strait of Hormuz.”The IRGC said the US attack had killed three soldiers and wounded two citizens. Iran’s Mehr news agency quoted the IRGC as saying its air defences shot down a US MQ-9 drone over the strait, causing it to crash ‌into Gulf waters.How the Iran war unfolded: every attack and oil price change – visualisedRead moreThe US said all missiles fired towards US forces in Jordan had been intercepted with no significant impact.The White House claim that the US now controls the strait and ships are free to navigate its waters is heavily contested. Tanker Trackers, an independent tracking agency, said on Sunday: “Past seven days daily average of crude oil exports via the strait of Hormuz was 3.8m barrels per day. During the formal ceasefire period (which in effect only lasted for 25 days), it was 9.8m.” The agency said Iranian crude exports had been at zero for some time.A meeting of G20 finance ministers in the US is likely to lead to a clash over American demands that more countries impose sanctions on Iran or face punitive action by Washington. The German finance minister, Lars Klingbeil, who is facing difficult regional elections, is to urge the US to bring the conflict to a diplomatic end, pointing to the war’s inflationary impact.The US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, echoing Trump, claimed on Monday the resumed exchanges of fire showed Iran was “lashing out” because the fresh sanctions were taking ​a heavy toll on its already battered economy.View image in fullscreenScott Bessent speaks to reporters as he arrives for the G20 finance ministers meeting in Asheville, North Carolina.Photograph: Allison Joyce/AFP/Getty Images“They’re taking it very seriously ... they’re in shock at the state of their ‌economy,” Bessent told reporters at the G20 finance ministers ‌meeting in North Carolina. “I would think that they are lashing out kinetically because they are losing economically.”China, a key Iranian customer for its oil, has said it opposes the new US sanctions campaign. In Kyrgyzstan, Pezeshkian will be looking for concrete assurances from the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, that he will not allow the US to spread economic chaos through Iran.Explore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranIranStrait of HormuzUS foreign policyDonald TrumpMiddle East and north AfricaUS militarynewsShareReuse this content

title: Iran’s economy in crisis as US launches new sanctions campaign | Iran | The Guardian
description: Trump’s Operation Economic Outcast is expected to push many Iranians into deeper poverty as food inflation soars
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Trump’s Operation Economic Outcast is expected to push many Iranians into deeper poverty as food inflation soars
Content: A bazaar in Tehran in June. Iranians’ buying power is being decimated by runaway food and fuel inflation and currency depreciation.Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPAView image in fullscreenA bazaar in Tehran in June. Iranians’ buying power is being decimated by runaway food and fuel inflation and currency depreciation.Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPAIranIran’s economy in crisis as US launches new sanctions campaignTrump’s Operation Economic Outcast is expected to push many Iranians into deeper poverty as food inflation soarsPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorMon 31 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor many Iranians, the new US sanctions campaign, called Operation Economic Outcast, seems superfluous given the grim economic situation in their country.Iranians are facing runaway food inflation, closed petrol stations and a seemingly never-ending depreciation of the nation’s currency caused by a lack of foreign exchange reserves.Vegetable oil in Iran in August cost 383% more than a year ago. The price of eggs rose by 294%, chicken by 177% and red meat by 148%.The cratering economy leaves the country’s political class on edge as they try to prevent economic conditions leading to social chaos.In truth, long before Donald Trump’slatest sanctions push, Iran’s economy had become a parallel battlefield in which the country’s economic commanders were struggling to maintain control.On 23 August, the US dollar reached roughly 2m rials on Iran’s open market, a new record.Three days later, Iran’s statistical centre announced that year-on-year inflation in August reached 84.4%; the rolling annual average rate was about 65%.How the Iran war unfolded: every attack and oil price change – visualisedRead moreAs purchasing power in Iran collapses, households are buying fewer goods.Diets are changing, clothes are being patched up and repaired rather than replaced, and medicine is in short supply, though it can be found on the hidden market.According to the Mehr news agency, demand for red meat fell by 50% in April 2026 compared with the same period last year. There has also been a leap in the consumption of potatoes, leading to shortages.Basic goods like eggs are now unaffordable to middle- and working-class families, Golshan Fathi, an Iranian feminist, recently said. “They don’t understand that people can no longer afford even a normal life.”Mohsen Zavaar, a biomedical engineer, said: “For part of the population, the issue is no longer buying a house or a car; the issue is cutting out meat, reducing food quality, postponing medical treatment, and scraping by until the end of the month.”Frustrated by the inability of officials to tackle the problems, he added: “The people don’t want miracles – they want decisions.”The crisis has spread beyond food and clothes. Long lines of cars stretched through parts of Tehran and the north-eastern Iranian city of Mashhad on Tuesday and Wednesday as motorists queued for fuel, with some lines blocking entire streets. Many petrol stations, including some of the largest, were closed.View image in fullscreenDrivers queue outside a petrol station in Tehran on Tuesday.Photograph: Vahid Salemi/APOfficials blamed isolated panic buying caused by rumours of a government-planned price increase, or Israeli bombs that destroyed two of Tehran’s three main oil depots.Inside the government, anxious discussions have been under way for weeks about increasing the price of oil to reduce costly subsidies, but the political class know from past experience that there could be significant pushback. A sudden overnight petrol price rise of 50% in November 2019sparked week-long violent protests.Public anger has been exacerbated by an admission that vested interests in the government made it hard to tackle fuel smuggling.Saqab Esfahani, deputy to Iran’s president, said: “Both political factions in the country are involved in fuel smuggling, and if I were to shut down their operations, they would break my windows.”Masoud Pezeshkian, Iran’s president, has been urged to investigate the remarks.View image in fullscreenIran’s leaders have appealed to the public’s sense of patriotism as they try to weather the country’s economic downturn.Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPAHowever, transparency over the economic conditions in Iran is likely to decrease.FatemehMohajerani, a spokesperson for the Iranian government, said recently that future poverty statistics would only be published with the permission of the country’s supreme national security council, making the decline in living standards akin to a classified state secret.Iran’s leaders now cast the home front as part of the war against America. Hojatoleslam Taeb, the new head of the Basij paramilitary force and a close ally of Mojtaba Khamenei, Iran’s supreme leader, recently delivered a speech that conjured up an image of resistance against market forces distorted by US sanctions.Iran seeks to criminalise all contact with foreign media in ‘chilling’ crackdownRead moreAs part of this war, he said it was necessary to reduce petrol consumption by as much as 10% to reduce the need for expensive imports. Avoiding unnecessary travel would be an act of patriotism, he implied.But these patriotic appeals increasingly have an air of desperation as the economic crisis becomes worse.Mohsen Rezaei, the new, more hardline secretary of the supreme national security council, said: “I advise young people to start producing the products they and society need in their homes, just as they gather in public spaces.”Mohammad Taheri, editor of the economics magazine Tejarat Farda, said the advice reminded him of Mao’s “backyard steel furnaces” during the Great Leap Forward. Mao encouraged people to produce their own steel, with disastrous effect.Amirhossein Hashemi-Javid, an energy expert, said Iran’s true economic crisis was its inability to export oil due to the US blockade. “The channels for selling Iranian oil are drying up.“Oil that cannot reach customers from the well provides no revenue for the Iranian economy; it is simply barrels that incur increasing production, storage and risk costs every day,” he said.At some point, the Iranian government will have to decide if it might achieve more through diplomacy than through continued confrontation.Only six months on from starting a war, after Trump promised protesters in January thathelp was on its way, the only commodity the US is now offering Iranians is deeper poverty.Explore more on these topicsIranDonald TrumpEconomicsMiddle East and north AfricaInflationnewsShareReuse this content

Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: US attacks Iranian rocket launchers on island in strait of Hormuz and Tehran targets US bases in Jordan and UAE
Content: The islands of Hormuz (top), Larak (centre) and Qeshm (left). The strikes were the first known American attacks since July.Photograph: Maxar Tech/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe islands of Hormuz (top), Larak (centre) and Qeshm (left). title: Bhutan hosts first ‘conscious food summit’ amid threats to global supplies | Food | The Guardian
description: Organisers say people must revive spiritual relationship with food amid double threat of climate crisis and conflict
Author: Fiona Harvey
Headline: Organisers say people must revive spiritual relationship with food amid double threat of climate crisis and conflict
Content: A market in Paro, Bhutan. The country’s PM said food ‘lies at the intersection of many of the defining challenges of our time’.Photograph: Robert Harding/AlamyView image in fullscreenA market in Paro, Bhutan. The country’s PM said food ‘lies at the intersection of many of the defining challenges of our time’.Photograph: Robert Harding/AlamyFoodBhutan hosts first ‘conscious food summit’ amid threats to global suppliesOrganisers say people must revive spiritual relationship with food amid double threat of climate crisis and conflictFiona HarveyEnvironment editorMon 31 Aug 2026 04.38 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 04.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMending the broken food system under the threat of climate-driven weather extremes will require more than economic fixes and intensive agriculture, according to the organisers of a pioneering summit this week, who say the world must revive its spiritual relationship with food.Delegates from more than 60 countries and the UN will gather for the next five days in Paro in the tiny Himalayan nation ofBhutanfor the world’s first “conscious food summit”, which will bring together governments and farmers, mindfulness experts and yoga therapists.Tshering Tobgay, Bhutan’s prime minister, said: “Food lies at the intersection of many of the defining challenges of our time – hunger, poor nutrition, poverty, climate change, biodiversity loss, and increasingly food security is also being disrupted by conflict and geopolitical instability. Our central message is simple: transforming our food systems requires both inner and outer change.”Conscious eating is at the heart of these talks, which will promote regenerative practices and Indigenous knowledge. “Consciousness can cultivate compassion, empathy, resilience, creativity and a stronger connection with nature,” Tobgay said in an interview with the Guardian. “This does not mean choosing spirituality over science. It means recognising that our values and mindsets influence how science, policy, finance and technology are used.”View image in fullscreenTshering Tobgay: ‘Food systems are ultimately shaped by human choices.’Photograph: Mike Bowers/The GuardianThe impacts of the climate crisis have been brought home close to Bhutan’s borders with thedisaster in its near neighbour Nepallast week where a glacial collapse led to floods and landslides that killed hundreds.This year and next as the “super El Niño” hits, the World Food Programme has warned that50 million people could be pushed close to starvation. Food shortages andhigher prices for staplesare likely around the world. It follows a summer in the northern hemisphere in which harvests have beendevastated by drought, intense heat and wildfires.Jerry Spooner, of Regenerative Vanua, a Pacific NGO, said the threats would push global food systems to their limit. “As we face the growing impacts of climate change, a potential super El Niño, biodiversity loss and increasing global instability, it is becoming clear that our food systems are not resilient enough for the challenges ahead,” he said. “The opportunity in Bhutan is to move beyond discussing how we produce more food and instead focus on how we build food systems that regenerate ecosystems, strengthen communities, celebrate culture and improve our collective resilience.”View image in fullscreenCows searching for food in a pasture in Tecoluca, El Salvador, where the lack of rainfall has reduced the availability of grass and other forage for livestock.Photograph: Marvin Recinos/AFP/Getty ImagesTobgay said people must articulate the values they wanted to see reflected in the way food is produced and consumed, instead of relying on businesses and governments to shape food choices. “Food systems are ultimately shaped by human choices, institutions, incentives, relationships and values,” he said. “So we must address root causes as well as symptoms.”Farmers and rural people were often at the mercy of markets and global forces. “Too often, policies are developed for these groups rather than with them,” Tobgay said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘The world needs to pay attention’: Nepalis and Tibetans in New York City respond to the Himalayan disasterRead moreThe summit will focus not on bombastic political speeches and promises but on fostering inner change, with the help of “spiritual masters” such as mindfulness practitioners. Food had become acommodity on world marketsand was treated carelessly as a result, leading to waste and unhealthy eating, and those attitudes must be reversed, Tobgay said.“Outer change is agriculture, markets, finance, public policy and consumption,” he said. “Consciousness has value only if it influences our decisions and changes how we act. For example, a conscious approach to production would care for both the land and the farmer. It wouldregenerate soils, not deplete them. It would protect water. It would reduce pollution and deforestation and recognise the dignity and wellbeing of the people who produce the food that sustain us.”Tobgay begins each day at 5am with a bowl of porridge and a banana, eaten sitting by a small stream that runs near his house. “I listen to the birds that are up and about by that time, I listen to the stream and the water,” he said.Anyone could try conscious eating, he added. Many cultures have a tradition before meals of reflecting on the food, its provenance and preparation, and giving thanks. Reviving such practices would take almost no time but could, he hopes, be one of the first steps to a revolution in the way we treat the planet and each other.Explore more on these topicsFoodFarmingBhutanSouth and central AsiaFood & drink industryWasteFood securitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Monday briefing: Nepal and Tibet’s floods are a warning for the future | Nepal | The Guardian
description: In today’s newsletter: As rescuers search for survivors after catastrophic floods, the disaster offers a stark warning about the climate risks facing the region, and the world
Author: Hettie O'Brien
Headline: In today’s newsletter: As rescuers search for survivors after catastrophic floods, the disaster offers a stark warning about the climate risks facing the region, and the world
Content: A boy looks at the devastation caused by flash flooding along the Trishuli River in Nepal’s Nuwakot district.Photograph: Niranjan Shrestha/APView image in fullscreenA boy looks at the devastation caused by flash flooding along the Trishuli River in Nepal’s Nuwakot district.Photograph: Niranjan Shrestha/APFirst Edition newsletterNepalMonday briefing: Nepal and Tibet’s floods are a warning for the futureIn today’s newsletter: As rescuers search for survivors after catastrophic floods, the disaster offers a stark warning about the climate risks facing the region, and the worldHettie O'BrienMon 31 Aug 2026 01.44 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 06.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGood morning. Over the weekend, rescue workers in Nepal andTibetraced to find people who are still trapped in villages affected by catastrophic flash floods. As of this morning, the death toll stands at 903, and more than4,000 people are missing.For those of you reading this in a place where life continues as usual, the scale of devastation is hard to fathom. In a matter of minutes, a torrent of mud and debris engulfed entire villages, snapped bridges and swept away people’s homes and families. Some survivors are marooned on top of buildings that rescue workers can’t reach. Others are trapped in tunnels beneath the ground. Many have no idea if their loved ones are still alive.The floods exemplify a wider threat. The delicate processes that have shaped our climate for centuries are unwinding at a terrifying pace. Scientists are still investigating the precise sequence of events that caused these floods, but as the planet heats up and glaciers melt, events like this will keep happening.The Guardian has been covering the floods extensively – you can read ourvisual guideto the disaster, and our latest report on ithere. For this morning’s newsletter, I spoke to our south Asia correspondentHannah Ellis-Petersen, who is on the ground in Kathmandu. She’s been speaking to survivors and reporting on the rescue operation since Thursday. That’s after the headlines.Weekend roundupUK politics| PC Andrew Harper’s killerswill remain in prisonafter Andy Burnham announced changes to the early release scheme that will see anyone convicted of unlawful killing, including all forms of manslaughter, excluded from the scheme.Milo Yiannopoulos| Far-right British media provocateur Milo Yiannopouloshas been deported from the US back to the UKby Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in connection with what the agency said was expired authorisation to be in the country.US-Iran| Iran has launchedretaliatory strikes on airbasesin Jordan after the United States attacked Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the strait of Hormuz, the first such strikes in a month.Iceland| In a blow to Brussels, Iceland hasheld a referendumthat has narrowly ⁠rejected ⁠the government’s proposal ​to hold ⁠accession talks with ⁠the ​EU.Nepal-Tibet disaster| A headteacher in Nepalevacuated 900 children from a schoolmoments before a deadly wall of water struck their town amid the devastating flash floods that have killed almost 800 people and left thousands missing.In depth: An ‘absolute catastrophe’View image in fullscreen‘Everything was either submerged in mud, or mangled’Photograph: cnsphoto/ReutersAt 8:37am on Wednesday morning, an enormous chunk of ice from a glacier in the Himalayas broke off and crashed on to a mountain near the border betweenNepaland Tibet. It caused a fearsome avalanche of ice and rock, which surged downstream into the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers, submerging villages and sweeping roads away.At first, the scale of damage was unclear. Nepal is prone to natural disasters, and many of the villages affected by these floods are extremely remote. Early satellite images of the region were obscured by thick clouds of dust, and scientists initially assumed that an earthquake must have caused the flood, rather than a glacier collapse. By Wednesday night, as more images and reports emerged, it became clear that the floods were an “absolute catastrophe,” Hannah says. On Thursday, she boarded a flight to Kathmandu, the capital city near the destruction.When Hannah arrived in Bidur, a small city two hours from Kathmandu, on Friday morning, most of its buildings had been destroyed, their carcasses exposed like matchsticks. A team of rescue workers in yellow hard hats were working to clear the roads. “There was a bank, an ATM machine, and a truck that was lying on its side,” she says. “Everything else was either submerged in mud, or mangled.”The race to save livesThe Nepali army has been organising the rescue operation from a military base in Bidur. Large sections of the road that links Bidur to villages higher in the valley have been washed away, so rescues are happening by air, and the sound of helicopters is nearly constant. Every two to three minutes, a chopper lands, deposits survivors, and sets off again. The mud is so thick in some places that helicopters have struggled to land. Rasuwa, an area where entire villages were destroyed, was still inaccessible when I spoke to Hannah on Sunday afternoon. “The ground zero of the floods has still not been reached by journalists, and is only just being reached by the army,” she says.Hundreds, if not thousands, of people have been rescued, and hundreds of people are now waiting outside the army base in Bidur scanning lists of survivors posted on the walls. At hospitals in Kathmandu, health workers have put up photos of bodies that are so disfigured their families have struggled to identify them. Authorities have begun burying human remains because there isn’t enough mortuary space to prevent them from decomposing. “I’ve spoken to people who have up to 12 relatives who have gone missing,” says Hannah, who visited hospitals in Kathmandu on Saturday. “And there’s no phone signal in the more remote villages. So another big cause of suffering is this huge uncertainty.”Thousands still missingSo far there are 4,247 people who are missing, according to Nepal’s disaster agency (592 of whom are foreigners, including 43Australians, and 48 from the UK, including 15 reported missing in China). Among them are 933 workers from Nepal and neighbouring countries who were working on hydroelectric power projects along the river. These rely on vast tunnel systems that are built deep into the ground, and rescue teams have to dig through mud and bore through tunnel walls to extricate trapped workers. On Saturday, the Nepali army had a small breakthrough when it successfully inserted a pipe into a tunnel at a hydroelectric site in Trishuli, allowing air to be pumped into the tunnel. In the early hours this morning, rescue efforts were “intensified” at the site, with a team of 90 people deployed.The army is racing against time to rescue the living. “People are stuck in areas that have no drinking water, or access to food. They’re completely cut off,” Hannah says. The picture of devastation has emerged more quickly in Nepal than in Tibet, where the Chinese government retains a tight grip on information. On Friday, as the official death toll in Nepal rose to 538 people, China estimated that just five people had died in Tibet. The Chinese authorities have since revised their numbers, and estimate that at least 16 people are dead and 546 missing.The long road to recoveryIt will take months to clear away the mud, and some people will never find their relatives’ bodies. Some were pushed so far down the river that they have washed up in India. “People have lost everything,” says Hannah. “I saw one woman clutching a bottle of cooking oil, because it’s the only thing she had left.” Climate stories in the global south often struggle to break through, so it’s encouraging that these floods have been covered so widely. But when the news cycle has moved on, Nepal will be left with the enormous task of rebuilding. It estimates that cost could be between $4bn to $5bn, almost a tenth of its economy.“It’s getting increasingly difficult for Nepal to pick itself up,” Hannah tells me. In Kathmandu, buildings destroyed by the 2015 earthquake, which killed nearly 9,000 people, are still in ruins. The EU has committed €2m to Nepal to help with the floods, and Britain has committed £5m. There’s also been a lot of focus on the need for better early monitoring systems. All of this matters. But as Sunil Acharya, a climate policy specialist based in Kathmandu, wrote in thisinteresting Opinion column, it also obscures a more fundamental problem: systems to monitor these events were designed for yesterday’s risks, not today’s extremes. Nepal’s warning systems were destroyed before they could alert people near the source of the flood.Looming over all this is the fact that nations like Nepal, which has contributed a minuscule amount to historic greenhouse gas emissions, will suffer the worst effects of the climate crisis. It needs far more assistance to cope with the consequences of richer nations’ actions. And it needs those nations to rapidly cut their emissions, before the crisis gets worse.The week to comeTuesday| Justice secretary Alex Norris is due to present the government’s revised plans for the prisoner early release scheme, which includes a headroom review aimed at freeing up more space in the system.Thursday| In the first UK visit by an EU leader of Andy Burnham’s tenure, the prime minister is will host talks with French president Emmanuel Macron.Saturday| Officials from Jamaica will visit the UK to lodge a petition with King Charles to seek legal guidance from the privy council on the country’s request for reparations over Britain’s involvement in the slave trade, on the anniversary of the 1781 Zong slave ship departure from West Africa.What else we’ve been enjoyingView image in fullscreen‘I’ve had a very hectic career’ … Mario Balotelli on his football career.Photograph: Luca Bruno/APAfter 15 years of headlines, it’s hard to say anything new about the trials and tribulations ofMario Balotelli. ButEmanuele Giulianelli’s excellent interviewwith the controversial star brings it all to life again.Dipo Faloyin, newsletters teamThe worst place to be in England is “left behind”. I enjoyedthis thoughtful columnfrom John Harris on the places Andy Burnham’s devolution agenda risks leaving out.HettieI’ve really enjoyed learning in the past week about the impactDolly Parton’s Imagination Library.Esther Addley warmly remembers the time Partoncame to Rotherham for the UK launch of the project.Diposkip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSportView image in fullscreenOllie Robinson of England celebrates taking the wicket of Azan Awais of Pakistan.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianCricket| Joe Roothas called on his playersto “celebrate in a sensible, grown‑up way” after they secured a first multi‑game series win since 2024 by beating Pakistan at Lord’s to take a 2-0 lead with one to play.Football| Cole Palmer eventuallymade the home win safeafter Brighton rallied from 3-0 down, with João Pedro scoring at both ends.Cricket| Yorkshire have beenclearedby the Cricket Regulator after a formal investigation into a £1.75m payment the county made to a company controlled by the club’s chief executive, Sanjay Patel, for the sale of the Northern Superchargers Hundred franchise.The front pagesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: The Guardian“Burnham keeps PC’s killers in jail but fears grow over prison capacity”, is theGuardian’s front page today, while theMirrorwrites “Killers told: You’ll do your time”. TheTimeswrites “Early release blocked for manslaughter prisoners”, while theMail’s take is “More dangerous criminals set to be freed early”, and theTelegraphsays “Burnham to free high-risk criminals”.Thei Papersplashes “Harry should pay for security costs in UK, say two-thirds of public in poll”, theExpressleads with “‘I fear Andrew’s staff won’t co-operate with police’”, and theFThas “Big Tech profits enjoy $160bn paper boost from stakes in other AI groups”. TheSun’s headline is “United for dad”.Today in FocusView image in fullscreenPhotograph: The GuardianBlack Box: episode 6 – Shut it down?For decades, Eliezer Yudkowsky has been trying to warn the world about the dangers of AI. Now people are finally listening to him, but is it too late? Guardian journalist Michael Safilooks into the world of artificial intelligence, exploring the dangers and promises it holds for society.Cartoon of the day | Tom GauldView image in fullscreenIllustration: Tom GauldThe UpsideA bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all badView image in fullscreenThe number of people living with dementia around the world is forecast to nearly triple to 153 million by 2050.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAResults from a 15-year study suggest that statins, the cholesterol-busting drugs,can lower the risk of dementiaby 15%. In the largest study of its kind, researchers tracked more than 132,000 people in Denmark between 2006 and 2021. Those who started on statins during the study period were 10% less likely to develop dementia. Those taking them early reduced their risk by 15%. The results were similar in women and men. The number of people living with dementia globally is forecast to nearly triple to 153 million by 2050. But, experts believe almost half of dementia cases could be prevented or delayed.Sign up herefor a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every SundayBored at work?And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. title: Rising microplastics in soil a threat to UK food security, MPs and campaigners say | Plastics | The Guardian
description: Report calls for legally binding targets to cut microplastic pollution as soil ‘is a complex living ecosystem’
Author: Damien Gayle
Headline: Report calls for legally binding targets to cut microplastic pollution as soil ‘is a complex living ecosystem’
Content: Microplastics are often shed by the breakdown of everyday plastic items such as synthetic textiles, packaging, paints, cosmetics or car tyres.Photograph: pcess609/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenMicroplastics are often shed by the breakdown of everyday plastic items such as synthetic textiles, packaging, paints, cosmetics or car tyres.Photograph: pcess609/Getty Images/iStockphotoPlasticsRising microplastics in soil a threat to UK food security, MPs and campaigners sayReport calls for legally binding targets to cut microplastic pollution as soil ‘is a complex living ecosystem’Damien GayleEnvironment correspondentMon 31 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe accumulation of microplastics in soil presents an emerging threat to the UK’s food security, according to scientists, MPs and campaigners who have called for legally binding targets to cut microplastic pollution.UK agricultural soils have been identified as among the most contaminated by microplastics in Europe, often as a result of repeated applications of sludge from water treatment works as fertiliser, according to a report published by the all-party parliamentary group (APPG) on microplastics.With extreme weather caused by climate breakdown already placing new pressures on agriculture, protecting soil from additional and unknown pressures is becoming increasingly important, it argues.Alberto Costa, the MP for South Leicestershire and chair of the APPG, said: “Despite the evidence, the UK’s response remains limited. Existing measures tackle only a tiny proportion of microplastic emissions. We urgently need a preventative approach focused on reducing microplastic releases at source to protect human health and food security.”Prof Cressida Bowyer, the director of the Revolution Plastics Institute at the University of Portsmouth, was the senior author on the report, produced in collaboration with the APPG and the Women’s Institute. The report follows up an earlier collaboration that focused onplastic microfibres from synthetic textiles.Microplastics are pieces of plastic between 1 micrometre and 5 millimetres in size. They are often shed by the breakdown of everyday plastic items such as synthetic textiles, packaging, paints, cosmetics or car tyres.Nanoplastics are particles smaller than 1 micrometre, which makes them small enough to permeate through biological membranes. “Everywhere we look, we find them,” Bowyer said. “Doesn’t matter how deep, how high, how obscure the sampling site, we will find microplastics. And similarly we’re finding microplastics now throughout the human body.”She added: “We’re starting to realise that our exposure to microplastics is happening across the whole of the plastics lifecycle. So not just during the production phase and at the disposal end, where most people think of microplastics contamination occurring. But also during our use of plastic, when we’re using plastic packaging or when we’re wrapping ourselves in that lovely soft, cosy blanket on the sofa, or chopping our mushrooms on that plastic chopping board.”Submissions of evidence to the report showed particular concerns around the presence of microplastics in soil, which Bowyer said “impacts the biological, the chemical and the physical functioning of the soil and the soil fertility itself”.According to Bowyer, plastic particles affect the soil structure, changing the water capacity of soil; they affect the microbial community, the bacteria and fungi that are crucial to soil health; and they affect the soil fauna, with earthworms ingesting microplastics undergoing physiological changes.She said it was important to remember that “soil is not an inert material. It’s a complex living ecosystem; it’s very finely balanced. [It is a] complex ecosystem that supports the growth of crops that feed us. The second thing to remember that’s really important is that microplastics, they’re not just polymer particles … they’re basically chemical cocktails.”There are more than 16,000 chemicals used in plastics. About 4,000 are known to be harmful to health, while most of the rest have never undergone safety testing, the report notes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Microplastics can also pick up from the environment further contaminants,” Bowyer said. “So they become like sponges or magnets for other things like bacteria, heavy metals, viral particles, other chemicals.”The report makes five policy recommendations: legally binding targets for cutting microplastic pollution, regulation of the largest sources of microplastic releases, extended producer responsibility to reduce releases across the plastics lifecycle, improved wastewater, sewage sludge and soil protections, and a coordinated national monitoring and evidence system to oversee the issue.The report’s co-author Dr Antaya March, the director of the RevolutionPlasticsInstitute’s Global Plastics Policy Centre, said: “The UK has an opportunity to move from a fragmented response to a coordinated strategy that tackles microplastics across the plastics lifecycle. We should not wait for every scientific uncertainty to be resolved before acting where the evidence already shows that intervention can prevent pollution and reduce future risks.”The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs was contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsPlasticsSoilPollutionEnvironment policynewsShareReuse this content

title: UK houses near top state secondary schools cost £40,000 more, research reveals | House prices | The Guardian
description: Premium of nearly 10% paid by housebuyers comparable with cost of a cheaper private school over seven years
Author: Rob Davies
Headline: Premium of nearly 10% paid by housebuyers comparable with cost of a cheaper private school over seven years
Content: Price differences vary across the country but the biggest premium is 54% in Sutton Coldfield.Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPrice differences vary across the country but the biggest premium is 54% in Sutton Coldfield.Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/Getty ImagesHouse pricesUK houses near top state secondary schools cost £40,000 more, research revealsPremium of nearly 10% paid by housebuyers comparable with cost of a cheaper private school over seven yearsRob DaviesMon 31 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA house near a top state secondary school costs an extra £40,000 on average, according to research that reveals education premiums that rank alongside some private school fees.The average property in a postcode district that includes a top 50 state secondary commands a price tag of £415,791, compared with £375,217 across the wider local authority areas in which those schools are located, a UK-wide analysis by the estate agent Yopa found.The £40,574 extra, a premium of about 11%, can be compared with an average annual fee of £23,000 charged by private schools, according to the GoodSchoolsGuide.However, some charge less than £6,000 a year, indicating that over seven years of secondary education parents could end up paying a similar sum to the average extra cost of a house near a top state school.The increased price tag for such properties varies significantly across the country, according to the research, although individual cases can be less informative than the overall average, due to local market factors.Bishop Vesey’s grammar school in the well-to-do West Midlands town of Sutton Coldfield tops the table of schools where buyers are likely to pay much more than in the surrounding area.Homes across the B74 postcode district go for an average of £509,964, a premium of £275,814 compared with the average of £234,150 in Birmingham, which includes more economically deprived areas.In London, the biggest premium is paid by people living close to Henrietta Barnett school, a grammar academy for girls. The average property across its NW11 postcode is valued at 37% more than in the rest of the surrounding borough of Barnet, equivalent to an additional £354,288.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUK house prices flat in July, says Lloyds, as buyers struggle with affordabilityRead moreHowever, there are some outliers to the trend. Across the postcode district home to Reading school and Kendrick school, the average property costs £276,870. That is £84,373 below the wider Reading average of £361,243.Verona Frankish, the chief executive of Yopa, said: “For many homebuyers with children, the quality of local schools is one of the most important considerations when deciding where to live and, with the new school year approaching, education will be front of mind for many families considering their next move.”Separate research reveals that in London, homebuyers with children who go to a nearby private school are opting in to a double whammy of extra costs, with properties near a top fee-paying establishment – which are often located in the most upmarket areas – going for premiums of up to 77%.Queen’s college, London, tops the table. Homes across the W1 postcode command an average price of £1.92m compared with the wider Westminster average of £854,198.Westminster school and Francis Holland school, Sloane Square follow. Both are located within the SW1 postcode, where the average property price stands at £1.49m, a premium of 54.5% compared with Westminster as a whole.Explore more on these topicsHouse pricesPropertySecondary schoolsPrivate schoolsSchoolsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Conservative reshuffle: who’s who in Kemi Badenoch’s top team?  | Conservatives | The Guardian
description: From a darling of the Tory right to a moderate former army officer, we profile the key players
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: From a darling of the Tory right to a moderate former army officer, we profile the key players
Content: Kemi Badenoch measures up Andrew Griffith, her newly appointed shadow chancellor, for a shirt in December last year.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PAView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch measures up Andrew Griffith, her newly appointed shadow chancellor, for a shirt in December last year.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PAConservativesConservative reshuffle: who’s who in Kemi Badenoch’s top team?From a darling of the Tory right to a moderate former army officer, we profile the key playersAndrew Griffith and Tom Tugendhat join Badenoch’s top team in Tory reshuffleHelena HortonandHarry CockburnMon 31 Aug 2026 14.45 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKemi Badenoch has kicked off the return to parliamentwith a reshuffleof her top team in order to take on Andy Burnham and Reform UK. She has made sweeping changes to the shadow cabinet and ruthlessly axed her shadow chancellor. Here is a run-down of the new characters sitting across from Labour on the opposition frontbench.Andrew GriffithGriffith, the MP for Arundel and South Downs, replaces Mel Stride as shadow chancellor, a role he has reportedly long coveted. He is loyal to Badenoch and was one of her first backers for leader in 2024.Previously the chief financial officer and chief operating officer of Sky and the chair of Just Eat, he entered parliament as an ally of Boris Johnson after allowing the former prime minister to use his £9.5m townhouse as his leadership campaign HQ in 2019. He later became Johnson’s business adviser in government before running for election later that year.Griffith was a backer of Liz Truss for leader and as her treasury minister was partially responsible for the disastrous mini-budget which caused economic chaos. He continued to defend the budget and said the market turmoil was linked to global events.He wasspotted last yearat the launch of a climate denial group with Truss and Nigel Farage. Of his attendance, he said: “In any year, I attend hundreds of external events with business organisations and thinktanks, none of which automatically imply my endorsement.” He also recently spoke at a hard-right Cpac event organised by Truss.Claire CoutinhoWidely tipped as one of the party’s rising stars, Coutinho made a fierce opponent to Ed Miliband when he was energy secretary and she shadowed his brief. A cabinet minister in Rishi Sunak’s government, she has been shifted to Badenoch’s economic unit and made shadow business secretary. Before parliament she was an investment banker at Merrill Lynch and KPMG, and has recently been holding the Labour government’s feet to the fire over rising energy bills.View image in fullscreenClaire Coutinho.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesColleagues describe her as forensic, she delights in doing her own research about what she terms “the hidden cost of net zero” and has spoken up in parliament for whistleblowers at the national energy systems operator.She became the first person to represent a political party at PMQs while pregnant earlier this year. Julia Lopez, the MP for Hornchurch and Upminster, will cover for her until the new year while she is on maternity leave. Coutinho is a keen cook in her spare time and once appeared on Nigella Lawson’s cooking gameshow The Taste.Tom TugendhatBadenoch has made a show of purging the more “woke” MPs from the party, banning those who believe in pursuing net zero from standing at the next election for example, so the choice of the moderate Tugendhat as shadow foreign secretary surprised some.View image in fullscreenTom Tugendhat.Photograph: House of Commons/PAHe replaces Priti Patel, who was sacked from the shadow cabinet. Tugendhat has experience in foreign affairs and previously served in the cabinet as security minister from September 2022 to July 2024. A former British army officer, he served in Afghanistan and Iraq.A remainer, he has also said he does not support leaving the European convention on human rights, which puts him at loggerheads with Badenoch.Tugendhat stood as the moderate option in the Tory party leadership contest in 2022, but was beaten by a long way by Truss. He tried and lost again against Badenoch when Sunak stood down in 2024.He wasbanned from drivingfor six months in 2022 for using his mobile phone at the wheel.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKatie LamA darling of the Tory right, Lam was only elected in 2024. She has been given the role of shadow housing and communities minister, and is likely to relish being Angela Rayner’s opposite number. She is a former special adviser to Johnson, and she worked on Sunak’s first leadership bid. Outside politics she worked at the PR company Portland Communications and the AI company Faculty.View image in fullscreenKatie Lam.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesShe has sometimes been tipped as a potential defector to Reform after saying many immigrants should “go home” and supporting the policy of revoking indefinite leave to remain. Her comments on immigration have gone further than official Conservative policy at some points.Lam has written five musicals, including an adaptation of The Railway Children.Other changes and those staying onChris Philp remains shadow home secretary. He supported Badenoch’s successful leadership campaign and has held the role since she became party leader.James Cartlidge stays on as shadow defence secretary, a position he has held since Sunak appointed him to the role in 2024.Andrew Bowie takes up Coutinho’s previous role as energy secretary.The shadow health secretary, Stuart Andrew, quit the frontbench to “focus on constituency work”, and Damian Hinds assumes his brief.Explore more on these topicsConservativesKemi BadenochTom TugendhatnewsShareReuse this content

title: More public control is the way to grow UK economy, Burnham to tell MPs | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Prime minister wants to ‘bring back hope’ by tackling cost of living as MPs call for electoral reform
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Exclusive: Prime minister wants to ‘bring back hope’ by tackling cost of living as MPs call for electoral reform
Content: Andy Burnham took over from Keir Starmer as prime minister in July, shortly after parliament’s summer recess began.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham took over from Keir Starmer as prime minister in July, shortly after parliament’s summer recess began.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAAndy BurnhamMore public control is the way to grow UK economy, Burnham to tell MPsExclusive: Prime minister wants to ‘bring back hope’ by tackling cost of living as MPs call for electoral reformJessica ElgotDeputy political editorMon 31 Aug 2026 14.13 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham will drive home his pledge to bring more essential services back into public control, telling MPs in the Commons on Tuesday that it will be the only way to improve growth across the country.Burnham will address the house for the first time in 16 years from the frontbench, and six weeks since he became prime minister, after spending the summer recess announcing a slew of policies that will now be put before MPs.He will use the statement to put public control of services at the heart of his priorities for the coming months, sources told the Guardian, saying he would make the case that it would unlock investment, jobs and growth.Burnham will say that the cost of everyday services to family budgets is holding back the economy and promise a plan to regain control of the costs.A No 10 source said: “Andy is optimistic about our country’s future. He has a clear plan for how we turn things round. He is determined we make this the moment we bring back hope.”The prime minister will face an early test of his commitment to public control as he mulls legislation to make it easier to bring struggling utilities such as Thames Water under government ownership. The Guardian reported last week Burnham was considering laws to make it easier to put companies into insolvency proceedings and then take control of them afterwards.View image in fullscreenThe prime minister has said taking water companies such as Thames Water into public control is crucial to his vision for the country.Photograph: Maureen McLean/ShutterstockHe will also face crunch decisions on possible changes to the immigration bill to exempt carers, as well as pressure from MPs to back moves towards electoral reform. A quasi-judicial decision on whether to allow more North Sea drilling is also expected soon: ahighly divisive issue within the party.Burnham will tell MPs that he wants to “bring back hope” in politics and pledge to work constructively with opposition parties.On Monday, the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, sacked her shadow chancellor Mel Stride and shadow foreign secretary Priti Patel, promoting Andrew Griffith in Stride’s place in the hope of making further inroads in attacking Burnham’s economic approach. Patel is replaced byTom Tugendhat.View image in fullscreenAndrew Griffith, right, with Kemi Badenoch and former chancellor Jeremy Hunt, second from right, during a visit to Godalming, Surrey earlier this year.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PABurnham will give a scathing analysis of how privatised services have done little for the public, saying that utilities and transport have not been run in the public interest and are neither reliable nor affordable.He will point to action already being taken to bring more bus routes under public control, including through a partnership between No 10 North and the West Midlands Combined Authority. The Liverpool City Region will start taking control of bus services from next weekend.Burnham has promised a10-year projectto take public control of utilities which is expected to be a major focus of his next few months in power. Allies have said the prime minister is “completely committed” to putting utilities such as energy and water companies into public control, and is looking at every option.As well as setting out key priorities for his first months in office, Burnham will face a two-hour grilling from MPs about policies announced over the summer – including a cut to VAT on energy bills, £2 bus fares, the scrapping of digital ID, a major expansion of devolution and a plan for a national care service.Opposition MPs are expected to ask tough questions on how the pledges will be funded as well as how Burnham expects to filla £4.7bn gap in the defence investment planleft by his predecessor, Keir Starmer.On Tuesday, the justice secretary, Alex Norris, will also present the government’s plans to cut the number of prisoners eligible for early release, including the killers of PC Andrew Harper.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThough the decision will see most of those convicted of manslaughter remain in prison to serve longer sentences, it has also raised alarm that the number of prison places may reach crisis point faster.Why are prisons overcrowded? Because no government will stand up to the tabloids | Zoe WilliamsRead moreLater in the week, Burnham will face Badenoch for his first prime minister’s questions and will also need to navigate the growing number ofLabourMPs who are heaping pressure on him to toughen up the representation of the people bill which returns to the Commons this week.Nearly 100 MPs havecalled on Burnham to back a commission on electoral reform, given the prime minister has previously been a vociferous supporter of changing the voting system. MPs have also been angered by the decision to drop any cap on party donations, after pressure from trade unions, despite the prime minister havingpreviously backed a cap of £500,000.TheLiberal Democratssaid on Monday they would put their full backing behind an amendment from the Labour MP Alex Sobel that calls for a commission on electoral reform to be established within 100 days.The party’s leader,Ed Davey, said it was a chance for Burnham to prove he was different to Starmer. “Reform stand to benefit from our terrible voting system and could manipulate it all the way to No 10,” he said.Davey added: “Keir Starmer never would have agreed to a national commission. He failed to grasp that it is our role as progressives to fix the broken system theConservativescreated. The only question now is: what kind of politician is Andy Burnham? Is he willing to do the right thing?”Reform will host its party conference this week in Birmingham, with Farage speaking on Friday.In the latest poll from More in Common, Labour hold a four-point lead over Reform, with the Tories a point behind. The latest Opinium poll found that Burnham’s net approval rating had increased over the last fortnight by three points.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamLabourEd DaveyKemi BadenochTom TugendhatReform UKLiberal DemocratsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Andrew Griffith and Tom Tugendhat join Badenoch’s top team in Tory reshuffle | Conservatives | The Guardian
description: Conservative leader sacks shadow chancellor Mel Stride and shadow foreign secretary Priti Patel
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Conservative leader sacks shadow chancellor Mel Stride and shadow foreign secretary Priti Patel
Content: Kemi Badenoch with Mel Stride (right) and Andrew Griffith (left) in December 2025. Stride has been sacked while Griffith is the new shadow chancellor.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch with Mel Stride (right) and Andrew Griffith (left) in December 2025. Stride has been sacked while Griffith is the new shadow chancellor.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyConservativesAndrew Griffith and Tom Tugendhat join Badenoch’s top team in Tory reshuffleConservative leader sacks shadow chancellor Mel Stride and shadow foreign secretary Priti PatelConservative reshuffle: who’s who in Kemi Badenoch’s top team?Jessica ElgotDeputy political editorMon 31 Aug 2026 14.07 EDTFirst published on Mon 31 Aug 2026 06.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKemi Badenoch sacked her shadow chancellor, Mel Stride, and the shadow foreign secretary, Priti Patel, in a sweeping Conservative reshuffle on Monday, replacing Stride with Andrew Griffith, and Patel withTom Tugendhat.Stride, who had been shadow chancellor since Badenoch became leader, was widely seen among Tories as failing to make an impression at a time when Labour had been under pressure over the economy.Griffith, who was previously a high-profile businessman, moves from the shadow business brief, where he will be replaced by Claire Coutinho, the former shadow energy secretary.A senior Conservative source described Griffith, the former chief operating officer of Sky and chair of Just Eat, as “a no-nonsense, pro-growth shadow chancellor with real business experience”.“Kemi is changing the way the Conservative party approaches economic policy and creating a new economic leadership team for the next phase, focused on growth, higher living standards and fiscal credibility,” the source said.View image in fullscreenAndrew Griffith, the MP for Arundel and South Downs, moves from the shadow business brief, where he is replaced by Claire Coutinho.Photograph: Gary Roberts Photography/ShutterstockBadenoch paid tribute to Stride but confirmed in a statement that he would return to the backbenches. “He helped us steady the ship, rebuild economic credibility and become an effective opposition, and I am genuinely grateful for his contribution,” she said, calling him “exceptionally loyal, and I will always be grateful to him for the work he has done”.Stride said he would continue to back Badenoch’s leadership. “The Conservative party must continue to champion an approach which is both radical and deliverable … TheConservativeshave a good story to tell on this now, and one that I know will continue to grow stronger and stronger under Kemi’s leadership,” he said.Badenoch has also sacked Stuart Andrew, the shadow health secretary, who said in a post on X he would be returning to the backbenches.Tugendhat, a former security minister, was a leadership candidate who had previously declined to join the shadow cabinet. Katie Lam, the hardline anti-migration MP who has been a key media voice for the Conservatives, will replace James Cleverly as shadow communities secretary, after he resigned from the shadow cabinet torun for London mayor.View image in fullscreenTom Tugendhat, the MP for Tonbridge, previously declined to join the shadow cabinet under Badenoch.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersTugendhat, who has been outspoken on China and Iran since returning to the backbenches, said: “We’re facing the most dangerous moment in a generation. Too often, the government has responded with weakness. As shadow foreign secretary, I’ll ensure Britain chooses strength again.”Patel announced on Sunday night that she would be leaving as shadow foreign secretary but said she would take on an “international role” with the party to build ties with other rightwing parties across the world.In a statement, Patel said she also wanted to spend more time in her Essex constituency. “I’m pleased to continue supporting Kemi and the Conservative party in a new role strengthening our relationships with fellow conservatives and centre-right parties around the world,” she said. “At a time of profound global uncertainty, when our values and freedoms are under threat, conservatives must work more closely together.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenPriti Patel (left) and James Cleverly (right) are among those being replaced by Badenoch (centre).Composite: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Getty Images ; Jonathan Brady/PACoutinho will go on maternity leave shortly and will be covered by Julia Lopez, who had shadowed the now abolished science, innovation and technology department. Helen Grant, the shadow solicitor general, has also asked to leave the shadow frontbench.Cleverly, who announced his run for London mayor on Sunday, denied he had quit the shadow cabinet following a shift to the right under Badenoch’s leadership. “I am going to put forward a classic Conservative case to be the mayor ofLondon, and it’s about enterprise, it’s about opportunity,” Cleverly told Times Radio.Cleverly, who lost the Conservative leadership race to Badenoch, is considered a more moderate voice in a party that has moved to the right as support for Nigel Farage’s rightwing Reform UK has grown.But the appointment of Tugendhat as shadow foreign secretary would bring a key voice from the party’s more centrist One Nation grouping into the fold, though Tugendhat is hawkish on foreign affairs.Badenoch has kept Chris Philp as shadow home secretary and James Cartlidge as shadow defence secretary. Joy Morrissey will be the new shadow minister for women and equalities, and Harriet Cross, another MP from the 2024 intake, is expected to become the new shadow Scotland secretary.Damian Hinds replaces Andrew as shadow health secretary and Andrew Bowie, who was key to the Tories recent byelection win in Aberdeen, will be shadow energy secretary.Explore more on these topicsConservativesKemi BadenochTom TugendhatPriti PatelJames CleverlyMel StrideForeign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: US army secretary Dan Driscoll resigns over reported friction with Pete Hegseth | US military | The Guardian
description: Resignation comes after months of turmoil at Pentagon, from leaked investigation to ousting of senior officials
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Resignation comes after months of turmoil at Pentagon, from leaked investigation to ousting of senior officials
Content: Secretary of the army Dan Driscoll was second in line to defense secretary Pete Hegseth.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSecretary of the army Dan Driscoll was second in line to defense secretary Pete Hegseth.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesUS militaryUS army secretary Dan Driscoll resigns over reported friction with Pete HegsethResignation comes after months of turmoil at Pentagon, from leaked investigation to ousting of senior officialsGuardian staff and agenciesMon 31 Aug 2026 19.09 EDTFirst published on Mon 31 Aug 2026 18.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArmy secretary Dan Driscoll has handed his resignation to Donald Trump, the White House said on Monday, becoming the latest high-profile figure to depart the defense department.The army official, who is second in line to defense secretaryPete Hegseth, had reportedly been eyeing an exit from the Pentagon amid apparent friction with the secretary.“Secretary Driscoll has been highly effective in advancing President Trump’s agenda to Make America Strong Again at the Department of the Army by providing outstanding leadership during historic military operations, restoring an emphasis on readiness and lethality, assisting with negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, and more,” White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said in a statement to the Associated Press.“The United States Army is more powerful than ever thanks to his work alongside the Commander-in-Chief and Secretary of War,” she added.The news was first reported by the Wall Street Journal.The resignation comes after months of turmoil at the defense department, which has seen numerous incidents, from leak investigations and budget issues to the ousting of several senior officials including the army chief of staff Randy Georgein April. In June, the army’s commander of its forces in Europe and Africa, Gen Christopher Donahue,unexpectedly stepped down.Driscoll was a George ally, and lamented his departure, as did Republican and Democratic lawmakers. Driscoll told Congress in April that he and his family drove to George’s house following his resignation “and we all gave him a hug”.“That being said, the civilian leadership, the design of our system, is that they get to pick the leaders that they want,” Driscoll added.Driscoll is an Iraq war veteran, tech investor and former adviser to JD Vance, whom Driscoll met at Yale law school. When nominating Driscoll in 2024, Trump called him “a disruptor and change agent”.As army secretary, Driscoll was tapped for the unusual role of key negotiator to try to end the war between Russia and Ukraine. He was also a major force behind trying to cut the red tape for military contractors to quickly develop more drones and counter-drone capabilities as warfare rapidly changes around the world.The Senate confirmed him in February 2025, voting 66-28, following an armed services committee hearing that was largely non-confrontational and focused on how the army could modernize its systems, improve recruiting and beef up the military industrial base.Explore more on these topicsUS militaryTrump administrationPete HegsethUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hiker, 91, becomes oldest person to complete grueling Appalachian Trail | US news | The Guardian
description: Dale Sanders said he fell 71 times on the trail, but completed the journey as ‘people are motivated … by my efforts’
Author: Lucy Campbell
Headline: Dale Sanders said he fell 71 times on the trail, but completed the journey as ‘people are motivated … by my efforts’
Content: Appalachian Trail hiker Dale Sanders wades across Big Wilson Stream on the 100-Mile Wilderness north of Monson, Maine, Wednesday, July 29, 2026.Photograph: Robert F Bukaty/APView image in fullscreenAppalachian Trail hiker Dale Sanders wades across Big Wilson Stream on the 100-Mile Wilderness north of Monson, Maine, Wednesday, July 29, 2026.Photograph: Robert F Bukaty/APUS newsHiker, 91, becomes oldest person to complete grueling Appalachian TrailDale Sanders said he fell 71 times on the trail, but completed the journey as ‘people are motivated … by my efforts’Lucy Campbelland agenciesMon 31 Aug 2026 18.17 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 18.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 91-year-old hiker has reclaimed his record as the oldest person to complete the more than 2,000-mile Appalachian Trail.By his count, Dale Sanders, ofTennessee, fell 71 times during the feat, six of which he said were hard falls and one which required a brief hospitalization and another just 200 yards from the end. The 2,193-mile trail runs between Springer Mountain in Georgia and Mount Katahdin in Maine.The Appalachian Trail Conservancy defines a thru-hike as completing all of the trail’s sections in any order within a year, allowing for pauses. Sanders began his hike on 6 September 2025 in West Virginia and, allowing for some brief breaks, he completed his journey on Monday atop Maine’s highest peak, where he paused to pray at the sign marking the summit.“I had to thank God, and I had to thank my support team and everybody that got me here,” Sanders, whose trail name is Grey Beard, told the Associated Press.View image in fullscreenDale Sanders celebrates after completing a difficult section of Mt Katahdin in Baxter state park in Piscataquis county, Maine.Photograph: Robert F Bukaty/APSanders first set the Appalachian Trail record in 2017 when he was 82, only to be overtaken four years later by his 83-year-old friend MJ Eberhart, whose trail name is Nimblewill Nomad.Within months, Sanders announced his comeback plan. But despite six months of training, he told the AP, he still was not in the best condition. “And even today, I feel that I should probably be in better shape than I am,” he said last month. “But I just have to always go back and say: ‘But I am 91, so I’m blazing new ground hiking long distances like this.’”In June, Sanders was descending Killington Mountain in central Vermont when he fell forward in a boulder field, scraping his legs, arms and hands. “Thank God nothing got broken, but I was banged up,” he said. “I didn’t rub the blood off, I just kept hiking.”Weeks later, his left arm went numb and he ended up at a hospital in Maine with what turned out to be a pinched nerve. But although he was soon cleared to resume hiking, he at that point considered giving up.When he returned home to Tennessee in early August to be with his wife, whose mother had just died, she convinced him to press on with his mission.Some of Sanders’ best days were inPennsylvania, where he said he enjoyed well-maintained trails and treats delivered by “trail angels”. “When people are taking care of you and bringing you caramel frappes on the trail, the rocks don’t matter,” he said.Also pushing him to keep going were his thousands of followers on social media. “I wanna get [my record] back, but right now, that’s secondary,” he told the AP. “Right now, what’s the most important thing – and it’s one of the things that surprised me – is that people are motivated and given encouragement by my efforts.”View image in fullscreenSanders takes a brief power nap near Monson, Maine, on 28 July 2026.Photograph: Robert F Bukaty/APSanders was born in Kentucky in 1935, two years before the Appalachian Trail was completed. Bullied as a child for his small size, he gained confidence in solo sports such as acrobatics and swimming. He later served in the navy and retired in 2002 after a long career in parks and recreation.He holds numerous other age-related records, including becomingthe oldest personto paddle the entire length of the Mississippi River in 2022, an 87-day trip he started on his 87th birthday.Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsUS newsTennesseePennsylvaniaAdventure travelnewsShareReuse this content

title: US trade regulator and 22 states accuse Amazon of taking $20bn with secret surcharges  | Amazon | The Guardian
