description: FTC alleges in lawsuit that online retailer ‘secretly and systematically overcharged’ advertisers for years
Author: Dara Kerr
Headline: FTC alleges in lawsuit that online retailer ‘secretly and systematically overcharged’ advertisers for years
Content: ‘Amazon has millions of advertising customers who were misled into paying significantly higher prices,’ the FTC chair says.Photograph: Charles-McClintock Wilson/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Amazon has millions of advertising customers who were misled into paying significantly higher prices,’ the FTC chair says.Photograph: Charles-McClintock Wilson/NurPhoto/ShutterstockAmazonUS trade regulator and 22 states accuse Amazon of taking $20bn with secret surchargesFTC alleges in lawsuit that online retailer ‘secretly and systematically overcharged’ advertisers for yearsDara KerrandBlake MontgomeryMon 31 Aug 2026 15.41 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 17.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US’s main trade regulator and 22 states suedAmazonon Monday, alleging the online retailer “secretly and systematically overcharged” advertisers on Amazon.com.The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) said these practices led to higher costs for customers on items like groceries and other essential goods that are sold onAmazon.“Amazon has millions of advertising customers who were misled into paying significantly higher prices. These higher costs were largely passed on to American consumers,” said Andrew Ferguson, the FTC chair.The agency accused the company of taking in more than $20bn from “hidden surcharges”, in what it deems an “ad-rigging scheme”. Amazon’s advertising business has grown significantly in recent years, becoming the third-largest online advertising marketplace after Google and Meta. The FTC says Amazon generates more than $68bn in ad revenue on its website.The lawsuit alleges that 1.2 million advertising customers were overcharged since 2019, including more than 500,000 small- and medium-sized businesses.An Amazon spokesperson pointed the Guardian to ablog postthe company published in response to the legal action, which calls the legal action a “misguided lawsuit”.“Amazon strongly disagrees,” the post reads.The government’s case hinges on Amazon’s advertising auction system, called “second-price auctions”, that lets the winning bidder pay only slightly more than the second-highest bid. Regulators allege that with this system, Amazon could secretly raise the second-highest bids with a higher “shill” bid of its own.“We believe Amazon manipulated its ad auctions to inflate what sellers had to pay, adding billions of dollars in costs that ultimately get passed on to customers with higher prices,” said Jeff Jackson, the attorney general for North Carolina, one of the states involved in the suit.The suit alleges Amazon tested how much it could increase the amount it charges without advertisers flinching. Internal documents show one manager allegedly describing the company’s pricing strategy as “hoping that advertisers don’t notice and decrease bids or ad spend”.Amazon denied these allegations and said the company gives “customers the lowest prices every day across the widest selection of products”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“After reviewing approximately 1.5 million pages spanning six years, the FTC leans on a handful of simplified communications to allege a companywide effort to deceive,” Amazon wrote in its blog post. “That is patently false.”Rob Bonta, the attorney general for California, noted in a press conference that the lawsuit arises from a partnership between conservative states, liberal ones, and the federal government. He said this lawsuit is focusing on Amazon’s alleged unlawful activities and its deception around those practices.“Amazon’s price inflation is illegal, plain and simple,” Bonta said. “This is a massive corporation. They can be wildly successful and also follow the law.”The federal agency and states are asking the court to bar Amazon from continuing the allegedly deceptive advertising practices, along with paying civil penalties and refunding advertisers.Explore more on these topicsAmazonLaw (US)E-commerceInternetAdvertisingnewsShareReuse this content

title: As US-Canada tensions flare, who’s calling the shots in Trump’s trade team? | US news | The Guardian
description: US trade representative Jamieson Greer has a level-headed reputation but commerce secretary Howard Lutnick and White House adviser Peter Navarro also have key roles
Author: Robert Tait
Headline: US trade representative Jamieson Greer has a level-headed reputation but commerce secretary Howard Lutnick and White House adviser Peter Navarro also have key roles
Content: Peter Navarro, Jamieson Greer, Howard Lutnick.Photograph: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeter Navarro, Jamieson Greer, Howard Lutnick.Photograph: Getty ImagesUS newsAs US-Canada tensions flare, who’s calling the shots in Trump’s trade team?US trade representative Jamieson Greer has a level-headed reputation but commerce secretary Howard Lutnick and White House adviser Peter Navarro also have key rolesRobert Taitin WashingtonMon 31 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 14.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHaving reportedlyreadVictor Hugo’s Les Misérables, in French, during a military tour of duty in Iraq, Jamieson Greer considered himself an unlikely target for accusations of francophobia.But Donald Trump’s US trade representative, hitherto one of the president’s less high-profile cabinet members, found himself in that uncomfortable position amid the acrimonious collapse of bilateral trade talks with Canada that now threatens to degenerate into an all-out trade war between the two close trading partners whose economies are tightly intertwined.An apparent pending deal between Washington and Ottawa aimed at avoiding damaging tit-for-tat tariffs broke down at the last minute, with Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, claiming his country had come “under attack” from the US.Detroit despairs as ‘insanity’ of Trump’s Canada trade war punishes cityRead moreAmong the multiple and complex points of disagreement was a Canadian accusation that US negotiators had pressed for a weakening of legal protections for the French language, which is most heavily spoken in the province of Quebec.Canadian provisions include legislationthat mandates streaming and online video companies to invest in and promote Canadian content and promote the French language. Carney cast US objections to such regulations as a deal-breaker, and said they amounted to “threats to French language and culture”.For Greer, a fluent French speaker who once served as a Mormon missionary in Belgium, France and Luxembourg, the charge was too much. “I speak French, too,”he told CNBC, dismissing the claims as “a funny, fake story”.“My kids speak French,” he said. “One of my kids was born in Paris. So I like the Québécois, and I like that they speak French. What we don’t like is a situation where Canada, the federal government, forces American tech companies to take their earnings and give a percentage to their competitors in Canada.”The controversy may be the closest glimpse the public will see of Greer being rattled. By Thursday, in what was being being seen bysome Canadian officialsas a potential olive branch, he was peddling a softer line on the language issue.“President Trump, myself and the US government recognizes the importance and sensitivity of the French language in Canada,” hetold CBC, the Canadian broadcaster. “We know that this is quite sensitive and quite important, and we actually champion the use of French.”The impact was undermined hours later, however, when Trump publicly signed aretributive executive ordersupposedly changing the name of Lake Ontario – one of the Great Lakes which has shores on both countries – to Lake America. Petty as the act was, it seemed to graphically illustrate the limited freedom of manoeuvre held by anyone representing a president so preoccupied with trade.And Greer is not the only official seeking to steer the president’s aggressive agenda on trade – raising questions over who is really in control.Moving the goalpostsThose who have met and worked with Greer describe the 46-year-old – who served as a military lawyer in Iraq, where he is reported to have read Hugo’s classic novel between bombardments – as a model of calm and expertise.“I have high respect for him. He been pretty creative in terms of trying to thread the needle with other countries as he tries to promote Trump’s trade policies,” said Wendy Cutler, a former US trade representative’s negotiator who has met Greer several times. “From a professional viewpoint, he’s extremely impressive. His reputation as being very level-headed, a very calm demeanor, and not someone who loses his temper or who grandstands.”It is not known if Greer retained his sang-froid in private as the talks with Canada unravelled, just days after Trump himself publicly declared a deal was at hand.According to reports, the agreement was derailed after Howard Lutnick, the US commerce secretary, objected to the scale of proposed tariffs reductions on imports of Canadian steel, aluminium and cars, sectors falling under his responsibility after Trump declared them areas of national security under the1962 Trade Expansion Act.double quotation markIt appears Greer was willing to go farther than Lutnick wasWilliam ReinschCarney, explaining why Canada decided to abandon the talks, pointed to disunity among the US negotiators. The White House has denied claims of division between Greer and Lutnick, but seasoned commentators are skeptical.“Lutnick viewed all this as his turf, and here is Greer, who is the designated guy to be effectively the trade minister, if you think about it in the context of other countries, conducting the negotiations,” said William Reinsch, a senior adviser to the Center for Strategic and International Studies and a former undersecretary for commerce. “It appears Greer was willing to go farther than Lutnick was.“From the Canadian point of view, this was a disagreement that developed late in the day and led the Canadians to believe that the United States was moving the goalposts.”Cutler, who served Republican and Democratic administrations during a 27-year stint as a US trade negotiator, said tensions within negotiating teams were not unprecedented, but were normally ironed out before talks reached the critical stage.“I think the challenge under this administration is that you have Greer in charge of the trade portfolio, but Lutnick’s in charge of section 232 investigations [restricting foreign import on national security grounds] and that’s where a lot of the sensitive issues are,” said Cutler, now vice-president of the Asia Society Policy Institute.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘Trump whisperer’Greer cut his trade negotiating teeth as chief of staff to Robert Lighthizer, US trade representative in Trump’s first presidency, who played the leading role in renegotiating Washington’s economic ties with Mexico and Canada, and the former North America Free Trade Agreement (Nafta), which was replaced with the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) in 2020.He was chosen for the position when Lighthizer apparently indicated he did not wish to be considered for the post a second time. “Greer plays the same role that Lighthizer played,” said Reinsch, who noted, however, that Greer lacked his former boss’s intimate understanding of Congress.“He figures out legal ways to do what Trump wants to do, and to get as much of Trump’s objectives accomplished as is possible within the framework that he has to operate in,” added Reinsch. “So that allows him to come back to Trump on occasion and say, ‘there’s a better way to get what you want than what you’ve employed so far.”Another complicating element may be Peter Navarro, the president’s senior counsellor for trade and manufacturing.He is reckoned by analysts to be a “Trump whisperer” on Canada, despite a belief that his influence has been marginalized compared with the first Trump presidency, when it was widely joked, according to Reinsch, that Lighthizer was reluctant to travel outside Washington for fear that Navarro would persuade the president to adopt impractical trade policies in his absence.Navarro,who went to jail for contempt of Congressafter refusing to comply with a subpoena from the committee investigating the 6 January 2021 insurrection, vented in an appearance on the C-Span network last week.Asked to respond to anarticlein the Guardian by the Canadian writer Jen Gerson, who wrote that US retaliation should be taken as a warning by other western allies, Navarro said: “Madam, your country screws us. You’re in bed with the Chinese and playing games with us.“Look in the mirror at your tariffs codes. You are the problem.”Blame gameNavarro has voiced concern that Canada has allowed the import of nearly 50,000 Chinese-manufactured electric vehicles under a most favoured nation agreement, which he fears will ultimately end up crossing the border to be sold in the US.“Navarro’s worried that the whole USMCA negotiation is really about how do we prevent Canada and Mexico from being a backdoor to Chinese stuff,” Reinsch said. “He would probably have argued last week that the deal wasn’t any good because it wouldn’t shut down Chinese imports in the United States.”double quotation markOther countries are watching the developments with Canada very closelyWendy CutlerYet the focus on Trump’s advisers cannot obscure the president’s own fixation with tariffs. Carney referred to agreements being “signed in pencil”, suggesting that Trump would try to change terms even after the details had been hammered out.“The larger Canadian objection was not due to interagency American disagreement,” Reinsch said. “Trump has very strong fixed views on trade. He thinks tariffs are good. So if you’re going to blame somebody, don’t blame Lutnick or Greer. Blame Trump, because I’m quite confident he had the last word on this.”Regardless of where blame is apportioned, the consequences of Carney’s defiance will reverberate beyond Canada, analysts say, as other countries forced to confront Trump’s threats of tariffs reassess and recalibrate how they should respond.“Other countries are watching the developments with Canada very closely,” said Cutler. “Some of our other trading partners have expressed similar frustrations [to the Canadians] to me privately, and so we could be at a turning point.“It is possible that what we’re experiencing with Canada now spreads to other countries.”Explore more on these topicsUS newsCanadaUS economyTrump tariffsDonald TrumpTrump administrationEconomicsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Revenge of the Rust belt’: Starbucks film-maker on Baristas vs Billionaires | Starbucks | The Guardian
description: Director Mark Mori followed coffee chain workers’ struggle to unionize: ‘These young kids are so inspirational’
Author: Michael Sainato
Headline: Director Mark Mori followed coffee chain workers’ struggle to unionize: ‘These young kids are so inspirational’
Content: Director Mark Mori attends a Baristas vs Billionaires special gathering on 19 November 2025 in New York City.Photograph: Johnny Nunez/WireImageView image in fullscreenDirector Mark Mori attends a Baristas vs Billionaires special gathering on 19 November 2025 in New York City.Photograph: Johnny Nunez/WireImageStarbucks‘Revenge of the Rust belt’: Starbucks film-maker on Baristas vs BillionairesDirector Mark Mori followed coffee chain workers’ struggle to unionize: ‘These young kids are so inspirational’Michael SainatoMon 31 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs the food service industry was pushed on to the frontlines of the Covid-19 pandemic in 2021, workers atStarbucksstores in the Buffalo region of New York went public to announce their union-organizing campaign.Their efforts, and Starbucks’ responses, have culminated in one of the most expansive union-organizing campaigns – and one of the most aggressive union-bustingcampaigns – in modern US history.In the new documentary film Baristas vs Billionaires, Starbucks workers in Buffalo recount their experiences with the billionaire Howard Schultz descending on the city to attempt to quell the unionization efforts.Narrated by the actor Susan Sarandon, with Alec Baldwin serving as a contributing producer, the film was directed and written by Mark Mori, who received an Academy Awardnominationin 1991 for the documentary Building Bombs andreceivedan Emmy award for a 2001 documentary on the Kent State shootings.View image in fullscreenA protest at Starbucks.Photograph: Courtesy of Barista vs Billionaires“Even though the Starbucks workers’ fight for a living wage was so public, I had no idea of the twists and turns and heartbreak connected to their struggle,” said Sarandon.In an interview with the Guardian, Mori said his former background as a steelworker and a union member with the United Steelworkers – and in political activism – had informed his decision to take on the project. He began reading about the union drive at Starbucks and spoke with a friend who would shoot the film for him.“We just went out and started interviewing baristas,” Mori said. “To me, I looked at it as the beginning of a long upsurge in the labor movement. I looked at this as we were in the 1930s, the 21st-century version of that.”Mori sees the Starbucks union-organizing drive as a counter to the drastic decline of the manufacturing industry in the US midwest in recent decades that has decimated the working class.“I call it the revenge of the Rust belt. Many of these kids are the children or grandchildren of the steelworkers from Bethlehem Steel in Buffalo, the grain silos in Buffalo, all of these factories across the Rust belt that were shut down. Their parents and grandparents lost their pensions, lost their homes, and these kids don’t see any future,” said Mori.View image in fullscreenMark Mori with Alec Baldwin at a fall 2025 screening event.Photograph: Isiah Babilonia/Courtesy of Barista vs Billionaires“These young kids are so inspirational, and they’re showing one way to deal with what’s going on, and there are many other ways. But the real number one thing about this is these young people taking matters into their own hands and inspiring other people to stand up against these billionaires.”US employers spend more than $1.5bn a year to fight labor unions, report findsRead moreHe explained the Starbucks workers who led the union-organizing drive reminded him of Vietnam war activists in the 1960s and 70s.“This is part of what some refer to as a wealth gap,” he added. “These kids can’t make enough money to pay off their student loans, to get married, to buy a house, to have children, They’re so brave and articulate in what they’re doing. I’m of an older generation, I was in the anti-Vietnam war movement. They reminded me very much of that.”The film is currently only available viascheduled screenings, though a distribution deal is in the works.The film comes as tensions between Starbucks and the union continue to escalate. Starbucks Workers Unitedlauncheda boycott on 25 August against Starbucks over the company’s failure to reach a first contract with the union.More than 700Starbucks stores have won union elections since 2021.View image in fullscreenBehind the scenes of Baristas vs Billionaires.Photograph: Courtesy of Barista vs BillionairesThe union is pushing for a $17-an-hour minimum wage, improved staffing and scheduling, and workplace protections, and for Starbucks to resolve the unfair labor practice charges.Administrative law judges and the National Labor Relations BoardfoundStarbucks committed more than 500 labor law violations, and hundreds of unfair labor practice charges at the agency are still unresolved.A spokesperson for Starbucks did not directly comment on the movie or the union’s boycott.“Starbucks has competitive pay, industry-leading benefits, and meaningful opportunities to grow a career,” the spokesperson said in an email. “People love working at Starbucks which is why we have the lowest turnover in the industry and why more than 1 million people every year apply to wear the green apron. As we have always been, we’re committed to engaging in productive bargaining.”Explore more on these topicsStarbucksUS unionsSusan SarandonAlec BaldwinDocumentary filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Anthropic sued over alleged theft of ‘tens of thousands’ of songs  | Music industry | The Guardian
description: AI company faces multibillion dollar lawsuit over misuse of copyrighted songs to train Claude models
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: AI company faces multibillion dollar lawsuit over misuse of copyrighted songs to train Claude models
Content: Music publishers have claimed Anthropic’s models ‘scraped’ smash hits including Mariah Carey’s All I Want For Christmas Is You.Photograph: Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for MCView image in fullscreenMusic publishers have claimed Anthropic’s models ‘scraped’ smash hits including Mariah Carey’s All I Want For Christmas Is You.Photograph: Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for MCMusic industryAnthropic sued over alleged theft of ‘tens of thousands’ of songsAI company faces multibillion dollar lawsuit over misuse of copyrighted songs to train Claude modelsDan MilmoGlobal technology editorMon 31 Aug 2026 08.42 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAll AI wants for Christmas is a vast back catalogue of songs without paying for it, according to a multibillion-dollar lawsuit against the startup behind the Claude chatbot.Sony Music Publishing and Warner Chappell, music publishers who manage the copyright of songs on behalf of songwriters and composers, are seeking damages for alleged misuse of “tens of thousands” of copyrighted works byAnthropic.The compositions include Mariah Carey’s All I Want for Christmas is You, Ain’t No Mountain High Enough, originally performed by Marvin Gaye and Tammi Terrell, and Survivor’s Eye of the Tiger.The plaintiffs claim they are victims of “one of the largest and most blatant ongoing thefts of intellectual property in history”.The lawsuit, filed in a California court, targets Anthropic and its chief executive, Dario Amodei, as well as co-founder Benjamin Mann. It alleges the defendants breached copyright law by “torrenting, scraping and downloading” lyrics from copyrighted works to train its family of Claude AI models – as well as reproducing those lyrics in responses to users’ prompts.It claims that Mann and Anthropic downloaded at least 7m copies of books from pirate websites, including the lyrics and sheet music to songs such as Bon Jovi’s Livin’ on a Prayer and Leonard Cohen’s Hallelujah.The figures are from a recent copyright case against Anthropic brought by US authorswhich the company settled for $1.5bn.Thelawsuit, filed on 28 August, was first reported by trade publication Music Business Worldwide. Other songs allegedly having their copyright infringed included Mark Ronson’s Uptown Funk and Katy Perry’s California Gurls.It also claims that Anthropic acquired copies of songs in other ways including scraping lyrics from legal sites like Musixmatch and LyricFind, and datasets on archive sites such as Common Crawl. In another section of the claim, the publishers allege that Anthropic stripped identifying information from songs while processing the texts, which denied copyright owners “valuable attribution” to their work.“Defendants specifically elected to harvest unauthorized copies of Music Publishers’ works so that they would not have to pay Music Publishers a licensing fee to use their works in AI training and development,” said the plaintiffs.The music publishers are seeking damages that could run into billions of dollars, based on a claim of up to $150,000 per infringed piece of work and $25,000 for each removal or alteration of identifying data.The suit implies at least 20,000 works are involved in the suit, referring to the unlawful copying of “tens of thousands of Music Publishers’ copyrighted musical compositions”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEd Newton-Rex, a UK-based composer and campaigner for protecting artists’ copyright, said he was “not surprised” that rights holders were defending themselves against a company with a “history of downloading and training their AI models on huge libraries”.Alongside the authors’ lawsuit, Anthropic has also faced claims from Universal Music Group and Concord Music Group.In a separate case this month, AI music generator Suno lost a copyright infringement case against German licensing agency GEMA, which alleged illegal use of songs including Boney M’s Daddy Cool to train its technology.A spokesperson for Anthropic, which is preparing for a stockmarket listing that could value the company at $2tn, said: “We disagree with the publishers’ claims and we intend to defend ourselves robustly in court.”Explore more on these topicsMusic industryAnthropicAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: AI could cause global economic downturn, Bank of England governor tells G20 | Global economy | The Guardian
description: Andrew Bailey, in role as financial stability watchdog chief, warns advanced models risk destabilising system
Author: Simon Goodley
Headline: Andrew Bailey, in role as financial stability watchdog chief, warns advanced models risk destabilising system
Content: The Bank governor recently told City bosses: ‘No country can seal itself off from the cross-border nature of systems that are prevalent today.’Photograph: Richard Drew/APView image in fullscreenThe Bank governor recently told City bosses: ‘No country can seal itself off from the cross-border nature of systems that are prevalent today.’Photograph: Richard Drew/APGlobal economyAI could cause global economic downturn, Bank of England governor tells G20Andrew Bailey, in role as financial stability watchdog chief, warns advanced models risk destabilising systemSimon GoodleyMon 31 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTFirst published on Mon 31 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Bank of England’s governor,Andrew Bailey, has joined the throng of figures warning about the global risks posed by the most advanced artificial intelligence technology.In a two-page letter sent to international finance ministers and central bank governors as part of his role as chair of the international Financial Stability Board (FSB), Bailey said “frontier” AI models were “showing increasingly sophisticated autonomy and problem-solving abilities, as well as threat capabilities”.He said the models risked destabilising the “highly interconnected” global financial system via cyber-disruption that “can spread across jurisdictions”.Bailey wrote toG20finance ministers and central bank governors before their meeting in North Carolina, US, this week: “Recent developments have also highlighted to me that many jurisdictions do not have the protocols in place to manage the development, release, and deployment of advanced frontier AI models, heightening risks for the financial sector and beyond”.His letter adds to alarm bells about AI that have been sounded by prominent technologists over the past few weeks – and mirrors his previous calls for internationalcooperation to tackle growing AI threats, when he told City bosses: “No country can seal itself off from the cross-border nature of systems that are prevalent today.”View image in fullscreenAndrew Bailey has raised concerns about high valuations in the AI markets.Photograph: Christian Ohde/AlamyLast month, a letter signed by 1,367 researchers and engineers at frontier AI labs – mainly OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind – also shone a light on the concerns of the engineers working on the technology every day.It stated: “There is a real risk that capability developmentrapidly accelerates beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems,” before going on to ask for the US government’s support for “an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development”.Earlier this month, it also emerged thatOpenAI staff observed signs of rogue behaviour among its cutting-edge AI agentsweeks before they escaped their training environment to launch an unprecedented hacking crusade that spread global alarm.Extending this theme into the world of financial policy, Bailey continued: “For the financial system, the most immediate concern is the potential impact of frontier AI on cyber-risk. Frontier AI may have the ability materially to alter the speed, scale and economics of cyber-risk, which could undermine market confidence system-wide, especially due to highly concentrated third-party service providers.”Bailey called on those tasked with safeguarding the world’s financial systems to prioritise “appropriate steps to support safe and responsible model release and deployment on a global basis”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe letter also noted Bailey’s concerns about the increased use of leverage in bond and equity markets, which he said was combining with high valuations in concentrated financial markets – particularly fuelled by investor optimism about the prospects of AI – in a way that could amplify a future market correction.“I remain concerned therefore that a large shock or combination of shocks could concurrently trigger multiple vulnerabilities,” Bailey wrote.Bailey has beengovernor of the Bank of Englandsince March 2020, and previously headed both the Financial Conduct Authority and the Prudential Regulation Authority, the UK’s two main financial regulators. He wasappointed chair of the FSBlast year.The FSB, based in Basel, Switzerland, coordinates the work at international level of national financial authorities and international standard-setting bodies in an effort to develop effective regulation and policies in the interest of financial stability.Explore more on these topicsGlobal economyAI (artificial intelligence)Financial sectorEconomicsG20Andrew BaileyComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Saka settles gruelling battle with Aston Villa to extend Arsenal’s winning start | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Bukayo Saka scored the only goal of the game as Arsenal held off a much improved Aston Villa to make it two wins from two in the Premier League
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: Bukayo Saka scored the only goal of the game as Arsenal held off a much improved Aston Villa to make it two wins from two in the Premier League
Content: Bukayo Saka wheels away, accompanied by Ben White and Kai Havertz, after scoring the only goal of the game.Photograph: David Klein/ReutersView image in fullscreenBukayo Saka wheels away, accompanied by Ben White and Kai Havertz, after scoring the only goal of the game.Photograph: David Klein/ReutersPremier LeagueSaka settles gruelling battle with Aston Villa to extend Arsenal’s winning startBen Fisherat Villa ParkMon 31 Aug 2026 17.08 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe smile on Declan Rice’s face with six minutes of normal time remaining said it all. He had just shut down Ian Maatsen as theAston Villafull-back zoomed into the box. Arsenal, for whom Bukayo Saka scored the only goal, were authoritative and seemingly took great satisfaction in keeping Villa at arm’s length.Unai Emery’s work‑in‑progress side struggled to test the champions, David Raya untroubled. The records will show Villa have lost their first two league matches of a season without scoring for the first time since 2002 but, despite successive defeats, this time there was no capitulation.Emery’s new team begin to emerge as Aston Villa rebuild on and off the pitch | Jonathan WilsonRead moreFor Villa, this was a marked improvement on defeat at Brighton in their opener. After 31 minutes in their previous game, they trailed 4-0 and after 40 were down to 10 men.Here they could take plenty of encouragement from a promising if not fruitless performance, the debutants Zion Suzuki and Nicolas Jackson impressing, having taken the No 1 and No 11 shirts vacated by Emiliano Martínez and Ollie Watkins respectively. Suzuki and Jackson were the only changes to Villa’s starting XI but they appeared far more cohesive. Suzuki’s eye for a pass was particularly noticeable, pinging 50-yard passes to George Hemmings, the 19-year-old who kept his place, and John McGinn within a few minutes of each other.Emi Buendía smacked the crossbar after Boubacar Kamara overawed Christos Tzolis – Martin Ødegaard subsequently asked questions of the referee, Jarred Gillett – but Jackson otherwise created Villa’s best opening. The Senegal forward, who worked under Emery at Villarreal, pinched possession from Gabriel Magalhães a few yards into the Villa half and galloped into the other before sending a near-perfect cross in from the right. Hemmings burst into the six-yard box but was unable to convert. Villa are just the second team to fail to register a shot on target in their first twoPremier Leaguematches in a season since 2003-04, along with Swansea City in 2017-18.This fixture last season ended in despair forArsenal, their players splayed across the turf after Buendía’s 95th-minute winner with the last kick of the game. Arteta said that defeat still haunts him and reminded his players as much before this game. “That was still in my tummy and I spoke to my players about it, the image of the players on the floor, totally gutted,” the Arsenal manager said. “We used that [as inspiration].”View image in fullscreenZion Suzuki, Aston Villa’s new goalkeeper, applauds the home fans after the final whistle.Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesIn that game last season Eberechi Eze was at fault for Matty Cash’s opener and was subsequently hooked at half-time. Here it was a case of role‑reversal, Eze shining after coming on for the second half in place of Christos Tzolis, who was booked after a foul on Cash and muted.“I think he learnt a lesson,” Arteta said of Eze, who was involved in Arsenal seizing the lead approaching the hour. Arsenal slowed things down and then punished Villa for switching off. Cristhian Mosquera pushed a pass to Eze, who was afforded space by Cash, Villa’s defender concerned about an unmarked Riccardo Calafiori. Eze promptly spied Calafiori’s underlapping run and the Italian steered the ball across the six-yard box where Saka beat Maatsen to the punch and scrambled the cross into the net.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis is a new-look Villa, on and off the pitch. A handful of staff in hard hats were positioned in the closed North Stand moonlighting as ball boys; the corner of rubble between the remaining skeleton and the Trinity Road Stand remains akin to an excavation site. Ibrahim Mbaye, whose £47m move from Paris Saint‑Germain is to be announced on Tuesday, was in the directors’ box. Taylor Harwood-Bellis is also poised to sign in a £25m deal from Southampton. Six of Villa’s starting XI from their Europa League triumph may have departed but Emery has made no complaints and has relayed his no-excuses mantra to his squad. “We do not look backwards,” he said.Villa’s frustrations were palpable. McGinn, in a hurry to get Villa level, was booked for wiping out Merino. Aaron Wan-Bissaka replaced Cash for his Villa debut and his first job was to stretch his legs to muffle an advancing Eze. Alejandro Garnacho entered in place of Ross Barkley. Arteta introduced Ezri Konsa for his debut, adding further steel.Villa could not find a way through and Arsenal’s winning habit already appears ominous. “It is painful to lose,” Emery said. “But we can feel optimistic with how we competed.”Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueAston VillaArsenalmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Who would fall in love with a fake NFL player? Plenty of sensible people | NFL | The Guardian
description: The FBI has charged Daejon Love after he allegedly pretended to be a 49ers receiver. Although football isn’t as glamorous as it looks, it easy to see the attraction
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: The FBI has charged Daejon Love after he allegedly pretended to be a 49ers receiver. Although football isn’t as glamorous as it looks, it easy to see the attraction
Content: NFL players can earn good salaries but careers are often short.Photograph: Charles Rex Arbogast/APView image in fullscreenNFL players can earn good salaries but careers are often short.Photograph: Charles Rex Arbogast/APNFLWho would fall in love with a fake NFL player? Plenty of sensible peopleDave SchillingThe FBI has charged Daejon Love after he allegedly pretended to be a 49ers receiver. Although football isn’t as glamorous as it looks, it easy to see the attractionMon 31 Aug 2026 13.44 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 13.46 EDTShareIs romance dead? Yeah, probably. There have never been more options for finding a mate – dating apps, Instagram DM slides, hanging out next to a gas station at 2am – but it’s also never been harder. Meeting someone who is compatible, stable, and even remotely attractive is akin to putting a square peg in a round hole. Blindfolded. From a mile away. Underwater. So, I can’t blame anyone for falling for an elaborate hoax like the one allegedly perpetrated by Daejon Love.Love is now infamous around the world for allegedly posing as an NFL player in order to scammore than 20 women out of $1.3m. Now that Love and his alleged accomplice, Taylor Jamie Chen, have beencharged by federal authorities, prosecutors are claiming they are a flight risk. They certainly seem like they have the money to flee the country. According to court documents, Love managed to fabricate an entire online persona as a San Francisco 49ers player – posting photos and videos in Niners gear, posing with expensive cars, and even performing football drills (badly) to bolster the alleged grift. Love allegedlyused AI to trick search engine resultsto add credibility to his claims on football success with the 49ers. There’s even a video of Love running wide receiver routes on the beach. In a helmet. Do real NFL players carry their helmets in the car, just in case?You never know when you may risk a concussion while laying in the sand.The FBI claims Love enticed women into romantic correspondence, then asked them for money to place into “lucrative investments.” In one of many videos obtained by TMZ, Love states he was looking for “genetically superior women.” Then again, aren’t we all?I feel awful for anyone who lost money in this alleged scam, but I can’t help but wonder why “NFL player” was the choice for this particular scheme. There’s no definitive data on the average career lifespan for anNFLplayer, but The Athletic cited a 2011 conference call by NFL commissioner Roger Goodell saying the average career length was around six years. Obviously, in practice, a football career could be much longer … or much shorter. Injuries, declining skill, and team compatibility can affect how long someone could last in the league. Football may be a glamorous occupation, but it’s not exactly one with a ton of job security.On top of that, while a player can make a lot of money during their career, it’s not guaranteed to be enough to live on for the rest of their lives, especially if, as Love claimed, that money gets spent on Lamborghinis and multiple houses that sit mostly empty. Sports Illustrated reported that themean NFL salary is $5.2m, but that figure is inflated by stars like Patrick Mahomes and Joe Burrow who earn more than $50m a year – the median salary is much lower and the rookie minimum is $840,000. Love presented a Pro Bowler lifestyle, but most NFL players don’t make the Pro Bowl. For a player who isn’t a huge star, once you take agent fees and taxes out of the equation, a five- or six-year career won’t guarantee a luxurious lifestyle in retirement. That’s why you see former athletesowning and operating car dealershipsor getting into sales. I can think of numerous professions with more longevity and security: Wall Street analyst, house painter, horse trainer.Maybe not White House Press Secretary, but that’s probably not the ideal job to scam people with anyway.I’d like to believe most people are aware of the NFL pay scale, but sadly, they’re not. Romance is a mysterious, elusive thing, and very few things are more seductive than wealth. Society is well past the days when financial security is explicitly the reason for getting together with someone, but it’s still there,especially among women looking for men, the demographic Love was allegedly targeting. This is why my dating app profile is just photos of my washer and dryer. What says “secure provider” more than that? Maybe a thermostat set to a luxurious 70F?As wonderful as central air can be, it’ll never beat a Lambo and a Richard Mille watch. Even if the NFL isn’t the permanent wealth generator many believe, it’s still more attractive than what most of us can offer. Don’t blame the alleged victims of Daejon Love. We all want to win the love lottery. Who can say no if someone thinks a winning ticket just fell in their lap?Explore more on these topicsNFLSan Francisco 49ersUS sportscommentShareReuse this content

title: Lionel Messi’s international retirement serves as a reminder: Watch him while you still can | Argentina | The Guardian
description: The Argentine’s career with Argentina was singular, and his exit is a reminder that all good things come to an end
Author: Pablo Iglesias Maurer
Headline: The Argentine’s career with Argentina was singular, and his exit is a reminder that all good things come to an end
Content: Lionel Messi ended his international career with three major titles.Photograph: Peter Cziborra/ReutersView image in fullscreenLionel Messi ended his international career with three major titles.Photograph: Peter Cziborra/ReutersArgentinaLionel Messi’s international retirement serves as a reminder: Watch him while you still canThe Argentine’s career with Argentina was singular, and his exit is a reminder that all good things come to an endPablo Iglesias MaurerMon 31 Aug 2026 14.51 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 19.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIIt was among the defining moments of the 2026 World Cup: Lionel Messi standing arms akimbo, looking up towards Argentina’s fervent supportersafter losing the final. Tears streamed down his face after his team’s embarrassing loss to Spain in what we now know was Messi’s final match wearing that famous Argentina kit.It was not the first time he’d cried at the tournament. There had been tears of joy in Argentina’s opening match, when Messi rolled back the clock to his glory days with a trio ofspectacular goalsagainst Algeria. There had been more when his brace against Austria pushed Argentina through to the knockout round as group winners, and even more when hisequalizer against Egyptthrewla Albicelestea much-needed lifeline. Later, the world found out that Messi had been struggling all the while with thehealth struggles of his father, Jorge, a fact that clearly weighed heavily on him as Argentina made a dramatic return to the final in a bid to defend their 2022 title.Argentina’s Lionel Messi retires from international football: ‘This hurts me a lot’Read moreThere were tears in the weeks that followed the tournament as well, when Jorge passed away. It led Messi – among the most private, reserved megastars in the world, football or otherwise – to provide a rare moment of public vulnerability as he mourned the loss of his father on social media. But buried in that remembrance was something that caught many football fans off guard.“All I did was play football,”Messi wrote, “and now I have serious doubts that I’ll do it for much longer.”Messiannounced his retirement from international footballthis week at age 39, a move that was somewhat expected given his age and the sheer emotional exhaustion that had clearly accompanied his final tournament. He finishes his Argentina career with the most men’s World Cup appearances of all time – 34 spread across six tournaments, the joint-most tournaments played alongside Cristiano Ronaldo and Guillermo Ochoa. He scored or assisted 185 times in his 207 caps, a record 35 of which came at a major tournament. And of course, he was the leading figure in that legendary run that saw Argentina win the 2021 Copa América, the 2022 World Cup, and then defend their Copa América title in 2024. Internationally, there was little left for him to accomplish.View image in fullscreenMessi won the 2022 World Cup with Argentina, his crowning international honor.Photograph: Friedemann Vogel/EPAYet Monday’s announcement still came as a bit of a surprise to many, largely because Messi’s brilliance is still so readily apparent. Few, if any players, have assembled the run of major tournament performances that Messi just put together, regardless of age.He remains the best player in Major League Soccer as well. Just this past weekend, the Argentinianscored four goalsand provided an assist against Montreal, pushing him into the lead for the league’s golden boot.He remains under a guaranteed contract at Miami through 2028, but Messi’s international exit has now cast understandable doubt on whether he will play that deal out. Messi essentially runs the show at Miami, a club that signs and discards players and coaches at his whim. Guaranteed contracts mean little to the club’s megastars. Just last year, Jordi Alba walked away from a three-year contract after just a few months, choosing retirement and making theMLSCup final his last professional game. Messi is an idol at the club and would seemingly face little resistance if he chose to bring his career to a close at the end of this season.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenLionel Messi scored four goals for Inter Miami over the weekend.Photograph: Chandan Khanna/AFP/Getty ImagesAll of which is to say: If you’re in North America, or if you can make it there, go seeLionel Messinow, while you still have a chance.Three years after his arrival, those of us who live and breathe soccer in Canada and the US have grown almost accustomed to Messi’s presence and all of the magic that accompanies it because it has become so routine. Miami’s traveling bazaar of Messi and aging European megastars was a genuine sensation at first but has since retreated into the shadows at times along with the rest of MLS. Hisfour-goal effort against Montrealwould have made international headlines in 2023 but now does little to move the needle. If anything, it’s to be expected. Even in Miami, where Messi was embraced readily, Messi’s presence no longer guarantees the hysteria it once did.Yet Messi’s level, in MLS at least, has not declined. He remains a must-see player and Miami remain a must-watch team. MLS has a sometimes deserved reputation for being a “retirement league,” yet that same reputation provides fans in North America with an opportunity few of them would have otherwise: to witness global greatness in person, and for a relative bargain.For other players – Thierry Henry, David Beckham and the like – those moments of greatness were sometimes sporadic in MLS. Messi, though, seems to provide those moments at each and every turn.His star no longer shines as brightly as it did years ago at Barcelona or even months ago, in anArgentinashirt. Yet even the slightly dimmed, more fleeting light Messi produces in Miami is worth watching. His first, presumably permanent, exit from the global stage is a good reminder that soon enough it will be gone for ever.Explore more on these topicsArgentinaLionel MessiInter MiamiMLSUS sportsWorld Cup 2026World CupfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tennessee to wear Dolly Parton tribute on helmets during 2026 college football season | College football | The Guardian
description: The Volunteers will be honoring Dolly Parton with a helmet sticker this season, the college football team’s head coach, Josh Heupel, announced on Monday
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Volunteers will be honoring Dolly Parton with a helmet sticker this season, the college football team’s head coach, Josh Heupel, announced on Monday
Content: Dolly Parton performs before Tennessee’s game against Georgia in 2023.Photograph: Wade Payne/APView image in fullscreenDolly Parton performs before Tennessee’s game against Georgia in 2023.Photograph: Wade Payne/APCollege footballTennessee to wear Dolly Parton tribute on helmets during 2026 college football seasonBeloved singer died last week at the age of 80Parton was born 30 miles from college campusAgenciesMon 31 Aug 2026 16.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Tennessee Volunteers will be honoringDolly Partonwith a helmet sticker this season, the college football team’s head coach, Josh Heupel, announced on Monday.Parton, a Tennessee native,died last weekat the age of 80 from cancer.“I’d be remiss if I didn’t also talk about the passing of Dolly Parton,” Heupel said Monday. “All that she’s meant across the world, this country, and certainly, the queen of EastTennessee– a lady that was extremely proud of her roots.”Dolly Parton obituaryRead moreThe singer grew up in Sevierville, roughly 30 miles east of Knoxville, where the University of Tennessee is located.“You look at [Parton’s] impact, you know, just her ability to give back, make an impact to people, certainly here in East Tennessee. She means a lot to people across this country,” Heupel said. “We’ll be wearing a sticker patch on the back of our helmet to recognize her accomplishments and everything that she’s meant.”Parton often spoke about her upbringing as one of 12 children in what she described as a “dirt poor” family. Inspired by her youth, Parton led several initiatives to give back to her home town, including her nonprofit Imagination Library, which provides children with access to free books.The sticker, in the Volunteers’ signature orange, features a butterfly similar to the one in the logo of Dollywood, Parton’s theme park. The logo also has “Dolly” written at its center.Parton had a close relationship with the university. She twice played on Tennessee’s campus during world tours. In 2023, before a football game, she was walked to the stage at Neyland Stadium by former NFL and Tennessee star Peyton Manning. She then led the crowd in a rendition of Rocky Top, a staple at Volunteers games.Tennessee host Furman in their season-opener on Saturday.Explore more on these topicsCollege footballTennesseeCollege sportsUS sportsDolly PartonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Will US Open defeat force Novak Djokovic to reconsider his end game? | Novak Djokovic | The Guardian
description: The Serb has his heart set on defending his Olympic title in Los Angeles in 2028, but his ageing body is screaming a resounding ‘no’
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: The Serb has his heart set on defending his Olympic title in Los Angeles in 2028, but his ageing body is screaming a resounding ‘no’
Content: Novak Djokovic holds an ice pack to his head while seated at a change of ends during his defeat by Mariano Navone.Photograph: Robert Deutsch/IMAGN IMAGES/ReutersView image in fullscreenNovak Djokovic holds an ice pack to his head while seated at a change of ends during his defeat by Mariano Navone.Photograph: Robert Deutsch/IMAGN IMAGES/ReutersNovak DjokovicAnalysisWill US Open defeat force Novak Djokovic to reconsider his end game?Tumaini Carayolat Flushing MeadowsThe Serb has his heart set on defending Olympic title in 2028 but his ageing body is screaming a resounding ‘no’Mon 31 Aug 2026 15.46 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareAs the scoreline continued to cascade and the prospect ofNovak Djokovicwinning even one match in New York this year became increasingly remote, the 24-time grand slam title winner’s suffering and toil drove the Arthur Ashe Stadium crowd to its feet in the early hours of Monday morning. With Djokovic trailing 3-1 in the fifth set, thousands of spectators stood in unison to salute their champion and urge him on. The moment reduced Djokovic to tears.This was quite a familiar scene. Five years ago, the same crowd similarly offered a tearful Djokovic a standing ovation as his match against Daniil Medvedev slipped away. The circumstances surrounding those results, however, could have hardly been any different. Back in 2021, Djokovic stood three sets away from winning the calendar year grand slam, the ultimate achievement. Here, he was losing in the first round of the US Open against a clay-court specialist ranked outside the top 50, an opponent he would usually crush with disdain.Ailing Novak Djokovic falls in US Open first round for earliest grand slam exit in 20 yearsRead moreDjokovic’s four hours and 36 minutes on court, by far the longest grand slam first‑round match of his career, was already a struggle from about 20 minutes in. He spent much of the match vomiting, cramping and understandably voicing his dismay to his team as he lost 7-6 (5), 5-7, 4-6, 6-2, 6-1 against a courageous Mariano Navone.At 39, and after a record 84 grand slam main‑draw appearances, these physical issues have been a large part of Djokovic’s story this year. When he has been relatively fit, he has played at a remarkable level considering his age, but his ageing body is his greatest rival. In Australia, his miraculous run to the final after his five-set win against Jannik Sinner ended with Djokovic being devoid of energy in his match against Carlos Alcaraz, despite receiving a walkover and retirement victory en route. He was ravaged by injuries for months in the build‑up to the French Open, which was reflected in him again vomiting and cramping in his five‑set third‑round defeat against an excellent João Fonseca. Although he was more physically prepared for Wimbledon, the tank was empty for his semi‑final with Sinner.In New York, this result had been foretold by his defeat in the second round of the Cincinnati Open, where he struggled badly in humid conditions. As in Cincinnati, Djokovic said he has been dealing with physical issues for some time and these episodes are no longer a surprise. Djokovic is the sport’s greatest physical titan who has pushed men’s tennis to greater heights with his physicality and endurance. The evidence suggests increasingly that his body cannot keep up.Losing matches is difficult enough, but his time on court in New York this year just looked like a completely miserable experience from the beginning. Instead of being able to embrace the battle and focus on problem solving, he was in survival mode throughout, trying to endure the pain for as long as he could. It looked like a horrendous experience. It came as no surprise that, when Djokovic came off the court, he almost immediately explained how much he despised his time on the court.View image in fullscreenNovak Djokovic acknowledges the rousing support he got from fans as he leaves the court.Photograph: Matthew Stockman/Getty ImagesThis was Djokovic’s first opening-round defeat at a grand slam tournament since 2006, and his first at the US Open. He leaves New York with perhaps the most serious period of reflection for his future ahead of him. Time comes for everyone. Despite how masterfully he has evaded it for so long, continuing to perform at such a high level while on the verge of turning 40, it is gaining on him quickly.The long final stretch of Djokovic’s career has been an incredible sight. He has achieved more than anyone at his age and demonstrating his enduring passion for the sport has been a pleasure. If his struggles with his body continue, if his physical discomfort continues to generate misery on the court, it is clear that Djokovic will have to reflect on how long he is willing to put himself through this.He has long identified the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics as his ultimate target, a chance to defend his gold medal from Paris 2024. At 39, nearly two years is an eternity and the prospect of trying to keep his body together seems a daunting task. Still, this is Novak Djokovic, who has won more than any other man in history. It is a reflection of his success and resilience that it is still unclear whether this is the defeat that causes the Serb to consider an end to his unprecedented career.Explore more on these topicsNovak DjokovicUS Open Tennis 2026US Open tennisTennisanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Aryna Sabalenka begins US Open title defence with victory against Camila Osorio | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: Aryna Sabalenka said she is determined to look ahead after beginning her US Open women’s singles title defence with a 6-2, 6-4 win against Camila Osorio
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Aryna Sabalenka said she is determined to look ahead after beginning her US Open women’s singles title defence with a 6-2, 6-4 win against Camila Osorio
Content: Aryna Sabalenka: ‘If I win the tournament or lose the tournament, today is a new day, and I have to stay in the moment.’Photograph: Sarah Yenesel/EPAView image in fullscreenAryna Sabalenka: ‘If I win the tournament or lose the tournament, today is a new day, and I have to stay in the moment.’Photograph: Sarah Yenesel/EPAUS Open Tennis 2026Aryna Sabalenka begins US Open title defence with victory against Camila OsorioReigning women’s singles champion wins 6-2, 6-4Men’s 10th seed Arthur Fils beaten by Stefanos TsitsipasTumaini Carayolat Flushing MeadowsMon 31 Aug 2026 15.36 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAryna Sabalenka said she is determined to look ahead, rather than dwell on a difficult past few months, after beginning her US Open title defence with a 6-2, 6-4 victory against Camila Osorio.“The good thing for me is not looking back no matter what, if it’s good or bad, because I feel a good result can also stop you from performing well because you’re basically focusing on the past,” Sabalenka said. “I never look back. If I win the tournament or lose the tournament, today is a new day, and I have to stay in the moment.”Venus Williams bows out after 2am following latest start in US Open historyRead moreSabalenka’s No 1 ranking is at risk after failing to reach a final for four months, with Elena Rybakina having a strong chance of taking top spot. Sabalenka produced a professional opening performance, serving well and overpowering Osorio from the baseline. She eased through the first set, and quickly rolled through the concluding three games of the second to close out the match.“I had opportunities, I tried to step in,” Sabalenka said. “She played great. She brought the fight and she battled really well, and I just tried to stay as aggressive as possible.”The Cincinnati Open champion Arthur Fils, meanwhile, endured the biggest upset of the second day at Flushing Meadows: he was defeated 4-6, 7-6 (3), 6-1, 6-4 by the former world No 3 Stefanos Tsitsipas. Fils, the 10th seed, arrived in New York considered one of the title contenders in an open men’s draw, but after leading 6-4, 5-2 the Frenchman balked while attempting to serve for the second set.Once he allowed Tsitsipas back into the match, the Greek served and struck his forehand brilliantly until the end, while Fils failed to regain the intensity and quality with which he began the match.“Once the energy went down at the end of the second, I never felt again a good energy,” Fils said. “I have to talk with my team, but at my level to do such a mistake is almost unprofessional.”It is an enormous result for Tsitsipas, twice a grand slam singles finalist, who fell as low as No 88 in the ATP rankings this year and now sits at No 53.The 28‑year‑old recently chose to split from his father, who had coached him on‑and-off since his childhood. Their relationship had become increasingly tense this year, leading Tsitsipas to declare that he does not intend to work with him again. This result is a significant step forward as he tries to re-establish himself.A positive run of first‑round results for British players early in the tournament continued on Monday as Harriet Dart followed up her strong performances in the qualifying draw by recovering from a set down to defeat the world No 55 Peyton Stearns, 3-6, 6-3, 6-2.She was followed into the second round by Jacob Fearnley, a lucky loser, who trailed by two sets to one before outlasting the world No 65 Martin Landaluce 4-6, 6-2, 4-6, 7-5, 6-3. Fearnley had fallen in the final round of qualifying in three tight sets before a flurry of late withdrawals allowed him to enter the tournament as a lucky loser.As with Toby Samuel, another qualifier, after his first‑round win on Sunday, Fearnley’s victory moves him back into the top 100 of the live rankings, meaning there will likely be five British men inside the ATP top 100 after the tournament: Arthur Fery, Cameron Norrie, Jan Choinski, Samuel and Fearnley.Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026Aryna SabalenkaUS Open tennisTennisnewsShareReuse this content

title: South African airline defends dramatic low-level flyby before rugby union clash | Rugby union | The Guardian
description: A pre-game stunt involving two passenger jets flying dramatically low over a  stadium in South Africa drew huge cheers from the crowd, but also sparked a major debate over safety risks
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A pre-game stunt involving two passenger jets flying dramatically low over a stadium in South Africa drew huge cheers from the crowd, but also sparked a major debate over safety risks
Content: An aircraft performs a low flyby before the match between South Africa and New Zealand in Cape Town.Photograph: Jamie Rossouw/ReutersView image in fullscreenAn aircraft performs a low flyby before the match between South Africa and New Zealand in Cape Town.Photograph: Jamie Rossouw/ReutersRugby unionSouth African airline defends dramatic low-level flyby before rugby union clashCape Town stunt sparks major debate over safety risksAirlink insists flyby conducted according to regulationsAssociated PressMon 31 Aug 2026 09.44 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA pre-game stunt involving two passenger jets flying dramatically low over a stadium in South Africa drew huge cheers from the estimated crowd of 56,000 people, but also sparked a major debate over safety risks. The flyby by two Embraer jets, operated by the local airline Airlink, happened on Saturday before the second rugby union Testbetween South Africa and New Zealandin Cape Town.The flight tracking service Flightradar24 estimated that the lead jet passed just 41-46 feet (12-14 metres) above the roof of Cape Town Stadium, with the crowd and the world’s top-ranked rugby teams below. The second jet, which was very close behind, flew through a cloud of pink dust that shot up from the stadium roof as part of the show.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueAirlink, a sponsor of theSouth Africarugby union team, said the flyby was conducted according to safety regulations. The airline said that it was carefully planned and rehearsed, with the aircraft flying at 150 knots (172 mph), when they went over the stadium. Each jet had three senior captains on board, Airlink said, operating in the roles of a commander, a co-pilot and a safety officer. The jets were not carrying any passengers.“Airlink notes the concerns expressed in various social media and online forums regarding yesterday’s formation flyby over Cape Town’s DHL Stadium,” Airlink said on Sunday. “The flight demanded careful planning and rehearsal, as it required navigating at low altitude, at around 150 knots. The South African Civil Aviation Authority and Air Traffic Navigation Services provided valuable guidance, approval and support to ensure a safe flyby.”View image in fullscreenThe planes fly above the stadium before kick-off.Photograph: Gallo Images/Getty ImagesSouth African rugby union has a tradition of stadium flybys at big games, starting when a Boeing 747 flew over a stadium in Johannesburg before the 1995 World Cup final between the same teams, who are fierce rivals. But the flyby last weekend was especially low and dramatic, generating global interest after it was shown as part of the pre-game broadcast, and sparking a flurry of videos shot by witnesses.View image in fullscreenThe second jet flies through a cloud of pink dust that shot up from the stadium roof as part of the show.Photograph: APSome aviation experts questioned whether the margin for error was too small. “Basically, that lead aircraft … was kind of like dodging over the roof and climbing over the one side and dipping below and then climbing over the other side. That was a little bit uncomfortable,” Chris Martinus, president of Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association South Africa, said. “[If] something adverse happens, you just don’t have options at that kind of altitude.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKeith Tonkin, an Australian aviation consultant and former military and commercial pilot, said yesteron Monday that the Embraer passenger jets – which are small-to-medium jets designed for regional flights – were not designed or intended for that kind of low-level operation and warned against the precedent.“The bigger picture is that a benchmark has been established and others may expect to do something similar, and that’s not going to end well,” Tonkin said. He added that turbulence or a bird strike at such a low altitude could leave the pilots with too little room to manoeuvre without hitting the stadium.Airlink said flight data recorded by both aircraft confirmed their flights were performed within civil aviation safety limits for speed and altitude.Explore more on these topicsRugby unionSouth AfricaSouth Africa rugby teamNew Zealand rugby union teamAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Manchester City gazump Spurs over Iliman Ndiaye and eye Enzo Fernández deal | Transfer window | The Guardian
description: Manchester City are poised to bolster their attack by buying Everton’s Iliman Ndiaye for up to £65m and have opened talks with Chelsea over a deal to sign Enzo Fernández
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: Manchester City are poised to bolster their attack by buying Everton’s Iliman Ndiaye for up to £65m and have opened talks with Chelsea over a deal to sign Enzo Fernández
Content: Iliman Ndiaye will have a medical at Manchester City with a £65m deal having been agreed with his club, Everton.Photograph: Robbie Hoad/Every Second Media/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenIliman Ndiaye will have a medical at Manchester City with a £65m deal having been agreed with his club, Everton.Photograph: Robbie Hoad/Every Second Media/ShutterstockTransfer windowManchester City gazump Spurs over Iliman Ndiaye and eye Enzo Fernández dealCity agree £65m deal with Everton for Senegal wingerRicharlison to stay at Spurs, who agree Mudryk loanJacob SteinbergandJamie JacksonMon 31 Aug 2026 15.32 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester City are poised to bolster their attack by buying Everton’s Iliman Ndiaye for up to £65m and have opened talks with Chelsea over a deal to sign Enzo Fernández.City’s hijack of Tottenham’s deal for Ndiaye came after their attempts to sign Liverpool’s Cody Gakpo broke down. The Senegal international is poised to undergo a medical after a fee of £60m plus £5m in add-ons was agreed withEverton, who have little time to find a replacement for one of their most important players before the transfer window shuts on Tuesday night.Chelsea’s perfect yet unserious start to the Premier League season | Jonathan WilsonRead moreIt had seemed that Ndiaye would move to Spurs after they agreed a deal in principle with Everton on Sunday. Richarlison was poised to move in the opposite direction but that transfer stalled on Monday. Richarlison released an emotional statement on social media and said that he would not allow his future to be decided for him. The Brazilian is cool on a move to Everton and is expected to stay at Spurs.City registered their interest in Ndiaye last week and moved in after Liverpool pulled out of an £85m deal for Gakpo. Spurs have moved on and agreed to sign Mykhailo Mudryk on loan fromChelsea.The Ukraine winger, who is free to play again after his doping ban was resolved this summer, played for Roberto De Zerbi at Shakhtar Donetsk and favoured a reunion with the Tottenham manager after Leeds and Brentford also contacted Chelsea about him.Spurs have also agreed a deal to sign Chelsea’s defender Tosin Adarabioyo on a permanent deal.Chelsea are poised for a busy end to the window and have finally been contacted by City about Fernández. The Argentina midfielder wants to leave and has his heart set on a move to City. Fernández has a close relationship with City’s manager, Enzo Maresca, who left Chelsea this year.Chelseaset a price of £120m for Fernández this summerand may push for a higher fee with the deadline drawing close. Another consideration for the Stamford Bridge club as they face up to losing one of their biggest players is the need to improve their squad.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChelsea have sounded out Roma’s Manu Koné and Monaco’s Lamine Camara as potential replacements for Fernández. They have been met with resistance in attempts to sign Bournemouth’s Alex Scott while Crystal Palace want to keep Adam Wharton. Chelsea are tracking Morgan Gibbs‑White but know Nottingham Forest are unlikely to sell at this stage.The goalkeeper Robert Sánchez is poised to leave Chelsea as he nears a loan to Como. Sánchez lost the No 1 spot after Emiliano Martínez’s arrival.Explore more on these topicsTransfer windowManchester CityEvertonChelseaTottenham HotspurnewsShareReuse this content

title: Argentina’s Lionel Messi retires from international football: ‘This hurts me a lot’ | Lionel Messi | The Guardian
description: Lionel Messi has confirmed he is retiring from international football with immediate effect, seven weeks after Argentina were beaten by Spain in the World Cup final
Author: Billy Munday
Headline: Lionel Messi has confirmed he is retiring from international football with immediate effect, seven weeks after Argentina were beaten by Spain in the World Cup final
Content: Lionel Messi after Argentina’s defeat against Spain in the World Cup final.Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLionel Messi after Argentina’s defeat against Spain in the World Cup final.Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesLionel MessiArgentina’s Lionel Messi retires from international football: ‘This hurts me a lot’Argentina great’s last game was in World Cup finalPlayer’s father Jorge died earlier in AugustBilly MundayMon 31 Aug 2026 11.19 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLionel Messi has announced his retirement from international football seven weeks after Argentinawere beaten by Spain in the World Cup finalin the US. The 39-year-oldcaptained Argentina to World Cup glory in 2022and two Copa América titles after winning his first cap in 2005.On Monday, Messi posted a picture on Instagram of notes that he wrote on 21 July, two days after the World Cup final, confirming he was ending his Argentina career and saidthe death of his father, Jorge, in early Augustmade him feel “more convinced than before”. Messi was often visibly emotional during the tournament and revealed in the knockout stages that Jorge was undergoing medical treatment.Messi’s statement, addressed toArgentinafans, read: “After the time that has passed since the final, thinking a lot, I want to let everyone know that I am retiring from the national team. It is a decision that hurts my soul but I know it is time. I can say for sure that I always gave everything, not only in the last few years when we won everything [but] before as well, and I always fought and gave everything for the shirt, to give you joy and make you proud of being Argentinian through football.“There’s not long left and chapters are coming to an end – and this is one that hurts me a lot. I love, have loved and I will always love being part of the national team. I have emptied myself: now I have nothing more to give and, besides, there are great young players coming through who deserve to be [selected].”Messi thanked his family for accompanying him on a “beautiful but difficult journey”. He previously announced his retirement from international football in 2016 after Argentinalost on penalties to Chile in the 2016 Copa América final– at the time his fourth defeat in a major final out of four. The then Barcelona forward was often criticised for not producing his club form at international level and comparisons were constantly made with the World Cup-winning Diego Maradona. However, Messi was persuaded to continue and finally lifted silverware with his countryat the 2021 Copa América in Brazil.“I take with me unforgettable memories and moments,” his statement said. After victory against Brazil at the Maracanã in the 2021 Copa América final, Messi was central to Argentina’s first World Cup triumph since 1986 and scored in every knockout round in Qatar, including twice in the final against France –two years after the death of Maradona.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Argentinadefended their Copa América title in 2024amid speculation that Messi, by then playing for Inter Miami, would call it a day. He turned 39 during the World Cup this summer, briefly becoming the tournament’s all-time record scorer before being overtaken by Kylian Mbappé.His statement finished by returning to address Argentina fans: “I go with the satisfaction and the pride of having, along with my teammates, giving you moments we dreamed about. I love you! I thank God for making me Argentinian.”Messi retires as Argentina’s record appearance maker – he won the first of his 207 caps in a friendly against Hungary in August 2005 and was sent off almost immediately for catching Vilmos Vanczak with an elbow. He is also Argentina’s record scorer with 125 goals. Before playing for the senior team, he won the Under-20 World Cup and also won Olympic gold in 2008.Since the end of his sixth World Cup, Messi has featured seven times for Inter Miami andscored four goals in the 7-1 rout of Montrealin Major League Soccer on Saturday. Messi signed a contract extension last year to 2028, when he will be 41.Ángel Di María, who scored for Argentina in the 2021 Copa América and 2022 World Cup finals, led tributes from Messi’s former teammates, writing: “All I know is that I was born in the right century to be able to see you, enjoy you and, above all, share with you all these years [together] with the national team.” The midfielder Rodrigo de Paul posted: “Thank you for making us so happy. You can’t imagine how many times you made people smile. You are eternal.”As a teenager, Enzo Fernández wrote to Messi to plead with him to reverse his 2016 decision to retire from Argentina duty, trying to work out if he would be old enough to play alongside him one day. “That kid was so lucky … Thank you for letting me share a part of your story,” Fernández said. “We’re going to miss you so much,capitán,” said the striker Lautaro Martínez.Explore more on these topicsLionel MessiArgentinanewsShareReuse this content

title: Arsenal trying to lure Julián Álvarez after agreeing deals to sell Martinelli and Jesus | Arsenal | The Guardian
description: Arsenal are running out of time to convince Julián Álvarez to join them from Atlético Madrid after agreeing late sales worth more than £70m
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Arsenal are running out of time to convince Julián Álvarez to join them from Atlético Madrid after agreeing late sales worth more than £70m
Content: Julián Álvarez at Atlético Madrid training on Sunday after being left out of the matchday squad on Saturday.Photograph: Rodrigo Jimenez/EPAView image in fullscreenJulián Álvarez at Atlético Madrid training on Sunday after being left out of the matchday squad on Saturday.Photograph: Rodrigo Jimenez/EPAArsenalArsenal trying to lure Julián Álvarez after agreeing deals to sell Martinelli and JesusAtlético say they will not allow Barcelona to buy ÁlvarezJesus poised for Barça and Martinelli for Al-HilalEd AaronsandBen FisherMon 31 Aug 2026 18.36 EDTFirst published on Mon 31 Aug 2026 06.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArsenal are running out of time to persuade Julián Álvarez to join them fromAtlético Madridafter agreeing to sell Gabriel Martinelli, Gabriel Jesus and Fábio Vieira in deals collectively worth more than £70m.Álvarez has his heart set on joining Barcelona despite Atlético’s insistence theywill not sellto their La Liga rivals – he returned to training on Sunday after being left out of their squad for the win against Sevilla.Transfer latest: Juventus in Woltemade loan talks, Everton pushing for BalogunRead moreMikel Arteta, the Arsenal manager, is understood to have spoken last week to Álvarez in an effort to persuade the former Manchester City forward to return to the Premier League and to have been informed the Argentina international wants onlyBarcelona.Asked directly about Álvarez after victory at Aston Villa on Monday, Arteta replied: “I don’t know.
