The MIT-affiliatedCorticoproject provides tools that surface under-heard community perspectives from recorded conversations, and is now organizing listening sessions atlibrariesacross the country. The US non-profit-builtTalk to the Cityuses AI to analyze large datasets of stakeholder input. The US startupRemeshhas a commercial offering that uses AI to generate recommendations from dialogue, which has beentestedin policy development scenarios.Mark Zuckerberg says the future of AI is for everyone. But who owns it? | Raffi KrikorianRead moreThere is a long and proud tradition of this sort of “civic technology” in the United States. Two decades ago, the spirit ofinnovationto develop software for better politics and civic engagement was so strong in organizations like Code for America and the Obama 2008 campaign that Congress funded a new executive agency to bring these ideas to government: the US Digital Service. (The Trump administration repurposed the USDS to become the US Doge Service in 2025.)One signal that candidates and political parties may start adopting these kinds of tools came this spring from Higher Ground Labs. The Democratic-aligned campaign tech investment firm launched a newfundtargeting, in part, “AI-Native Campaign Systems” and “community-Led Messaging Platforms that surface authentic, bottom-up insights from real conversations”.AI is a multifaceted issue that deserves to be on the table in the midterms. So far, the powerful force ofpolarizationin US politics seems to be separating the parties into the AI skeptics versus the AI boosters. We urge both voters and politicians toseparatethe technology of AI from its profiteers. We want big techmoneyout of politics, holding the AI companiesaccountablefor the harm their models cause,taxingtheir revenues, and maybe evennationalizingthem if the AI bubble bursts.But we also think congressional candidates in the US midterms seeking authentic connection with voters, and seeking to differentiate themselves from their opponents, should be looking to use AI responsibly in their campaigning. The broad listening and deliberation tools pioneered by others around the world could make US politics more transparent, responsive and community-driven. The impact of AI on campaigning doesn’t have to be all bad.Bruce Schneier is a security technologist who teaches at the Harvard Kennedy School and the University of Toronto’s Munk School of Global Affairs & Public PolicyNathan E Sanders is a data scientist affiliated with the Berkman Klein Center of Harvard University and co-author, with Bruce Schneier, of the book Rewiring Democracy: How AI Will Transform Our Politics, Government, and CitizenshipThis article was amended on 31 August 2026. An earlier version incorrectly described CrownShy as a non-profit.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionUS politicsJapanScotlandcommentShareReuse this content

title: Space junk punched a new hole in the moon. It’s not ours to abuse | Moriba Jah | The Guardian
description: The space industry treats the sky as a place to dump what it no longer wants. We must develop a new model of accountability
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The space industry treats the sky as a place to dump what it no longer wants. We must develop a new model of accountability
Content: An undated view, left, of the Moon's surface and an image taken between 11 and 12 August showing a crater that formed after a Falcon 9 upper stage struck the Moon's surface.Photograph: Nasa Goddard/Intuitive Machines/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn undated view, left, of the Moon's surface and an image taken between 11 and 12 August showing a crater that formed after a Falcon 9 upper stage struck the Moon's surface.Photograph: Nasa Goddard/Intuitive Machines/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionSpaceSpace junk punched a new hole in the moon. It’s not ours to abuseMoriba JahThe space industry treats the sky as a place to dump what it no longer wants. We must develop a new model of accountabilityMon 31 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTShareOn 5 August, a piece of a derelict SpaceX rockettraveling at 5,400 miles an hourmet with the moon and punched a fresh hole into itnear Einstein Crater. Astronomers were thrilled. The European Southern Observatorycaught sodium and lithiumflaring in the debris plume and called it a bonus. The mediacalled ita light show. Nobody was physically hurt, so nobody is responsible, and within a week the story was gone.I have spent 20 years tracking the junk humanity leaves behind in space for a living, and I want to tell you plainly what that crater actually is: a receipt. It’s what you get when an entire industry treats the sky, and now the moon, as a place to dump what it no longer wants, and calls the dumping “normal operations” or “space exploration”.Here’s my thesis, and I won’t soften it: we don’t own the moon, but we’re behaving as though we did, and that behavior has a name. It’s the oldest colonial instinct there is, dressed up in aerospace engineering. Take what you want, leave what you don’t, and let someone else, or something else, absorb the cost.Stewardship asks what we owe a place. Ownership asks what we can extract from it before anyone stops us. Right now, in cislunar space, ownership is winning by default, because nobody with power has bothered to claim the alternative, and power doesn’t reside in controlling outcomes but rather in the ability to make choices. Remember this.We are preparing to transform the moon and Mars. The public must have a say in this future | Ben BrambleRead moreSo, let’s start with the plain facts of the object itself. The Falcon 9 upper stage that hit the moon launched in 2025 carrying lunar landers, finished its job, and was simplyabandoned in a high orbitthat happened to cross the moon’s path. Nobody designed a deliberate end for it. The curvature of spacetime and the sun’s radiation pressure did the steering instead, for months, until a predictable, computable trajectory ended predictably, in a fresh scar.SpaceX didn’t choose to hit the moon. But it did not prevent the collision, which, in an industry with the money and the trajectory software to do otherwise, is probably a choice all the same. That is my first point, and it is not an isolated one. Companies have the power to not allow their rockets to hit the moon. Moreover, rocket bodies have hit the moon before, in 2022 and earlier still, and are always treated as curiosities rather than as pattern.The pattern is the second point, and it’s where I stop being generous. Look at what we have already done to low Earth orbit, the space closest to home. Tens of thousands of tracked fragments, and uncountable smaller ones, now circle the planet because for 60 years, operators launched first and asked about disposal never. Abandonment is not disposal, but those with power have chosen it to be so.Starlink alone accounts for more active satellites than the rest of the world’s operators combined, and its own operatorsreport rising near missesas the constellation grows. We built that congestion through a very specific kind of confidence (AKA hubris): the belief that space is big enough to absorb whatever we throw into it, forever, without a bill ever coming due.It’s the same hubris a mining company has about a river, or a fleet has about a fishery, right up until the fish are gone. We are simply exporting the same appetite further out, because the moon, unlike the ocean or the atmosphere, has no way to fight back. No air to burn up what we drop on it. No tide to wash away what we leave behind. Whatever debris we send there is, for all practical purposes, permanent. You’ll still find bags of astronaut poop on the lunar surface from the Apollo program.Which brings me to the third point, the one under all the others: why does this keep happening, when the physics has been understood for decades and the fixes are neither exotic nor expensive?The honest answer is entitlement. Not carelessness – entitlement. There is a difference between not knowing better and knowing better and doing it anyway because nobody will stop you.This is the same posture empires have always taken toward frontiers they didn’t build and don’t have to live inside the consequences of. Plant a flag, extract the value, leave the mess for whoever comes next, and call the mess someone else’s problem, or better yet, call it nobody’s problem, because there was never an owner to complain.That isn’t a metaphor. It’s a fairly literal description of how spacefaring nations and companies currently treat the moon, a place that legally belongs to no one and is treated, in practice, as though it belongs to whoever gets there first with a bigger engine. People love to own the profits without owning the consequences of them left in their wake.Let’s stop going into space. There’s nothing to see and no one to talk to | Zoe WilliamsRead moreTo be sure, I don’t think most of the engineers doing this work are villains, and I don’t think this particular impact was reckless in the way, say, a rocketexploding over the Caribbeanand scattering debris over a populated area would be (wink). This piece of debris hit an empty stretch of lunar terrain in daylight, and it genuinely did hand scientists a rare, useful dataset. Some operators are also trying to do better. Companies now design certain missions with deliberate deorbit plans, and there is real, if slow, movement toward international norms for orbital debris mitigation.I don’t want to pretend none of that exists. But good intentions from a minority don’t change the system’s default setting, and the default setting, according to recent evidence, is still: launch, abandon, hope nothing important gets hit. Isolated best practice is not governance. It is public relations for an industry that still has none.So no, nobody owns the moon. Under the 1967 OuterSpaceTreaty, no nation can claim it, and no company can either, whatever their marketing suggests about future colonies and mined regolith. But ownership was never really the problem. Nobody owned the lands where Native Americans thrived either. The problem is that we are acting out ownership’s oldest habits, extraction without accounting, expansion without consequence, on a body we all agreed, on paper, to hold in common.A crater near Einstein Crater is a small thing by itself. What it represents is not small at all.We have a narrow window left in which the moon still looks the way it has looked for billions of years, before the coming decade’s hundred-plus missions turn “who hit it this time” into a monthly headline instead of a rare one. We can spend that window building the tracking, the disposal rules and the accountability that stewardship actually requires. Or we can keep doing what we did on 5 August: witness something we built come out of the dark, watch it hit a place we don’t own as if we did, and call it a light show.Moriba Jah is a professor of aerospace engineering and engineering mechanics at the University of Texas at Austin and a MacArthur “Genius” fellowExplore more on these topicsSpaceOpinionSpaceXThe mooncommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s plan to sell off a part of Yosemite is what oligarchy looks like | Rebecca Solnit | The Guardian
description: Public lands belong to all of us. No one should plunder those lands for profit
Author: Rebecca Solnit
Headline: Public lands belong to all of us. No one should plunder those lands for profit
Content: ‘To give away a piece of land is one form of harm to the parks.’Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘To give away a piece of land is one form of harm to the parks.’Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesOpinionUS newsTrump’s plan to sell off a part of Yosemite is what oligarchy looks likeRebecca SolnitPublic lands belong to all of us. No one should plunder those lands for profitMon 31 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 13.37 EDTShareDo people still say a car was “sold for parts”? Because the US is being sold for parts or just handed over to the oligarchy. It’s a fire sale, a bankruptcy auction, it’s a planned dismantling of everything from its military to its institutions of higher education to its scientific research to its public lands.And while the threat to sell off part of Yosemite national park is about a quarter-mile parcel on the park’s edge, Yosemite is a crown jewel in the national park system and, arguably, the world’s first national park.To let any bit of it be sold off for the benefit of a corporation’s planned development on the park’s western border would compromise the inviolability of national parks and sacrifice public good for the sake of private profit. This is of course the ongoing agenda of theTrump administration.Public lands belong to all of us, a gift from the past because people worked hard to protect these forests, mountains, canyons, and a trust for the future, because the public should include everyone in this country alive now and everyone yet to come.The Trump administration’s ruthless efforts to turn over public lands for mining and logging and fossil fuel exploitation while it also dismantles the US Forest Service and National Park Service is about turning long-term wellbeing for the many, human and more than human, into short-term profit for an elite.These public lands have many kinds of value – the trees and grasslands are sequestering carbon as part of a natural climate amelioration, the mountains are watersheds, and most of these natural places now are key to rural tourism and outdoor recreation economies.White people first entered Yosemite valley in the early 1850s, on a military campaign to punish, displace, or exterminate the Indigenous people there who were interfering with another era’s environmental destruction: the Gold Rush, whose miners were hunting out the game, cutting down the trees, polluting the rivers, and massacring the region’s original inhabitants.Some of the early visitors recognized Yosemite’s extraordinary scenic beauty of its oak grasslands, high canyon walls, waterfalls. By the 1860s, photographers such as Carleton Watkins and Eadweard Muybridge had made images of Yosemite that were shown internationally. The place became iconic before many white people had visited it.In the spring of 1864, Abraham Lincoln signed into law a bill establishing that “Yosemite Valley’s premises shall be held for public use, resort, and recreation; shall be inalienable for all time.” It was originally managed by the state of California, since the federal government had little presence in the west and was busy fighting the civil war.Yellowstone national park, on the other hand, was set aside eight years later as a federally managed preserve because Wyoming and Montana were not yet states and is usually recognized as the first national park.The document Ulysses S Grant signed said the place was to be “reserved and withdrawn from settlement, occupancy, or sale under the laws of the United States, and dedicated and set apart as a public park or pleasuring-ground for the benefit and enjoyment of the people.”There was always a lie in the foundation of Yosemite, Yellowstone, Death Valley, the Grand Canyon and many other parks, in that they were Indigenous peoples’ ancestral homelands long before Columbus set sail or Lewis and Clark headed west.In Yosemite, those wrongs have been addressed over the past 30 years by changes in signage, representations of the place’s history, and opening to the traditional usage and ceremony of the original inhabitants’ descendants. The flawed premise of national parks matters, but so does the fact that the system kept these places from being privatized, developed and destroyed.But that is what is now happening to the park service as a whole: Trump has been funneling Park Service money meant to be spread across the country to his pet projects at the White House and in Washington DC including gilding statues and the incompetent $16mpaintingof the reflecting pool.Michael Schererreportsin the Atlantic that there’s a fast-track approval process for funding Trump projects out of park service funds, while the National Park Service as a whole is being starved. He notes there’s “a decrease of $854m, or 68%, in spending on projects in park regions outside the Washington area in the first eight and a half months of fiscal year 2026, compared with the full prior fiscal year. During that same period, spending around Washington increased by about $100 million.”The Trump administration proposes to further slash the number of park service employees, who had already been reduced by 24% in 2025.To give away a piece of land is one form of harm to the parks, to take away the park’s workers, whose labors protect endangered species, waterways and land, prevent fires and provide public services from search and rescue operations to education to clean restrooms is another.To open up the ancient sacred site of Chaco Canyon in New Mexico to fracking is yet another form of destruction by the Trump administration under way. The same is true of the 90% reduction of Bears Ears and Escalante in Utah.As the Associated Pressreportedearlier this month that this radical shrinkage undoes “protections established by his Democratic predecessors on public lands that are sacred among many Native Americans. Trump administration officials and congressional Republicans have sought to expand drilling, mining and logging on public lands, while removing protections for imperiled species and rolling back rules for conservation.”Yosemite was first established as protected land during one civil war. Another is under way about whether the federal government exists to serve the good of the many or the profiteering of the few. A small parcel in Yosemite is nevertheless a big indicator of who this country belongs to and whose rights and interests matter.Rebecca Solnit is a Guardian US columnist. She is the author of Orwell’s Roses and co-editor with Thelma Young Lutunatabua of the climate anthology Not Too Late: Changing the Climate Story from Despair to PossibilityExplore more on these topicsUS newsOpinionTrump administrationcommentShareReuse this content

title: OnlyFans and AI training: why gen Z doesn’t care where our money comes from | Alice Lassman | The Guardian
description: With traditional goals such as stability and home ownership feeling out of reach, young people are focused on the present
Author: Alice Lassman
Headline: With traditional goals such as stability and home ownership feeling out of reach, young people are focused on the present
Content: ‘Take away the feasibility of long-term goals and our willingness to wait for “the good life” collapses.’Photograph: Michael Simons/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Take away the feasibility of long-term goals and our willingness to wait for “the good life” collapses.’Photograph: Michael Simons/AlamyOpinionMoneyOnlyFans and AI training: why gen Z doesn’t care where our money comes fromAlice LassmanWith traditional goals such as stability and home ownership feeling out of reach, young people are focused on the presentMon 31 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 12.17 EDTShareBy now, we all know the shape of financial nihilism: the throw-your-money-at-anything reaction to the dissolution of the slow, linear path to wealth; theprediction markets,meme stocks,cryptocurrenciesandmicroluxuriesgrowing in its place. We’re left in an economic no man’s land. But financial nihilism only describes where we put our money. What about how we earn it in the first place?The modern economy has long relied on our need for stable employment – to pay the mortgage, to keep our kids fed, or, for some, to chase prestige and power – to generate the work ethic that keeps the wheel of production turning. None of this is going well for young people. Our jobs areinsecure, we can’t afford houses, we’re deferring having kids (if we have them at all), and only 6% of ussaya leadership position is our primary career goal. Hope is one of the economy’s most productive inputs,poweringour willingness to endure long hours. When the production function of income – the mechanism that turns hard work into a stable salary, then a mortgage, then a pension – breaks down, so does our relationship with the input. I call this production nihilism: my generation’s growing indifference to the kinds of work we’re willing to participate in, and where we’re willing to earn.We are witnessing the slow death of the prestige career | Alice LassmanRead more“Normal people are asleep. Good,” a young woman running her craft business at night-time tells the camera in Shopify’slatestcommercial. Partially thanks to all-in-one e-commerce platforms like Shopify, many of us have mastered the art of polyworking. These are jobs our high school career advisers could hardly have imagined – platforms such as Mercor, where white-collar workerstrain LLMsto do their job; “YouTube empires”; the much-covered millions being made byyoung womenon OnlyFans; non-sexualizedescorts. Some are supplementary, some are enough to eventually become a primary source of income. Americans seem to be coming around to the idea of “portfolio careers”, withmore than halfcalling them more desirable than traditional careers for a future workforce.Take away the feasibility of long-term goals and our willingness to wait for “the good life” collapses. So we redirect our motivation to grind and save into channels that pay out sooner – cash, yes, but also autonomy, flexibility or a sense of identity. Fifty-seven per cent of gen Zreporthaving a side hustle, well over double the boomer rate. Day jobs start to function as financial anchors, paying the rent while our side gigs do the identity work. After all, “writer” plays far better on a Hinge profile than “analyst”.With no solid formula for our futures, more of us are experimenting with what it means to interact with the economy at all. The cultural counterpart to this economic logic is a series of attitude shifts to work, nervously cataloged as trends: thegen Z stare, orfaked productivity. I recently wrote about theslow death of the prestige career, where – thanks to AI – companies no longer require a robust team of entry-level workers to scale.We’re living through a transition in our economic relationship with the future. The cultural theorist Lauren Berlant described how an “anticipatory present” kept people bound to an economic system: enduring the short term in the hope for a promised version of the long term. Profoundly unable to imagine – let alone attain – a prosperous future, young people may be among the first generations to name this for what it is:foreclosed. When the promise of a future stops working, we “maxx” for the present, extracting value as quickly as possible with whatever assets late-stage capitalism permits us to spend. It’s the other side of the “little treat” economy.Boomers v millennials: how have different generations reacted to falling house prices? | Fiona KatauskasRead moreNeoliberalism, the system that raised us, offers a convenient way forward: everything can be commodified if we try hard enough. When western society was first learning this lesson, France’s artists gave voice to the unease of their postwar consumer boom. The film-maker Jean-Luc Godard’s Two or Three Things I Know About Her follows Juliette, a Paris housewife, as she prostitutes herself to keep up with the lifestyle being aggressively marketed to her. She decides to sell her afternoons, her time, her body. It’s a precursor, in many ways, to the gig economy of platform capitalism: Juliette optimizes any assets at her disposal to enjoy the present moment.The New Wave tried to warn us against the relentless tide of commodification. But where Godard and his contemporaries channelled their anxiety through women as objects, gen Z reclaims Juliette’s image – not as a helpless, bored object, but as subject. We are agents of our own relationship with the economy. Less despairing, less passive, less accepting: gen Z’s nihilism feels distinctly active. Production nihilism leans into a new definition of work, forcibly detaching us from the neoliberal “good life” fantasy that’s clearlystopped delivering. Nietzsche described nihilism of this kind as a process of clearing away dead values. Which is what production nihilism does: it detaches us from the neoliberal “good life” fantasy that’s clearlystopped delivering. Refusing to accept the current economic system as the endpoint of our search for meaning, we improvise a new set of values as we go.But is there real agency here? There’s an idea circulating in Silicon Valley: that “high-agency” individuals – those who think for themselves and act without being told – will be the ones to survive the comingAI disruption. This isn’t really agency. It’s the anticipatory bind Berlant warned us about, another story about how to succeed in an economy where fewer of us will realistically be able to. No wonder we’ve stopped caring about where our income comes from, when its source no longer determines where we end up.Alice Lassman is an economist who writes The Intimacy Economy, a Substack and forthcoming book on the economics of connection, care and relationshipsExplore more on these topicsMoneyOpinionUS economyEconomicsUS personal financeGenerational inequalityAI (artificial intelligence)US work & careerscommentShareReuse this content

title: The Nepal floods seem a world away – but make no mistake, climate breakdown will affect us all | Nesrine Malik | The Guardian
description: Richer countries might have more resources to deal with catastrophe, but this problem grips the entire planet, however much leaders may want to deny it, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
Author: Nesrine Malik
Headline: Richer countries might have more resources to deal with catastrophe, but this problem grips the entire planet, however much leaders may want to deny it, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
Content: Aftermath of flash floods in Nepal's Nuwakot district, 29 August 2026.Photograph: Prabin Ranabhat/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAftermath of flash floods in Nepal's Nuwakot district, 29 August 2026.Photograph: Prabin Ranabhat/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionNepal-Tibet flood disasterThe Nepal floods seem a world away – but make no mistake, climate breakdown will affect us allNesrine MalikRicher countries might have more resources to deal with catastrophe, but this problem grips the entire planet, however much leaders may want to deny itMon 31 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 07.48 EDTShareClimate breakdown is happening on one Earth, but two different worlds. In one, its impacts increasingly encroach on everyday life; longer periods of discomfort and shorter periods of sharp pain. Endless, hotter summers, and within them sudden wildfires, evacuations, homes burned to cinders in a matter of hours. In another, catastrophe. This summer has been a snapshot of that split-screen. The hottest day on record in parts of Europe, and a wave of water, mud and ice inNepalthat so far has claimed more than 750 lives. Thousands of people are still missing.The difference is also one of resources. The climate crisis has an economic cost, but some places can absorb it better than others. Responses to this summer of wildfires in Europe included a rapid scrambling by the French government to provide everything fromtax breaksfor businesses affected by the fires to relocation costs andaid to rebuild homes. The UK government haddeployed almost £100mbefore the summer to strengthen wildfire resilience.Entire industries exist to absorb the impact, undergirded by sophisticated technology, disposable income and evolved sectors. Wildfire insurance in the US is beingpowered by AI, which spits out numbers to estimate risk based on location and construction material. Outside North America and Europe, there is little of that buffer. The result is asymmetry. While developed countries will still be stressed as events triggered by climate breakdown become more regular and chronic, and they are still not immune toglobalised outcomes– rising food costs,droughts, water shortages – what they experience and how disruptive that will be are far removed from other parts of the world.The difference in scale and resources is colossal. What is needed to rebuild Nepal’s flood damage may constituteup to a 10thof its entire economy – something like $5bn, and that’s not even factoring in all the technical foreign assistance, equipment, expertise and labour required. Also colossal is the difference in exposure to the obliterative effects of events.Take the death of coral reefs, and how that disproportionately affectscoastal populations. Across the Caribbean, coral bleaching caused by rising ocean acidification and temperatures not only dramatically reduces marine life, which is a source of food and income for entire populations –90% of Jamaica’s economic incomeis generated alongside its coasts – but also increases the scale and intensity of storms. Coral reefs are a sort of natural storm barrier, absorbing the force of sea waves and buffering coastal areas from flooding. The intersection between these geographical and economic features means countries in the Caribbean are being pummelled on the weather front (climate breakdown also increases the power of hurricanes through warming ocean water), as well as having their incomes drastically reduced and therefore their ability to bounce back.Then there is the heat. Temperatures are not just jumping far above the average in Europe but also in warmer areas where the base temperatures are already high. Last week, aHarper’s Index summaryof estimated heat-related mortality in India showed some staggering numbers: 3,400 excess deaths “caused by a single day of extreme heat”; 30,000 deaths “caused by five consecutive days of extreme heat”. In April of this year,all 50 of the world’s hottest cities were in a single country, India, something which according to the air-quality monitoring platform AQI “has no modern precedent across global weather data”.2:04‘I have lost everything’: survivors reflect after deadly flood in Nepal – videoThis is another double whammy for poorcommunitieswithout access to shelter or cooling systems of unlimited fresh water. These are the so-calledclimate breakdown hotspots, identified as “areas where strong physical and ecological effects of climate change come together with large numbers of vulnerable and poor people and communities”. Few places on Earth demonstrate this category more vividly than Sudan. A country already in the grip of war and food insecurity is nowsuccumbingto the delayed rains caused by the El Niño climate pattern, cracking the dry earth and draining the Nile. The risk of famine stalks populations that are already acutely hungry.And what is felt asymmetrically has been caused in that way too. These poorer, more vulnerable countries are paying the price for the emissions caused by wealthy countries, and not even being extended thefull, remedial supportfrom the coffers of those nations that accumulated the wealth generated by industries that contributed to climate breakdown and global heating. We are not just battling complacency, or indifference to the importance of climate justice, but a political climate that has in recent years, led by Donald Trump’s second term, seen its own collapse.Look closer and the problem isn’t only historical failure but a casual disregard, an adventurism that launches wars and stresses economies with buffers already damaged by the climate crisis. The Iran war in combination with El Niño is a weather and politics collaboration that has hiked fertiliser costs on the one hand and choked rain on the other. More broadly, what was a generously named albeit tenuously implemented “rules-based order”, which at least had some bedrock of global cooperation and aid, has been cancelled altogether. Trump’s withdrawal from the Paris agreement set the tone, while the dismantling of USAID cut the funds that divertedbillions of dollarsfrom the rich to the developing world to help with the fallout of extreme weather and reduce greenhouse gas emissions.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNepal-Tibet flood: this is the cost of not acting in the face of the climate crisis | Sunil AcharyaRead moreHere is another cascade. As the US withdraws from its commitments, sending the signal that there are no rules or duties, and indeed no problem with climate breakdown at all, pressure will rise on other countries to contribute more. They will need to figure out a way to hold together a coordinated response in the shadow of a destabilising hegemon, as well as try to foster that sense of social obligation in a time of political sociopathy.The foolish shortsightedness of it all is that even though there is a large gap between experiences, and so a sense that glaciers and floods and famines are happening all the way over there, their knock-on effects and food supply challenges, and political and refugee crises, will affect us all. Things will get dramatically worse for the hotspots, but there is still no outrunning it all in the long term. It seems that at precisely the moment when this realisation should yoke us together in all the ways life is rapidly changing, we are all being untethered. But ultimately, whatever different spheres we inhabit, we are all still trapped on the same planet.Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterOpinionNepalClimate crisisIndiaSudanCaribbeanDonald TrumpcommentShareReuse this content

title: The datacentre power spat highlights a hidden truth: we’re not building renewables fast enough to meet our needs | Alison Reeve | The Guardian
description: A battle over datacentre power sources is only part of the picture. Australia needs a much bigger electricity system to meet all future demand
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A battle over datacentre power sources is only part of the picture. Australia needs a much bigger electricity system to meet all future demand
Content: ‘If we restricted electricity emissions, the coal and gas v renewables part of the datacentre debate could be avoided … Focus would be on the impact of datacentres on power prices and the reliability of supply.’Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘If we restricted electricity emissions, the coal and gas v renewables part of the datacentre debate could be avoided … Focus would be on the impact of datacentres on power prices and the reliability of supply.’Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesOpinionDatacentres - AustraliaThe datacentre power spat highlights a hidden truth: we’re not building renewables fast enough to meet our needsAlison ReeveA battle over datacentre power sources is only part of the picture. Australia needs a much bigger electricity system to meet all future demandMon 31 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 20.31 EDTShareAnthony Albanese has been clear that he wants a set of national standards to ensure datacentre growth accelerates Australia’s push to renewables and keeps a lid on power prices. At the centre of his desired policies was a “BYO power” requirement – a condition that all new datacentres would be powered by 100% renewable electricity.But last week these aims collided with the Queensland and Northern Territory governments’ desire torely on their state-owned gas and coal power stationsto power datacentres.As a result, we got a national cabinet communique that was carefully worded to allow every first minister to claim a win, but little clarity about what rules would apply.On Friday, the energy minister, Chris Bowen, reiterated the federal government’s intent to legislate binding national standards for datacentres across the country which will require them to use 100% renewables, backed by firming – which can be gas.The potential for a carve-out is still there, with Bowen saying the federal government would consider concessions –but only if state-owned generation can provide a cheaper power mix.What will we get out of the AI boom? The data suggests lots of noisy, energy-hungry datacentres and not much elseRead moreAt first glance, this looks unlikely. Electricity costs are about 10% of total expenditure for a datacentre.Gasis the most expensive form of generation, and new coal is more expensive than new renewables. Even existing coal gets undercut by cheap solar for much of the day. Existing centres are already choosing to run on about 70% renewable electricity, through a power purchase agreement with a wind or solar farm, because they want to keep their costs down.Using gas and coal power (as Queensland and the NT are pushing for) would probablyincreaseelectricity costs for datacentres. It would also probably delay their development, because the waitlist to receive new gas turbines is years-long.In any case, the energy source for potential new datacentres is only one part of the picture.Most datacentres need to be close to population centres to allow customers to send and receive data instantaneously. This is why the vast bulk of existing datacentres in Australia, and 85% of the proposed ones, are located in Sydney and Melbourne.If a fossil-fuel driven datacentre boom hasn’t happened in Australia’s north already, it’s not likely to in the future, unless the population shifts markedly and datacentres develop a taste for expensive electricity.This doesn’t mean NSW and Victoria can take future datacentre development for granted. If new wind and solar farms can’t be built as fast as new datacentres, this will act as a brake on growth. For the federal legislation to have an impact, all three governments need to double down on making it easier to finance and build new renewables.The spat over datacentre guidelines exposes more than just federal and state differences. It highlights the two biggest problems in the energy sector: there are no restrictions on electricity emissions, and we’re not building fast enough to meetallsources of new demand, not just datacentres.Anthony Albanese says he wants to do AI ‘the Australian way’ – videoApart from the two years whereAustralia had a carbon price, electricity generators have never been forced to reduce their emissions. Instead, governments have focused on pushing more renewables into the electricity mix. Provided they could push these in faster than demand was growing, emissions went down, as coal generators were undercut and lost market share.We are now bumping up against the limits of this approach.If we restricted electricity emissions, the coal and gas v renewables part of the datacentre debate could be avoided. The “BYO power” push could be technology-neutral because the restrictions would have taken care of the emissions impact. Focus would be on the impact of datacentres on power prices and the reliability of supply.Datacentres make up just 17% of future power demand growth. The rest is from increased take-up of electric vehicles, households and businesses converting to electricity and population growth.Even if datacentres went elsewhere, we would still be facing the problem that we’re not building enoughelectricity infrastructure fast enough to meet our needs. This includes new renewables, but also the transmission lines to connect them to demand centres, the batteries and storage to keep the system reliable and the back-up generation to ride through the few days of the year when renewables alone can’t support the whole system.The future Australia economy should run on electricity: it’s cheaper, cleaner, and more efficient. Meeting all these needs will require a much bigger electricity system. Datacentres are the first test of how well we meet this challenge.If we start constraining electricity emissions, and make it easier to build electricity infrastructure, we’ll give ourselves the best chance of doing so.Alison Reeve is the energy and climate change program director at the Grattan InstituteExplore more on these topicsDatacentres - AustraliaOpinionRenewable energyAustralian politicsEnergyFossil fuelsGasCoalcommentShareReuse this content

title: The law won’t save us from Meta’s ‘pervert glasses’. The only solution is mockery | Jonathan Liew | The Guardian
description: These things are undermining not just our public spaces but the very nature of being human. Let’s shame them off the streets, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Liew
Author: Jonathan Liew
Headline: These things are undermining not just our public spaces but the very nature of being human. Let’s shame them off the streets, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Liew
Content: Mark Zuckerberg presents Meta’s smart glasses at a company event in Menlo Park, California, on 17 September 2025.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersView image in fullscreenMark Zuckerberg presents Meta’s smart glasses at a company event in Menlo Park, California, on 17 September 2025.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersOpinionWearable technologyThe law won’t save us from Meta’s ‘pervert glasses’. The only solution is mockeryJonathan LiewThese things are undermining not just our public spaces but the very nature of being human. Let’s shame them off the streetsMon 31 Aug 2026 10.56 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 13.33 EDTShareSo far I am yet to be tempted into purchasing a pair of Ray-BanMetaglasses. To a certain extent this is a function of possessing a large, misshapen and comically convex head upon which no pair of sunglasses has ever looked remotely appropriate. Nor am I one of those consumers who professes to be “really into gadgets”, a preference I’ve always found weirdly unspecific. It’s subtly telling when people claim to be into “gadgets”, because they’re never talking about, say, a tin opener. What they really mean is something gimmicky and expensive that almost certainly requires the services of a datacentre and enough water to irrigate Kent.And even if I were to surmount these two obstacles, you then get into the ethics of the thing. I’m nobody’s idea of a PR expert, but if your shiny new product keeps requiringpatches and updatesto prevent people from using it todo degenerate thingsto women, perhaps it might be worth walking it back to the research and development stage.Of course, Meta has no intention of doing anything quite so dignified or responsible as that. The prospect that users of its new glasses might wish to film people covertly and without consent appears not to have occurred to one of the world’s leading tech companies. Nor the possibility that owners might try todisable or cover up the little LEDthat displays when the camera is recording. Instead, the company has embarked ona publicity blitz, reassuring us all that our privacy is, if not quite their number one priority, then certainly there or thereabouts.But unlike most items of consumer tech, smart glasses are not the sort of thing to which one can simply opt in or out. These things arealready out there– around nine million from Meta alone – scanning our streets, capturing and processing content, blurring the boundaries between the real and the virtual.Unlike security cameras, they are not fixed but mobile, arbitrary and largely unregulated. They raise issues that go far deeper than a piece of overpriced eyewear, deeper even than the dense thicket of technology and regulation, into the most basic questions of how we treat each other, how societies function. Specifically: what happens to our shared public spaces when we are forced to confront the presumption that we are all being filmed, broadcast, processed? What happens to our cities? What happens to our trust, our bonds, our relationships with our fellow humans?Much of the current concern over smart glasses has understandably focused on the lurid and the macabre: the creeps and the perverts, the changing room voyeurs, the internetprankstersandschool bullies. But while any new technology will attract its share of malign actors, nefarious intent is not in fact a prerequisite to harm.Simply put, the very act of filming somebody without their permission – for whatever purpose – is in itself a form of violation, perhaps even of theft. On a philosophical level, it is the blithe assertion of one person’s liberty and rights over those of another. On a political level, it expresses an asymmetry of power, a very capitalistic form of resource extraction. It strips the unsuspecting individual of agency and mines them for content.And yes, we have long been bleakly aware of the surveillance apparatus around us: traffic cameras, security cameras, personalised ads, some bored ladat GCHQwith a list of keywords and access to the emails of everybody you know. ButKylie Jennerisn’t posing suggestively on the A46 trying to sell you a speed camera. Wearables, by their very nature, straddle the realms of fashion and culture, and are thus the perfect vehicle for reimagining the public panopticon, the AI training zoo, as a kind of chic lifestyle choice.For the same reason, legislative fixes – inevitably reactive rather than proactive – only get us so far. Denmark recently introduced an innovative copyright lawgranting citizens ownership of their own likeness, which mostly covers deepfakes and AI-generated imitations. But who realistically has the time and will to trawl the entire internet for illicitly procured content? In any case, by the time it’s up, it’s up, and by a similar logic the tech giants have long operated under a praxis of launching first and dealing with the fallout later.Which is why social stigma remains one of the most powerful weapons. The increasingly pervasive deployment of the term “pervert glasses” is a decent start, but other perfectly good slurs remain unclaimed: Stalker Specs, Nonce Goggles, Depraviators. Above all the ridicule must be merciless and unstinting, a ritual shaming entirely in proportion to the magnitude of deviance.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut of course, even if society succeeds in killing the Meta glasses, others will surely learn and follow. Samsung and Google are launching their own glasseslater this year. Apple’s effort will probably emergesometime in 2027. And perhaps the thing few have considered is who – with the exception of the partially sighted, hard of hearing and those otherwise in need of assistive technology – asked for any of this? If smart glasses are the answer, what was the question? Perhaps, as with AI chatbots and fridges with web browsers, there was none: just the lavishly funded persistence of a tech sector intent on manufacturing consent for the things it has decided we must have.In so doing, it may succeed in turning the high street into an unwitting hub of surveillance. A society fearful of itself, paranoid and mistrustful. A public sphere exposed and disassembled and reduced to its constituent pixels. Where there is no longer a right to be anonymous, to be inattentive, to be forgotten or left alone by our fellow citizens. Where something as simple and innocent as a human gaze has been reimagined as an item of transaction.Jonathan Liew is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsWearable technologyOpinionMetaSurveillancePrivacyPrivacy & the mediacommentShareReuse this content

title: Defence spending is an insatiable beast. John Healey is right to tame it | John McTernan | The Guardian
description: The MoD grossly overspends then claims poverty. It’s high time it was treated as just one part of a progressive government, says John McTernan, former special adviser to the Ministry of Defence
Author: John McTernan
Headline: The MoD grossly overspends then claims poverty. It’s high time it was treated as just one part of a progressive government, says John McTernan, former special adviser to the Ministry of Defence
Content: Chancellor John Healey during Andy Burnham’s first Cabinet meeting in Downing Street, 21 July 2026.Photograph: Eddie Mulholland/Daily Telegraph/PAView image in fullscreenChancellor John Healey during Andy Burnham’s first Cabinet meeting in Downing Street, 21 July 2026.Photograph: Eddie Mulholland/Daily Telegraph/PAOpinionLabourDefence spending is an insatiable beast. John Healey is right to tame itJohn McTernanThe MoD grossly overspends then claims poverty. It’s high time it was treated as just one part of a progressive governmentMon 31 Aug 2026 08.10 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 10.21 EDTShareNowhere was the confidence of the prime minister, Andy Burnham, shown as clearly as in his appointment of chancellor. There wereweeks of speculationthat this appointment was a choice between the energy secretary, Ed Miliband, and the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, with their contrasting political economies.It has been a hallmark of Burnham’s politics that he and his team do not get involved in briefing wars, so it was only when former defence secretary John Healey appeared in Downing Street together with Mahmood that it was clear that the prime minister had cut the Gordian knot,reassuring the marketswith a cool, calm political operator with extensive Treasury experience as chancellor. Healey’s two years in defence meant that he would know both sides of the argument when it came to one of the biggest questions of the forthcoming budget: how to meet the bold new Natodefence spending targetswithout derailing the social ambitions of the Burnham government.Just last week, it was revealed that the question of getting the right balance of the competing demands of defence, social care, council housing and devolution would be deferred to a spending review next year, and thatthis October’s budgetwould be a low-key, continuity affair. That’s a good thing, because the facts about the Ministry of Defence are stark – the stridency of its claims of underfunding are only matched by its record of overspending. TheNational Audit Officehas a series of reports detailing the failures of the MoD’s control of spending.When I was a special adviser in the MoD during the Gordon Brown government, there was a saying that if you wanted to know what was going on in procurement you just needed to speak to BAE Systems. It was a sardonic acknowledgment of the extent of producer capture by the UK defence industries. Now, there are more elevated phrases like “sovereign capability” or references to seemingly objective measures like percentages of GDP – “3% by the next parliament and 3.5% by 2035”. But they all mean the same thing: like the Cyclops in The Odyssey, the military industrial complex is hungry.This is one of the strongest arguments for the appointment of Wes Streeting as defence secretary. He has, it seems, tamed the NHS appetite for overspending. TheInstitute for Fiscal Studiesreported last week that “last year the NHS saw no spending top up for frontline services from the Treasury reserve or capital budgets for the first time since 2013-14”.Of course, geopolitics looms over the defence spending question. The godfather – in all meanings – of the Hague investment plan, which committed the US’s Nato allies tohigher defence spending, was President Trump, despite his repeated threats to the territorial integrity of members of that alliance. Keir Starmer decided that a mixture of flattery in the form of asecond royal visit, and subservience – embarrassedly picking up the president’s dropped papers – was the right formula. The problem is that going along with a bully just reinforces their behaviour.The more appropriate political response is being modelled by Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney. He sketched out a new emerging world order in a speech at Davos in January, and most Canadianssupport his stancesince his resoluteresponse to US trade talksand Trump’s attempted “renaming” of Lake Ontario. This led Carney to float the possibility of adeepening partnershipbetween Canada and the European Union – an arrangement that could set a precedent for the UK to realign with the EU without rerunning the entire Brexit debate.Political entrepreneurship on that level is already being demonstrated by Miliband, now foreign secretary, who has chosen to take the UK seat on the World Bank rather than delegating it to a junior minister. That shows an intent to shape rather than respond to the emerging international situation, and should give space for the prime minister to deal with a pressing domestic agenda.The question that is rarely addressed in the defence debate is what kind of country we are fighting for. With his mantra of “growth in every postcode”, fixing social care, devolving power and building council houses, Burnham has laid out his programme. Simply setting out his stall has greatly increased Labour’s support. Now he has to build that better Britain – a socially democratic one in which defence spending is taken seriously but doesn’t prevent other societal needs from being fulfilled.Of course, in politics, one of the huge advantages of having a positive vision of what you are for is that you can go negative on your opponents. Here, defence can be a huge wedge for Burnham. On the right, both the Conservative party and Reform UK were so eager to support Trump that they wanted the UK to commit to the quagmire of the Iran war. They should never be allowed to forget that they put US interests above the UK’s. On the centre-left the attack lines are easy, too. The SNP wants to be a member of an imaginary non-nuclear Nato and never address the challenge ofRussian infractionsinto Scottish waters and airspace. Likewise, the Greens are split on whether to be in Nato and have no idea of why the UK should have defence forces.All in all, defence is returning to the right space in UK politics. Neither an unfeasible demand on resources, nor a neglected backwater, but a positive tool for a progressive government.John McTernan was political secretary to PM Tony Blair and is now a political strategist for Burson GlobalExplore more on these topicsLabourOpinionJohn HealeyAndy BurnhamDefence policycommentShareReuse this content

title: More and more undergrads are living at home. That’s a crying shame – here’s why  | Rohan Sathyamoorthy | The Guardian
description: Spiralling rental costs have made living with parents the only option for some students. That fails to prepare them for the realities of adult life, says writer Rohan Sathyamoorthy
Author: Rohan Sathyamoorthy
Headline: Spiralling rental costs have made living with parents the only option for some students. That fails to prepare them for the realities of adult life, says writer Rohan Sathyamoorthy
Content: ‘Ucas data shows a marked rise in the number of students planning to live at home with their parents.’Photograph: redsnapper/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Ucas data shows a marked rise in the number of students planning to live at home with their parents.’Photograph: redsnapper/AlamyOpinionStudent housingMore and more undergrads are living at home. That’s a crying shame – here’s whyRohan SathyamoorthySpiralling rental costs have made living with parents the only option for some students. That fails to prepare them for the realities of adult lifeMon 31 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 06.05 EDTShareIf the headlines are to be believed, no one should want to be a student in England any more. And yet this September and October, a record number of school leavers will begin their journey at university, unwilling to let rising costs, a regressive loan system and dimming graduate job prospects blot out the promise of the best years of their lives. The burden now placed on today’s students has grown so heavy, though, that it is reshaping people’s experience of higher education: new data from the university admissions service Ucas shows a marked rise in the number of students planning tolive at home with their parents, rather than moving away to study.It’s first worth stressing that this new arrangement is not, for the most part, a voluntary one. That’s clear in the gap between those “choosing” to stay at home and those who have no choice at all: among students from England’s poorest neighbourhoods,more than halfnow expect to live at home while studying, compared with just under a fifth from the least-deprived areas.The student rental market is the main culprit – it is now forcing many teenagers to fork out more than £10,000 a year just for basic accommodation, even in cities outside London. Since the liberalisation of housing regulations in the 1980s (alongside an influx of wealthy international students), private landlords have been given free rein to jack up prices while housing standards worsen, with damp, rat-infested accommodation now becoming a normalised part of thestudent experience. A recent study by the National Union of Students found that an appalling84% of students reported significant issues with their housing, with almost half living with mould, despite the extortionate costs many are now paying. It’s no surprise, then, that many of my peers feel they have no option but to stay at home.This may seem like an easy solution, but it, too, comes with its personal costs. A lack of personal space as well as family conflict can mean worsening mental health for some students who stay at home. Many will also inevitably miss out on the life skills a person only learns when living independently. Then there’s also the very real risk of being excluded from the cultural and social highs of university life – the joys that make it worth persevering through gruelling deadlines and exam schedules. That trade-off is evident in those around me who have already made the reluctant retreat to study from home: all have struggled with isolation, and some have dropped out of university entirely. With graduate prospects collapsing, it’s the lifelong friendships built on campuses and in student accommodation that count more than ever in the university experience. Take that away and replace it with an hour-long commute from your childhood bedroom, and you begin to wonder if any part of getting a degree is really worth it.Meanwhile, students on difficult terms with their parents are left in an impossible position, forced to cough up eye-watering sums simply to maintain a healthy distance from them. In this respect, particularly for those who have experienced restrictive upbringings, the freedom to explore adult life at university remains an invaluable part of discovering our real selves. Crippling costs therefore make what should be the most liberating chapter of our lives so far instead feel like trading one set of restrictions for another.It has always been fashionable for older generations to bemoan the laziness of “today’s youth”. Yet how can anyone expect a generation to properly grow up while being denied the hallmarks of adult life? Stuck under a parent’s roof at university, and denied the economic mobility that comes with a graduate job once they leave, my generation is being condemned to live out its own twisted Peter Pan fairytale.Luckily, it’s not all doom and despair. The recent Renters’ Rights Act has provided much neededbreathing room for students, shifting the needle back in favour of tenants over Britain’s landlords for the first time in decades. Certainly, the ability to cut our tenancy short has been a gamechanger over the summer; previously, we had to keep paying rent for rooms we couldn’t stay in. But students will need more than just tweaks to their current arrangements; we need rent controls, a shift out of the private rental market, and investment into affordable, purpose-built complexes designed for university life.There is one silver lining to all this: earlier this year the UK’s biggest student landlord warned thatprofits could slidebecause of lower room occupancy, which could be exacerbatedas students choose to study from home, so the tower of cards is looking awfully close to coming crashing down. Perhaps if this model has finally run out of road, then students’ housing needs can finally be released from thegrip of profiteers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRohan Sathyamoorthy is a writer from south-west LondonExplore more on these topicsStudent housingOpinionStudent experienceStudentsRenting propertyHousingStudent financeHigher educationcommentShareReuse this content

title: The hill I will die on: No self-respecting adult should use the term ‘picky bits’ | Laura Snapes | The Guardian
description: It’s the Boaty McBoatface of dinner time. Britons, resist the supermarkets’ cutesy branding and have some dignity, says the Guardian’s deputy music editor, Laura Snapes
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: It’s the Boaty McBoatface of dinner time. Britons, resist the supermarkets’ cutesy branding and have some dignity, says the Guardian’s deputy music editor, Laura Snapes
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThe hill I will die onSupermarketsThe hill I will die on: No self-respecting adult should use the term ‘picky bits’Laura SnapesIt’s the Boaty McBoatface of dinner time. Britons, resist the supermarkets’ cutesy branding and have some dignityMon 31 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 10.22 EDTShareIt’s a bittersweet time of year. The season of tiny shorts is giving way to wondering whether the trousers you last wore in May still fit. I’ve already seen Christmas tat in The Works; only Sainsbury’s winter-spiced bleach is the greater festive harbinger of mortality. At least we’ve hopefully seen the end of the heatwaves. And, with it, the scourge of the phrase “picky bits”.For the blissfully uninitiated, picky bits is apparently the new national name for spending £8 on three trays of pastry-wrapped “exotic” confections in a tragic facsimile of the delicious, high-quality deli items our European neighbours enjoy every day of their goddamn lives. Every summer, the ranges get more off their nuts: who knew your picnic needed Turkish grilled pepperoncini and dressed salsa verde chickpeas? (It doesn’t.)Before brands such as M&S, Waitrose and the Co-op leapt on the cutesy phrase as a way of bankrupting you for sticks of cheese wrapped in ham (and loads of plastic), picky bits had more innocent origins as one of the many terms that Britons use for slapping tomatoes, coleslaw and crisps on the table and letting everyone choose their own dinner.Its potentially infinite variety demands almost as many names. Back when Twitter was fun, discussions of regional – or just family – difference like this knocked hours off British productivity levels. You call it a picky tea? Table dinner? Lovely. My friend’s mum calls it, quite wonderfully, “a cold collation”. Mine calls it “salad”, despite the sad bistro leaves (served in bag, obviously) being the last thing anyone wants, compared to the salami and dips. Salad cream, however, is crucial. I love linguistic quirks such as this. You call a roll a breadcake, a barm, a cob? Delightful!That is, until brands get on board. Suddenly, endearing domestic chatter becomes mortifying when shouted from a 4ft-tall poster at the train station. Removed from the context of the family’s novelty salt and pepper shakers and a sibling squabble over the last sausage roll, picky bits feels – as the New York Times once wrote in acanonical 1994 report about Mr Blobby– like “a metaphor for a nation gone soft in the head”.Every time I see the phrase in public life it makes me want to do civil disobedience. It’s the Boaty McBoatface of dinner time, exposing our once-repressed nation’s surprisingly twee core and total disregard for shame. Sure, my own personal lexicon is full of embarrassing nonsense, but you’re never going to see [REDACTED] on a billboard overhanging the A4.Also, most of these supermarket picky bits taste incredibly underwhelming. Have some self-respect and tear a rotisserie chicken apart with your bare hands next time you go to the park.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLaura Snapes is the Guardian’s deputy music editorExplore more on these topicsSupermarketsThe hill I will die onFood & drink industryFoodRetail industrycommentShareReuse this content

title: I’m giving birth as a battle rages over maternity care in Ireland. We shouldn’t have to pay to feel safe | Caelainn Hogan | The Guardian
description: An unfair two-tier system is, at last, giving way to universal state care. But private interests and highly paid doctors are resisting, says journalist Caelainn Hogan
Author: Caelainn Hogan
Headline: An unfair two-tier system is, at last, giving way to universal state care. But private interests and highly paid doctors are resisting, says journalist Caelainn Hogan
Content: Ireland has a worryingly low obstetrician-to-patient ratio.Photograph: Halfpoint Images/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIreland has a worryingly low obstetrician-to-patient ratio.Photograph: Halfpoint Images/Getty ImagesOpinionIrelandI’m giving birth as a battle rages over maternity care in Ireland. We shouldn’t have to pay to feel safeCaelainn HoganAn unfair two-tier system is, at last, giving way to universal state care. But private interests and highly paid doctors are resistingMon 31 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 11.07 EDTShareThere were no chandeliers in the public ward where I spent my first days as a mother, at the oldest continuously operating maternity hospital in the world. The room echoed with cries, the well-worn floor bouncing under footsteps, the windows looking out on Dublin’s city centre.Now the Rotunda hospital, where I’m due to give birth again soon, is counting down to its 1 millionth baby. It is also at the centre of a bitter debate over plans to reform Ireland’s two-tier state healthcare system, so that those who pay to “go private” in public hospitals no longer gain an unfair advantage over those who don’t.A chandelier is the background for the Rotunda Private’ssoft-lit webpage, which lists fees of up to €4,500 to be treated privately in this public hospital. Maternal healthcare in Ireland is provided free by the state, and there are no stand-alone private maternity hospitals in the country. But in the public hospital system,patients who can afford it can payto access continuity of care with a private consultant, private scans and the right to request a private room after birth.Ireland is anoutlier in Europeby not providing free universal primary healthcare. But at least in public hospitals, its two-tier arrangements could finally be ending. Aradical overhaulof the state healthcare system seeks to ensure equal access for every citizen. The “Sláintecare” plan was launched nearly 10 years ago with cross-party support and aims to deliverequal access to health servicesbased on individual patient need, not on ability to pay. But it has still not been fully implemented.Under the reform, hospital consultants on new public-only contracts are barred from carrying out private work in public hospitals. More than 60% of consultants have signed up to the new contracts in exchange forpay that can exceed€300,000(with on-call duties and overtime). With no private maternity hospitals, giving birth is finally set to be made entirely public.But a backlash has exposed both a worryingly low obstetrician-to-patient ratio, and the resistance of these highly paid senior doctors to a fairer, single-tier health system. Ireland has fewer hospital consultants than most countries in the EU, with many medicalgraduates emigrating. Thelowest uptakefor the new public-only contracts is in obstetrics and gynaecology, at just over half.The extent of private activity in Ireland’s public healthcare system and the fight for a single-tier system puts us at the centre of aEurope-wide debateover separating the two.The government recentlyprevailed in a long-running standoffwith the Rotunda’s management by threatening to cut funding. This followed the revelation that, despite the ban, consultants on public-only contracts were stilltreating private patientsin this public hospital, using public resources, whilebilling insurers for hundreds of thousandsof euros of care, with the Rotunda’s board’s permission.Allegations thatprivate consultants gave financial gifts as high as €1,500to public-only colleagues to deliver their private patients’ babies on weekends fuelled the controversy.Senior figures at the Rotunda have argued thatwomen should be able to choosebetween public and private. But if there is a shortage of consultants, surely all their time needs to go to higher-risk pregnancies whether the mothers can pay or not?A Rotunda staff member who sees public and private patients assured me that births take place in the same delivery rooms, and that patients are meant to be seen according to need. “The sickest women often get the best care,” she said.She suggested the dispute was less about maternal “choice” than about a revenue stream that hospitals don’t want to give up. A fully public system was “the only way to have truly equitable care”, she said.Beyond maternity, there are wider concerns about unfair use of public hospital resources for private healthcare. Despite Ireland being a wealthy country withhigh spending on health, public hospital corridors are often lined with patients on trolleys, sometimes waiting days for a bed, while children spend years in agony on lists for spinal consults.Nearly half the Irish populationrelies on private health insurance, as in many cases this means they can skip the long waiting lists in public hospitals. I have basic health insurance, but I went fully public for maternity care during my first pregnancy, paying for prenatal testing, which I feel should be free.As a public patient without complications, I was cared for by midwives at the Rotunda.Ireland has low maternal mortality but one of Europe’s highest C-section rates, and midwife-led care can offer less intervention and should be expanded, asthe WHO advocates.View image in fullscreenCaelainn Hogan in the Rotunda hospital, Dublin, with her first baby.Photograph: Caelainn HoganMidwives gave me freedom in labour, helped my baby latch, taught me to use a blanket with the smell of my skin to get him to sleep, while I bled in shared toilets and fed myself one-handed. Now, just a few years later, some of the free midwife-led antenatal classes I found crucial are stripped back. And not everyone in Ireland can access midwife-led care. Our government, seemingly championing public care, is also overseeing a crisis in midwifery staffing, driven by state cuts.Around aquarter of pregnant women in Irelandgo private or “semi-private”, an option that the state health service still officially says is available inall maternity unitsin the country. In practice, however, private maternity care is gradually being eliminated. At the National Maternity hospital, an unprecedented 150women were turned awayfor private care in just six weeks in June and July, fuelling a campaign against women losing this “choice”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut any patient who requires it should be able to see a dedicated consultant obstetrician on a public-only contract. And while many women have traumatic experiences of giving birth in Ireland, surely we should be fighting for every pregnant person to have access to the care they need – not just those who can pay.A health worker I know opted for private care for her second baby after experiencing missed complications and absent consultants during her first public maternity. But in her work she sees consultants “using the public system to their advantage and funding a lot of their private practice through it.”Weeks ago, a still-developing body inside my belly flickered on ultrasound. I was told to come back in a month because of a borderline concern. As a public patient, I worried about falling through the gaps.Since then, a brilliant midwife and public sonographers referred me to consultants including top foetal medicine specialists listed on the Rotunda Private site. I see them for nothing as a public patient. This is how the system is meant to work, escalating care according to need.Yet it is gutting to know there is a perception that I could be risking my baby’s health by not “going private”, for the continuity of care that paying patients receive and which midwives have beendemanding be made standard for all.I trust the people working hard to provide strong public care, and we shouldn’t have to “go private” to feel safe. If everyone is equally relying on one system, there is real pressure for change.There is a history in Ireland of bishops, doctors and conservative politiciansrailing against free healthcarefor mothers and children, desperate to maintain control and profit.I want a fully public, equitable health system. For that to work, those in power must ensure resources and accountability.My Rotunda maternity ward looked across to a statue of Charles Stewart Parnell, the first president of the Irish National Land League – a mass movement against private monopolies. Ireland’srevolutionary proclamationenvisioned “cherishing all the children of the nation equally”. What better way to cherish every child equally from their first breath than a fully public maternity system?Caelainn Hogan is a journalist and the author of Republic of Shame: How Ireland Punished ‘Fallen Women’ and Their ChildrenExplore more on these topicsIrelandOpinionPregnancyEuropeFamilyParents and parentingHealth & wellbeingcommentShareReuse this content

title: It is now almost certain the world will warm past 1.5C. But ‘net-negative’ emissions are still possible | Wesley Morgan for the Conversation | The Guardian
description: Climate change is the greatest threat to the Pacific, with fuel shortages and missile tests also on the agenda as Anthony Albanese heads to Palau
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Climate change is the greatest threat to the Pacific, with fuel shortages and missile tests also on the agenda as Anthony Albanese heads to Palau
Content: The Rock Islands Southern Lagoon in Palau. As the world comes perilously close to the Paris agreement’s 1.5C temperature goal, a record-breaking El Niño looms in the Pacific Ocean.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe Rock Islands Southern Lagoon in Palau. As the world comes perilously close to the Paris agreement’s 1.5C temperature goal, a record-breaking El Niño looms in the Pacific Ocean.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersThe ConversationPacific Islands ForumIt is now almost certain the world will warm past 1.5C. But ‘net-negative’ emissions are still possibleWesley Morgan for the ConversationClimate change is the greatest threat to the Pacific, with fuel shortages and missile tests also on the agenda as Anthony Albanese heads to PalauSun 30 Aug 2026 22.07 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 02.03 EDTShareAnthony Albanese is in Palau this week for the annualPacific Islands Forumand regional security is expected to top the agenda.China is testingnuclear-capable missilesin the Pacific, prompting talk of a new regional agreement. The United States-Iran war has exposed a reliance on costly fossil fuels that is undermining Pacific economies.And as the world comesperilously closeto the Paris agreement’s 1.5C temperature goal, a record-breakingEl Niño looms in the Pacific Ocean.But the forum will be missing key leaders – Solomon Islands’ prime minister, Matthew Wale, made a shock departure, flying out of Palau just hours after arriving, in order to deal with a looming leadership challenge back home.Nepal-Tibet flood: this is the cost of not acting in the face of the climate crisis | Sunil AcharyaRead moreAnd the Kiribati president, Taneti Maamau, the Samoan prime minister, Laʻauli Leuatea Schmidt, and Vanuatu’s prime minister, Jotham Napat, are also not attending. It is unclear if Fiji’s prime minister, Sitiveni Rabuka, will be present.Pacific nations will want Albanese to address the world’s key security threat – climate change. Aspresident of negotiations of the Cop31climate talks in November, Australia can work with the Pacific to keep 1.5C within reach and secure much-needed finance for island nations at the climate frontline.China’s missile testSince the second world war, the United States has maintained fortified bases in the Pacific and an unrivalled deep-water navy (the US also regularly testslong-range missiles in the region). However, China’s investment in military capabilities has challenged the status quo.In July, China launched a nuclear-capable test missile that flew over multiple Pacific nations and hit waters close toTuvalu’s exclusive economic zone.This sparked calls for a new regional security agreement: Wale said China’s missile test was“not the act of a friend”.Ironically, it was Solomon Islands thatsigned a security deal with Chinain 2022. This changed the security dynamics of a region long aligned with the US and Australia (notwithstanding concerns about nuclear testing and decolonisation).Since then, Canberra has pursued a web of bilateral deals to shore up Australia’s place as Pacific security partner – first with Tuvalu(2023), then Naoero (formerly Nauru)(2024), Papua New Guinea(2025)and Vanuatu(2026). Discussions are ongoing with Tonga and Solomon Islands. The most recent agreement, anOcean of Peace Alliancesigned with Fiji in July, is a mutual defence pact that is open to other Pacific nations to join.Canberra was already pursuing a treaty allowing for coordinated regional responses todisasters and other crises. China’s missile test may have opened the door for something more.Renewables the solution to fuel crisisThe Middle East conflict has pushed the Pacific toward an energy crisis. About 80% of the region’s energy relies onimported oil products, much of which would normally transit the strait of Hormuz. Even before the US-Iran war, Pacific island countries spent an eye-watering percentage of GDP(between 10% and 25%)buying fossil fuels to run power plants, generators, boats and vehicles. This compares with a regional average of8% spent on education and 6% on health.The Middle East conflict has only added to the bill. According toa new report, Fiji’s annual refined fuel import costs could rise by US$375m (A$520m) if high oil prices persist. This is more than Fiji’s entire healthcare budget.Renewable energy offers a clear solution. Replacing diesel generators with grid-scale solar and battery storage could save Pacific countries aboutUS$700m (A$520m) each year in avoided fuel costs.Datacentres are a ticking timebomb. We must make sure AI’s benefits outweigh the costs | Nicki HutleyRead moreThe incoming chair of the Pacific Islands Forum, the Palau president, Surangel Whipps Jr, wants the region to become the first in the world100% powered by renewables.
