He says investment of US$120m (A$ 166m) is needed for Palau to add60MW of solar and battery storage, which would enable 90% of its power needs to be met by renewables.The greatest Pacific threatWhen climate change was first debated at the UN Security Council in 2007, Pacific countriesarguedthe impacts of a warming planet were “no less serious than those faced by nations and peoples threatened by guns and bombs”.Since then, Pacific Islands Forum leaders have explicitly reaffirmed climate change is“the single greatest threat”to Pacific security.In 2025, Earth was1.44C warmerthan the long-term average. Pacific countries are reeling from stronger cyclones, dying reefs and ocean acidification. Without urgent action to shift away from coal, oil and gas impacts will get much worse. Just this week, the world’s oceans are thewarmest on record, fuelled by climate change and a rapidly intensifying El Niño event.It is nowalmost certainthe world will warm past 1.5C. Yet it remains possible, following atemporary “overshoot”, that countries can limit warming to 1.5C by the end of the century. This will require deep and immediate emissions reductions and some carbon dioxide removalto achieve “net-negative” emissions.Limiting global warming to 1.5C is a line in the sand for low-lying Pacific nations – “1.5 to stay alive” is the slogan. Pacific negotiatorshelped securethis temperature goal in the 2015 Paris agreement.Pacific nations expect Australia to reaffirm global commitment to 1.5C. Australia is helping Fiji and Tuvalu host apre-Cop summit in Octoberthat will remind world leaders the survival of island nations is at stake.Pacific countries will also seek new finance for aPacific-owned climate fundto invest in community-scale adaptation projects.Some argue collaboration with the Pacific in the lead-up to Cop31 isan expensive exercise. But climate action is crucial to Australian strategy in the region. Investing in renewables and adaptation in the Pacific is an investment in shared security, even as geopolitical competition sharpens between China and the US.Wesley Morgan is a research associate at the Institute for Climate Risk and Response, UNSW. title: The Guardian view on regulating big tech: Meta has got off too lightly | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: New child safety measures are welcome, but the wider risks posed by these platforms remain unaddressed
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: New child safety measures are welcome, but the wider risks posed by these platforms remain unaddressed
Content: Members of Colorado's trial team celebrate after Meta’s settlement on 26 August 2026 in Oakland, California.Photograph: Noah Berger/APView image in fullscreenMembers of Colorado's trial team celebrate after Meta’s settlement on 26 August 2026 in Oakland, California.Photograph: Noah Berger/APOpinionMetaThe Guardian view on regulating big tech: Meta has got off too lightlyEditorialNew child safety measures are welcome, but the wider risks posed by these platforms remain unaddressedMon 31 Aug 2026 13.04 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShare“Hook, hold, harvest and hide” was how Megan O’Neill, a lawyer for the US state of California, characterised Meta’s business model in thetrialthat ended last week with an $18bn settlement, to be shared between the states and territories that brought the case. It was a clever way to describe the company’s approach to users’ attention and data. But the sharpness of her words was not matched by the deal. While the strengthening of child safety features is welcome, the tech giant once again batted off efforts to alter its products.Meta’s decision to settle enabled it to avoid any admission of liability. It put a stop to the awkward questions being asked of witnesses includingAdam Mosseri, Instagram’s CEO, and the damaging claims made by whistleblowers such asArturo Béjar. This former Meta safety engineer told the court that his own daughter had been sent unsolicited photos of male genitals on Instagram.View image in fullscreenAdam Mosseri, head of Instagram.Photograph: Karl Mondon/AFP/Getty ImagesThe $18bn that Meta agreed to pay over 10 years, some of which is conditional on other platforms making similar changes, will hardly dent its profits (Meta plans to investup to $145bnthis year). More significant by far are its concessions in relation to child users. Safety features will become “opt-out” instead of “opt-in”, increasing the likelihood of their being switched on. Parents will be able to change the settings on young people’s accounts so that their feeds no longer show personalised, algorithmically driven content.A new two-hour daily limit, blocks on use during the night and on notifications during school hours, backed up by compulsory age verification, improve on the current free-for-all. So does the commitment to disable obviously harmful “social comparison” features such as cosmetic surgery image filters.But the package falls short of the restrictions on social media companies’ access to children that Australia, the UK, Malaysia, Indonesia and the EU have either imposed or are in the process of imposing (UK ministers have indicated that in areas where US rules may be stricter, theyplan to follow suit). By accepting the terms that they did, while declining to raise the “digital age of consent” (at which accounts can be marketed to children) from 13, this deal’s negotiators left crucial aspects of Meta’s business, including its algorithms and addictive design features,largely untouched.There are good reasons why children’s mental health is a central focus of online safety campaigning. But the harm caused by big tech’s monetisation of attention goes wider. The addictive, tribalist and narcissistic behaviours that platforms are widely recognised to promote haveimplications for societiesas well as individuals.One of many outstanding cases against Meta is being brought by Abrham Mearag, whose father was murdered in Ethiopia in 2021, after Facebook’s algorithm allegedly promoted posts calling for his killing. A US courtblockedanother case against the company regarding its role in the Rohingya genocide.Measures designed to protect American children from anxiety, depression, unlawful data gathering and addiction are important. But they will not reduce the risk of social media being linked to murderous violence, or undermining democracy, elsewhere in the world. It is now for other courts, or foreign governments, to take the next steps in holdingMetaand its peer companies to account for their role as overseers of the global digital commons.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: ‘The whistling on the theme tune? That’s Dickie Attenborough!’ Hayley Mills on Whistle Down the Wind | Movies | The Guardian
description: ‘I’d just made two films in America. Shooting on a Lancashire farm was very different. There was mud everywhere – and we’d be eating dripping, jam butties and fried eggs in buns’
Author: Chris Broughton
Headline: ‘I’d just made two films in America. Shooting on a Lancashire farm was very different. There was mud everywhere – and we’d be eating dripping, jam butties and fried eggs in buns’
Content: ‘Just a fella’ … Hayley Mills and Alan Bates in the 1961 film Whistle Down the Wind.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Just a fella’ … Hayley Mills and Alan Bates in the 1961 film Whistle Down the Wind.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyHow we madeMovies‘The whistling on the theme tune? That’s Dickie Attenborough!’ Hayley Mills on Whistle Down the Wind‘I’d just made two films in America. Shooting on a Lancashire farm was very different. There was mud everywhere – and we’d be eating dripping, jam butties and fried eggs in buns’Interviews byChris BroughtonMon 31 Aug 2026 09.21 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 10.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHayley Mills,played Kathy BostockWhistle Down the Wind was originally a novel written by my mother, Mary Hayley Bell, about three children living on a farm in Sussex. The children – loosely based on my sister Juliet, my brother Jonathan and myself – discover a man in their barn. Thinking he’s Jesus, they decide to hide him and protect him from the adults because they don’t want the same thing to happen to him as before.Dickie Attenboroughthought it was a wonderful story, and convinced my parents it should be made into a film by the production company he’d set up with the actor and writerBryan Forbes. After the original director,Guy Green, pulled out, Bryan took over at the 11th hour. He’d never directed before. When Dickie asked if he could do it, he apparently said: “I’ve no idea. We’ll soon find out!”Keith WaterhouseandWillis Hallwere engaged as writers and made the brilliant decision to move the story to a remote part of Lancashire. The perfect location was found in the village of Downham, at the foot of Pendle Hill, famous for the witch hunts. Nearly all of the children in the film were local: the only experienced child actors were Roy Holder, who played Jackie, and me. I was 14 and a head and shoulders taller than most of the other kids. The sleeves on my coat were too short and my arms stuck out like a scarecrow’s.double quotation markBryan really whacked me! It wasn’t until cameras stopped rolling that I criedI’d just made two films in America for Disney. Shooting on a Lancashire farm in winter was very different: there was mud everywhere, and we often had to walk very carefully on duckboards. But I always loved filming in England. We’d be eating dripping, jam butties and fried eggs in a bun. Bryan was great at communicating what he wanted from the children without just getting them to parrot him. In the scene where the boy slaps me in the playground, the hand in the closeup was actually Bryan’s. He really whacked me! Kathy isn’t supposed to show that she’s been affected, so it wasn’t until cameras stopped rolling that I cried.Watch a trailer for Whistle Down the WindArthur Ibbetson’s black and white cinematography wonderfully captured the stark, leafless trees and the mist blowing across the hills. It had a sort of film noir quality, and as a child I loved the night shoots. This was all beautifully complemented byMalcolm Arnold’s poignant, nostalgic music. His arrangement of We Three Kings was a perfect fit for the kids’ tiny figures leaping like hares on the brow of the hill – and that’s Dickie himself whistling on the main theme.I’ve always said Alan Barnes stole the show as my little brother, Charles. He was only seven. The first morning on location, there was a row of director’s chairs with the names of adult cast and crew members on them. He pointed at Alan Bates’s chair and said, “Ey up, they’ve spelled me name wrong.” By the next day, the props department had made a tiny chair just for him. One of his lines became the most quoted one from the film: “It isn’t Jesus. It’s just a fella.” He delivered it perfectly.Diane Poole (nee Holgate), played Nan BostockI was 10 when Bryan and Richard visited my school. I didn’t know who they were. The head teacher just said two men would be coming to the playground to watch us play, but not to bother about it. Afterwards, a few of us were grouped together and told the men were looking for children to be in a film. When I told my mum, she said: “Don’t be so ridiculous and get your dinner eaten.” But the next dayRichard Attenboroughturned up at the front door. She was horrified as it was a Wednesday – and she wasn’t due to scrub the front step until Friday.View image in fullscreen‘Us kids didn’t go to the cinema so I didn’t know who Hayley Mills was’ … Diane Poole, centre, with Alan Barnes and Hayley Mills.Photograph: Courtesy BFI National ArchiveI remember doing a screen test up at the farm where a lot of the film was made. We just had to look round the end of a stone wall and say, “Is he coming?” without looking at the camera. I’d done school plays before and played Snow White, which involved learning quite a lot of dialogue, so this seemed easy.Nan wasn’t the child who didn’t believe, and she wasn’t the one who was totally besotted. She kept the peace between the other two. I was probably a quiet child at home: I guess they saw that in my personality. Bryan kept some of our mistakes in the film, which helps make it feel more real. In one scene, I spell “Bible” wrong and in another I mispronounce “Christmas”.In those days, us kids didn’t go to the cinema so I didn’t know who Hayley Mills was. She was like a real big sister, though, and we would act the goat together. It was only when we went to Pinewood to film scenes set inside the farmhouse that we started seeing what footage had been shot. It was a revelation. We thought: “Oh, this is what it’s all about.” They borrowed the actual back door from the real farmhouse to use on the set. My dad had a haulage firm and got one of his drivers to deliver it.View image in fullscreenPoole and Mills with Bernard Lee as Mr Bostock.Photograph: Courtesy BFI National ArchiveAlan Bates was very pleasant and softly spoken, so in the scene where he suddenly shouts at the “disciples”, we thought: “Oh crikey, what have we done?” At the London premiere, he came up and swung me around and I didn’t recognise him until he spoke, because he’d shaved his beard off. I got sent to Harrods to choose a dress for the London premiere, but I insisted on wearing the one my granny had bought me.The scene I’m most proud of is when Kathy first tells Nan about Jesus being in the barn, while they’re in bed together. That was the last thing I did at Pinewood and by then I’d got used to it all. It was a long scene, but looking at it now I think: “Yeah, you did all right there, kid.”A new 35mm print of Whistle Down the Windscreens at the BFI Southbank, London, on 4 September,with a Q&A with Hayley Mills, Diane Poole and Alan Barnes. title: Reading and Leeds festival review – post-GCSE blowout shows how dominant dance music now is | Reading and Leeds festival | The Guardian
description: Charli xcx and Fontaines DC are spellbinding and there’s an awesome array of genres, but the biggest turnouts are for tech house names like Kettama and Josh Baker
Author: Archie Forde
Headline: Charli xcx and Fontaines DC are spellbinding and there’s an awesome array of genres, but the biggest turnouts are for tech house names like Kettama and Josh Baker
Content: Kettama performing at Leeds festival.Photograph: Matthew Baker/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKettama performing at Leeds festival.Photograph: Matthew Baker/Getty ImagesReading and Leeds festivalReviewReading and Leeds festival review – post-GCSE blowout shows how dominant dance music now isBramham Park, LeedsCharli xcx and Fontaines DC are spellbinding and there’s an awesome array of genres, but the biggest turnouts are for tech house names like Kettama and Josh BakerCharli xcx, Reading festival review – Pretentious? Just a bit. But Nietzsche would have loved itArchie FordeMon 31 Aug 2026 11.45 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 15.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReading and Leeds festival will probably always be a post-GCSE rite of passage: a gleefully riotous taste of freedom before having to make actual life decisions. But the sibling events have been struggling for a sense of identity beyond this, particularly post-Covid. In 2025, the festival decided to theme days based on genre, which felt out of touch – but, this year, organisers have decided to tackle gen Z’s borderless approach head on. There are new stages, such as the chandelier-adorned Ballroom, and overall the lineup is wonderfully mazy.On the festival’s second stage, you can catch everything from UK underground rap selector DJ EJ, warbly US rockers Geese, and raw, live-drummed jungle from 4am Kru. “I dedicate this one to all the bad bitches from small places. Let’s make a song about the bad bitches from Leeds,” Slovakian pop star Adéla gleefully giggles during her own set here, before launching into neon-streaked megahit Ain’t in LA. In a ping-ponging journey across styles, other highlights include London singer Dexter in the Newsagent’s blue-skied bedroom pop, Australian artist Mall Grab’s Game Boy grime beats and Bar Italia’s insouciant rock, which is significantly more fun and dance-y than their recent lukewarm album reviews might suggest.View image in fullscreenAdéla performing at Leeds festival.Photograph: Katja Ogrin/RedfernsThursday is headlined by a tired-sounding Kasabian, who don’t move a crowd of kids that, for good reason, would much rather be at LS23, the trippy dance stage in the woods. Chase and Status’ festival-sized drum’n’bass scratches that dance itch as Friday’s main stage headliner, while Charli xcx (reviewed in full here) and Fontaines DC are a spellbinding double bill on Saturday. The latter play new material from their forthcoming album Dopamine Chamber, including beguiling single Marianne, and an unreleased new track called Happy for You – it’s driven by a Sundays-sounding guitar line and a peppy rimshot, but moves with melancholy, the band members’ features obscured against a humming green light onstage. Their set is the best from a guitar band all weekend.Another new stage, the Canopy, replaces the BBC Introducing stage at both festivals and is a showcase of new artists curated by Festival Republic, who are majority owned by Live Nation – it has been dubbed the“nepo baby” stagefor platforming the offspring of Dave Grohl, Liam Gallagher and the Beckhams. For the most part, the programming is disastrously bad, and the stage is underattended until festivalgoers can catch a perfunctory glimpse of someone semi-famous. Then it swarms, making sets look like amomentthat doesn’t actually exist from the outside, and to the detriment of other artists who would benefit from not being juxtaposed with celebrities’ kids. The two best acts are young alt-rock four-piece Tooth and brilliantly talented singer Sade Olutola, and yet they only get 20-minute opening slots on the Saturday and Sunday.View image in fullscreenGeneral Levy performing with Chase and Status.Photograph: Matthew Baker/Getty ImagesIf Reading and Leeds can be defined by anything this past year, it is young people’s ongoing affinity for tech house DJs like Josh Baker, Omar+, Max Dean and Luke Dean; Irish producer Kettama’s set is one of the most packed-out of the weekend. These artists play perfectly engineered going-out music, with chantable vocal samples and mixes that build and change a little too fast, like doomscrolling in audio form.The dance music is mainly on the Warehouse stage, which is not unlike a mockup of Manchester’s Warehouse Project, and is where the most crowd energy is directed across the weekend. Issues with overcrowding mean that Silva Bumpa and a Skepta b2b with East End Dubs are cancelled, with calls online for Reading and Leeds to recognise the popularity of dance and move it to bigger stages. Baker clashes with Dave on Sunday, and despite cameos from Kano, Tems and Central Cee, the Dave crowd is by far the most sparse out of all the headliners.Daisy Chain Fields review – Olivia Rodrigo’s women-led festival is electric amid extreme heatRead moreYou can really see Reading and Leeds’ transformation at Hedex’s set, when the drum’n’bass DJ drops a mix that begins with a sped-up version of Nirvana’s Smells Like Teen Spirit. There’s a slight bit of confusion at a tune that once embodied this festival. Still, the crowd join in singing the verse, before Hedex pulverises the track to the same effect as the distorted drop in the original and everyone’s back to dancing with that same immediacy, that same teenage freedom.Explore more on these topicsReading and Leeds festivalMusic festivalsFestivalsPop and rockDance musicRapKasabianlive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Gen Z ‘Chinamaxxers’ fantasise about life in China. This journalist and this artist can never go back there | Comics and graphic novels | The Guardian
description: A graphic novel by Melissa Chan and Badiucao imagines China and the US at war in 2035. They hope to remind young people that ‘authoritarianism everywhere is bad’
Author: Kat Wong
Headline: A graphic novel by Melissa Chan and Badiucao imagines China and the US at war in 2035. They hope to remind young people that ‘authoritarianism everywhere is bad’
Content: ‘The younger generation feel like there is no meaningful method to change society,’ says Badiucao (right) with journalist Melissa Chan at Sydney’s Carriageworks.Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The younger generation feel like there is no meaningful method to change society,’ says Badiucao (right) with journalist Melissa Chan at Sydney’s Carriageworks.Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianComics and graphic novelsInterviewGen Z ‘Chinamaxxers’ fantasise about life in China. This journalist and this artist can never go back thereKat WongA graphic novel by Melissa Chan and Badiucao imagines China and the US at war in 2035. They hope to remind young people that ‘authoritarianism everywhere is bad’Mon 31 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 20.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDrinking Tsingtao beers, eating congee, walking with hands behind their backs: for many young people in western countries, “Chinamaxxing” has become all the rage. Some content creators have even gone beyond the jokes about being in “a very Chinese time in my life” and have followed this passion to the Middle Kingdom: making TikToks in Chongqing’s multilayered metropolis, bathing in Chengdu’s 24-hour spas or backflipping on the Great Wall of China.When your culture becomes a meme: the ‘jarring’ effect of ChinamaxxingRead moreThis irreverent, mostly ironic trend is jarring for some, but Chinese Australian artist Badiucao and Chinese American journalist Melissa Chan don’t want to lecture the so-called Chinamaxxers.“The younger generation feel like there is no meaningful method to change society. They feel defeated when they see what’s happening in Gaza – there’s been protests but the government doesn’t care and is collaborating with atrocities in wars. There’s also the Epstein files in America, which show how the elite is corrupt,” says Badiucao, who, along with Chan, is in Sydney to promote their new book, You Must Take Part in Revolution.“When you want to see change, there is the hard way, which is being innovative and finding a solution. And there is the lazy way, which is finding a cheap alternative and fantasising about a faraway, oriental, communist country that might be your future,” he says.View image in fullscreen‘We don’t want to just lecture,’ says Badiucao.Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianChan and Badiucao have both paid the price for criticising China’s one-party system. Chinese officials refused to renew Chan’s press credentials before expelling the former Al Jazeera journalist from China in 2012; and the previously anonymous political cartoonist Badiucao wasforced to reveal his identity in 2019after it was compromised and authorities threatened his family in China.You Must Take Part in Revolution, the pair’s debut graphic novel, portrays a dystopian future where China is at war with the United States in 2035.View image in fullscreenYou Must Take Part in Revolution by Badiucao and Melissa Chan.Illustration: Simon & SchusterThe graphic novel features a variety of characters from the Chinese-speaking diaspora, including from Hong Kong, Taiwan, the US and Tibet, as they decide what choices they are willing to make under authoritarian oppression.“It was intentional to show the panoply of Asian identities that have been impacted by a great power,” Chan says. “It opens up the possibility to get young people to better understand it’s not just a ‘Chinese time in my life’, that there’s a lot going on here … hopefully it can get a few people thinking about resistance movements both present and in the past.”“We don’t want to just lecture,” Badiucao adds. “We really want readers to put themselves in the eyes of those characters as if they were a real human being with a real life.”Chan now lives in Berlin and has written for the Atlantic, the Washington Post, Time, and others, while Badiucao, who lives in Melbourne, has exhibited works across the world. They started working on the graphic novel five years ago after first meeting in Germany during the late 2010s.View image in fullscreen‘If things are shit, they’re shit in any country,’ says Chan.Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianYou Must Take Part in Revolution starts off in the real-life Hong Kong protests of 2019, when almost two million people took to the streets to denounce a controversial law that would allow the extradition of suspects to mainland China. The law was viewed as a sign of growing mainland influence in Hong Kong.While the graphic novel is geographically grounded in an Asia governed by authoritarian China, it also portrays the US as a proto-fascist state, resisting the idea that criticising one necessarily means painting the other in a positive light.“This book happens to focus on China, but authoritarianism everywhere is bad,” Chan says. “We don’t want anyone to engage in whataboutism and I don’t think there needs to be a balance – if things are shit, they’re shit in any country.”Unlike other graphic novels such as Art Spiegelman’s Maus, Badiucao and Chan’s book takes its influence from Japanese manga. “There are great works like Attack on Titan which are not necessarily about specific history or political content that have so many metaphors reflecting important things like racism, war and equity,” Badiucao says.“It’s part of the reason this form is potentially more than just entertainment or some kid stuff, it really influences an entire generation.”You Must Take Part in Revolution was released in the US in 2025, but it is only just getting its Australian release this week and its UK release in October.Badiucao says readers across the world have contacted them about their own histories after reading it, including Ukrainian refugees who have escaped Russia’s invasion, and Czech communities who lived through the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic.View image in fullscreenThe artist recalls one interaction at a comic festival in New York, where a second-generation Chinese Canadian girl told him that she had hesitations about taking the book home. “I don’t think my mum would love it,” she said.A few minutes later, an older woman came up to Badiucao and explained she was an immigrant whose family had been through hardship during the Cultural Revolution. Flipping through the book, she said her daughter might like it, but she didn’t know if she would be open to learning about Chinese politics.Badiucao later discovered the two were mother and daughter.“I told the daughter her mum might be more open about political stuff, and I told the mum that your daughter might be interested too,” he says. “They ended up having an honest conversation, and they got a copy of the book … among all the interactions with readers, that was pretty special to me.”You Must Take Part in Revolutionby Melissa Chan and Badiucao is out now in Australia (Affirm Press; $39.99), as well as in the US. It is out in the UK on 8 October.This article was amended on 1 September 2026 to provide the UK release date of You Must Take Part in Revolution. A previous version said the book had already been published in the UK.Explore more on these topicsComics and graphic novelsFestivalsFictionArt and design booksAustralian booksChinafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Goodbye to Babylon Berlin, the 1920s TV drama that has eerily foreshadowed real-life politics | Television | The Guardian
description: The long-running drama reaches Hitler’s rise to power in its final season as its creators reflect on the unsettling parallels between Weimar Germany and the present day
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: The long-running drama reaches Hitler’s rise to power in its final season as its creators reflect on the unsettling parallels between Weimar Germany and the present day
Content: ‘We’re in the volcano itself’ … Volker Bruch (second, right) and Liv Lisa Fries on set of the fifth series of  Babylon Berlin.Photograph: Joachim Gern/Beta FilmView image in fullscreen‘We’re in the volcano itself’ … Volker Bruch (second, right) and Liv Lisa Fries on set of the fifth series of  Babylon Berlin.Photograph: Joachim Gern/Beta FilmTelevisionGoodbye to Babylon Berlin, the 1920s TV drama that has eerily foreshadowed real-life politicsThe long-running drama reaches Hitler’s rise to power in its final season as its creators reflect on the unsettling parallels between Weimar Germany and the present dayDeborah Colein BerlinMon 31 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s the global hit TV series that pulled audiences straight into the chaotic hedonism of 1920sGermany, dramatising the brilliance and brittleness of a newly built democratic system with unprecedented ambition.But in the 13 years that the German makers ofBabylon Berlinhave worked on the show, modern democracies from the US to Hungary to South Korea have come under pressure in ways the creators say they could never have imagined when they started.Now they are preparing to unveil the fifth and final season, culminating in Adolf Hitler’s rise to power, the same week that Germany will face one of the biggest tests of its postwar order in a watershed state election.The timing, they insist, is pure coincidence, but is fitting for an ambitious programme set a century ago during theWeimar republicthat has always felt eerily prescient.As the team gets ready to sign off, the inexorable end of the story is now upon the familiar characters of the noirish police procedural, with its lush period sets and frisson of impending doom.“It’s no longer a dance on the rim of the volcano,” said lead actorLiv Lisa Fries, using a German idiom for the explosion of avant garde culture and sexual liberation in the 1920s before the descent into fascism. “We’re in the volcano itself.”Fries plays the series’ intrepid working-class heroine Charlotte Ritter, who works her way up from secretarial duties and underworld sex work to become the first female detective on the Berlin police force.Her co-star Volker Bruch is Gereon Rath, a shellshocked first world war veteran whose eventful odyssey through the trauma of his era bears a resemblance toChristopher Nolan’s summer blockbuster, The Odyssey.But the more striking parallel isGermanyin 2026.View image in fullscreenPower struggle … episode 12 of series four of Babylon Berlin.Photograph: Frédéric Batier/ARD/Sky StudiosThe far-rightAlternative für Deutschland, anextremist, anti-constitutional partyfounded around the same time that work on the series began, is now leading national opinion polls.On Sunday 6 September, it could win its first absolute majority in a state election, in Saxony-Anhalt, and two weeks later may beat its opponents in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. In Berlin, it is polling close to the far-left party Die Linke.With German democracy facing such a stress test, Bruch said the political “parallels” jumped out. But he resisted overly simplistic comparisons, citing an old adage: “History doesn’t repeat itself that way – it rhymes.”The blurred lines between life and art took on sometimes surreal dimensions during the course of the production.Series three was filmed in part at the neo-baroque Villa Adlon, which in November 2023 served as the real-life venue for asecret meetingof AfD officials and neo-Nazis to discuss a “remigration” plan for mass deportations if the party came to power.Series five sees Hitler’s appointment as Reich chancellor, just as an medical file goes missing that casts new light on his time as a soldier in the first world war.Although it was always clear how the series would end, watching Babylon Berlin has meant hoping to the last that history would take another turn.That poignancy transformed a sophisticated crime show into something more affecting, and perhaps more enduring.Across 50-odd hours, the show, based partly on a series ofnovels by Volker Kutscher, helped expand the scale and ambition of European television drama.“It was almost impossible even then when they started,” said Scott Roxborough, the European bureau chief of entertainment trade magazine the Hollywood Reporter.It was the product of a “pioneer time”, he said, when Germany was willing to throw massive resources at a chance to catch up with splashy shows from the US and Britain like Breaking Bad and The Crown.“I think it would be almost impossible to do it nowadays unless an Apple TV or a Netflix decided to finance everything,” something he said was increasingly unlikely as the global streaming companies take a morecautious, profits-first approach.Babylon Berlin has reached audiences around the world – 140 countries at last count – with its cautionary tale of a vibrant civilisation’s inherent fragility.“The secret to the series’s success in capturing the zeitgeist is definitely not that it mirrors the present. I don’t believe that,” one of its three creators, Tom Tykwer, said.Rather, audiences have been drawn to the “transformative force” of Berlin in the 1920s, when a weak government and a churning society left room for women, gay people and new immigrants to rewrite the rules.“That brings forth an incredible number of wonderful, positive, beautiful blossoms, but because it’s so experimental, they’re also destroyed again almost immediately,” he said.“We’ve tried to explore the universal themes that stem from the fact that political systems are people-centred so are always under threat. It will always be that way.”Tykwer also co-composed much of the original music for the series, including the haunting theme song To Ashes, to Dust. The fifth season features a plot excursion to Paris and an on-screen rendition of the tune by French neo-chanson starZaho de Sagazan.In series five, Tykwer and his team have also revived the 1920 queer anthemDas Lila Liedwith its rousing chorus “Wir sind nun einmal anders als die andern” (We’re just different from the others) for the series.It is rousingly sung in a nightclub frequented by cross-dressing patrons and uniformed, gay SA officers – a startling melange the producers say was not uncommon before thebrutal Nazi crackdown on the LGBTQ+ community.While Tykwer bristles at the notion that the series should deliver any sort of “message” to Germans about their choices at the ballot box this month, fellow creator Henk Handloegten said he was proud to have “struck a nerve” with audiences around the world who find themselves at a political crossroads.“I believe that we’ve taken a clear political stand, even now in the final series, and I find it very necessary,” he said.For Handloegten, the pressure on democracy in many countries where the show is watched, “has really motivated me”.“It’s given me the justification to engage with [this era] for so long and so deeply, because I felt there was a relevance to it in today’s world. And for me, in a strange way, that’s political work – something we’ve been doing here for 13 years now.”Explore more on these topicsTelevisionGermanyEuropeAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)featuresShareReuse this content

title: British Museum hosted Palantir founder Peter Thiel in private viewing of Bayeux tapestry | British Museum | The Guardian
description: Concern among staff that fragile artwork’s scarce ‘light hours’ given to someone with no known interest in museum
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Concern among staff that fragile artwork’s scarce ‘light hours’ given to someone with no known interest in museum
Content: Peter Thiel. The museum has a careful plan for light-hour allocations, agreed with colleagues in France.Photograph: Gage Skidmore/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPeter Thiel. The museum has a careful plan for light-hour allocations, agreed with colleagues in France.Photograph: Gage Skidmore/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockBritish MuseumBritish Museum hosted Palantir founder Peter Thiel in private viewing of Bayeux tapestryConcern among staff that fragile artwork’s scarce ‘light hours’ given to someone with no known interest in museumNadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentMon 31 Aug 2026 04.50 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe British Museum privately hosted the Donald Trump-supporting tech billionaire Peter Thiel in the exhibition space of theBayeux tapestryearlier this month, the Guardian understands.The museum’s director of development, Charlotte Appleyard, hosted the PayPal founder at a VIP viewing of the tapestry, which is yet to open to the public, on 18 August.In response to queries from the Guardian, a source at the museum confirmed that the visit took place. It is understood the museum chair, George Osborne, was aware of the viewing but did not attend with Thiel.It is understood that senior museum leaders were warned about the possible public perception of special treatment for someone with connections to Jeffrey Epstein, and whose public software company, Palantir,plays a controversial role in the British state.View image in fullscreenGeorge Osborne and France’s culture minister, Catherine Pégard (C), look at the Bayeux tapestry during a visit to its unveiling at the British Museum in July.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/AFPThere were concerns among some staff that scarce “lux hours” for the tapestry – a combined measure of light intensity and exposure time used to track and limit cumulative light damage to sensitive artefacts – were given up to someone with no known interest in the museum.The exhibition gallery is still under construction, and only limited viewings of the tapestry have been possible across a range of stakeholders. Among those receiving special access are Osborne and his podcasting partner, Ed Balls, who will record the next episode of their Political Currency show from the gallery,the noteson the most recent episode suggest.TheBritish Museumhas a careful plan for light-hour allocation, agreed in partnership with colleagues in France. It is understood that no light hours have been taken from the allocation for public visitors. Thiel is not a donor to the museum and no money has been received via him or his businesses.Members of the public keen to see the Bayeux tapestry faced online queues of up to nine hours when tickets went on sale for the first time earlier this summer. There were reports of 40,000 people queueing by mid-morning, with that figure ballooning to almost 80,000 by mid-afternoon.On Friday, the museum announced that the next wave of public tickets for the tapestry will go on sale on 21 October at 10am.View image in fullscreenMuseum staff adjusting protective covers on the Bayeux tapestry.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/AFP/Getty ImagesGuests at One Aldwych hotel, where rooms cost more than £1,000 a night, are also able to get ticketswithout joining the online queues.Thiel is the founder of Palantir, a public software company that builds data integration, analytics and artificial intelligence platforms for government agencies and large corporations. Palantir has a swathe of British public contracts, including, most controversially, a£330m deal with the NHS, which it has held since 2023.The company also works for the US, Israeli and UK militaries. Its use of its AI-powered software to support military strikes in Gaza and Iran, US ICE immigration raids and access to NHS data has stoked concern.Last month, a second parliamentary committee urged Labour to scrap Palantir’s NHS contract. The cross-party group of MPs cited “serious mistrust” among the public and the medical profession of its NHS system, contested evidence of its benefits, and cited the availability of other tools that could deliver similar results.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBayeux tapestry crosses Channel in dead of night for historic UK exhibitionRead moreIn May, Sadiq Khan, the London mayor,blocked the Metropolitan police from awardinga £50m contract to Palantir after saying Londoners wanted to see public money being paid to companies that “share the values of our city”. Palantir is challenging the decision in the high court.Thiel recently hit the headlines forhosting a series of lecturesphilosophising about who the antichrist could be and warning that Armageddon was coming. He has also recently become powerful in US conservative politics, with close ties to Donald Trump and JD Vance, and has helped bankroll Republicans’ 2026 midterm campaigns.The Epstein files showed that Thiel remained in contact with the financier for years after his 2008 conviction for soliciting prostitution from a minor, with multiple references to lunches and meetings between the pair from about 2014 onwards.Epstein’s Southern Trust Company also invested about $40m (£29.5m) in a venture fund co-founded by Thiel, while correspondence from 2018 shows Epstein inviting Thiel to visit him in the Caribbean. Thiel has said he never visited Epstein’s island and there is no suggestion that he was involved in Epstein’s sexual abuse or trafficking.Thiel and Palantir have been approached for comment.Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsBritish MuseumPeter ThielBayeux tapestryPalantirMuseumsLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Rise of Chicken Shop Date highlights how YouTube turned the tables on TV | YouTube | The Guardian
description: Amelia Dimoldenberg says publicists ignored her interview show for years but she can now be picky over A-list guests
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Amelia Dimoldenberg says publicists ignored her interview show for years but she can now be picky over A-list guests
Content: Shania Twain was a guest on Chicken Shop Date in 2023.Photograph: Chicken Shop DateView image in fullscreenShania Twain was a guest on Chicken Shop Date in 2023.Photograph: Chicken Shop DateYouTubeRise of Chicken Shop Date highlights how YouTube turned the tables on TVAmelia Dimoldenberg says publicists ignored her interview show for years but she can now be picky over A-list guestsMichael SavageMedia editorMon 31 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 14.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJust a decade ago,Amelia Dimoldenbergfound it impossible to drum up any mainstream celebrities to come on her mock date YouTube show, in which she chats awkwardly with guests over chicken and chips.Even persuading a local actor connected with her London youth club to come on took years of prodding. Managers of A-listers with movies or albums to push instead battled to claim a spot on the hallowed cushions of the primetime TV chatshow sofa.Yet after those early years of rejection, Dimoldenberg has said that she has reached a watershed moment. Such is the influence of her Chicken Shop Date show, she says it now ranks alongside Graham Norton’s chatshow or BBC Radio 1 for celebrities seeking media cut-through.“When I started the show in 2014, no publicist and no manager would let their talent come on aYouTubeshow – that was just insane,” she told the Edinburgh TV festival. “I would be banging down the doors, it was just so challenging. Now it’s so fascinating because it’s the opposite.“If your publicist is coming to you and you’ve got a movie out, or you’ve got an album rollout campaign, now I do think one of the first things up there on the list of things to do would be to come on Chicken Shop Date.“That has always been the ambition – my ambition – to make it as important as going on Graham Norton or going on Greg James, Radio 1, for example. So I’ve achieved that goal.”Dimoldenberg’s rise is a prime example of how digital platforms have radically reshaped the media world, with viewers across all ages switching to YouTube,especially under-35s.Dimoldenberg has shared the ketchup with Ed Sheeran, Charli xcx and Jennifer Lawrence, although Lawrence got Dimoldenberg’s name wrong. Even Paul McCartney turned up for a date in a vegan chicken shop this year, declining Dimoldenberg’s suggestion that he adopt a pet otter.Dimoldenberg initially focused on interviewing figures from the UK rap and grime scene when she launched Chicken Shop Date in 2014. She secured her first big name, the actor Daniel Kaluuya, because he was a fan of the show.Her interviews have repeatedly gone viral since then, thanks toLouis Theroux rappingor the chemistry between Dimoldenberg and the actor Andrew Garfield. “I didn’t realise fully how much the audience would catch on to how obsessed he is with me,” she said.View image in fullscreenAmelia Dimoldenberg flirting with Andrew Garfield at the British GQ awards in 2022.Photograph: British GQShe is increasingly picky over guests and rejects anyone who wants to be on the show only as part of a “press run” publicising their latest project.It marks a shift in the media hierarchy and underlines YouTube’s muscle. The platform’s rise has become so all-consuming in the TV world that Pedro Pina, YouTube’s head for Europe, the Middle East and Africa, was invited to give the keynote MacTaggart lecture at the Edinburgh TV festival last week, the industry’s most important get-together of the year.Pina used the speech to insist YouTube was “not the villain” about to destroy the TV industry, though he made clear the age of monopoly for TV networks was over.Sure enough, the temptation of having total creative control – as well as scooping up the ads, sponsors and brand deals that can follow – is now enticing more established media names to try their luck on YouTube.The presenterHolly Willoughbylaunched her YouTube channel over the summer, amassing 22,000 subscribers so far. Amol Rajan will finish as a presenter of BBC Radio 4’s Today programme this week and launch a YouTube show, The Amol Rajan Connection. The road from TV personality to YouTuber is already well established in the US.Yet in a media world that continues to converge, Dimoldenberg is moving in the other direction, seeking success in conventional movies and television. She is writing a teen drama for the BBC, similar to the showSkins, which ran for seven series on E4.She is also writing a Hollywood romcom, in which she will star as a journalist who finds romance with a celebrity after interviewing them. Other than the chicken, it is a plot that sounds close to home.“It’s a character that I’ve been playing half my life, so I feel like I know it very well,” she said. “It’s definitely just an exaggeration of who I am.”Explore more on these topicsYouTubeEdinburgh International Television FestivalTalk showsTelevision industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Future Starts With Us by Gordon Brown review – the ex-PM’s recipe for beating populism | Politics books | The Guardian
description: Global crises are tightly linked to how we treat each other at the local level, argues this optimistic book
Author: Gaby Hinsliff
Headline: Global crises are tightly linked to how we treat each other at the local level, argues this optimistic book
Content: Gordon BrownPhotograph: Margaret Mitchell/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGordon BrownPhotograph: Margaret Mitchell/The GuardianPolitics booksReviewThe Future Starts With Us by Gordon Brown review – the ex-PM’s recipe for beating populismGlobal crises are tightly linked to how we treat each other at the local level, argues this optimistic bookGaby HinsliffMon 31 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn times of crisis, there is one person to whom the left still turns for guidance.More than a decade and a half after leaving government,Gordon Brownhas mellowed into the Labour party’s favourite wise elder; one who has never disappointed the faithful by going off to make a ton of money, remaining quietly committed to public service and deeply engaged with the world’s knottier problems. Having successfully led the global response to the financial crash of 2008, and advocated powerfully during the pandemic for global cooperation against the virus, he was never going to simply sit back and shrug as the world spiralled into conflict and chaos under Donald Trump.But still, I thought, as I opened his latest book on the collapse of the old world order, it’s barely three years since his last tome on fixing the general mess (Permacrisis, written with the economists Mohammed El-Erian and Michael Spence). Does he really have anything new to say, or is this prolific output born mostly out of frustration that the world has seemingly stopped listening?A bit of both, it turns out. The new twist involves some polling commissioned to back Brown’s hunch that deep down voters actually crave a return to the more stable, orderly, benevolent world of the 2000s, despite voting repeatedly for the opposite. But to reach this research, readers must first wade through multiple chapters ramming home once again what’s wrong with the world, which will have many readers nodding in agreement without telling them much they didn’t already know. What could have been a deep, rich essay thus becomes a book: essentially a sermon on the moral failings of neoliberalism, ending in a rousing hymn to hope, echoing both the rhythm of his best party conference speeches and the broad themes of Andy Burnham’s first few weeks in power. (So much so, indeed, that you wonder how much the two men have been talking lately.)What is new for Brown, however, is that this book is preoccupied less with economics than with the argument that collapsing civic ties – the fact that we’re less likely now than a generation ago to be part of a club, trade union, church or community group – have helped undermine “the very idea that we are all in this together, that there are common causes worth fighting for”.What could be just another nostalgic, even reactionary, argument for a bygone age when everyone knew their neighbours is tempered by Brown’s willingness to acknowledge that much of this togetherness was built on the unpaid labour of women stuck at home. But it’s also brought up to date by his argument that this fraying of social bonds – especially in towns fallen on hard times, now leaning towards populist politicians – is actively connected to fragmentation and the retreat from multilateralism on the world stage. It’s time, he argues, to stop treating breakdown at home and breakup abroad as separate phenomena.Beating populism obviously means tackling the economic grievances – the disappearing jobs and hollowed-out high streets – on which it feeds in post-industrial communities across the US and Europe. Yet the general rolling chaos that populists tend to unleash on the world stage makes it actively harder for everyone else to build stable and prosperous economies, creating a vicious circle of decline.Brown’s answer is to build a virtuous circle instead, from the ground up. Strengthening civic ties should make people feel less lonely, more secure and trusting, and thus hopefully more relaxed about their governments acting generously and collaboratively at an international level. That, of course, is key to tackling everything from the climate crisis, to global poverty, to forming the kind of alliances with other middle-ranking powers that might prevent a country like the UK being totally steamrollered in a standoff between the US and China. At least, that’s the theory.The idea that dying high streets at home and rogue superpowers overseas are different threads of the same great unravelling does at least create a clear narrative hook on which a new Labour prime minister can hang lots of otherwise seemingly disparate ideas, and seek political buy-in for them both in the “red wall” and among big-city liberals. There’s material here too for a foreign secretary capable – as Ed Miliband arguably is – of thinking big and acting local, connecting foreign policy much more closely to progress at home. But just how plausible is it?Enter the new polling, of 32,000 people across 20 developed countries, from Argentina to the UK to South Korea. It distinguishes between “zero sum” thinkers – people who believe they can only win if others lose, colouring their attitudes to everything from trade to immigration – and a more generous “civic core”, open to some compromise for the greater good, on whom progressive governments depend. In the UK, at least, the latter group still outweighs the former, with a significant group lying between the two that Brown reckons could be persuaded to heed the better angels of their natures.He then calculates the impact of measures like reducing economic grievances, or increasing people’s face-to-face interaction with others from different religious or racial backgrounds, on propensity to vote for populists. To cut a long story short: deploy all the virtuous circle measures together, and with luck (and time), you might have a potent means of tackling populism from the ground up.Rather less convincing, however, is his formula for restoring the international rules-based order, starting with a new universal charter to which responsible countries could sign up. We already have plenty of grand statements of intent and bodies to enforce them, from the international criminal court to the Paris climate change accords: what’s missing is governments prepared to actually stick to the rules.Unusually for Brown, the best of this book isn’t in the big-picture thinking on globalisation or the rise of China, but in lessons learned at neighbourhood level. After a life spent trying to push through huge decisions, he writes, only recently has he begun thinking that he should have started small.One obvious hurdle is that the neighbourly civic engagement he favours is of the decidedly muscular, worthy kind. The clubs Brown sees as capable of teaching “active citizenship” are those that demand the most time and effort from volunteers – and they have died out. Just signing up for fun times doesn’t count. Like the good son of the manse he is, Brown personally practises what he preaches in Kirkcaldy, where he is heavily engaged with local charities. I’m not sure your average Briton, spending their downtime from work scrolling exhaustedly on the sofa, will feel the same.Then again Brown does say that cynicism like mine is part of the problem; that if liberal politics is to compete with demagogues, it can’t simply confine itself to the art of the possible – it must “show it can make the desirable possible”. Even if, just occasionally, that sounds like wishful thinking.The Future Starts With Us by Gordon Brown is published by Simon & Schuster (£25). To support the Guardian order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsPolitics booksGordon BrownEconomicsSociety booksreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Gems, ghosts and GTA VI: the biggest video games for autumn 2026 | Games | The Guardian
description: There are juggernauts and indie gems aplenty for when the nights draw in, from an ingenious puzzle game to blockbusters such as Marvel’s Wolverine and Call of Duty
Author: Jordan Erica Webber
Headline: There are juggernauts and indie gems aplenty for when the nights draw in, from an ingenious puzzle game to blockbusters such as Marvel’s Wolverine and Call of Duty
Content: Work to be done … There Are No Ghosts at the Grand and GTA VI.Composite: Guardian Design/Friday Sundae/Rockstar GamesView image in fullscreenWork to be done … There Are No Ghosts at the Grand and GTA VI.Composite: Guardian Design/Friday Sundae/Rockstar GamesAutumn arts preview 2026GamesGems, ghosts and GTA VI: the biggest video games for autumn 2026There are juggernauts and indie gems aplenty for when the nights draw in, from an ingenious puzzle game to blockbusters such as Marvel’s Wolverine and Call of DutySee all of our unmissable autumn arts recommendations hereKeith StuartandJordan Erica WebberMon 31 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTShareOnimusha: Way of the SwordAfter 20 years away, Capcom’s hyper kinetic action adventure returns, pitting skilled samurai Miyamoto Musashi against hordes of warriors and demons in Edo-period Kyoto. Master the complex combat then prepare for flashing blades, disembodied limbs and geysers of spraying blood.4 September; PC, PS5, Switch 2, XboxScreenboundBilled as the first ever 5D platformer, Screenbound has you navigating a 3D landscape while simultaneously playing an on-screen handheld console, which contains a 2D mirror world. Everything you do in one affects the other in mind-bending ways. The most ingenious puzzle game we’ve seen in a long time.10 September; PC, PS5, XboxView image in fullscreenMind-bending originality … Screenbound.Photograph: Crescent Moon GamesMarvel’s WolverineThe team behind the brilliant Marvel’s Spider-Man titles is back with a very different kind of hero. The open-world New York setting is gone in favour of a globe-trotting narrative following Logan on his quest to protect vulnerable mutants. The visuals are gorgeous, while the slick combat brings literal meaning to the term bleeding edge.15 September; PS5Fire Emblem: Fortune’s WeaveThe tactical role-playing adventure series returns to the realm explored in the acclaimedFire Emblem: Three Houses. This time, hopeful contestants arrive at the glorious city of Dagsion to compete in a contest where the winner is granted a single wish. Deep combat, lush settings and fraught relationships are guaranteed.17 September; Switch 2Silent Hill: TownfallSilent Hill comes to the east coast of Scotland in a beautifully gloomy new horror adventure. You play as Simon Ordell, returning to a quiet harbour town with no memory of whatever catastrophe has taken place there. The place seems abandoned, but you are not alone for long …24 September; PC, PS5View image in fullscreenBeautiful gloom … Silent Hill: Townfall.Photograph: Screen BurnControl ResonantRemedy Entertainment sets out to disprove the notion that all video game sequels are more of the same. This follow-up to the successful2019 sci-fi shooterhas a new lead character with supernatural powers, a whole new role-playing adventure feel, and a fresh take on Manhattan, where a reality-bending monster awaits …24 September; PC, PS5, XboxRatatanThe latest gorgeously strange game from Patapon creator Hiroyuki Kotani is a rhythm action platformer set in a colourful world where enemies are defeated with songs and players can work together to produce devastating melodies. Imagine Dead Cells merged with PaRappa the Rapper and you’re getting close.15 October; PC, PS, Switch, XboxCall of Duty: Modern Warfare 4The world-beating mega shooter packs its bags full of guns, grenades and macho dialogue and heads for Korea, in another Modern Warfare instalment. There will be epic battles, sanitised politically adjacent themes and rip-roaring online multiplayer – plus, moustached SAS figurehead Captain Price will be tagging along for the ride. Resistance is futile.23 October; PC, PS5, Switch 2, XboxGrand Theft Auto VIAfter a decade in development and several delays, Rockstar’s entertainment behemoth returns, following loved-up criminals Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos as they take on every scumbag Vice City has to offer. Already looking vibrant, expansive and lascivious, this is Bonnie and Clyde for the digital generation.19 November; PS5, XboxThere are No Ghosts at the GrandChris David has inherited a grand old hotel, but now there’s work to be done renovating the decrepit building during the day and then exorcising unwanted ghosts into the night. Like all old English buildings, this charming game is filled with secrets and puzzles, and of course there will be ancestral revelations aplenty.TBC: PC, Xbox

title: Tilda Swinton’s blast from the past, Kevin Bridges at large and a deepfake ballet: theatre, comedy and dance to see this autumn | Stage | The Guardian
description: Swinton takes a dead man’s identity, Glasgow’s heir to Billy Connolly heads on tour and Gillian Anderson, Keira Knightley and Natalia Osipova all hit the stage
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Swinton takes a dead man’s identity, Glasgow’s heir to Billy Connolly heads on tour and Gillian Anderson, Keira Knightley and Natalia Osipova all hit the stage
Content: Kevin Bridges tours his standup show and Tilda Swinton stars in Manfred Karge’s Man to Man.Composite: Guardian Design/Andy Hollingworth/Sølve SundsbøView image in fullscreenKevin Bridges tours his standup show and Tilda Swinton stars in Manfred Karge’s Man to Man.Composite: Guardian Design/Andy Hollingworth/Sølve SundsbøAutumn arts preview 2026StageTilda Swinton’s blast from the past, Kevin Bridges at large and a deepfake ballet: theatre, comedy and dance to see this autumnSwinton takes a dead man’s identity, Glasgow’s heir to Billy Connolly heads on tour and Gillian Anderson, Keira Knightley and Natalia Osipova all hit the stageSee all of our unmissable autumn arts recommendations hereTheatre picksArifa Akbar. Comedy picksBrian Logan. Dance picksLyndsey WinshipMon 31 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTShareTheatreBloodsport: After Helen of TroyAva Pickett has an impressive track record of imaginative historical dramas, including her award-winning Tudor-era play1536, which had a West End run this year.Alongside co-writing a film about Joan of Arc with Baz Luhrmann, she has reconceived this ancient epic, with Michelle Dockery playing Helen returning to war-ravaged Troy.Theatre Royal Stratford East, London, 3 September-10 OctoberMan to ManAt the Edinburgh festival in 1987, Tilda Swinton played a German widow who takes on the identity of her dead husband in a prose poem by the Berliner Ensemble’s Manfred Karge. Almost 40 years later, she returns to the role of Ella/Max in a revised version, again directed by Stephen Unwin.Royal Court theatre, London, 5 September-24 October.Traverse theatre, Edinburgh, 29 October-7 NovemberThe Standard of LivingView image in fullscreenPriceless … Thomas Flynn, Rory Kinnear and Natalia Osipova star in The Standard of LivingWhat greater “event theatre” than a new James Graham play? This one brings a twist to Keynesian economics. Directed by Nicholas Hytner, it stars Rory Kinnear as John Maynard Keynes and explores his relationship with the Bloomsbury group and his impact on arts funding. Royal Ballet principal Natalia Osipova co-stars, making her West End debut.Theatre Royal Haymarket, London, 21 September-12 DecemberWho’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?The celebrification of the West End continues apace with this version of Edward Albee’s 1962 play, bringing two starry screen talents together, although both Gillian Anderson and Billy Crudup have proved themselves on stage before now. Directed by Marianne Elliott, they will engage in toxic slanging matches, psychological warfare and marital meltdown.@sohoplace, London, 21 September-19 DecemberI’ll Be Seeing YouView image in fullscreenRhinestones guaranteed … Simon Russell Beale in rehearsals for I'll Be Seeing You.Photograph: Olivia Attwooll-KeithThere is much to excite about this world premiere – a meta Martin Sherman play about the flamboyant pianist Liberace, with Simon Russell Beale taking the lead role. Fra Fee co-stars in the production directed by Alan Cumming and Ben Occhipinti. It promises rhinestones aplenty.Pitlochry Festival theatre, 22 September-11 OctoberAs You Like ItAn all-male production of Shakespeare’s pastoral comedy comes amid some striking gender reversals at the RSC – Harriet Walter is also reprising her Brutus in Phyllida Lloyd’s all-femaleJulius Caesar. This show, directed by Daniel Evans, features Tony award-winner Jonathan Groff as Rosalind and the talented Fisayo Akinade as Celia.Royal Shakespeare theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon, 26 September-7 NovemberView image in fullscreenEagerly awaited … Inua Ellams.Photograph: Dave Benett/Getty ImagesOnce Upon a Time in SokotoPoet-playwright Inua Ellams earned enormous praise forBarber Shop Chroniclesand his adaptation of Chekhov’sThree Sisters. His Alfred Fagon award-winning drama sounds promising, with the exploration of an unlikely friendship between an enslaved woman and her former master in the lead-up to the formation of Nigeria.Royal & Derngate, Northampton, 28 September-10 October.Touring until 13 FebruaryKing LearView image in fullscreenDavid Threlfall will perform as King Lear at the Royal Exchange, Manchester.Illustration: David StewartThere is more than one big-name Lear in store this autumn. Ian McKellen takes on the role (again!) in Simon Stephens’s radically re-spun production at the Yard in east London,opening in November, while David Threlfall returns to Manchester’s Royal Exchange after almost three decades in director Matthew Dunster’s reimagined adaptation for the theatre’s 50th anniversary.Royal Exchange theatre, Manchester, 2 October-15 NovemberBalloon GirlLouisa Maud Evans, otherwise known as Mademoiselle Albertina, was a young Welsh firebrand who died while parachuting during a balloon flight at the Cardiff Exhibition of 1896. Writer-director Hannah McPake creates an upbeat adventure that honours her spirit of curiosity and endeavour.Sherman theatre, Cardiff, 9-24 OctoberThe Lives of OthersView image in fullscreenHigh stakes … Stephen Dillane, Keira Knightley and Luke Thompson in The Lives of Others.Photograph: Oliver Rosser, Feast CreativeKeira Knightley and Stephen Dillane star in an adaptation of Florian Henckel von Donnersmarck’s 2006 film, a high-stakes love story set in Stasi-era east Germany. It may follow the trend for transposing hit films to the stage but is helmed by Robert Icke, who at his best makes old stories blazingly new.Adelphi theatre, London, 14 October-9 JanuaryComedySam CampbellThe success of Channel 4’s oddball mockumentaryMake That Movie, and his stint on Amazon hit Last One Laughing, broadcast more widely what insiders have long known: Aussie act Sam Campbell is one of comedy’s most unpredictable talents. Touring set Kid Giblet offers new fans a glimpse of the indelible live experience.Bristol Beacon, 31 August. Touring until 1 DecemberKevin BridgesHaving unfussily built a reputation as one of the UK’s greatest live standups, and off the back of his acclaimed World Cup curtain-raiser on the telly, In Search of the Beautiful Game, Glasgow’s heir to Billy Connolly returns with his keenly awaited new tour, Here If You Need Me.Eventim Apollo, London, 1-3 September. Touring until 20 FebruaryFlo & JoanView image in fullscreenKeyed up … Flo and JoanNot many comedy acts ascend to the next level by absenting themselves from the stage. Musical duo Flo & Joan (AKA Rosie and Nicola Dempsey) managed it with One Man Musical, their for-the-ages bio showabout a certain West End composer. In With Feeling, a new suite of comic songs, the pair return to their own spotlight.Gala theatre, Durham, 19 September. Touring until 12 DecemberAhir ShahAfter winning the Edinburgh comedy award three summers ago, then conquering Netflix, with a counterintuitive and feelgood show about multicultural Britain and his family history, the Londoner now takes to the road with its follow-up, Golden, inspired (in typical boffinish fashion) by Nietzsche and Gerard Manley Hopkins.Soho theatre, London, 5-17 October.Touring until 14 MarchView image in fullscreenUnlike anyone else … Frankie Thompson: Horrible Things.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianFrankie Thompson“If you laugh, it’s comedy; if you don’t, it’s live art”: so the cult clown-comic (and live artist!) Frankie Thompson describes her new set, Horrible Things. If we can credit her previous, unlike-anyone-else offerings at the Edinburgh fringe and beyond, expect another heart-and-funny-bone-teasing hour of uncategorisable performance.Soho theatre, London, 12-24 OctoberDanceLondon City BalletA mix of revivals, forgotten gems and brand-new choreography is the signature of London City Ballet. Its autumn tour programme differs at each venue, but all shows include a revival of Glen Tetley’s Firebird, marking Tetley’s centenary – his version is about a young woman breaking free from the constraints of her family.York Theatre Royal, 18-19 September. Touring until 24 OctoberJess & Morgs: DeepfakeThe creators of Scottish Ballet’s award-winning Coppélia – which set the classic ballet in an era of AI – return with a new work exploring the possibilities and pitfalls of technology. Using cutting edge tech, the set-up is an interview between a politician and a journalist. The question is: can you tell what’s really real?Jerwood DanceHouse, Ipswich, 25 September.Sadler’s Wells East, London, 1-3 OctoberEnglish National Ballet: Romeo & JulietView image in fullscreenAction-packed ballet … Isaac Hernández as Romeo and Erina Takahashi as Juliet.Photograph: Laurent LiotardoAlmost 50 years have passed since Rudolf Nureyev created his ballet of Romeo & Juliet, a version less often seen in the UK than Kenneth MacMillan’s but just as powerful. It’s a ballet packed with fast-paced steps and heightened drama from the two feuding families plus Prokofiev’s sumptuous, stirring score.Liverpool Empire, 15-17 October. Touring until 24 JanuaryMeet the HatterJust one dancer and a stageful of magical projections is enough to create a wonderland in this multimedia family show from Joss Arnott Dance. Arnott’s take on one of Lewis Carroll’s best-loved characters sees the Mad Hatter turn up for a tea party – but there’s no one there, so his imagination takes over.Pavilion Dance South West, Bournemouth, 24 October. Touring until 26 JuneThe Last HamletParis’s Théâtre de la Ville is dedicating a whole season this autumn to dance-theatre maker Ben Duke, AKA Lost Dog – quite the honour. On home soil, you can see his new work The Last Hamlet, musing on the idea of Hamlet’s last-ever performance, deconstructing Shakespeare’s tragic hero with characteristic wit.Sadler’s Wells East, London, 4-7 November

title: Dolly Parton laid to rest in private Nashville funeral | Dolly Parton | The Guardian
description: The queen of country was interred next to her late husband in an intimate ceremony attended by close family
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: The queen of country was interred next to her late husband in an intimate ceremony attended by close family
Content: Dolly Parton at a Los Angeles event in 2019.Photograph: Mario Anzuoni/ReutersView image in fullscreenDolly Parton at a Los Angeles event in 2019.Photograph: Mario Anzuoni/ReutersDolly PartonDolly Parton laid to rest in private Nashville funeralThe queen of country was interred next to her late husband in an intimate ceremony attended by close familyOwen MyersMon 31 Aug 2026 12.17 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 14.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDolly Partonwas laid to rest in a private ceremony in Nashville on Friday, her family has confirmed.The queen of country music, whodied aged 80 on 25 August“after bravely facing a brief battle with cancer”, was interred at Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum alongside her husband of 60 years, Carl Thomas.From Jolene to Islands in the Stream: Dolly Parton’s 10 best recordingsRead moreParton’s great-niece Lainey Parton wrote onInstagramon Saturday: “I wanted to wait until after my granny was laid to rest yesterday before I tried to put any of this into words.“From the time I was little, my granny always had a way of making me feel like I was enough. She never made my dreams feel too big or made me feel like I couldn’t do something. She believed in me before I even knew how to believe in myself.“Because she couldn’t have kids of her own, she always made us feel like we were hers,” Lainey continued. “She loved us that way, and I’ll forever be grateful for that.”View image in fullscreenDolly Parton’s burial site next to her late husband at Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum in Nashville.Photograph: Tammie Arroyo/AFF-USA/ShutterstockOnly immediate family attended the small ceremony,Peoplereported. Parton had her name engraved on the large mausoleum plaque at the cemetery before she died, as well as an engraving of the cabin in Sevier county, Tennessee, where she grew up.On Saturday, Parton’s niece Jada Star took to the stage at Nashville’s Grand Ole Opry as part of a tribute concert to the country legend. Starperformeda song titled The Orchard that she had recorded with Parton for her 2024 album Smoky Mountain DNA: Family, Faith and Fables.Dolly Parton was a rare singer who proved herself to be an electric movie starRead moreIn anInstagram postahead of the performance, Star said, “I am walking around in a fog of sadness, like all of you have.“I do not take this honor lightly. I will stand on that stage tonight, the stage she loved so much, and share my song I wrote for her and for my whole family.”On Monday, the estate of Parton announced DollyFest, a two-weekend event which will take place in Nashville and London next year. Before her death, Parton had been planning the festival for January 2026 but had to take a step back due to health issues.“As far as a traditional memorial goes, that is not something Dolly wanted,” said Parton’s manager, Danny Nozell, in a press release. “So, instead, it feels more appropriate for us to take a beat, let all the tributes that immediately make sense occur naturally, and then, see through this festival-style concept that was truly dreamed up by Dolly.”View image in fullscreenDolly Parton’s niece Jada Star performs at a tribute to Parton at the Grand Ole Opry, Nashville, Tennessee, on Saturday.Photograph: Seth Herald/ReutersLast week, Parton’s team confirmed that the projects she was working on before her death would continue to be brought to life, including a line of coffee grounds, a home decor collection and a Broadway musical to launch in New York later this year.“Dolly worked up until the day she died,” Nozell said. “As the leader of the team responsible for overseeing her legacy, we will ensure the many dreams she had yet to fulfill are brought to life.”Active projects that Parton was working on at the time of her death also include Dolly Parton’s SongTeller Hotel and Dolly’s Life of Many Colors Museum, which are both scheduled to open next month in Nashville. Meanwhile, Dolly Dolls and a range of Dolly’s Dog Treats are scheduled to be released in the coming months.The family has asked for donations in Parton’s memory to be dedicated toImagination Library, the organization she founded to encourage literacy and the love of reading in children.Explore more on these topicsDolly PartonCountrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Met Gala exhibition honoring John Galliano is cancelled after backlash | John Galliano | The Guardian
description: Fashion designer was convicted of hate crime by French court in 2011 after series of racist and antisemitic remarks
Author: Anna Betts
Headline: Fashion designer was convicted of hate crime by French court in 2011 after series of racist and antisemitic remarks
Content: John Galliano in December 2017.Photograph: Jeff Spicer/BFC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJohn Galliano in December 2017.Photograph: Jeff Spicer/BFC/Getty ImagesJohn GallianoMet Gala exhibition honoring John Galliano is cancelled after backlashFashion designer was convicted of hate crime by French court in 2011 after series of racist and antisemitic remarksAnna BettsMon 31 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 15.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe controversial fashion designerJohn Gallianoannounced on Monday that an exhibition honoring his work that New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art had scheduled to open for the upcoming spring’s Met Gala is not going to go forward.The museum’s decision to honor Galliano, who wasconvictedof a hate crime by a French court in 2011after aseries of racist and antisemitic remarks, had drawn controversy and backlash.“After much reflection and discussion with all those involved, I have decided, with great sadness, that it is best for the exhibition not to take place at this time,” Galliano wrote in astatementposted on Instagram on Monday morning.The exhibition, titledJohn Galliano: Horizons, wasannounced in early Augustand was set to have been kicked off by the annual Met Gala.In his statement on Monday saying that the exhibition was off, Galliano wrote: “I remain fully accountable for the pain caused by my words in the past, particularly the hurt I caused to the Jewish and Asian communities, and I remain deeply sorry.“I understand that meaningful atonement is not achieved through an exhibition, institutional recognition or a single public gesture. It is a continuing responsibility, demonstrated through listening, learning and one’s conduct over time.”He also wrote: “I do not want the debate surrounding me to place the Met in a difficult position or distract from the remarkable work of the Costume Institute. I also recognize and respect that an exhibition honoring my work would be painful for some.”In a separatestatementon Monday, the Metropolitan Museum of Art director and chief executive officer, Max Hollein, said: “Following thoughtful discussions with John Galliano, we have together decided not to proceed with the exhibition.”The Met trustee Anna Wintouradded: “John’s decision that the exhibition devoted to his work should not take place at this time is very courageous and a measure of the man he is.“I believe this is the right decision, and both he and the museum have my full support.”TheNew York Timeshad reported on Friday that opposition to the museum’s plans with respect to Galliano had grown in recent days among Jewish leaders in New York City and beyond. The newspaper also reported that some donors had contacted Met executives and threatened to withdraw gifts to the museum if the exhibition went ahead as planned.The New York City council speaker, Julie Menin, alsosent a letterto the Met leadership, calling the museum’s decision to honor Galliano “a mistake”.
