Menin also urged the institution to reconsider.On Monday, Menin wrote on social media: “Museums such as The Met must be held to a high standard of inclusiveness and tolerance, and I am pleased that they have listened to the concerns I have raised and reacted with the right decision.”Menin also described herself as the daughter of a Holocaust survivor and the first Jewish speaker of theNew YorkCity council, saying, “This decision was personal to me, and the Jewish community and I felt a strong obligation to speak out.”TheNew York Timesreported that the Met’s board of trustees had been scheduled to gather on Monday morning to discuss the exhibition.The museum said on Monday that details about “a new spring Costume Institute exhibition and the 2027Met Galawill be announced at a later date”.The remarks which resulted in Galliano’s hate crime conviction in France also led to his being fired as creative director of the famous fashion brand Christian Dior.Explore more on these topicsJohn GallianoMet GalaNew YorknewsShareReuse this content

title: Anthropic sued over alleged theft of ‘tens of thousands’ of songs  | Music industry | The Guardian
description: AI company faces multibillion dollar lawsuit over misuse of copyrighted songs to train Claude models
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: AI company faces multibillion dollar lawsuit over misuse of copyrighted songs to train Claude models
Content: Music publishers have claimed Anthropic’s models ‘scraped’ smash hits including Mariah Carey’s All I Want For Christmas Is You.Photograph: Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for MCView image in fullscreenMusic publishers have claimed Anthropic’s models ‘scraped’ smash hits including Mariah Carey’s All I Want For Christmas Is You.Photograph: Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for MCMusic industryAnthropic sued over alleged theft of ‘tens of thousands’ of songsAI company faces multibillion dollar lawsuit over misuse of copyrighted songs to train Claude modelsDan MilmoGlobal technology editorMon 31 Aug 2026 08.42 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAll AI wants for Christmas is a vast back catalogue of songs without paying for it, according to a multibillion-dollar lawsuit against the startup behind the Claude chatbot.Sony Music Publishing and Warner Chappell, music publishers who manage the copyright of songs on behalf of songwriters and composers, are seeking damages for alleged misuse of “tens of thousands” of copyrighted works byAnthropic.The compositions include Mariah Carey’s All I Want for Christmas is You, Ain’t No Mountain High Enough, originally performed by Marvin Gaye and Tammi Terrell, and Survivor’s Eye of the Tiger.The plaintiffs claim they are victims of “one of the largest and most blatant ongoing thefts of intellectual property in history”.The lawsuit, filed in a California court, targets Anthropic and its chief executive, Dario Amodei, as well as co-founder Benjamin Mann. It alleges the defendants breached copyright law by “torrenting, scraping and downloading” lyrics from copyrighted works to train its family of Claude AI models – as well as reproducing those lyrics in responses to users’ prompts.It claims that Mann and Anthropic downloaded at least 7m copies of books from pirate websites, including the lyrics and sheet music to songs such as Bon Jovi’s Livin’ on a Prayer and Leonard Cohen’s Hallelujah.The figures are from a recent copyright case against Anthropic brought by US authorswhich the company settled for $1.5bn.Thelawsuit, filed on 28 August, was first reported by trade publication Music Business Worldwide. Other songs allegedly having their copyright infringed included Mark Ronson’s Uptown Funk and Katy Perry’s California Gurls.It also claims that Anthropic acquired copies of songs in other ways including scraping lyrics from legal sites like Musixmatch and LyricFind, and datasets on archive sites such as Common Crawl. In another section of the claim, the publishers allege that Anthropic stripped identifying information from songs while processing the texts, which denied copyright owners “valuable attribution” to their work.“Defendants specifically elected to harvest unauthorized copies of Music Publishers’ works so that they would not have to pay Music Publishers a licensing fee to use their works in AI training and development,” said the plaintiffs.The music publishers are seeking damages that could run into billions of dollars, based on a claim of up to $150,000 per infringed piece of work and $25,000 for each removal or alteration of identifying data.The suit implies at least 20,000 works are involved in the suit, referring to the unlawful copying of “tens of thousands of Music Publishers’ copyrighted musical compositions”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEd Newton-Rex, a UK-based composer and campaigner for protecting artists’ copyright, said he was “not surprised” that rights holders were defending themselves against a company with a “history of downloading and training their AI models on huge libraries”.Alongside the authors’ lawsuit, Anthropic has also faced claims from Universal Music Group and Concord Music Group.In a separate case this month, AI music generator Suno lost a copyright infringement case against German licensing agency GEMA, which alleged illegal use of songs including Boney M’s Daddy Cool to train its technology.A spokesperson for Anthropic, which is preparing for a stockmarket listing that could value the company at $2tn, said: “We disagree with the publishers’ claims and we intend to defend ourselves robustly in court.”Explore more on these topicsMusic industryAnthropicAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: Tupac Shakur murder trial: jury begins deliberations after hearing closing arguments | Tupac Shakur | The Guardian
description: Former gang leader Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis, 63, is accused of ordering the killing of the hip-hop star in 1996
Author: Gabrielle Canon
Headline: Former gang leader Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis, 63, is accused of ordering the killing of the hip-hop star in 1996
Content: Duane Davis enters the courtroom during his murder trial, related to the 1996 killing of rapper Tupac Shakur, in Las Vegas, Nevada, on 27 August 2026.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDuane Davis enters the courtroom during his murder trial, related to the 1996 killing of rapper Tupac Shakur, in Las Vegas, Nevada, on 27 August 2026.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesTupac ShakurTupac Shakur murder trial: jury begins deliberations after hearing closing argumentsFormer gang leader Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis, 63, is accused of ordering the killing of the hip-hop star in 1996Gabrielle CanonandRoque PlanasMon 31 Aug 2026 17.42 EDTFirst published on Mon 31 Aug 2026 09.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Las Vegas jury is now deliberating after hearing closing arguments in the trial of the South Side Compton Crips gang leader Duane “Keffe D” Davis, who is accused of ordering the murder of hip-hop legendTupac Shakur.Davis, 63, is accused of leading a group of men to kill Shakur in retaliation for the beating of his nephew, though not of pulling the trigger himself. Davis has pleaded not guilty.Police said they long suspected Davis, but did not have enough evidence to ​charge him until he went public with his ‌story in media appearances and a memoir he published in 2019. The book, as well as tapes of secret meetings with investigators, make up most of the prosecution’s case.Over the weeks-long trial, Marc DiGiacomo, the Clark county district attorney, and Binu Palal, the chief deputy district attorney, brought 25 witnesses to the stand – including some who had to be ordered by the court because they were reluctant to testify.During the proceedings, Davis’s attorney, Michael Sanft, tried to frame the stories and statements as the exaggerated and embellished claims of a man hoping to benefit from the public interest and unanswered questions around Shakur’s murder.In the final moments of the trial, prosecutors hammered home their arguments that Davis called the shots for the attack on Shakur that night based on Davis’s own statements.Palal told jurors on Monday that Davis ​wanted revenge after Shakur’s entourage beat up his nephew, Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson, in the lobby of the MGM Grand casino and hotel on 7 September 1996. Anderson, who died two years later in an unrelated shootout, was a member of a rival gang in Compton, California.“So ‌what did [Davis] do? He acquired a firearm, got his group together, and went hunting for Mr Shakur,” Palal said.Davis’s defense attorney, however, questioned the integrity of theLas Vegasmetropolitan police department’s investigation, describing its officers as “dirty”. Sanft portrayed his client’s book as a fictionalized, and at least partially ghost-written, account that could not be taken as a factual confession.“What did he really confess to that was true?” Sanft said.Sanft showed the jury video footage of Davis appearing confused by an interviewer’s questions about whether he and others with him were carrying guns the night of Shakur’s murder.“Does that sound like someone who wrote his own book?” Sanft said.But DiGiacomo, the county prosecutor, said during rebuttal that the case was a “slam dunk” and that Davis’s only defense was to hope that the jury members “somehow don’t believe a fully corroborated confession”.“Go and read his book if you want, you will not be smarter for it,” DiGiacomo said. “He shouldn’t be out there profiting on a murder in our jurisdiction.”“Mr Davis is attempting to escape responsibility for a crime everybody knows he committed, even him and he admits to it – for seven or eight times over the course of 30 years and there’s no evidence contradicting that fact,” DiGiacomo added. “Hold him accountable to the crime he committed.”Davis sat stone-faced through closing arguments.Prosecutors have argued Davis’s story is generally consistent and that he has essentially admitted to arranging Shakur’s killing, which under Nevada law is enough to be charged with murder. Prosecutors played eight hours of recordings, taken from four separate events in different years, during which Davis shared in his own words what happened the night of the shooting.Shakur and the founder of his label, Marion “Suge” Knight, had attended a Mike Tyson boxing match at the casino when the altercation with Anderson took place, and were on their way to an after-party. A white Cadillac pulled up next to them while they were stopped at a red light, and someone in that car began shooting, according to investigators.In his book, Davis claimed to have been in that car, and that he had brought a .40-caliber Glock with him. “Them jumping on my nephew gave us the green light to want to do something to their ass,” he wrote. “Pac chose the wrong game to play.”At the trial earlier this month,prosecutors played a 2008 recordingof Davis telling detectives that he handed a pistol to his nephew Anderson, who fired the shots that killed Shakur.Anderson died in a 1998 shootoutin Compton, California. The two other men in the car have since died as well.While the trial has finally come to an end, family members had been left to wonder for years why it took so long for investigators to reach a conclusion in the case.“We’ve been waiting 30 years to grieve properly,” Zayd Akinyela, Shakur’s cousin, told reporters outside the courtroom when the trial was under way. “A lot of people don’t get to grieve until they understand what happened to their loved one and how it happened.”Reuters and the Associated Press contributedreportingExplore more on these topicsTupac ShakurLas VegasLaw (US)newsShareReuse this content

title: Les Siècles/Lehmann La Damnation de Faust review – vivid colour, soaring solos and a sharp-suited demon | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: Period instrument grain and an energised Jakob Lehmann did a fair job with Berlioz’s concert setting of the drama, but the hall’s murky acoustic buried some of the sparkle
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: Period instrument grain and an energised Jakob Lehmann did a fair job with Berlioz’s concert setting of the drama, but the hall’s murky acoustic buried some of the sparkle
Content: ‘All black suit, scarlet tie and eyebrows’ … Gerald Finley  as Méphistophélès in Berlioz’s La Damnation de Faust, conducted by Jakob Lehmann.Photograph: Mark AllanView image in fullscreen‘All black suit, scarlet tie and eyebrows’ … Gerald Finley  as Méphistophélès in Berlioz’s La Damnation de Faust, conducted by Jakob Lehmann.Photograph: Mark AllanProms 2026ReviewLes Siècles/Lehmann La Damnation de Faust review – vivid colour, soaring solos and a sharp-suited demonRoyal Albert Hall, LondonPeriod instrument grain and an energised Jakob Lehmann did a fair job with Berlioz’s concert setting of the drama, but the hall’s murky acoustic buried some of the sparkleErica JealMon 31 Aug 2026 09.18 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 10.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBerlioz wrote hissetting of the Faust storyfor concert performance, counting on the fact that what went on in his audience’s mind’s eye would be more fantastical than anything that could be portrayed on stage. The forces he employed aren’t on the same scale as those for his Requiem – written almost a decade earlier, in 1837, andheard here earlier this month– but are still huge. Here they came in the form of the period-instrument orchestra Les Siècles, plus the Choeur de Radio France and, joining in the closing five minutes, the Radio France children’s choir – conducted byJakob Lehmann, making an energised Proms debut.Les Siècles’ period instruments brought their own grainy texture to the palette, from the chattering piccolos representing Méphistophélès’s malignant spirits and the silky violin swoops lulling Faust to sleep, down to the inclusion in the orchestra of an ophicleide, an instrument that’s an evolutionary dead end on the tuba’s family tree. The Hungarian March sounded snappy, as did the brass fanfares, echoed at one point by a small band up in the gallery.View image in fullscreenRadiant  … Véronique Gens as Marguerite in La Damnation de Faust.Photograph: Mark AllanYet alongside the vividly colourful passages were some that made you wish you could pick the performance up and put it down in a different, less tricky venue. In this very particular hall, Berlioz’s teemingly detailed music often needed more space from Lehmann or a crisper, more forensic approach to ensemble. As it was, the palette at times turned murky, the accompanying figures merging into a blur. And while it was in some ways a treat to hear the choral music sung so well – the Choeur de Radio France was 80-strong, and you rarely get to hear a professional choir on that scale – their well-blended sound didn’t always cut ideally through the orchestra.The soloists were a strong team, with John Osborn’s tenor soaring incisively yet smoothly up to the heights in the title role, the soprano Véronique Gens singing especially radiantly in Marguerite’s first aria, and Thomas Dolié dispatching Brander’s drinking song with vigour. But it was Gerald Finley’s entrances as Méphistophélès – all black suit, scarlet tie and eyebrows – that made the dramatic aspect of this legend come alive.Available on BBC Soundsuntil 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsProms 2026Choral musicClassical musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Performance and belonging: Rio de Janeiro’s ballroom scene – photo essay | World news | The Guardian
description: A look at the ballroom scene across Maré, Lapa, Gamboa and the city centre. The photographer Juliana Bizzo has documented a movement born from Black and Latinx LGBTQ+ communities in the US that has more recently evolved in Rio, growing from the city’s first ball in 2016
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A look at the ballroom scene across Maré, Lapa, Gamboa and the city centre. The photographer Juliana Bizzo has documented a movement born from Black and Latinx LGBTQ+ communities in the US that has more recently evolved in Rio, growing from the city’s first ball in 2016
Content: Lua Brainer vogues during Ocupação Noite das Estrelas, an artistic project celebrating LGBTQIAPN+ memory and presence in Maré. Photograph: Juliana BizzoA look at the ballroom scene across Maré, Lapa, Gamboa and the city centre. The photographer Juliana Bizzo has documented a movement born from Black and Latinx LGBTQ+ communities in the US that has more recently evolved in Rio, growing from the city’s first ball in 2016ByJuliana BizzoMon 31 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy first encounter with Rio de Janeiro’s ballroom scene was in 2023, during Noite das Estrelas, an artistic occupation that moved through the streets of Maré. From the top of a sound truck, the performer and drag queen Preta Queen B Rull, of the Kiki House of Mamba Negra, sang as people followed her through the neighbourhood. Before we had even reached our destination, the procession had changed the rhythm of the street.View image in fullscreenPreta Queen B Rull performs from a sound truck during Noite das Estrelas.View image in fullscreenTainá Mattos (known as Princess Tai Ninja in the Mainstream scene and Legendary Tai Lafond in the Kiki scene) performs during the ball that concluded the Ocupação Noite das Estrelas in Maré.At the end of the day, two rows of people shouted, pressed against one another and took photographs, forming a runway inside a warehouse. I had gone simply to watch, but I had my camera in my bag. I did not know whether to admire, photograph or try to understand what I was seeing: dance, fashion, performance, movements I did not yet know how to name. I left certain that I would return.That day, I learnt that photographing a ball demands quick decisions: hesitate, and the moment disappears. But what drew me back was the energy between the runway and the people gathered around it, the shouts for the houses, the response of the crowd, the vibration that seemed to pass through the body. After attending many balls, this has never become ordinary to me. What I feel there is a force built from presence and belonging, as if, for a few hours, no one has to make themselves smaller in order to fit into the world.View image in fullscreenVitória Jovem, wearing a mirrored visor, joins others at the Noite das Estrelas ball.Ballroom culture began to take shape in New York between the late 1960s and the 1970s. It was created by Black and Latinx LGBTQ+ people in response to racism and exclusion within drag pageants. Organised into houses, chosen families that provide guidance and support, participants compete at balls in categories involving dance, fashion, performance and gender expression.In Rio, the scene began to organise around 2015 and 2016 through voguing and exchanges with pioneers from other Brazilian states. Conferência das Bruxas, held in May 2016, is locally recognised as the first ball in the state of Rio de Janeiro. The House of Cazul and the House of Kínisi later played pioneering roles in consolidating house culture in the region. Since then, the scene has developed according to Rio’s own geographies and rhythms, incorporating funk, carnival, the cultures of the city’s peripheries and local political struggles.View image in fullscreenParticipants and audience members cheer for friends competing in the Transconexão Ball.Names also indicate belonging and position within the ballroom. Members often adopt the name of their house as a surname, while 007 identifies someone who is not affiliated with a house. Mother, Father, Prince and Princess designate positions within a house; Legendary recognises a sustained record of excellence, influence and contribution to the scene. Because the Kiki and mainstream circuits have their own houses and systems of recognition, the same person may use different names and titles in each.I have watched the scene attract larger audiences, enter higher-profile cultural venues and expand into other parts of Rio. But this does not mean leaving the periphery behind.View image in fullscreenAzch 007 Kiki (left) works on a costume with Mother Rebecaza de Ra, in preparation for Pajuball.I usually arrive while the venue is still empty. I prefer to observe and follow what unfolds. I photograph at close range because the spaces are generally small, although the audiences continue to grow. I allow flashes, arms, heads and mobile phones into the frame. They are part of the scene and do not disturb me.Before Pajuball, Azch 007 Kiki was helping a close friend, Mother Rebecaza de Ra Kiki Colombia, finish her outfit. Azch told me that the two had not seen each other for three years, while Rebecaza was living in Colombia. They had first met at a ball, later discovered that they were neighbours and became best friends. That evening, Rebecaza wore the outfit and won the grand prize.View image in fullscreenMadah Sodré, a member of the House of La Bella Mafia, wears an outfit made from materials discarded after carnival.I also photographed the House of La Bella Mafia at Sustenta Carnaval, a project created by Mariana Pinho, artistic director of Gandaia Arts. The project collects costumes discarded after carnival and puts them back into use, preventing them from ending up in landfill. Madah Sodré, who was responsible for the creative direction of the shoot, stepped into the street wearing one of the looks she had just created. At that moment, a VLT tram passed and the passengers turned to look at her.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenKill Bill Balenciaga (left) performing during the Pink & White Mainstream Ball, and Vitória Jovem walking in the Runway category as part of Presença Festival at Circo Voador, in LapaView image in fullscreenLua Brainer Kiki, a femme queen, during Ocupação Noite das Estrelas.In Maré, Legendary Lua Brainer Kiki represents another form of continuity. Born and raised in the area, she and Kill Bill Balenciaga help to build the local scene through Ballroom na Maré, creating spaces for ballroom culture within Maré itself.View image in fullscreenIn the final image, the ball is already behind them. Outside, Legendary Runway Vitória Jovem 007, Daniela Raio Klandestina, Legendary Vini Ventania 007 and others talk and laugh before heading in different directions. My work is also moving in that direction: beyond the runway, towards the everyday lives of the houses and the relationships that make a performance possible. I will keep returning because I want to understand what remains when the runway disappears.Explore more on these topicsThe Guardian picture essayAmericasPhotographyBrazilShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Judi Dench and Ian McKellen share stories, secrets and a little mischief | Television | The Guardian
description: The stage and screen legends reminisce over tea. Plus: Fred Sirieix checks into one of Marrakech’s grandest hotels. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Priya Elan
Headline: The stage and screen legends reminisce over tea. Plus: Fred Sirieix checks into one of Marrakech’s grandest hotels. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Pure gold … Ian McKellen in Tea With Judi Dench.Photograph: Mindhouse/PAView image in fullscreenPure gold … Ian McKellen in Tea With Judi Dench.Photograph: Mindhouse/PATV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Judi Dench and Ian McKellen share stories, secrets and a little mischiefThe stage and screen legends reminisce over tea. Plus: Fred Sirieix checks into one of Marrakech’s grandest hotels. Here’s what to watch this eveningPriya Elan,Phil Harrison,Hollie Richardson,Jack SealeandSimon WardellMon 31 Aug 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTea With Judi Dench9pm, Sky ArtsJudi and her potty-mouthed parrot Sweetheart invite Ian McKellen for a natter in the return of this charming show. Ian reminds her of when they first met, performing a play in 1967, and how Judi saved him from stage fright. Then it’s a warm, naughty hour as they share anecdotes about Ann Summers knickers, ponder the future (Judi’s eyesight is now very bad) and watch a clip of cinema flopCats: “I was frightful in the film,” says Judi. Pure gold with two icons.Hollie RichardsonMillionaire Hot Seat7.30pm, ITV1The new season of the accelerated version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? opens with six new hopefuls (sadly there’s no “Coughing Major”). The tighter format means that contestants don’t have time to doubt themselves as they ascend the money ladder. And if they get a multiple-choice question wrong, they will be eliminated.Priya ElanThe Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo8pm, BBC OneView image in fullscreenAnswering the call … Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo at Edinburgh Castle.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianRebus star Richard Rankin narrates the annual bonanza at Edinburgh Castle, which takes on the theme A Call to Gather. Expect Highland dancers, a ceremonial performance from the RAF’s King’s Colour Squadron, international music and, of course, lots of bagpipes.HRFred’s Ultimate Hotels8pm, Channel 4Fred Sirieix embarks on a luxurious new travel series, starting in Marrakech. He checks into – and has a go at being the general manager of – the exclusive Royal Mansour hotel, where the personal service is impeccable and the hammams are opulent. Then he leaves the site to check out some souks and fly in a hot-air balloon.Jack SealeMy Life Is Murder8pm, U&AlibiA lawyer is killed at an elite pub quiz, which calls for investigator Alexa Crow and sidekick Madison to – you’ve guessed it – go undercover and schmooze with the wealthy suspects. They’re a competitive bunch with a lot of history behind them, so the pair have got their work cut out before the night is over.HR24 Hours in A&E9pm, Channel 4There’s some brilliant detective work in Queen’s medical centre, Nottingham. Claire has arrived in the unit after collapsing during a run. Her case seems straightforward but doctor David has noticed something very troubling in the results of a routine blood test. As ever, impressive and affirming.Phil HarrisonFilm choiceView image in fullscreenFlair to spare … Milla Jovovich in The Fifth Element.Photograph: Gaumont/Sportsphoto/AllstarThe Fifth Element (Luc Besson, 1997), 7pm, Sky Sci-FiGiven that one of the first sci-fi films was French (Georges Méliès’ A Trip to the Moon, 1902), it’s a pity there have been so few great ones from the country since. But Luc Besson’s hyperactive movie should be up for consideration. Bruce Willis plays a cabby in 23rd-century New York who finds himself in an end-of-days race against time when he meets the “ultimate warrior”, Leeloo (Milla Jovovich), who was created to defeat an evil entity. Featuring costumes by Jean Paul Gaultier, it’s got flair and wit to spare.Simon WardellLive sportSnooker: British Open,12.30pm, Channel 5The first round from the Centaur in Cheltenham.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightJudi DenchIan McKellenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Switzy by Emma Cline review – this Booker-listed account of a man’s last days is profoundly moving | Fiction | The Guardian
description: Struggling with Alzheimer’s, the central character sets out on his final journey to a euthanasia clinic
Author: Chris Power
Headline: Struggling with Alzheimer’s, the central character sets out on his final journey to a euthanasia clinic
Content: Journey’s end … Emma Cline.Photograph: PRView image in fullscreenJourney’s end … Emma Cline.Photograph: PRBook of the dayFictionReviewSwitzy by Emma Cline review – this Booker-listed account of a man’s last days is profoundly movingStruggling with Alzheimer’s, the central character sets out on his final journey to a euthanasia clinicChris PowerMon 31 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 02.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe word “Alzheimer’s” never appears in Switzy, Emma Cline’s third novel, which arrives pre-endorsed as a Booker prize longlistee. But we can be certain that it is the disease afflicting its central character, David Hastings – certain in a way he finds it increasingly hard to be about anything.When the novel begins, David and his assistant Cody are aboard a private jet flying from his home in the US to the UK. Landing at London City airport (which the book, experiencing its own senior moment, situates in the countryside), they visit David’s daughter and her family before travelling on to Zurich (hence “Switzy”). One more appointment, a catchup with an old boarding school roommate called Tom, awaits just over the French border, after which David will be euthanised at a facility resembling Dignitas.David is wealthy. Not wealthy enough to own the jet he’s flying around in – that’s a loan from his boss – but someone to whom its polished doors, “that slid silently and obligingly out of sight”, are of a piece with the comfortable, largely frictionless world through which he moves. He has had a career in business, chief financial officer of some undefined entity – one large enough for a forensic accounting firm to be required when it became apparent David, in an early sign of the seriousness of his impairment, had mistakenly scattered its money into “an archipelago of overseas accounts”.For all the capital he has accumulated, David has been “a support person, a man whose name would never be known”, who sat at a desk and “made certain numbers swell up and other numbers recede”. Has it been a happy life? Well, the revelation or otherwise of that is one of the strands running through this extraordinarily well-made novel.How ill is David? Not so ill as to disqualify him from choosing euthanasia, but enough that navigating the world, from finding his hotel room to operating a phone, holding up his end of a conversation or understanding how and why he has offended someone, has become deeply problematic. He has reached the stage of his illness where, we learn from references to past events, he has woken up in his car uncertain of how he came to be there, soiled himself, upset employees, even lost the ability to tie his shoelaces. Sometimes he forgets he has eaten until a burp, tasting of lunch, reminds him of the fact. At other times he experiences the feeling “of coming into a room and the room offering no answers as to why he was there”. His world is full of aftermath but often frustratingly empty of cause.double quotation markBehind his chaotic decline hums a perfectly calibrated narrative machine, as smooth in its operation as the doors of his private jetHe compares his situation to that of a “mental ice floe, populated only by David, floating off into the polar darkness”. The text elegantly reflects this, its atomised paragraphs separated by white space – treacherous voids across which the thread of David’s awareness might not stretch from one moment to another. Yet as his comprehension thins, our own deepens. As his self-referential and fragmented stream of consciousness, often rich in similes, rebounds between the inputs of wherever he happens to be – in a car, at a restaurant, walking the streets of one city or another, always with Cody beside him – and his piecemeal memories, we begin to catch the resonances he no longer can.I think it is probably impossible to remain unmoved by David’s journey towards death, but as I accompanied him on it, I registered a nagging doubt that became increasingly insistent. David’s condition is worsening; he knows the day is coming when “he’d find that the contents of his brain had been excised with an ice-cream scooper instead of these dainty little teaspoons, here and there”. But in the case of the storyline involving Tom, David’s faltering memory just so happens to fall into precisely the pattern of revelation employed by a traditional trauma-plot novel.Characters in such books, as the New Yorker critic Parul Sehgal noted in her 2021 essay on the subject, “work to fill in the gaps of partial, haunting recollections”. Throughout Switzy, clues bob to the surface of David’s consciousness about some shameful event that soured things between himself and Tom at boarding school in the 1960s. One involves Tom’s sister “narrowing her eyes at him across the lawn at graduation”. No further context for the look is provided, for us or David, but as soon as it was mentioned I felt confident that the closer the meeting with Tom came, the more would be revealed about their shared past.This certainty that novelistic convention would be obeyed works against the uncertainty Cline otherwise evokes so brilliantly. It’s true that with Alzheimer’s long-term memories can persist as short-term memories cease to imprint. But David, too, appears to be searching for precisely what happened between himself and Tom. The memory is conveniently unavailable, provoking suspense, and then, just as conveniently, it returns to provide satisfaction. The reader’s knowledge that David will remember – an expectation drummed into us from myriad stories that work this way – runs counter to the reality of his predicament, to which neither narrative nor real-world logic applies. Behind his chaotic decline, the “unknowable soup” of his reality in which cause and effect have become terrifyingly uncoupled, hums a perfectly calibrated narrative machine as smooth and obliging in its operation as the doors of his private jet.When the novel moves past the Tom storyline, as it does with about 50 pages to go, it becomes its best self. Untethered from the duties of revelation it can fully immerse us in David’s pocked reality: impressionistic, arresting, upsetting, even funny. Earlier in the book, when reflecting on losing the name for the plastic cap on a shoelace (an aglet), he thinks that that one “was probably okay. Sure, toss it overboard.” By contrast – although it’s tempting fate to say it – the last pages of Switzy, which mingle horror, beauty, absurdity, and a sense of profound finality, will probably stay with me for ever.Switzy by Emma Cline is published by Chatto & Windus (£18.99). title: ‘Sometimes you just need a good cry’: why Little Women is my feelgood movie | Drama films | The Guardian
description: The latest in our series of writers highlighting their go-to comfort films is an ode to the teary 1994 adaptation of the classic novel
Author: Vivian Ho
Headline: The latest in our series of writers highlighting their go-to comfort films is an ode to the teary 1994 adaptation of the classic novel
Content: At its core, Little Women is a letter to girlhood and a coming-of-age tale about four March sisters growing up in New England during the civil war.Photograph: United Archives GmbH/AlamyView image in fullscreenAt its core, Little Women is a letter to girlhood and a coming-of-age tale about four March sisters growing up in New England during the civil war.Photograph: United Archives GmbH/AlamyMy feelgood movieDrama films‘Sometimes you just need a good cry’: why Little Women is my feelgood movieThe latest in our series of writers highlighting their go-to comfort films is an ode to the teary 1994 adaptation of the classic novelVivian HoMon 31 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 13.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIhave an ongoing argument with some friends about how I refuse to watch Interstellar again, despite considering it a beautiful and well-crafted film. It’s just so sad, I tell them, even with its hopeful ending. A desperate, choking lump forms in my chest as soon as I hear the futuristic swells of Hans Zimmer’s score and I have to remove myself before I am overtaken by emotion.‘A bit like meditation’: why Saw is my feelgood movieRead moreBut at the same time, the movie I choose as my feelgood film is one that has reduced me to a sobbing, snotty mess time and time again, whether I’m watching it curled up with my cat on the couch, swaddled in blankets while sick in bed or jostling with my seatmate for the armrest on an airplane. And just like with the score from Interstellar, the moment I hear Thomas Newman’s wistful little oboe intro of the 1994 version ofLittle Women, I can feel my eyes well up with tears.As you’ve probably discerned already, I tend to feel things very strongly. Probably one of my most psychotic traits is that I have to spoil the endings of most movies before I watch them for the first time because if I get too attached to a character and that character dies, it could take me several days to recover. But sometimes you just need a good cry, and that’s exactly what Gillian Armstrong’s Little Women is for me.At its core, Little Women – a coming-of-age tale about four March sisters growing up in New England during the civil war – is a love letter to girlhood. Originally a novel by Louisa May Alcott published in 1868, the storyhas repeatedly been adaptedfor film, television and stage over the past century, in part because of the timelessness of its characters. Generations of girls have grown up identifying with the hopes, dreams, struggles and triumphs of Jo, Meg, Beth and Amy – arguably the original quartet of female archetypes for girls to attach their personalities to, the predecessor of Sex and the City’s “I’m such a Samantha” or “You’re so Carrie” (Maturity is understanding that women contain multitudes and recognizing that we probably embody the qualities of multiple characters – on some days, like my astrological chart, I identify as a Jo sun, Amy rising and others as a Jo sun, Beth rising).Tearful moments abound throughout Little Women, played out magnificently by the 1994 cast. There’s the grief and fury of Winona Ryder as Jo when she discovers her burned manuscript, the quiet fortitude ofSusan Sarandonas their mother Marmee as she gathers her girls in a hug before leaving to care for their war-injured father. Coming-of-age stories are not always sad, but by definition, to grow up means closing a chapter in your life and letting go of the innocence of childhood – a bittersweet experience, no matter the circumstances. Little Women captures that bittersweetness through a number of milestones for the sisters – and then turns the emotional dial into a knife in your chest in the second act with the death of Beth. Nothing symbolizes the end of childhood quite like the devastating gutpunch of the kind, timid Beth dying quietly in her childhood bed. Claire Danes as Beth plays this moment with a heart-wrenching sweetness, her chin trembling as she tells a crying Jo that she is not afraid and that she can be brave like her.Beth’s death is such a well-known tearjerker in the cultural milieu that it’s used as a punchline in the sitcom Friends. “Beth is really, really sick,” Joey tearfullytells Rachelin the episode where he reads Little Women for the first time. I go into every rewatch knowing that I will be inconsolable within an hour or so. And yet I keep returning because as sad as it is, I emerge from my tears feeling content, with my heart full. This is the benefit of a good cry, a release of bottled-up emotions. With Little Women, my release of emotions is always tempered with a sort of fuzzy nostalgia that comes with revisiting your childhood. The 1994 version will always be my go-to because that is the version I grew up with and watched with my own sister when we were girls. But I also love Greta Gerwig’s interpretation of the story in the 2019 remake, just as I’m sure I will love any and all future remakes. One time I lucked out on a long trip home for the holidays and both adaptations were available on the in-flight entertainment. I treated myself to a tear-heavy double feature and deboarded that plane feeling lighter, happier and more dehydrated than ever.Little Women is available to rent digitally in the US, on Channel 4+ in the UK and to rent digitally in AustraliaExplore more on these topicsDrama filmsMy feelgood movieLittle WomenWinona RyderSusan SarandonClaire DanesKirsten DunstFilm adaptationsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Parasomnia review – sleep-schedule horror conjures up a succubus on the loose in waking nightmare | Movies | The Guardian
description: Debut director James Ross II shows promise in this gore fest, but the fear factor suffers from an overly complex plot
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: Debut director James Ross II shows promise in this gore fest, but the fear factor suffers from an overly complex plot
Content: Wandering a hellish labyrinth … Jasmine Mathews as Riley in Parasomnia.Photograph: Courtesy of Shudder. A Shudder Release.View image in fullscreenWandering a hellish labyrinth … Jasmine Mathews as Riley in Parasomnia.Photograph: Courtesy of Shudder. A Shudder Release.MoviesReviewParasomnia review – sleep-schedule horror conjures up a succubus on the loose in waking nightmareDebut director James Ross II shows promise in this gore fest, but the fear factor suffers from an overly complex plotPhil HoadMon 31 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSleep has been part of the horror genre repertoire since The Cabinet of Dr Caligari, and the anxieties around it are spiking as the “sleep economy” becomes a thing. This ambitiously structured gore fest about a woman suffering from waking nightmares comes with an all-black cast, but race isn’t a central preoccupation here. Instead, as night terrors burst the banks into reality, debut director James Ross II concentrates on maintaining an appropriately scrambled and claustrophobic experience – perhaps to the detriment of the fear factor.On her 15th birthday, Riley (Jasmine Mathews) is paralysed in a waking/sleep state at her foster home, able to observe but powerless to intervene to stop a care worker going berserk. Since this massacre, Riley keeps a strict sleep protocol as an adult, making sure anyone under the same roof drops off before her, which apparently protects them from the malevolent presence invading her nights. Old foster home pal David (Stephen Barrington) accepts an invitation to the house where Riley’s dad murdered her mum, but gets the willies when a pallid demon begins manifesting in the small hours. It turns out that Riley’s boyfriend, Cam (RJ Brown), has been lax in letting her fall asleep before him – and now her resident succubus is on the loose again.The levels of cause and effect, reality and fantasy, in Riley’s dreams are confusing at first: she inhabits the perspective of the eyeball-plucking fiend (a nod toETA Hoffmann’s Sandman?) and wanders a hellish labyrinth in which past victims are trapped. Thankfully, Ross clarifies everything with a burst of guiding lore in an ingenious third-act switchback that revises the previous two acts.Despite this sturdy constriction, the film remains only mildly scary – maybe because of the interruptions and vagaries of the complex setup. The middling performances don’t feel extreme enough, and the generic, chalk-faced, taloned bogeyman is a mere stain on Freddy Krueger’s jersey. But there is an undeniable astuteness and agility in the storytelling here on which Ross can build.Parasomnia is on Shudder and AMC+ from 4 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsSleepreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Bel review – the powerful life force and haunting absence of a traumatised singer-songwriter | Movies | The Guardian
description: Beldina Odenyo alchemised the pain of exile, loss and racism into music as Heir of the Cursed before her death in 2021, as this attentive tribute explores
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: Beldina Odenyo alchemised the pain of exile, loss and racism into music as Heir of the Cursed before her death in 2021, as this attentive tribute explores
Content: Deep wounds … Bel.Photograph: Euan RobertsonView image in fullscreenDeep wounds … Bel.Photograph: Euan RobertsonMoviesReviewBel review – the powerful life force and haunting absence of a traumatised singer-songwriterBeldina Odenyo alchemised the pain of exile, loss and racism into music as Heir of the Cursed before her death in 2021, as this attentive tribute exploresPhil HoadMon 31 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 04.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleInstead of an artist in a booth, a lone amplifier plays the music of singer-songwriter Beldina Odenyo for a cluster of microphones to pick up during the posthumous recording of her debut album. It is a haunting encapsulation of the absence and presence at the heart of Louise Lockwood’s documentary, which makes a commendably thorough exploration of the mental illness that led to Odenyo killing herself in November 2021, and its roots: exile, loss and racism.Performing under the moniker Heir of the Cursed, a translation of the Tetela name ofassassinated Congolese leader Patrice Lumumba, Odenyo was on the verge of bigger recognition at the end of 2021 after a successful performance at Edinburgh’s Usher Hall. But hemmed in by successive Covid lockdowns, the 31-year-old is clearly unwell in a discomfiting backstage interview. Squirming, monosyllabic, she seems to be regressing to the non-verbal state of shock in which she arrived in Dumfriesshire from Kenya as a young child.Lockwood’s film plays as if Orpheus was the one being rescued from the underworld. As well as gathering Odenyo’s demos into a finished album, her half-sister Leah attempts to reconstitute her sibling, her traumas and her life force. Being ripped away fromKenyaand her mother, who later died prematurely, is clearly at the heart of things. The harassment and violent physical abuse, including being set on fire, that she encountered in the village of Kirkconnell and nearby Dumfries deepened the wound – as did losing another sister to leukaemia. She might have been a born musician, but having to alchemise this pain gives Odenyo double the force; her keening top range recalls PJ Harvey, but she frequently dips into the kind of baleful quaver Nina Simone once knocked audiences flat with.With her singing face sometimes a rictus, Odenyo felt no obligation to pander to her audience, as poet Jackie Kay notes here. But visibility – part of her curse growing up in Dumfriesshire, but a source of connection on stage – remained a profoundly ambivalent matter. She wrestled, like Kurt Cobain, with the idea of commercialising her inner woes. Compelled to keep mining that source, especially in the pandemic pressure cooker, she starts to experience music as a chore. In the end, it’s not enough to save her; the Usher Hall triumph seems like it happened by dying force of will. As well as being an attentive tribute, Lockwood’s film weighs up the compulsive and healing halves of art; it is Orphic to a fault.Bel is atFilmhouse, Edinburgh, from 4 September, then tours.Explore more on these topicsFilmMusic documentaryDocumentary filmsKenyaScotlandreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Black Garden review – haunting study of growing up in war-torn Nagorno-Karabakh | Movies | The Guardian
description: Alexis Pazoumian’s documentary follows Samvel and Avo, two preteen boys whose lives will be unavoidably scarred by brutal conflict
Author: Phuong Le
Headline: Alexis Pazoumian’s documentary follows Samvel and Avo, two preteen boys whose lives will be unavoidably scarred by brutal conflict
Content: Unwavering pride … Samvel and Avo in The Black Garden.Photograph: True StoryView image in fullscreenUnwavering pride … Samvel and Avo in The Black Garden.Photograph: True StoryMoviesReviewThe Black Garden review – haunting study of growing up in war-torn Nagorno-KarabakhAlexis Pazoumian’s documentary follows Samvel and Avo, two preteen boys whose lives will be unavoidably scarred  by brutal conflictPhuong LeMon 31 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, a decades-long territorial dispute exploded in the region of Nagorno-Karabakh, as its largely Armenian population fought against countless military campaigns from the Azerbaijani army. Shot over the course of three eventful years, which culminated in thesurrender of Nagorno-Karabakh’s separatist government in 2023, Alexis Pazoumian’s haunting documentary harnesses the collective turmoil that dominated generations of Armenians. From the elderly to the very young, the community are united by an unwavering sense of pride, one that carries them through never-ending bloodshed and displacement.The film opens with the harrowing sight of a bombed-out school in the small village of Talish, where childlike innocence contrasts with wartime trauma. Samvel and Avo, two preteen boys, roam through the wreckage and scavenge for remains of past normalcy, like the scattered notebooks left behind by their former classmates. The threat of the enemy, however, is drilled into every aspect of their daily life. At school, they learn how to assemble guns, and at family gatherings, they join in songs that speak of heroic valour. That the children here – boys and girls – will grow up to become soldiers is a foregone conclusion.Pazoumian’s film, however, steers clear of nationalist ideologies to lay bare the human cost of conflict. In one early scene, we see twentysomething Armenian recruit Erik performing energetic somersaults in his military uniform. Later on, the once-beaming young man returns from the frontline a shadow of his former self, having lost a leg. Still, Erik regains his optimism as he undergoes physical therapy and rehabilitation; his resilience, too, is a kind of cultural inheritance. Though the film could have been enriched by more detailed sociopolitical context, the emotional weight of such scenes makes it a profound work of remembrance.The Black Garden is on True Story from 4 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsArmeniaAzerbaijanNagorno-KarabakhEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Katie Norris: Mother Succubus review – gothic comic enters a wickedly funny new era | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Norris swaps her larger-than-life Farm Fatale persona for something more autobiographical in this easygoing musical comedy
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Norris swaps her larger-than-life Farm Fatale persona for something more autobiographical in this easygoing musical comedy
Content: Singled out … Katie Norris changes tack after 143 failed first dates.View image in fullscreenSingled out … Katie Norris changes tack after 143 failed first dates.Edinburgh festival 2026ReviewKatie Norris: Mother Succubus review – gothic comic enters a wickedly funny new eraPleasance Courtyard, EdinburghNorris swaps her larger-than-life Farm Fatale persona for something more autobiographical in this easygoing musical comedyBrian LoganMon 31 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 04.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKatie Norris is on a familiar trajectory in standup, from debuting as a version of herself so heightened as to be caricature, to settling into a lower-key Katie she’s happy to be on stage. And happy, too, is anyone who’s followed that journey from2024’s fantastic Farm Fatale, which established her gothic, cat-batty spinster persona, to this new show – more straight-bat autobiographical standup, about Norris leaving behind the male gaze.But let us not overstate the case: there’s nothing normie about Norris in her third outing, in which she appears, imposing as ever, with a crow perched on her arm. In a show whose theme can best be described as loose-fitting, she’s here to address one reviewer’s description of her as “a man-eating succubus”. Far from it, she retorts. After 143 failed first dates, Norris is forswearing straight men and their favour, and entering a new era – where women join choirs, go wild swimming and fearlessly untangle roadkill from the undercarriage of their Ford Fiestas.There’s an easygoing, urgency-free swing to all this, as Norris renders her life phase in song, faintly threatening backchat with the audience, and lurid standup painting herself in chiaroscuro as a premature old maid. But that characterisation is scaled back here, as we’re offered clearer-cut routines about starring as a Victorian sex worker, aged nine, in her school play; and fangirling the eye-opening 00s TV show Eurotrash.Dom McGovern: Prize Hog review – a sharp standup who is sure to go stellarRead moreI’m just as delighted by dialled-down Norris as I was by her larger-than-life forebear, as she roleplays a communal dip in Hampstead ponds, and performs a pop medley in character as a member of the Military Wives choir. Neither convinces you she’s quite ready to join their gang – even as this committed singleton’s narrative takes an unexpected turn towards coupledom. For Norris-watchers aware of her long-term stepmum ambitions, that finale, with its entertaining song about dating a weekend dad, can’t help but be cheering – before the show (at least when seen on the Edinburgh fringe) ends more than 10 minutes shy of the hour mark. I could have had more. Norris’s new era looks like being just as much fun as the previous one.AtSoho theatre, London, 14-19 SeptemberAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026ComedyEdinburgh festivalFestivalsSoho theatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: A Small and Quiet Light review – fractured portrait of a remarkable wartime spy | Theatre | The Guardian
description: A female secret agent’s extraordinary courage never quite comes to life in a drama that struggles to find tension in her high-stakes story
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: A female secret agent’s extraordinary courage never quite comes to life in a drama that struggles to find tension in her high-stakes story
Content: Restrained … Priyanga Burford (right) in A Small and Quiet Light at Minerva theatre, Chichester.Photograph: Marc BrennerView image in fullscreenRestrained … Priyanga Burford (right) in A Small and Quiet Light at Minerva theatre, Chichester.Photograph: Marc BrennerTheatreReviewA Small and Quiet Light review – fractured portrait of a remarkable wartime spyMinerva theatre, ChichesterA female secret agent’s extraordinary courage never quite comes to life in a drama that struggles to find tension in her high-stakes storyArifa AkbarMon 31 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 00.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNoor-un-Nisa Inayat Khan was a second world war spy codenamed Madeleine. A mixed-heritage British Indian and Special Operations Executive (SOE) agent in Nazi-occupied Paris who showed extraordinary courage, her story is ripe for dramatic retelling. So why does it feel so fractured and unsatisfactory in director Elin Schofield’s production?Perhaps because of the limited documentation of this medalled war hero’s life. That is not helped in the delivery of her story in playwright Stephanie Street’s non-sequential narrative, beginning with her interrogation in 1943, after being caught by the Germans, and shuttling back and forth across the years, from early family life to her death in Dachau concentration camp.Because the story is already filled with holes, it gains more lacunae in this broken-up telling to become less than the sum of its parts. It creates unnecessary confusion and does not relay who Khan was beneath the facts of her life, what drove her or exactly what she did in what turned out to be a highly dangerous lone mission.Priyanga Burford plays Khan across the decades, from a girl playing piano with her mother to a young woman getting ready for a date. We are told Khan wrote fiction but not much more. A character likens storytellers to spies but the play lacks the essential conflict and suspense of either. Burford’s performance is solid but workmanlike.View image in fullscreenShadowy … Caoilfhionn Dunne (right) in A Small and Quiet Light at Minerva theatre, Chichester.Photograph: Marc BrennerScenes are often short and static. Accompanying characters include Vera (Amanda Hadingue), the handler who sends Khan to France, as well as Viennot (Léa des Garets), Khan’s sometime lover, and Vogt (Caoilfhionn Dunne), her mild-mannered interrogator. There are others but sometimes it is not clear who they are, and they all remain shadowy.Khan’s American-born mother (also Hadingue) and her musician father (Paksie Vernon), who we hear knew Debussy and Tolstoy, provide backstory but do not illuminate what drove Khan. We are told that she feels a greater purpose on her mission but this sounds pat. There is a tantalising suggestion that she feels more herself as Madeleine, and that life as a spy is more real to her, but there is no follow-through.Overall, the tone is too polite and restrained, Nicola T Chang’s melodramatic compositions and Tingying Dong’s big sound design doing all they can to insert some charge.This is not the first attempt at dramatising Khan’s life.Kali Theatre’s production at the Southwark Playhouse in 2022was imperfect but did manage to capture the peril in her mission by focusing the action on her work in France. This play skirts around dramatising that. So scenes lack tension, despite the best attempts of the all-female cast to convey jeopardy, which seems like a fatal flaw for a drama about high-stakes espionage.It stalls itself at the end to remind us that we cannot nail down the story of Khan’s life (or death) with any certainty, that it is fraught with unknowns. This drama goes some way towards telling us who she was, and certainly conveys her heroism – but she never comes to life through these jagged pieces of a remarkable life.At Minerva theatre, Chichester until12 September, and thenOrange Tree theatre, London, 21 September-24 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreChichester Festival theatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: A$AP Rocky review – arena spectacular has plenty of helicopters but little sense of direction | Music | The Guardian
description: The polymath rapper’s stage show, which also features SWAT teams and a warship, is truly bravura stuff – but you can’t help feeling this is an artist at a creative crossroads
Author: Stevie Chick
Headline: The polymath rapper’s stage show, which also features SWAT teams and a warship, is truly bravura stuff – but you can’t help feeling this is an artist at a creative crossroads
Content: Quite the spectacle … A$AP Rocky.Photograph: Thepinkrosephotographyltd/Laura RoseView image in fullscreenQuite the spectacle … A$AP Rocky.Photograph: Thepinkrosephotographyltd/Laura RoseMusicReviewA$AP Rocky review – arena spectacular has plenty of helicopters but little sense of directionO2 Arena, LondonThe polymath rapper’s stage show, which also features SWAT teams and a warship, is truly bravura stuff – but you can’t help feeling this is an artist at a creative crossroadsStevie ChickMon 31 Aug 2026 09.47 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA$AP Rocky dangles precariously from a helicopter, while beneath him black-clad SWAT officers brawl with his white-masked followers. This isn’t some cliffhanger setpiece from the rapper/actor’s latest film – it’s just how shows on his Don’t Be Dumb tour open. It’s a big production: there are further prop helicopters, including a smaller one up in the rafters from which he also raps (a reference to his single Helicopter), while the stage recreates the top deck of a naval warship, for reasons that never become clear.The bizarre set underscores a sense of a man in career transition, unsure who he is any more. In the eight years since his last album, this survivor of homelessness and incarceration became a father, three times, with Rihanna; he’s pivoting towards movies –goodones– and co-chairs the Met Gala. His new record sought to redefine him as an artist, juggling more of his trademark pugilistic rap with ambitious stylistic experiments and unexpected collaborations (Damon Albarn! Danny Elfman!).View image in fullscreenGet to the chopper! … A$AP Rocky.Photograph: Laura RoseBut Rocky seemed paralysed by choice, unable to choose a lane. Was he a reformed Lothario declaring his devotion to Rihanna? Or the wildling of yore, “still smoking my weed” and rekindling beef with Drake? The album reached No 1 without offering a definitive answer. Now he’s got a warship to strut along (while pursued by 30 dancers in that SWAT gear), and a besotted audience starting circle pits to wonky fight song STFU, bouncing en masse to the death-rattle funk of Riot (Rowdy Pipe’n), and twirling their white shirts like helicopter blades at his command.Tonight, Rocky seems most energised performing the haunted dream-pop frug of Punk Rocky, or his swoonsome Thundercat collab, Stay Here 4 Life, or the hypnotic slither of L$D. The wildcard sound of these tracks suggests he’s searching for a creative mode that will fit him as well as his earlier sizzurp-slaked anthems. But as he ably negotiates the special effects and gonzo props of his big, bonkers stage show, it’s also hard to shake the suspicion that, if Hollywood offered Rocky a truly career-changing role, hip-hop wouldn’t see him for dust. He is a man in motion, for sure – but his direction remains undefined.A$AP Rocky plays 3Arena, Dublin, 2 September; thentours the UK until 5 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsMusicRapHip-hopA$AP Rockylive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: My search for the perfect Polish dumplings in Gdańsk | Poland holidays | The Guardian
description: Pierogi are a religion in Poland, but I’d never been a believer. Could a recce in the charming Baltic city convert me?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Pierogi are a religion in Poland, but I’d never been a believer. Could a recce in the charming Baltic city convert me?
Content: Gdańsk old town.Photograph: Poike/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenGdańsk old town.Photograph: Poike/Getty Images/iStockphotoPoland holidaysMy search for the perfect Polish dumplings in GdańskPierogi are a religion in Poland, but I’d never been a believer. Could a recce in the charming Baltic city convert me?Ben AitkenMon 31 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 02.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIused to live in Poland.I worked in a fish-and-chip shop in the western city of Poznań, boning cod and peeling potatoes for £1.50 an hour. With the exception of that job, I enjoyed everything about my time in the country, not least the food. I liked the chicken broth with noodles, the slippery herring, the knuckles of pork the size of basketballs, the cold beetroot soup that beats gazpacho hands down.One thing I was less delighted by were Polish dumplings – pierogi. It wasn’t that they weren’t nice – they were – it was more that they didn’t seem to warrant the extreme levels of affection and esteem Poles often bestow on the doughy parcels. By being ambivalent about them, I was going against a well-established grain.It is claimed by some that pierogi arrived in Poland via Marco Polo (actually a myth), and that the oldest written Polish recipe dates to 1682 (true). In short, these things have pedigree, and you denigrate them at your peril. I almost lost a Polish friend once for not being smitten with Poland’s answer to gyoza and ravioli. Such was her reaction, you’d have thought I’d denigrated the late Polish pope, John Paul II.“I don’t understand this mentality,” said Paulina. “Have you tried the ones filled with cheese and potato?”“Yep.”“Have you had the ones from the fancy place on the old square?”“Yep.”“Have you had the frozen ones from the supermarket?”“Uh-huh.”“Have you had the ones from the milk bar near Freedom Street?”“More than once.”“Hm. Have you tried my grandmother’s?”“Erm, no.”“Well there you are. Mystery solved. That explains your mentality. You have to reserve judgment and stop talking nonsense until you’ve tried the dumplings of ababcia.”I had versions of this conversation several times when telling Poles that I was merely fond of pierogi rather than hopelessly devoted. On each occasion, thebabcia(grandmother figure) in question was either dead or otherwise engaged, meaning that their dumplings couldn’t be tested, and my opinion – thatpierogi are just OK – couldn’t be validated.Until now perhaps. Having enjoyed searching forthe perfectsteak fritesin Paris, I set myself the task of giving pierogi a proper crack of the whip in one of Poland’s finest cities – its jewel on the Baltic coast, Gdańsk. Could the old port city cure me of my pierogiscepticism? Would the dumplings of a localbabciabowl me over? The answer was yes … and no.Gdański BowkeView image in fullscreenAfter a mooch around the picturesque old town(during which I learned that Daniel Fahrenheit, inventor of the temperature scale, spent his first years in Gdańsk before leaving as a teen, having realised how cold it got in winter), I pull up a pew on the riverside terrace of this well-regarded establishment. I have a mixed plate of the classics: potato and cheese, cabbage and mushroom, minced pork. They’ve been boiled then shallow fried, ensuring a slightly crisp finish, and are served with the traditional accompaniments: sour cream and bacon bits jostling in their own lardy juices.The first thing that strikes me is the size of these parcels. Boy, are they plump. Of the selection, potato and cheese triumphs, with the optimal mouthful requiring a touch of each topping: the bacon bringing a salty crunch, the lard adding an umami note, the sour cream resolving the whole. In short, solid grub in a lovely spot.£13, 7.5/10,gdanskibowke.comPanoramaView image in fullscreenComposite: Alexander Spatari/Getty ImagesNo chance of just happening on this restaurant: it’s on the 16th floor of what might be charitably called a nondescript building. The view isn’t postcard-perfect but it’s powerful: the vista is dominated by the city’s famous shipyard, where in 1980 trade union leader Lech Wałęsa and his unmerry men downed tools and gave communism the cold shoulder.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe boiled dumplings have been blackened with charcoal or squid ink, filled with a raspberry reduction and white Belgian chocolate, then decorated with strawberries and cream. This is a main course, by the way, not a dessert. I have fun pressing a fork through the foreboding dough and watching the innards spill. Gory but enjoyable. There’s a nice sourness from the raspberries, the chew on the dough allows the flavours to travel and combine, and I like the crunch you get from the tiny raspberry seeds. I had been tempted by the savoury pierogi option – rabbit with thyme sauce – but I went with madam’s suggestion and I’m glad I did. After all,babciaknow best.£11, 7.5/10,panoramarestauracjagdansk.plManduView image in fullscreenThe dumplings here are made on site and it’s a lovely thing to witness – the craft, the culture, the skill of thebabcia. The menu is extensive: 40 types, with baked, boiled and deep-fried options. Some of the fillings require a double take: chorizo, potato, mascarpone and … truffle paste, anyone?I’m pleased to see variety, though. As with the sandwich, conceivably a dumpling can be filled with anything. (In Cleveland, Ohio, I once encountered bacon cheeseburger pierogi – which I interpreted as evidence that multiculturalism was working just fine.)I have a baked half-dozen, filled with a mingling of beef, cheese, red onion and pickled cucumber. Small pies they are, befitting the etymology of pierogi. The filling is excellent, but the heavier carriage of the yeast-risen dumplings starts to weigh on me, and I find myself digging out the interior and foregoing the case. I would have appreciated a mixed plate option, to avoid things getting samey.£12, 8/10,pierogarnia-mandu.plStary MłynView image in fullscreenComposite: Ben AitkenThis pierogi specialist is housed in an old mill – hence the name, which translates as old mill – on the edge of what has become known as booking.com island, on account of its popularity with tourists. I have the mixed plate – nine iterations of Poland’s beloved comfort food. There’s a half-hour wait after ordering, while the dumplings are “cooked on the fly”, the ceaseless prep apparent at the back of the dining room. The wait gives me a chance to read a kids’ book I find on the merchandise stand (yep, there’s merch) about a dumpling that goes on an adventure and ends up as prime minister.The fillings are decent: beef rib, cod fillet, chicken and cheese – but they are somewhat overpowered by the dough. One shortcoming of Polish dumplings is that a plate of them, even a mixed one, can get a bit repetitive.Here’s an idea: individual dumplings, slightly enlarged, handheld, easily taken away and munched on the move? The largest pierogi ever made, incidentally, was about two metres long and weighed nearly 100kg, though the largest recognised by the Guinness World Records weighed 55.7kg – both, unsurprisingly, in the US.£15, 7/10,pierogarnie.comOberża 86View image in fullscreenGdańsk is officially in a relationship with two other cities – Sopot and Gdynia. Together they are known as the Trójmiasto,or Tricity. I take a short train ride to Gdynia, the ugly sister of the three. After vainly wandering around for an hour in search of pierogi, I’m about to abort the mission when I chance on Oberża 86. I confess my head is turned less by the name or the building and more by the word Michelin on the sign. I pop my head in and ask if they do pierogi. They do, as a starter, just the three pieces, filled with broad beans and served with a shallot sauce, which they suggest pairing with a wine from the north-west of Poland.I’m sold. And soon I’m smitten. The sauce has a zing that comes from the onions being slow-cooked with wine and lemon. The dough has the quality of pasta. The filling is gentle, and balances the tangy sauce. And there is the right amount – a lovable trio, rather than a testing half dozen. The wine helps, I must say. It’s lairy, with apple vibes and a slight fizz, the Johnny Rotten of the white wine world. After crowning Oberża 86 my winner, I waddle to the local beach for a swim, wondering if I’ll be more or less buoyant after all the pierogiI’ve taken on board the past couple of days.£12, 9/10,oberza86.plBen Aitken is the author of A Chip Shop in Poznan: My Unlikely Year in Poland. title: Rosie Mackean’s quick and easy recipe for cucumber rice with fudgy eggs | Food | The Guardian
description: An intriguing and refreshing hot-cold combo of eggy rice, butter, cold cucumber sauce and pickles
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: An intriguing and refreshing hot-cold combo of eggy rice, butter, cold cucumber sauce and pickles
Content: Rosie Mackean’s cucumber rice with fudgy eggs.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Georgia Rudd.View image in fullscreenRosie Mackean’s cucumber rice with fudgy eggs.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Georgia Rudd.Quick and easyFoodRosie Mackean’s quick and easy recipe for cucumber rice with fudgy eggsAn intriguing and refreshing hot-cold combo of eggy rice, butter, cold cucumber sauce and picklesRosie MackeanMon 31 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen cooking on a weeknight, it’s easy to forget that sometimes experimenting with temperature is as important as flavour. Hot things combined with very cold things are exceptionally refreshing in the summer, and also make the mundane more exciting and playful. This dish of hot rice, hot butter, cold cucumber sauce, hot egg and cold pickles might sound, well, a bit weird, but I promise it’s delicious, comforting and also cooling.Cucumber rice with fudgy eggsPrep10 minCook30 minServes2200g Japanese short-grain riceSalt and black pepper2 medium eggs40g soft salted butter3 spring onions, trimmed and finely slicedFor the pickled cucumbers200g baby cucumbers, or the same quantity of a large cucumber1 tsp flaky sea salt3 tbspcaster sugar75gwhite-wine vinegar1 tbsp olive oil1 small handfulfresh dill, leaves picked and chopped½ tsp dried mintFor the cucumber sauce1 large cucumber, peeled and deseeded100gcreme fraiche1 very generous pinch flaky salt1 garlic clove, peeled1ice cubeStart with the pickles. Slice the cucumber into rounds, put them in a heatproof bowl, add the salt and toss to coat. In a second heatproof bowl, mix 75ml just-boiled water with the sugar and vinegar, then pour this over the cucumber and set aside while you make everything else.Wash the rice under cold water until it runs clear, then drain. If you have a rice cooker, use that. Otherwise, put the rice in a saucepan with a tight-fitting lid and add 250ml cold water and a pinch of salt. Put the pan on a medium heat, bring it to a boil, then turn down the heat as low as possible and cover the pan with the lid. Leave the rice to cook for eight minutes, then take off the heat, and set aside, still covered, for 10 minutes, so it absorbs all the water.Meanwhile, blitz the peeled and deseeded cucumber in a blender with the creme fraiche, salt and garlic, until smooth. Transfer to the fridge with the ice cube to keep it lovely and cool.Cook the eggs in boiling water for seven minutes, then rinse under cold running water until they’re just cool enough to peel.Dress the pickled cucumber with the olive oil, dill and dried mint. Pile spoonfuls of the rice into the centre of two wide, shallow bowls, then dot with the soft butter – it will melt and pool in the rice (heaven). Pour the cucumber sauce around the rice, top with the pickles, the peeled and halved fudgy eggs, and some shredded spring onion, then serve with plenty of salt and pepper on the eggs.Good Time Cooking: Show-Stopping Menus for Easy Entertaining, by Rosie Mackean, is published by Pavilion Books at £26.
